Indicator: Years of life lost due to suicide
Rationale: Years of life lost is a measure of premature mortality and gives an estimate of the length of time a person would have lived had they not died prematurely. It can be used to compare the premature mortality experience of different populations and quantify the impact on society from suicide.
Definition: Years of life lost due to mortality from suicide and injury undetermined (ICD10 X60-X84, Y10-Y34)
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Definition of numerator: Years of life lost and deaths from suicide and injury undetermined classified by underlying cause of death (ICD10 X60-X84, Y10-Y34) registered in the respective calendar years (3 years pooled)
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts
Definition of denominator: Office for National Statistics, 2021 census based mid-year population estimates for respective calendar years (3 years pooled)Please note mortality rates presented include a full revision of the back series data which has been calculated using the 2021 census rebased ONS mid-year population estimates. Integrated care board (ICB) data has not been refreshed, and is awaiting the release of the ONS mid-year population estimates for LSOAs.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The number of years of life lost is calculated by summing over ages 15 to 74 years the number of deaths at each age multiplied by the number of years of life remaining up to age 75 years.
Disclosure control: Data that may potentially identify an individual have been removed
Notes:
Suicide definition The definition of suicide includes deaths given an underlying cause of intentional self-harm or an injury/poisoning of undetermined intent. In England and Wales it has been customary to assume that most injuries and poisonings of undetermined intent are cases where the harm was self-inflicted, but there was insufficient evidence to prove that the deceased deliberately intended to take their own life. However, this cannot be applied to children due to the possibility that these deaths were caused by unverifiable accidents, neglect or abuse. Therefore, only persons aged 15 years and over are included in the suicide figures.Registered deaths In common with most other UK mortality statistics, suicide figures are presented for deaths registered in a particular calendar year, which enables figures to be published in a timely manner. The alternative would be to publish statistics based on the year in which the death occurred. However, if ONS were to do this the release of the data would have to be delayed in order to allow enough time for the majority of the deaths that occurred in a given year to be registered. The Mortality Metadata publication found on the ONS website:  http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/user-guidance/health-and-life-events/index.html  reports figures on the number of late registrations (all deaths) that are not included in the relevant occurrence dataset. Due to the length of time it takes to hold an inquest, suicide rates presented in this tool are based on deaths that may have occurred months or even years before the reporting year. For example, in the Suicides in the UK 2013 Registrations Bulletin  http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/dcp171778_395145.pdf  the median registration delay for suicides in 2013 for England was 168 days. Of all the suicides in England registered in 2013, 51% occurred before 2013. In England, the average registration delay has gradually increased over time. More information and further analysis done by ONS on registration delays can be found in the Suicides in the UK Registration Bulletin, and in the Impact of registration delays on mortality statistics publication found on the ONS website:  http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/user-guidance/health-and-life-events/index.html .
Narrative conclusions There are around 30,000 coroner’s inquests held in England and Wales each year. The majority of these inquests receive a “short form” conclusion such as accident, misadventure, natural causes, suicide or homicide. The remaining inquests receive a “narrative conclusion”, which can be used by a coroner or jury instead of a short form conclusion to express their findings as the cause of death. Some narrative conclusions clearly state the intent (for example, accidental) and mechanism (for example, hanging, poisoning) of death. However, in other cases, the coroner may not indicate unambiguously whether the fatal injury was accidental, intentional or otherwise. Deaths where the intent has not been specified are defined as “hard-to-code”. The rules for coding cause of deaths mean that, if no indication of intent has been provided by the certifier, a death from injury or poisoning must be coded as accidental. There is considerable variation in the use of narrative conclusions between coroners. This leads to concerns that the use of narrative conclusions could be distorting local area suicide statistics. However, an analysis to assess the impact of narrative conclusions on suicide rates at regional level in England and Wales was undertaken by ONS in 2011. The results showed that, between 2001 and 2009, there was no statistically significant impact. More information on narrative conclusions can be found in the annual suicide registration statistical bulletins.

Indicator: Proportion of pulmonary TB notifications starting treatment within two months of symptom onset
Rationale: Reducing diagnostic delay is a key indicator in the Tuberculosis Action plan for England, 2021 to 2026. Reducing the proportion of pulmonary TB notifications starting treatment more than four months after symptom onset is a key indicator.
Definition: The annual proportion of pulmonary TB notifications known to have started treatment within two months of symtom onset (exclusions: TB notifications with no date of symptom onset or date of treatment start and TB notifications diagnosed post-mortem).For more information on how treatment delays where handled, please refer to the methodology and definitions of the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tuberculosis-in-england-2022-report-data-up-to-end-of-2021/tb-treatment-in-england-2021#methodology-and-definitions
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).
Definition of numerator: Annual number of pulmonary TB notifications notified to National Tuberculosis Surveillance system (NTBS) starting treatment within 61 days of symptom onset (exclusions: TB notifications with no date of symptom onset or date of treatment start and TB notifications diagnosed postmortem).For more information on how treatment delays where handled, please refer to the methodology and definitions of the https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tuberculosis-in-england-2022-report-data-up-to-end-of-2021/tb-treatment-in-england-2021#methodology-and-definitions
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Enhanced Tuberculosis Surveillance System (ETS)
Definition of denominator: Annual number of pulmonary TB notifications notified to National Tuberculosis Surveillance system (NTBS) with known start of treatment and symptom onset dates (exclusions: TB notifications with no date of symptom onset or date of treatment start and TB notifications diagnosed postmortem).
Source of denominator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Enhanced Tuberculosis Surveillance System (ETS)
Methodology: The number of pulmonary TB notifications starting treatment within61 days of symptom onset divided by the total number of pulmonary TB notifications with known symptom onset and start of treatment dates multipled by 100 to generate a percentage.
Confidence interval details: 95% confidence intervals were calculated using Wilson Score method
Disclosure control:
The data presented in the TB Strategy Monitoring Indicators are agreed measures of the service and care provided to people with TB. The data does not include direct or indirect identifiable information (such as exact dates, age, sex, location or ethnicity) that would allow an individual to be identified. Therefore, no disclosure control is applied to the data.
However, some Local Authority and Clinical Commissioning Group (CCG) data are suppressed to avoid presenting proportions that are based on small denominators. This is because these proportions can be misleading and vary considerably from year to year. The data are suppressed in a given area and year if the denominator for that indicator is 5 or less. In these situations, suppression is applied to the count, proportion and confidence interval data.
Caveats: Every effort is made to ensure accuracy and completeness of NTBS data, including web-based reporting, data cleaning and data integrity checks for data quality. However, responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of the data lies with the reporting clinic.Data for all previous years are updated using the most recent TB notification dataset. This update means that the values for a given area and year may be different (either smaller or larger) when compared to what has been shown on this profile in the past.
Copyright: The data shown in the TB indicator profiles are publicly available and there are no restrictions on their re-use

Indicator: Under 18s abortions rate
Rationale: Most teenage pregnancies are unplanned and around half end in an abortion. As well as it being an avoidable experience for the young woman, abortions represent an avoidable cost to the NHS.More background information and advice on tackling teenage pregnancy is provided in Public Health England's joint paper with the Local Government Association (LGA) published January 2016  https://www.local.gov.uk/good-progress-more-do-teenage-pregnancy-and-young-parents
Definition: Abortions in women aged under 18 per 1,000 females aged 15-17
Data source: OHID, based on Department of Health and Social Care and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: Number of abortions in women aged under 18 that are legal under the Abortion Act 1967.
Source of numerator: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), Abortion statistics in England and Wales
Definition of denominator: Number of women aged 15-17 living in the area
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 1,000
Disclosure control:
For 2023, all numbers are rounded to the nearest 5. Totals may not add up and counts of 0 can mean no or a small number of procedures in the given field. Percentages, rates and confidence intervals are calculated using rounded figures; therefore, percentages may not add up to 100. Rates are rounded to one decimal place.For 2022 and earlier years, York, North Yorkshire, Staffordshire, Stoke-on-Trent, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire have been randomly perturbed to prevent disclosing numbers of abortions in areas with very small population sizes that lie in the intersections of Local Authorities and sub-ICBs. This allows the values to be presented for these Local Authorities rather than being supressed as in previous years. Values have been randomly perturbed by a number between -5 and +5, excluding 0. While these adjustments affect the values and total within these Local Authorities the overall totals at Local Authority and age group level are preserved.
Some values have been suppressed to protect patient confidentiality.
Caveats: Deprivation decile calculations exclude any upper tier local authority values that have been suppressed.For 2023 the population is mid-2023 data published on 15 July 2024 (this population data has since been revised but the calculations were carried out before the revision). For 2022 data the population is mid-2022 data published in July 2023 (this population data has since been revised but the calculations were carried out before the revision). In previous years, the population year is often the one prior to the abortion year as latest population estimates are not released in time for abortion data updates.
Notes: This indicator is based on year of abortion.The year of conception version of the abortion rate is available in Table 6 of ONS annual conception statistics here:<a href="https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/conceptionandfertilityrates/datasets/conceptionstatisticsenglandandwalesreferencetables">https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/conceptionandfertilityrates/datasets/conceptionstatisticsenglandandwalesreferencetables

Indicator: Under 18s births rate
Rationale: Teenage parents are at increased risk of postnatal depression and poor mental health in the 3 years following birth. They are more likely than older mothers to have low educational attainment, experience adult unemployment and be living in poverty at age 30. Their children experience higher rates of infant mortality and low birth weight, A&E admissions for accidents and have a much higher risk of being born into poverty.More backgroundinformation and advice on tackling teenage pregnancy is provided in Public Health England's joint paper with the Local Government Association (LGA) published January 2016  https://www.local.gov.uk/good-progress-more-do-teenage-pregnancy-and-young-parents
Definition: Live births in women aged under 18 per 1,000 females aged 15 to 17
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: Number oflive birthsregistered in women aged under 18 years by area of usual residence
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts
Definition of denominator: Number of women aged 15 to 17 living in the area
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 1,000

Indicator: Chlamydia detection rate per 100,000 aged 15 to 24 years
Rationale: Chlamydia is the most commonly diagnosed bacterial sexually transmitted infection in England, with rates substantially higher in young adults than any other age group. It causes avoidable sexual and reproductive ill-health, including symptomatic acute infections and complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy and tubal-factor infertility. The National Chlamydia Screening Programme (NCSP) promotes opportunistic screening to sexually active young people aged 15 to 24 years. In June 2021,  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-the-national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp  were announced with a focus on reducing reproductive harm of untreated infection through opportunistic screening offered to young women aged under 25 years.The chlamydia detection rate among young people aged 15 to 24 years is a measure of chlamydia control activity, aimed at reducing the incidence of reproductive sequelae of chlamydia infection and interrupting transmission. An increased detection rate is indicative of increased control activity; the detection rate is not a measure of morbidity.Inclusion of this indicator in the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/public-health-outcomes-framework  allows monitoring of progress to control chlamydia and the delivery of accessible, high-volume chlamydia screening.The chlamydia detection rate is a PHOF indicator and local authorities should be working towards a detection rate of at least 3,250 diagnoses per 100,000 young women aged 15 to 24 years.
Definition:
All chlamydia diagnoses among young people aged 15 to 24 years attending sexual health services (SHSs) and community-based settings, who are residents in England, expressed as a rate per 100,000 population.Data excludes people accessing services located in England who are residents in Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland or abroad. The England total includes tests which did not have sufficient location information to be attributed to a local authority of residence.In this indicator, male or men refers to gender identity. Gender identity refers to a person’s sense of their own gender – whether male (men), female (women) or any other identity (such as non-binary). This may, or may not, be the same as their sex registered at birth.Sexual health services are those providing STI related care (Levels 1, 2 or 3). Further details on the levels of sexual healthcare provision are provided in the https://www.bashh.org/about-bashh/publications/standards-for-the-management-of-stis/ .
There are 8 categories of ‘testing service type’: sexual health services (specialist STI-related care) (SHS), GPs, sexual health services (non-specialist STI-related care), internet, termination of pregnancy (ToP), pharmacy, other and unknown.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: UK Health Security Agency's  https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp-data-tables .<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp-data-tables">
Definition of numerator: For the male indicator, the numerator is the number of diagnoses in young men aged 15 to 24 years in England.For the persons indicator, the numerator is the number of diagnoses in young persons aged 15 to 24 years in England.Chlamydia data is sourced from GUMCAD STI Surveillance System (Level 3) and CTAD Chlamydia Surveillance System (Levels 1 and 2), UKHSA. GUMCAD is reported by SHSs providing STI related care (Levels 2 or 3). CTAD is reported by laboratories conducting testing for any service (Levels 1, 2 or 3) providing chlamydia testing. All chlamydia diagnoses at SHSs providing specialist STI-related care previously diagnosed at another service have been removed from diagnosis totals to prevent double-counting. Details of the GUMCAD methodology are on theGUMCAD STI Surveillance Systempage.Data includes those diagnosed through NHS and local authority commissioned testing and excludes those diagnosed through private testing.A maximum of one chlamydia test or diagnosis per individual is counted within a 6-week period. Any further tests or diagnoses within the 6-week period are not counted. Diagnoses are kept in preference over negative results during this process. Patients cannot be tracked between clinics and therefore de-duplication relies on patient consultations at a single service.The clinical definition used to diagnose chlamydia is given atBASHH guidelines.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), GUMCAD STI and CTAD Chlamydia Surveillance Systems
Definition of denominator: For the male indicator, the denominator is the population of young men aged 15 to 24 years derived from ONS mid-year population estimates sourced from the 2021 Census.For the persons indicators, the denominator is the population of young persons aged 15 to 24 years derived from ONS mid-year population estimates sourced from the 2021 Census.Population estimates for 2025 were not available at the time of publication. Therefore, rates for 2025 are calculated using estimates from 2024 as a proxy.ONS population estimates are in relation to sex – which may, or may not, be the same as gender identity. Therefore, rates by gender identity are calculated using population estimates by sex as a proxy.Further details on the ONS census are available from the https://www.ons.gov.uk/census .
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: For the men indicator, the rate is per 100,000 population of young men aged 15 to 24 years. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.For the persons indicator, the rate is per 100,000 population of young persons aged 15 to 24 years. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Confidence interval method: Exact PoissonA confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically, it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.Confidence intervals have been calculated by the UKHSA using the Stata software package and are based on the exact Poisson method.

Caveats:
Every effort is made to ensure accuracy and completeness of the data, including web-based reporting with integrated checks on data quality. However, responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of data lies with the data submitter and service providers.Chlamydia diagnoses are recorded in both GUMCAD and CTAD data sets. Records are de-duplicated within the 2 data sets as part of data cleaning to prevent overestimation prior to publication.There may be some minor differences in the chlamydia totals reported in this indicator and in the  https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp-data-tables , where there are differences in how chlamydia testing by internet providers is reported to GUMCAD and CTAD.Missing data in CTAD: Leeds General Infirmary Laboratory did not submit data for July to September (Quarter 3) 2016 and Birmingham Women’s Laboratory did not submit data for October to December (Quarter 4) 2018. However, LSOA data reported to GUMCAD may not have the latest LSOA codes therefore, some LSOA data cannot be attributed to the correct ICB. The total for local authority data may not equal to the total for ICB.Population data for ICBs was derived from postcode of residence to ICB in the CTAD data using the  https://digital.nhs.uk/services/organisation-data-service/data-search-and-export/csv-downloads/ods-postcode-files .Values for the combined authorities (CAs) in England defined by 2 June 2026 have been provided directly. New CAs defined after 2 June 2026 and before the 2027 data refresh will be calculated automatically by the Fingertips software in the Sexual and Reproductive Health Profiles.Regions shown in the profiles are with reference to the Former Government Offices for the Regions (GOR) which may not match the UKHSA regions shown in the  https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp-data-tables .In 2012, several changes were made to the collection and reporting of chlamydia activity data, to deliver a simpler and more representative national surveillance system. Further information can be found on the  https://www.gov.uk/guidance/chlamydia-testing-activity-dataset-ctad  page.In June 2021, the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/national-chlamydia-screening-programme-ncsp  changed to focus on reducing the harms from untreated chlamydia infection. Given the change in programme aim the benchmarking thresholds have been revised and will be measured against females only. Please see the  /documents/Summary%20of changes to the NCSP PHOF DRI benchmarking December 2021.pdf  for more details.

Indicator: Cost per smoking quitter
Rationale:
Local NHS Stop Smoking Services offer support to help people quit smoking. This can include intensive support through group therapy or one-to-one support. The support is designed to be widely accessible within the local community and is provided by trained personnel, such as specialist smoking cessation advisors and trained nurses and pharmacists.
This indicator is a guide to how cost-effective local NHS Stop Smoking Services are, and to highlight disparities around the country, which might lead to further investigation and changes to the way local services are delivered.
Definition: Amount spent to achieve each successful smoking quitter
Data source: NHS England
Definition of numerator: The expenditure provided by each local authority (LA) in their return form. The return form asks organisations to provide a figure which relates to "all monies from whatever source which have been specifically allocated to, or spent on, smoking cessation services". Thus includes any costs of running the smoking cessation service including, the cost of training, sub-contracting, salaries and overheads and pharmacotherapies issued as part of this service. It also includes any money spent on marketing, or the appropriate part of any marketing or other spend where the intended outcome is increased attendance at local services. From 2011/12, organisations have been advised to only include monies spent on smoking cessation activity, not wider tobacco control measures. It excludes NRT, Bupropion (Zyban) and Varenicline (Champix) on prescription.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Statistics on NHS Stop Smoking Services in England (SSS)
Definition of denominator: Number of self-reported successful quitters at 4 weeks.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />Successful quitters are those smokers who successfully quit at the 4 week follow-up. A client is counted as a ‘self-reported 4 week quitter’ when assessed 4 weeks after the designated quit date, if they declare that they have not smoked, even a single puff on a cigarette, in the past 2 weeks. This information is collected on NHS Stop Smoking returns in line with requirements from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Statistics on NHS Stop Smoking Services in England (SSS)
Methodology: LAs submit returns to NHS England for smoking services, which include the total number of people who successfully quit smoking and the total expenditure. The total expenditure is divided by the number of quitters to calculate an average cost per successful quitter.
Confidence interval details: No confidence intervals available
Caveats: NHS England report that there is some evidence that in practice there may be a lack of standardisation in terms of the scope of expenditure items included in some organisation’s returns; this means figures may not always be calculated on a comparable basis locally.
Notes: NHS England have identified an issue with the data used to compile the Stop Smoking Services publication, originally released on 3rd September 2019. The annual dataset did not contain the revised data for Quarters 1 to 3 that local authorities had submitted along with their quarter 4 data; instead the provisional data for these quarters was included in the annual dataset. This has caused differences throughout the publication. Data for 2018/19 was updated on this tool on 1st October 2019.

Rationale: There is evidence that when doctors and other healthcare professionals advise patients to stop smoking, this is effective. This indicator examine whether smoking status is recorded in the patient record.The Government’s Tobacco Control Plan (Towards a Smokefree Generation: A Tobacco Control Plan for England, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/towards-a-smoke-free-generation-tobacco-control-plan-for-england ) published in July 2017 sets out the Government’s strategy to reduce smoking prevalence among adults and young people, and to reduce smoking during pregnancy.

Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Definition of denominator: Estimated list size 15+: the estimated number of patients listed on GP records within each area (age 15 years and over)
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Methodology: QOF GP level data (Recorded disease prevalence, achievements and exceptions: Smoking 15+) was downloaded and aggregated to higher geographical areas. Current smokers was calculated as a percentage of those registered with a GP aged 15 years or older.
Confidence interval details:
A confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.
Normal approximation methods can be used to calculate approximate confidence intervals for a wide variety of indicators. Any indicator value which is calculated as a mean of the observed values can be approximated with a Normal distribution as long as the sample size is sufficiently large. Distribution-specific methods should be used whenever possible, especially when the indicator is a rate with very low values, or a proportion with values close to zero or one, and the ease with which these can be applied through computation means it is rarely necessary to use normal approximation methods. However, in cases where the underlying distribution is complex or not known, normal approximation methods may be the only approach available.
The general form of all Normal approximation methods is: A 100(1 − α)% confidence interval for an indicator value, x, is given by: x ± z × SE(x) where α is the significance value specifying the width of the confidence interval, SE(x) is the standard error of the indicator value (estimated by different methods according to the statistic type) and z is the 100(1 − α/2)th percentile value from the Standard Normal distribution.
For example for a 95% confidence interval, α = 0.05 and z = 1.96 (the 97.5th percentile value from the Standard Normal distribution).
For proportions, SE(x) is estimated by: √(x(1 − x)/n) where x is the indicator value (the observed proportion) and n is the denominator of the indicator value.

Indicator: People invited for an NHS Health Check per year
Rationale: The NHS Health Check programme aims to help prevent heart disease, stroke, diabetes and kidney disease. Everyone between the ages of 40 and 74, who has not already been diagnosed with one of these conditions, will be invited (once every five years) to have a check to assess their risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney disease and diabetes and will be given support and advice to help them reduce or manage that risk. A high take up of NHS Health Check is important to identify early signs of poor health leading to opportunities for early interventions.
Definition: Percentage of the eligible population, aged 40 – 74 years, offered an NHS Health Check per financial year
Data source: OHID, based on NHS Health Check Programme data
Definition of numerator: Number of people aged 40-74 eligible for an NHS Health Check who were offered an NHS Health Check in the financial year.
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), NHS Health Check Programme
Definition of denominator:
Number of people aged 40-74 eligible for an NHS Health Check in the financial year.
OHID calculates the total eligible population (TEP) by using the latest available Office for National Statistics data (Census 2021-based mid-year ONS resident population estimates) minus the estimated number of people on existing disease registers. To estimate the number of people on existing disease registers and therefore not eligible for a NHS Health Check, the age and sex specific weightings used in the NHS Health Check Ready Reckoner tool are applied to the local population.
Since 2019/20, the TEP has also been adjusted to remove prisoners serving a sentence of 6 months or more.
• Those prisoners are included in ONS mid-year population estimates, however prisoners serving a sentence above 2 years receive checks commissioned by NHS England rather than by local authorities.
• Prisoners serving a sentence of at least 6 months but under 2 years were also excluded from the TEP because, although they aren’t eligible for an NHS England check, by virtue of them being in prison they can’t access a NHS Health Check provided by the local authority.
In addition, every year local authorities able to identify the eligible population from their local general practice clinical systems or who have undertaken a more accurate assessment of the eligible population can use this TEP estimate rather than OHID estimates.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), NHS Health Check Programme
Methodology:
Percentage of eligible population aged 40-74 offered an NHS Health Check: the number of eligible people aged 40-74 who were offered an NHS Health Check is divided by the number of eligible people aged 40-74 and multiplied by 100.
Note that this indicator is based mostly on general practice data,but data is collected and aggregated by local authorities responsible for managing the NHS Health Check programme locally.
Confidence interval details:
A confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.
The Wilson Score method1gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for proportions and odds based on the assumption of a Binomial distribution. It can be used with any data values, even when the denominator is very small and, unlike some methods, it does not fail to give an interval when the numerator count, and therefore the proportion, is zero. The Wilson Score method is the preferred method for calculating confidence intervals for proportions and odds, but it can also be used for rates, as long as the event rate is low (relatively rare events within the population) as the Binomial distribution is a very good approximation to the Poisson distribution when the event rate is low. The method is described in detail in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.2
1Wilson EB. Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference.J Am Stat Assoc1927;22:209-12.2Eayres D.Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.York: APHO; 2008. Available at http://www.apho.org.uk/resource/item.aspx?RID=48457
Disclosure control: None applied
Caveats:
The NHS Health Checks programme became the responsibility of Local Authorities in April 2013. There is still considerable variation between local authorities in the reported numbers of Health Checks offered and received. In some cases the variation may be the result of data quality issues. For example, for a few local authorities, the number of checks offered is the same as the number of checks received. Data quality issues may affect the indicator and England comparator values of both offers and received numbers of Health Checks should be interpreted together. The Health Check Programme aims to cover the eligible population over a 5 year period i.e. 20% of the eligible population invited for NHS Health Checks each year. The total number of people offered an NHS Health Check in the financial year does not, therefore, represent the total population eligible for a Health Check.Caution should be taken with local authorities that have small values due to the variation that can take place.This is the case particularly for the quarterly (91040, 91041, 91030) and uptake (91030, 91735, 91116) indicators.

For data at an ICB level, local authorities are allocated to their relevant ICB using the method developed by the Public Health Outcomes Framework (PHOF) profile. If a local authority sits within two or more ICBs, its population is mapped to each ICB to obtain a weighting based on resident population: the weighting is applied to allocate the eligible population, number of checks offered and number of checks completed by the local authority to the ICBs it is part of.

The ICB data has been backdated to 2019/20. This means that historical local authorities must also be split into ICBs even though they do not have a weighting. There are two cases of historical local authorities where this is the case: Northamptonshire and Cumbria. Northamptonshire is very simple to allocate to an ICB as it sits entirely within NHS Northamptonshire ICB. However, Cumbria is a more complex case as both Cumbria and the two local authorities it separated into, Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness, sit across two ICBs, NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB and NHS North East and North Cumbria ICB.

Value notes have been added to the affected ICBs which are NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB and NHS North East and North Cumbria ICB. This is because we are estimating the offers and checks that go into Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness from the Cumbria data before adding them into these two ICBs. It means the method for calculating historical values for these two ICBs is different from the method used for other ICBs.

NHS Health Check data is originally based on GP records then collated by LAs. By estimating ICB level data from LA level data, NHS Health Check data is being converted back to health geographies. It is important to note that ICB values obtained this way will be different from what would be obtained by directly aggregating general practices data.

Mapping using geographic boundaries doesn't necessarily align with the numerator, i.e. the weighting of the population does not necessarily reflect the distribution of offers and completed checks across the area. However, where the overall counts of LAs (eligible population, offers, completed checks) have been divided and allocated to two or more ICBs, this assumption has been made.

The PHOF method of separating local authorities made use of the total population to weight them, not the population specific to NHS Health Check (40-74 year olds). This impacts how local authorities are weighted if age is not distributed evenly throughout the area.
Impact of COVID-19: This indicator covers the period since March 2020 and includes the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Data re-use: These source data are publically available and there are no restrictions on their re-use.

Note that this indicator is based mostly on general practice data,but data is collected and aggregated by local authorities responsible for managing the NHS Health Check programme locally.
Confidence interval details:
A confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.
The Wilson Score method1gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for proportions and odds based on the assumption of a Binomial distribution. It can be used with any data values, even when the denominator is very small and, unlike some methods, it does not fail to give an interval when the numerator count, and therefore the proportion, is zero. The Wilson Score method is the preferred method for calculating confidence intervals for proportions and odds, but it can also be used for rates, as long as the event rate is low (relatively rare events within the population) as the Binomial distribution is a very good approximation to the Poisson distribution when the event rate is low. The method is described in detail in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.2
1Wilson EB. Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference.J Am Stat Assoc1927;22:209-12.2Eayres D.Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.York: APHO; 2008. Available at http://www.apho.org.uk/resource/item.aspx?RID=48457
Disclosure control: None applied
Caveats:
The NHS Health Checks programme became the responsibility of Local Authorities in April 2013. There is still considerable variation between local authorities in the reported numbers of Health Checks offered and received. In some cases the variation may be the result of data quality issues. For example, for a few local authorities, the number of checks offered is the same as the number of checks received. Data quality issues may affect the indicator and England comparator values of both offers and received numbers of Health Checks should be interpreted together. The Health Check Programme aims to cover the eligible population over a 5 year period i.e. 20% of the eligible population invited for NHS Health Checks each year. The total number of people offered an NHS Health Check in the financial year does not, therefore, represent the total population eligible for a Health Check.Caution should be taken with local authorities that have small values due to the variation that can take place.This is the case particularly for the quarterly (91040, 91041, 91030) and uptake (91030, 91735, 91116) indicators.

For data at an ICB level, local authorities are allocated to their relevant ICB using the method developed by the Public Health Outcomes Framework (PHOF) profile. If a local authority sits within two or more ICBs, its population is mapped to each ICB to obtain a weighting based on resident population: the weighting is applied to allocate the eligible population, number of checks offered and number of checks completed by the local authority to the ICBs it is part of.

The ICB data has been backdated to 2019/20. This means that historical local authorities must also be split into ICBs even though they do not have a weighting. There are two cases of historical local authorities where this is the case: Northamptonshire and Cumbria. Northamptonshire is very simple to allocate to an ICB as it sits entirely within NHS Northamptonshire ICB. However, Cumbria is a more complex case as both Cumbria and the two local authorities it separated into, Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness, sit across two ICBs, NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB and NHS North East and North Cumbria ICB.

Value notes have been added to the affected ICBs which are NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB and NHS North East and North Cumbria ICB. This is because we are estimating the offers and checks that go into Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness from the Cumbria data before adding them into these two ICBs. It means the method for calculating historical values for these two ICBs is different from the method used for other ICBs.

NHS Health Check data is originally based on GP records then collated by LAs. By estimating ICB level data from LA level data, NHS Health Check data is being converted back to health geographies. It is important to note that ICB values obtained this way will be different from what would be obtained by directly aggregating general practices data.

Mapping using geographic boundaries doesn't necessarily align with the numerator, i.e. the weighting of the population does not necessarily reflect the distribution of offers and completed checks across the area. However, where the overall counts of LAs (eligible population, offers, completed checks) have been divided and allocated to two or more ICBs, this assumption has been made.

The PHOF method of separating local authorities made use of the total population to weight them, not the population specific to NHS Health Check (40-74 year olds). This impacts how local authorities are weighted if age is not distributed evenly throughout the area.
Impact of COVID-19: This indicator covers the period since March 2020 and includes the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Data re-use: These source data are publically available and there are no restrictions on their re-use.

Indicator: Proportion of local smoking population who set a quit date
Rationale: Local NHS Stop Smoking Services offer support to help people quit smoking. This can include support through one-to-one or group interventions, either in-person or remotely. The support is designed to help smokers to quit in order to reduce health inequalities, particularly in areas where rates of smoking are higher than the general population. The services should be accessible in the local community and are provided by trained personnel, such as specialist smoking cessation advisors, trained clinical staff and pharmacists.This is an indicator of the coverage of local NHS Stop Smoking Services. The indicator should be viewed alongside 94243 as a measure of the effectiveness of local stop smoking services. It is recognised that in certain cases some time may need to be spent with clients before they are ready to set a quit date. However only actual quit attempts are counted for national monitoring.
Definition: Those setting a quit date as a proportion of current smokers, expressed as a percentage.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: The number of current smokers who set a quit date with a local NHS Stop Smoking Service.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Statistics on NHS Stop Smoking Services in England (SSS)
Definition of denominator: Population who currently smoke. Smoking prevalence estimates at local authority level for those aged 18+ (calculated from the Annual Population Survey) were multiplied by the corresponding ONS mid-year population estimates for age 16+ to calculate the smoking population.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Statistics on NHS Stop Smoking Services in England (SSS)
Methodology: The number of current smokers setting a quit date divided by the smoking population expressed as a percentage.
Confidence interval details: A simulation approach was used to produce confidence intervals because the denominator is an estimate with known uncertainty and the standard approach for confidence intervals assumes a fixed denominator. The standard deviation is estimated from the confidence intervals because standard deviations are not published.Prior to the simulation: 1) The prevalence is logit-transformed logit (prev) = (ln (prev / (1 – prev))2) The standard deviation (SD) of the logit-transformed prevalence is calculated. This is done by first calculating the Wilson Score confidence intervals for the prevalence, using n as the denominator and (prev × n / 100) as the numerator3) These confidence limits are then logit-transformed, and the difference between the logit-transformed upper and lower limits is divided by (2 × z1–α/2) to give an estimate of the SD of the logit-transformed prevalenceSimulation: for each iteration: 4) A random number between 0 and 1 is generated using the Mersenne Twister algorithm, and used to provide a random value from a normal distribution with mean = logit (prev) and SD = the SD of logit (prev)5) This random sampled value is transformed to a prevalence using the inverse of the logit function, and multiplied by pop to give a randomised estimated number of smokers in the LA (the denominator of the randomised indicator)6) A second random number is generated and used to provide a random value from a normal distribution with mean = num (eg the number of smokers who have set a quite date in the LA) and SD = sqrt (num) – this is the randomised numerator value7) The randomised indicator value is calculated by dividing the randomised numerator by the randomised denominator8) The randomised indicator value is added to an array of randomised indicator valuesAfter the simulation: 9) From the array of randomised indicator values, the (1–α/2)th centile smallest and largest values are identified and returned as the lower and upper confidence limits respectively (where α is the confidence level specified for the confidence intervals, eg 0.95)For further information see  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Basic_statistics/Confidence_intervals.html#estimation-of-confidence-intervals-using-simulation
Caveats: Data are collected on the basis of the local authority (LA) providing the stop smoking service. Clients are not restricted to attending stop smoking services in the LA with which they are registered or resident. This means that the number of smoking quits as a result of stop smoking services is not necessarily the number of smoking quits in the LAs own population. For those LAs whose residents go elsewhere for stop smoking services this will be an underestimate of the true quit rate. For those LAs who see many people for stop smoking services from outside the LA, this rate will be an overestimate.The numerator data are based on adults aged 16+. Smoking prevalence data from the Annual Population Survey is available for adults aged 18+. Since smoking prevalence is likely to be lower for younger people, this will result in an over estimate of the actual smoking population aged 16+. The impact is that the success of local services as measured as expressed by quit rates is likely to be slightly underestimated.Smoking prevalence as measured by the Annual Population Survey is self-reported and as such, prone to respondent bias. Also, the prevalence data is not age standardised. All issues of accuracy and completeness highlighted for smoking prevalence will also affect this indicator.It should be noted that as the majority of quitters do not use NHS Stop Smoking Services this indicator will not reflect overall quit attempts in the population.Please see the NHS England website for details of LAs not submitting data: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-nhs-stop-smoking-services-in-england
Notes: The Annual Population Survey has historically been designated as a National Statistic and provided a consistent time series of data. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, and in line with other government surveys, the response rate for the Annual Population Survey has fallen. The reduction in sample size impacts the ability to produce reliable estimates for smaller geographic areas. To mitigate this impact, the prevalence included in the calculation of this indicator is the 3-year APS-based smoking prevalence for local authorities.

Indicator: Premature births (less than 37 weeks gestation)
Rationale:
Globally premature birth (less than 37 weeks gestation) is the leading cause of death for children under the age of 5¹.
There is substantial evidence that smoking during pregnancy and exposure to second-hand-smoke can lead to premature birth² among many other adverse health effects including complications during labour, low birth-weight at full term and increased risk of miscarriage and stillbirth.
The inclusion of this indicator will help to monitor if the reduction in smoking prevalence and rates of smoking prevalence during pregnancy are having any effect on related health issues.

Indicator: Dementia: Short stay emergency admissions (aged 65 years and over)
Rationale:
Changes in the surrounding environment can increase the levels of anxiety and stress for an individual. People with dementia and alzheimer's can be more susceptible tothese changes, which can cause additional distress. Admissions to hospital, particularly ones of short duration should be avoided if at all possible for this population.
In areas where the admissions are above the national rate, further investigation is necessary to understand the factors contributing to higher rates. Factors can include the level of provision of primary care or community care services, both specifically for people with dementia or alzheimer's and general services that support older people with general health needs.
Definition: Percentage of emergency inpatient admissions for people (aged 65+) with a mention of dementia or alzheimer's in any of the diagnosis code positions that are short stays (1 night or less).
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: Hospital Episode Statistics - Admitted Patient Care
Definition of numerator: The number of finished discharge episodes (FDE), with an emergency admission method (ADMIMETH=2), ordinary admissions (CLASSPAT=1) with a spell duration of 1 night or less (SPELDUR=0 or 1) and with any mention of dementia or alzheimer's (F00-F03, G30, G318 & G310) in any diagnostic field position, in people aged 65+.Admissions are only included if they have a valid resident Local Authority code.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Definition of denominator: The number of finished discharge episodes (FDE), with an emergency admission method (ADMIMETH=2), ordinary admissions (CLASSPAT=1) and with any mention of dementia or alzheimer's (F00-F03, G30, G318 & G310) in any diagnostic field position, in people aged 65+.Admissions are only included if they have a valid resident Local Authority code.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Methodology: Emergency admissions data obtained from HES Inpatient data by ICD10 codes F00-F03, G30, G318 & G310. Short stays are defined as one night or less, with the episode ending in the financial year.
Disclosure control: All sub-national HES counts have been rounded to the nearest five in accordance with the latest disclosure guidelines.
Caveats:
HES inpatient data are generally considered to be complete and robust. However, there may be a question regarding the quality of external cause coding. Some of these cases may represent admissions for observation due to observed symptoms following an external cause event. There may be differences in admission thresholds. There may be variation between Trusts in the way hospital admissions are coded. There may be variation in data recording completeness.
The England figure is calculated as the local authority aggregate, therefore the England figure will not always match the value of the CCG aggregate.
NHS Digital has identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust (RXC) in 2018/19. Approximately 85,000 records erroneously had all diagnosis codes removed. Therefore, PHE have not published values for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 10% of patients from that area with missing diagnosis codes from RXC in the current year (2018/19). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients with missing diagnosis codes from RXC have been flagged to be treated with caution. For more details of the issue, see   https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/hospital-episode-statistics/the-processing-cycle-and-hes-data-quality#hes-data-quality-notes

Indicator: Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening: Hepatitis B Coverage
Rationale: To provide assurance that screening is offered and recommended to all eligible women and each woman accepting screening has a confirmed screening result.Coverage is a measure of the delivery of screening to an eligible population. Low coverage might indicate that:• not all eligible women were offered screening• those offered screening are not accepting the test• those accepting the test are not testedMonitoring coverage levels will highlight whether enough is being done to raise coverage levels and whether or not remedial action is required in areas where coverage is low. The benefits of screening will increase as the coverage levels increase.
Definition: The percentage of pregnant women booked for antenatal care for whom a screening result is available at the day of report.
Data source: NHS England, Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening Programme
Definition of numerator: Total number of eligible women for whom a confirmed screening result was available for hepatitis B at the day of report, including women who were known to be hepatitis B positive at booking and not retested.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Maternity Services Data Set (MSDS)
Definition of denominator: Total number of pregnant women booked for antenatal care during the reporting period, or presenting in labour without previously having booked for antenatal care, excluding women who:• miscarry between booking and testing• opt for termination between booking and testing• transfer out between booking and testing (do not have a result)• transfer in who have a result from a screening test performed elsewhere in the NHS in this pregnancy
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Maternity Services Data Set (MSDS)
Methodology: Percent coverage is calculated as the number of women tested divided by the number of women booked, multiplied by 100.
Confidence interval details: Wilson Score method used
Caveats:
Please be aware that the April 2019 to March 2020, April 2020 to March 2021 and April 2021 to March 2022 data covers the time period affected by the COVID19 pandemic and therefore data for this period should be interpreted with caution. https://phescreening.blog.gov.uk/2020/10/12/fourth-quarterly-kpi-2019-20 and https://phescreening.blog.gov.uk/2021/08/27/fourth-quarterly-kpi-data-for-2020-to-2021-published .

Indicator: GP prescribed LARC excluding injections rate / 1,000
Rationale: The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) Clinical Guideline CG30  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg30 advises that LARC methods, such as contraceptive injections, implants, the intra-uterine system (IUS) or the intrauterine device (IUD), are highly effective as they do not rely on daily compliance and are more cost effective than condoms and the pill. Implants, IUS and IUDs can remain in place for up to 3, 5 or 10 years depending on the type of product.A strategic priority is to ensure access to the full range of contraception is available to all. An increase in the provision of LARC is a proxy measure for wider access to the range of possible contraceptive methods and should also lead to a reduction in rates of unintended pregnancy.This indicator of GP prescribed LARC excludes injections, replacing an earlier indicator which included injections,because:- injections rely on timely repeat visits/administration withinthe year and consequently have a higher failure rate than the other LARC methods- injections are easily given in primary care and do not require the resources and training that other LARC methods require- injections are outside local authority contracts
Definition: Crude rate of GP prescribed long acting reversible contraception excluding injections per 1,000 resident female population aged 15-44 years
Data source: OHID, based on NHS Business Services Authority and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
Total number of implants, IUS and IUD in the calendar year (January to December) for women in all age groups.
Local authority assigned based on the location of the GP practice.
Source of numerator: NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), Prescription data (ePACT2)
Definition of denominator: ONS, Mid-year population estimates: single year of age and sex for local authorities in England (ages 15-44 years)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 1,000
Disclosure control: Small numbers are not be suppressed due to public availability of selected GP prescribing data - see 'links' section below.
Caveats: GP activity is assigned to the host local authority of the GP practice main base.Women, particularly younger women, may seek to use Sexual and Reproductive Health Services instead of GP services. Thus patterns of use may vary according to population characteristics and access to such services.Women may seek removal of LARC after a short time of use.In some cases LARC may be prescribed for menorrhagia, rather than for contraceptive purposes.GP prescribing data is prescription-item rather than person-based. Therefore it is not possible to use this data to derive an exact measure of the number of women prescribed implants, IUS and IUDs in general practice. The number of items prescribed in a yearis thus used as a proxy for the number of individuals prescribed implants, IUS amd IUDs.As LARC products can be in place for a number of years, this will be an undercount of the number of women actually using LARC in any year.A small number of ‘Unidentified doctors’ prescribed items have not been assigned to GP practices.The denominator population has been restricted to age 15-44 to allow direct comparison with the total abortion rate which is constructed on this basis. Indicator: Deprivation score (IMD 2015)
Rationale: Deprivation covers a broad range of issues and refers to unmet needs caused by a lack of resources of all kinds, not just financial. The English Indices of Deprivation attempt to measure a broader concept of multiple deprivation, made up of several distinct dimensions, or domains, of deprivation.
Definition: The English Indices of Deprivation 2015 use 37 separate indicators, organised across seven distinct domains of deprivation which can be combined, using appropriate weights, to calculate the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2015 (IMD 2015). This is an overall measure of multiple deprivation experienced by people living in an area.
Data source: OHID, based on Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government data
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2015
Source of numerator: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), English indices of deprivation
Source of denominator: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), English indices of deprivation
Methodology:
The English Indices of Deprivation 2015 are measures of multiple deprivation at the small area level. The model of multiple deprivation which underpins the indices of Deprivation 2015 is based on the idea of distinct domains of deprivation which can be recognised and measured separately. These domains are experienced by individuals living in an area. People may be counted in one or more of the domains, depending on the number and the types of deprivation that they experience. Each domain represents a specific form of deprivation experienced by people and each can be measured individually using a number of indicators. Seven distinct domains have been identified in the English Indices of Deprivation; Income Deprivation, Employment Deprivation, Health Deprivation and Disability, Education, Skills and Training Deprivation, Barriers to Housing and services, Living Environment Deprivation and Crime. Individual domains can be used in isolation as measures of each specific form of deprivation. They can also be combined, using appropriate weights, into a single overall Index of Multiple Deprivation which can be used to rank every small area in England according to the deprivation experienced by the people living there. Along with two supplementary indices, Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index and Income Index Affecting Older People Index, they form the English Indices of Deprivation. These statistics allow the most, and least, deprived areas of the country to be identified as well as providing information about the issues faced by people living in different parts of the country.Scores for geographies larger than LSOAs are population weighted averages of the LSOAs in that area.
Estimates for GP practices have been re-calculated in 2016 by building the population weighted average over the IMD scores of the LSOAs where the practice population lives with 2016 populations. The data source for mapping patient numbers to LSOAs (April 2016) was downloaded from the NHS digital website:  http://content.digital.nhs.uk/catalogue/PUB20480/gp-reg-patients-LSOA-MALE.csv  http://content.digital.nhs.uk/catalogue/PUB20480/gp-reg-patients-LSOA-FEMALE.csv 
For more information, see: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2015-technical-report
Notes: The Indices of Deprivation 2015 are relative measures of deprivation. This means it can tell you if one area is more deprived than another, but not by how much.The Indices of Deprivation 2015 is not a measure of affluence; all of the indicators used in the index are designed to identify aspects of deprivation, not affluence. Therefore the area ranked as the least deprived is not necessarily the most affluent. There were 19 small wards which had no LSOAs with the population weighted centroid of the LSOA inside the boundary of the ward. Figures for these wards could not be calculated.

Indicator: Direct standardised rate of mortality: People with dementia (aged 65 years and older)
Rationale: The rationale for including this indicator is to understand the geographical variation in the deaths of people with dementia or Alzheimer's disease.
Definition: Directly age standardised rate of mortality in persons (aged 65 years and older) with a mention of dementia or Alzheimer's disease reported death certificate per 100,000 population. This indicator uses resident based data.
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths with a mention of dementia or Alzheimer's disease (classified as either underlying cause of death or contributory cause) recorded as ICD codes F00 to F03, G30, G318 and G310 registered in the respective calendar years, in people aged 65 years and older aggregated into quinary age bands (65 to 69, 70 to 74,…, 90 and older)
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: Population-years for people of aged 65 years and older, aggregated into quinary age bands (65 to 69, 70 to 74,…, 90 and older)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates and Eurostat, European Standard Population (2013)
Methodology:
Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area.
These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area.
This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
Caveats:
Historical data for 2018 and 2019 have been updated with rebased population estimates that are consistent with Census 2021. Therefore all values may differ from those previously published.
Death counts included in this indicator relate to only those where dementia and Alzheimer's disease is recorded on the death certificate. However this does not necessaily mean a formal diagnosis was given and recorded in primary care records prior to death occuring.
Notes: For comparator indicators please see http://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/end-of-life

Indicator: Dementia: Recorded prevalence (aged 65 years and older)
Rationale:
This indicator quantifies the proportion of people aged 65 years and older with a recorded diagnosis of dementia.
Prime Minister's challenge on dementia 2015 to ' increase diagnosis rates through existing checks for over-65s' set out 'the first ever national ambition on dementia diagnosis that two thirds of the estimated number of people with dementia should receive a diagnosis and appropriate post-diagnosis support by March 2015 so that they can access the right care at the right time'.The second stage of the Prime Minister's challenge on dementia 2020 further pledged to 'create a society by 2020 where every person with dementia, and their carers and families, from all backgrounds, walks of life and in all parts of the country – people of different ages, gender, sexual orientation, ability or ethnicity for example, receive high quality, compassionate care from diagnosis through to end of life care'.
The recorded dementia prevalence provides an indication of the concentration, within a population, of the number of people aged 65 and older who have been diagnosed and who are now living with the condition. This indicator can be used to inform local service planning as to the scale of services required to provide treatment, care and support as needed, so those with dementia can live well with the condition.
Definition: The percentage of patients aged 65 years and older with dementia recorded on primary care (GP) practice disease registers.
Data source: NHS England
Indicator source:
Until September 2022, NHS Digital has been publishing recorded dementia diagnoses at GP practice level on a monthly basis. This publication was superseded by the Primary Care Dementia Data published by NHS England in October 2022 with regular quality monthly data extracts provided from April 2023 onwards. This indicator compiles epidemiological summary of the data extracted at 31st December but more contemporary monthly data is available directly from NHSE.Primary Care Dementia data: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/primary-care-dementia-data 
Recorded Dementia Diagnosis data: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/recorded-dementia-diagnoses

Patients aged 65 years and older recorded with dementia on primary care (GP) practice registers at 31st December, allocated to health geographies based on the postcode of the practice

This is a registered population based indicator. Where data are not available for a GP practice for the date specified, data are backfilled using recorded dementia diagnosis from previous months. Where this is not available, the 'Quality and Outcomes Framework QOF practice disease registers data' for all ages is used.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), multiple sources

Practice list size for people aged 65 years and older at 31st December, allocated to health geographies based on the postcode of the practice

ICB: The number of patients aged 65 years and olderregistered with a GP practice in each Integrated Care Board (ICB).
Sub-ICB: The number of patients aged 65 years and olderregistered with a GP practice in each Sub-ICB location.

Notes:
Interpretation of the different dementia prevalence indicators:
Dementia recorded prevalence (all ages) indicator is a companion metric based on QOF data, and provides a snapshot of dementia at 31st March each year.
However, the following three companion metrics are based on NHS monthly data, and they provide a snapshot of dementia prevalence at December 31st of each year.

Recorded prevalence (aged 65 years and older).
Crude recorded prevalence (aged under 65 years) per 10, 000.
Dementia (aged under 65 years) as a proportion of total dementia (all ages) per 100.

Supporting analysisFurther work on prevalence of dementia is available as part of https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/dementia/supporting-information/surveillance%20factsheet publication and https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/dementia/supporting-information/dementia%20new%20indicator%20factsheet , in particular part 1 on incidence and young onset dementia.Caveats

Data is extracted for open and active practices only. A small number of GP practices may not have denominator values, therefore the associated numerator values are excluded from this indicator. For geographies affected by this issue, the numerator counts provided here will not match those found in the relevant QOF publication.
This indicator is a measure of recorded prevalence and not actual prevalence and therefore under-reports groups who are less likely to be registered with a GP, such as ethnic minority populations, homeless people, migrants and travellers. Caution should be taken when interpreting this indicator - as a higher than average value may mean that the prevalence of the condition is high in an area, but it could also indicate that detection is better there; this is for local knowledge to determine.

Indicator: Percentage of broad-spectrum prescribed antibiotic items (cephalosporin, quinolone and co-amoxiclav class) by quarter
Rationale: The consumption of antibiotics is a major driver for the development of antibiotic resistance (AMR) in bacteria. The use of antibiotics is essential for saving lives in conditions such as sepsis.The UK government released a https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/385733/UK_AMR_annual_report.pdf in 2013 and a https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/784894/UK_AMR_5_year_national_action_plan.pdf in 2019, with ambitions to reduce UK antimicrobial use in humans by 15% by 2024.
Specific rationale: This indicator specifically shows broad-spectrum items prescribed by quarter. It is a target to reduce the proportion of broad-spectrum antibiotics consumed and monitor the trend of the proportion over time.
Definition: Broad-spectrum items prescribed in primary care settings includes the following antimicrobials; cephalosporin, fluoroquinolone and co-amoxiclav. Data is presented as percentage of broad-spectrum items prescribed over all prescribed antibacterials in the British National Formula (BNF) 5.1 category.The lower the precentage presented, the lower proportion of broad-spectrum items were prescribed.
Data source: NHS Business Services Authority
Indicator source: Prescribing data is supplied by general practices to NHS Digital and downloaded monthly to UKHSA. Data is aggregated to produce both quarterly and annual levels of consumption.
Definition of numerator: The items of broad-spectrum antimicrobials: cephalosporin, fluoroquinolone and co-amoxiclav, prescribed in a quarter.N<a href="http://www.hscic.gov.uk/">umerator data isa subset of the BNF 5.1 category. The full list of BNF formulae included can be found on  https://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/epact2 .
Source of numerator: NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), Prescription data (ePACT2)
Definition of denominator: The total items of antibacterials (BNF 5.1) prescribed in a quarter
Source of denominator: Not applicable (N/A)
Methodology: Quarterly consumption ofcephalosporin, fluoroquinolone and co-amoxiclav divided by the total number of antibacterials (BNF 5.1) prescribed in primary care settings, then multipliedby 100.Antibiotics derivatives are supplied with https://www.bnf.org/ (BNF) codes, detailing the full https://www.whocc.no/atc_ddd_index/ (ATC) code of the antibiotics and specifying the route of administration.
Caveats:
Profiles are generated for all practices in QOF 2020/21 with a list size of at least 750 patients and for other practices if they had according to NHS digital in April 2021 a list size of at least 750 patients and there exists valid GP patient survey data for the practice for the same year. For details see:  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/documents/Inclusionlist2020.xlsx .

Indicator: Total number of prescribed antibiotic items per STAR-PU by quarter - GP

Specific rationale: Specific Therapeutic group Age-sex weightings Related Prescribing Unit(STAR-PU) is an indirectly standardised ratiothat removes confounding effects of age and sex in the comparison of prescribing between different areas, as the demographic characteristics of the population may influence levels of prescribing. Definition: STAR-PU is weighted units to allow comparisons adjusting for the age and sex of patients distribution of each practice. A lower items per STAR-PU value is associated with fewer items of antibiotics being prescribed.

Indicator: C. difficile infection case counts and rates by Sub ICB Location (SICBL) and financial year
Rationale: Surveillance of C. difficile laboratory faecal samples in England and Wales was introduced in 1990 as part of the Public Health Laboratory Service’s voluntary monitoring of infectious diseases. Between 1990 and 2004 there was a rise in the number of C. difficile infections, from less than 3,000 in 1990 to more than 45,000 in 2004. Rates of C. difficile infections also rose over this time period in all age groups ≥40 years old. Due to the increasing incidence of C. difficile infections, the mandatory reporting of C. difficile infection in people aged ≥65 years was introduced in England in January 2004, this was a quarterly aggregate data return reported by NHS acute Trusts comprising data on the number of toxin-positive C. difficile faecal samples. Due to the continued rise of C. difficile infections among the population aged ≥65 years, the C. difficile mandatory surveillance scheme was enhanced in April 2007, to be patient-level and to cover all C. difficile infections in patients aged 2 years and over.A low value is indicative of a low rate ofC. difficile.
Definition:
C. difficile infection C. difficile infection in patients aged 2 years and above, diagnosed by one of the following five methods: 1.Diarrhoeal stools (Bristol Stool types 5-7) where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive*
2.Toxic megacolon or ileostomy where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive*
3.Pseudomembranous colitis revealed by lower gastro-intestinal endoscopy or Computed Tomography
4.Colonic histopathology characteristic of C. difficile infection (with or without diarrhoea or toxin detection) on a specimen obtained during endoscopy or colectomy
5.Faecal specimens collected post-mortem where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive or tissue specimens collected post-mortem where pseudomembranous colitis is revealed or colonic histopathology is characteristic of C. difficile infection
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/clostridium-difficile-guidance-data-and-analysis

rate = (cases for given period/CCG-level population estimate)*100,000
