Indicator: Percentage of people with type 1 diabetes who were offered the diabetes structured education programme within 12 months of diagnosis
Rationale:
Diabetes is one of the common endocrine diseases affecting millions of people in England. Effective control and monitoring can reduce mortality and morbidity. Much of the management and monitoring of diabetic patients is undertaken by the GP and members of the primary care team. However, type 1 and type 2 diabetes have different risk factors and management. There are differences in the population with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, leading to a discrepancy in receiving care processes and achieving treatment targets. Understanding this discrepancy at a local level is important for assessing the needs of the local population with diabetes and where improvements can be made.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Guidance provides the rationale for adults with diabetes need to acquire a large range of new skills and knowledge, such as how to manage their insulin therapy. Patient education enables self-management, which is important in diabetes management. It allows adults with type 1 diabetes to adapt their diabetes management to changes in their daily lives and to maintain a good quality of life. Managing type 2 diabetes involves lifestyle changes, and treatment can be complex. Structured education programmes can help adults with type 2 diabetes to improve their knowledge and skills and increase patient activation to self-manage effectively. These programmes should be offered in a timely manner following diagnosis, recognising that adults may be more open to change at this time, and key messages reinforced periodically. The first few months after diagnosis involve considerable adjustment, so although information should be given from diagnosis, a more intensive structured education programme will be more beneficial 6–12 months after diagnosis.
Definition: The percentage of people newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes within the calendar year who were offered the chance to attend the diabetes structured education programme within 12 months of diagnosis among practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit.
Data source: NHS England, National Diabetes Audit
Definition of numerator: Number of people newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in the calendar year who were offered diabetes structured education within 12 months of diagnosis.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator: Number of people newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in the calendar year.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Methodology: The number of people newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes who were offered diabetes structured education within 12 months of their diagnosis divided by the number of people newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Only includes people registered at a practice participating in the National Diabetes Audit.
Disclosure control: To avoid disclosive counts that could risk patient identification at any geography and through differencing, numerators and denominators are rounded to the nearest 5. To avoid disclosure of small numbers, numerators and denominators between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5.
Rounding: Numerators and denominators are rounded to the nearest 5. Values between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5. Values were calculated from these rounded values.
Caveats:
National Diabetes Audit data is collected covering a 15-month period between 1st January in the first year and 31st of March in the second year. Data reported for these indicators is assigned to the calendar year that new diagnoses occcured. Data for each year is reported by the subsequent audit period to allow enough follow-up time for those diagnosed to be offered/attend structured education. For example, data for 2020 is reported from the audit period 2021-22. However, there will be new diagnoses from 2020 that are only reported in the 2022-23 audit period. These are not captured by the data presented here, as it is not possible to differentiate new diagnoses from ones that were reported in the previous audit period, as these period overlap.

Indicator: E. coli bacteraemia 12-month rolling case counts and rates of hospital-onset, by reporting acute trust and month
Rationale: Escherichia coli(E. coli) is a Gram-negative bacterium and has been the predominant cause of bacteraemia in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, overtaking those caused byS. aureus(a Gram-positive bacterium), since 2003. Following a year-on-year increase in Gram-negative bacteraemia, as reported to PHE via the voluntary surveillance system (44% increase amongE. colibacteraemia alone between 2003 and 2011, from 16,542 to 29,777 voluntary reports), and a recommendation from the government advisory group Advisory Committee on Antimicrobial Resistance and Healthcare Associated Infections to commenceE. colibacteraemia surveillance, the Department of Health mandated NHS acute Trusts to report patient-level data on episodes ofE. colibacteraemia to UKHSA through the established enhanced mandatory surveillance Data Capture System from June 2011.
Definition: Laboratory confirmed cases ofE. colibacteraemia.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/escherichia-coli-e-coli-guidance-data-and-analysis
Definition of numerator:
All cases of E.coli meeting the 'Definition' section above occurring for thepast 11 months are summed with the current month to give arolling 12-month total. For the calculation of rates, the past 11 months are summed with the current month and the denominator is the sum of the bed-days (for trusts) or population (for CCGs) for the current month and preceding 11 months.

The rate for a month is then calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and multiplying by 100,000 to give a manageable value.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Healthcare Associated Infection Data Capture System (HCAI DCS) Mandatory Surveillance
Definition of denominator: Denominator values are calculated as an annual rolling sum. For any given month, the denominator includes the value for the occupied bed days for that month and the 11 preceeding months.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Bed Availability and Occupancy (KH03)
Methodology: The rate gives the annual rolling rate for a given month. In this calculation, the numerator is the sum of the cases for the current month and the 11 preceeding months. The denominator is the sum of the bed days for the current month and the 11 preceeding months.The rate for a month is then calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and multiplying by 100,000 to give a manageable value.
Confidence interval details: Confidence intervals are not calculated as the population value is known.
Caveats: These data do not provide a basis for decisions on the clinical effectiveness of infection control interventions in individual Trusts: further investigations considering potential confounders would need to be undertaken before this could be done.Nor do these data provide a basis for comparisons between acute Trust or CCGs. Rate information, using rate calculations as currently defined, is not appropriate for comparison. The counts of infections have not been adjusted to give a standardised rate considering factors such as organisational demographics or case mix. Rate information is of use for comparison of an individual organisation over time.Most acute trusts are expected to have higher rates of community-onset cases than hospital-onset cases. However, there are some specialist trusts for which this is not the case.

Definition: The number of respondents aged 19 and over, with valid responses to questions on physical activity, doing at least 150 moderate intensity equivalent (MIE) minutes physical activity per week in bouts of 10 minutes or more in the previous 28 days expressed as a percentage of the total number of respondents aged 19 and over.
Data source: OHID, based on Sport England data
Definition of numerator: Weighted number of respondents aged 19 and over, with valid responses to questions on physical activity, doing at least 150 MIE minutes physical activity per week in bouts of 10 minutes or more in the previous 28 days.Active Lives Adult Survey data is collected November to November.
Source of numerator: Sport England (SE), Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS)
Definition of denominator: Weighted number of respondents aged 19 and over, with valid responses to questions on physical activity.Denominator values in the Download data are unweighted counts. All analyses for this indicator have been weighted to be representative of the population of England.Latest update presents data from the Active Lives Adult Survey for the period mid November to mid November.
Source of denominator: Sport England (SE), Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS)
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100.The survey uses a 28 day reference period to record the number of minutes of physical activity (of at least 10 minutes) and then divides the number of minutes by four to calculate a weekly average (e.g. 2 hours of physical activity over the 28 days equates to 30 minutes per week). Number of minutes presented is the moderate intensity equivalent minutes of activity, which consists of moderate activity plus double the number of vigorous minutes of activity.The (broad) activities included in the estimates are grouped as sporting activities, fitness activities, cycling for leisure and sport, cycling for travel, walking for leisure, walking for travel, creative or artistic dance and gardening.The counts are weighted to be representative of the national population.
Confidence interval details:
An approximate 95% and 99.8% confidence interval was derived from 10,000 simulations of physically active prevalence for each age group within each area. Each prevalence simulation was calculated by

1 drawing a number of ‘successes’ randomly from a binomial distribution ~Bin(n,p) when n is the unweighted total population estimate and p is the weighted prevalence of physically active.

2 dividing the number of ‘successes’ by the unweighted total respondentsThe 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of these prevalence estimates were then found to give the 95% and 99.8% confidence intervals respectively.
Caveats: The values are calculated from the Active Lives Adult Survey a self report survey, which is subjective and is influenced by the respondent's ability to recall and assess their physical activity levels. Self reported data may also be affected by respondent desire to confirm to expectations and social norms (e.g. smoking under estimated and PA over estimated). However, although this might affect the absolute values, this should not affect comparisons if the bias is consistent across populations.

Indicator: Dementia: Crude Recorded Prevalence (aged under 65 years) per 10,000
Rationale: Young-onset dementia (also known as early or working age dementia) refers to dementia that is diagnosed before the age of 65 (the age at which people traditionally retired); however the age cut-off point has no medical or biological significance. People diagnosed with dementia under the age of 65 have different needs and commitments, they often follow a different clinical pathway, and may also need different forms of support, compared to people diagnosed with dementia over the age of 65 (1). This indicator is a companion metric and should be interpreted alongside the 'Dementia (aged under 65 years) as a Proportion of Total Dementia (all ages)' indicator. These metrics provide an indication of the concentration within a population of the number of people diagnosed and now living with the condition. The rationale for the provision of these indicators is to provide information that assists in the reduction of local variation in access to good quality care and support across England.1. Methodology: (Numerator/Denominator) x 10,000 Advantages of the crude prevalence method: Crude prevalence is simple and straight forward to calculate. It is readily understood by a wide audience. It is calculated when the total number of cases are divided by all persons of the relevant population, at one specific time-point. It is therefore useful at a localised level to determine service provision. In addition, the crude prevalence can be compared to the England value. Disadvantages of the crude prevalence method: The crude prevalence provides an overall average, but it doesn't take into account age differences. If two populations have unequal age distributions, it will distort the comparison of interest. ICB should not compare themselves to other ICB as the denominator for all areas differs (this includes local authorities). However, where the population structure is similar, then comparisons can be made between different areas.The Dementia Profile includes a 'Population distribution' chart for each geographical area and this may provide further useful information in relation to this indicator.

This indicator is a measure of recorded prevalence and not actual prevalence and therefore under-reports groups who are less likely to be registered with a GP, such as ethnic minority populations, homeless people, migrants and travellers. Caution should be taken when interpreting this indicator as a higher than average value may mean that the prevalence of the condition is high in an area, but it could also indicate that detection is better there; this is for local knowledge to determine.

Rationale: A summary figure of gonorrhoea cultures tested for azithromycin susceptibility. Primary diagnostic laboratories should test all specimens for antimicrobial susceptibility to first-line antimicrobials, which includes ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

The number of gonorrhoea diagnoses among people accessing care in England which were successfully cultured in primary diagnostic laboratories.

Indicator: Dementia: Quality rating of residential care and nursing home beds (aged 65 years and older)
Rationale:
The Prime Minister’s ‘Challenge on Dementia 2020’ highlights that people with dementia should have access to safe and high quality long term care services. In England, there are currently 498,221 people with a diagnosis of dementia (as of 31st December 2024), and it is estimated that 70% may eventually require long-term residential care. Therefore this indicator provides information regarding the quality of residential care home and nursing home beds, specifically those suitable for persons with dementia (aged 65 years and older).

Definition: This indicator illustrates the percentage of residential care home and nursing home beds, suitable for a person with dementia (aged 65 years and older), which are rated as ‘good’ or ‘outstanding’ by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), per ICB and local authority. It is highly recommended that this indicator is interpreted together with the companion metrics 'Dementia: Residential care and nursing home bed capacity (aged 65years and older)' and 'Dementia: Percentage of assessed residential care and nursing home beds (aged 65years and older)'.Therefore ICBs and local authorities must have both a high percentage of beds rated as 'good' or 'outstanding' and a high percentage of beds assessed in order to achieve a high value for this indicator. There are a number of beds per ICB and local authority, which have not been rated as yet, however these are still included in the total bed count. A low score on this indicator may occur due to two reasons - the beds may have received a low rating from the CQC, or there may be a number of beds which remain unassessed due to a variety of reasons, which include the recent registration of new residential care homes and nursing homes.

Source of denominator: Care Quality Commission (CQC), Care directory

Indicator: Major lower-limb amputation procedures for people with diabetes
Rationale:
A major diabetic lower-limb amputation (above the ankle) is an adverse outcome of diabetes. People with diabetes are at risk of lower-limb amputations due to reduced sensation after vascular and nerve damage. This can lead to infection after an injury (such as a skin ulcer) that -if not seen to - can lead to severe complications that may require the surgical removal of a toe, foot or part of the leg. However, severe cases requiring amputation are preventable if detected early and the correct intervetions are put in place.
The rate at which major amputations occur in a diabetic population can be used as an overall proxy measure of the effectiveness of healthcare and the diabetic foot care systems. Survival rates and quality of life for patients following a major diabetic lower-limb amputation can often be poor.
Specific rationale:
Clinical advice was sought on which demographic factors would be relevant to control for in the standardisation analysis. It was suggested that, in particular, efforts should be made to standardise for ethnicity and age. The reasons for standardising for ethnicity were twofold:
1.<span style="white-space: pre;"> Data from the 2015/16 NDA suggests there is considerable variation in the distribution of ethnicity between the registered population with diabetes at a commissioning level.
2.<span style="white-space: pre;"> The risk of adverse end outcomes of diabetes (including amputation) differ by ethnicity. There are UK data reporting that the relative risk of amputation was three times lower in black men (but not women) in London - risk reduction was reduced to two times lower after adjustment for smoking (1). The risk of amputation in South Asians was found to be four times lower than in Europeans in Manchester and South Lancs (2). A paper from New Zealand confirms the low incidence of amputation in East and South Asians when compared to Europeans (3). A paper from 2005 found “South Asians with diabetes in the U.K. have about one-third the risk of foot ulcers of Europeans (4). The lower levels of PAD, neuropathy, insulin usage, and foot deformities of the Asians account for approximately half of this reduced foot ulcer risk. Lower neuropathy is the main contributor to the reduced African-Caribbean ulcer rate, particularly in men”. Findings from the National Diabetes Foot Care Audit Report 2014-2016 suggest that after 12 weeks patients with Black or Asian ethnicity are more likely to be alive and ulcer-free than those with White ethnicity (5).
Therefore, controlling for the age and ethnicity of the patients with diabetes allows for more robust comparisons of the rate of amputations being carried out between areas.

(1) Leggetter S et al Arch Int Med 2002; 162: 73-8.
(2) Chaturvedi N Diabetic Med 2002; 19: 99-104.
(3) Robinson TE et al Diabet Med 2016; 33: 55-61.
(4) Abbott, et al Diabetes Care 2005. 28:1869–1875.
(5) The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership. 2017. National Diabetes Audit - National Diabetes Foot Care Audit Report 2014-2016.
Definition: Directly age and ethnicity standardised rate of major diabetic lower-limb amputation procedures per 10,000 population-years, over a three year period for those aged 17 and over.
Data source: NHS England, multiple sources
Indicator source: National Cardiovascular Intelligence Network (NCVIN)
Definition of numerator: Count of major amputation procedures for patients diagnosed with diabetes aged 17 and over within the three year period.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)
Definition of denominator: QOF registered population with diabetes aged 17 and over stratified by ethnicity and age, as inferred by applying proportions from the National Diabetes Audit registration data. This is a sum of 3 years of registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA) and Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Methodology:
Episodes of care within the specified three year period, which meet the criteria for major diabetic lower-limb amputation, are identified.
The full technical definition of a diabetic lower limb procedure is follows:
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> At least one diagnosis code (in any position) of: E10, E11, E12, E13 or E14.
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> A procedure code (in any position) of 'X09' - Amputation of leg

A sum of major amputation procedures is calculated. Procedures are assigned to the commisioning organisation of responsibility of that patient at the time.
Patients under 17 were removed. Patients with no STARTAGE assigned there ADMIAGE, otherwise they were removed. Patients with no commisioning organisation of responsiblity assigned (coded ‘59999’) or assigned to non-Englaish health geography were removed. Excluded those that were regular attenders or if the patient clasification was unknown. Patients who were the responsibility of a commissioning hub were removed.
Where patients had been coded as belonging to a commisioning organisation that subsequently changed, they were assigned to the most recently available organsiation code based on the changes that have taken place.
Procedures were collapsed into spells of care in hospital. These were assigned to a financial year based on the FYEAR field of the admission episode of the spell. Note: in some cases, the actual amputation procedure may have taken place in a different financial year if the operation episode took place later in the spell. The sum of major amputation procedures is stratified by age (<65, 65-79, 80+) and ethnicity (white/non-white) based on the patient’s HES records.
In each three-year period a small number of HES records did not have a valid ethnicity code assigned to the amputation spell. In these cases, patient’s past HES records (from inpatient and outpatient and emergency department records) were searched for episodes where a valid ethnicity code had been assigned. The most recent, valid ethnicity code was then assigned to the patient. Where we were still unable to identify a valid ethnicity code for a patient their ethnicity was imputed based on the known distribution of white/non-white diabetic patients in that area.
To calculate the at-risk population for the denominator, QOF registered population with diabetes were stratified by ethnicity and age, as inferred by applying proportions from the NDA registration data for the appropriate years. The denominator used in this indicator is a sum of 3 years of registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.
Category-specific rates of amputation are then calculated. These category specific rates are weighted against a standard population. The weighted category specific rates are summed to form a directly standardised rate and then mutlipled by 10,000.
Standard population/values:
An important consideration in the choice of a standard population is that the population should “not be considered abnormal or unnatural relative to the populations under study”. In our case this means the population should be representative of the population with diabetes in England. Therefore, data from the 2015/16 National Diabetes Audit was used to infer a standard population.
The NDA is an audit of the (mostly) primary care records of the registered population with diabetes. The audit collects information on the demographic characteristics of these patients. In 2015/16 81.4% of all GP practices in England took part in the audit – this equates to a collation of demographic information on 2,646,701 patients with diabetes from primary care records (information on 74,591 additional patients was also taken from secondary care records). For comparison, the entire registered population with diabetes in the Quality Outcomes Framework in 2015/16 was 3,033,529 patients. As such, the NDA offers a large, reliable, improving sample to make statistical inferences from regarding the characteristics of the English population with diabetes. The proportion of NDA registrations by age and ethnicity were calculated from the NDA. A hypothetical total population of 3,000,000 was used as a basis for creating our standard population.
Disclosure control: To avoid disclosive counts that could risk patient identification at any geography and through differencing, numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Rates have not been calculated for numerators of 7 or below.
Rounding: Numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Counts of 7 or less have been suppressed. Values were not calculated from these rounded values.
Caveats:
Rates are calculated for a pooled three years of data to allow for large enough counts of procedures to robustly standardise by age and ethnicity at a local level. When considering trends in amputation rates over time, this should be considered due to the impact a change in a single year of data can have over multiple data points. For example, during Spring 2020, there was a substantial drop in hospital activity due to the COVID-19 pandemic which impacted the number of amputation procedures taking place. This drop will impact the subsequent three data points where data for 2020/21 is included in the three year period.
Patients under 17 were removed as this indicator is also used to produce rates per 10,000 patients with diabetes and the denominator for this purpose (QOF diabetes register) does not include patients under 17.
To inform the use of HES ethnicity data for this analysis a scoping literature review was conducted and the findings suggested a white/ non-white dichotomy would be robust for the purposed of this analysis. The completeness of HES ethnicity coding has improved over time – from around 70% in 2001 to 91% in 2011. There are limited studies on the accuracy of HES ethnicity coding, but those that have addressed the question have found that:
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> Patients coded as white in HES also self-identify (or are identified in other data sources elsewhere) as white (98% concordance).
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> For those coded as non-white in HES there is considerably more discrepancy with self-reported ethnicity (and self-reported or primary care data sources). However, in general when there is a discrepancy patients have their ethnicity assigned to another non-white group. Meaning if the categorisation of HES data used is white/non-white then this would not be an issue.

Indicator: Minor lower-limb amputation procedures for people with diabetes
Rationale:
A minor diabetic lower-limb amputation (ankle or below) is an adverse outcome of diabetes. People with diabetes are at risk of lower-limb amputations due to reduced sensation after vascular and nerve damage. This can lead to infection after an injury (such as a skin ulcer) that -if not seen to - can lead to severe complications that may require the surgical removal of a toe, foot or part of the leg. However, severe cases requiring amputation are preventable if detected early and the correct intervetions are put in place.
The rate at which amputations occur in a diabetic population can be used as an overall proxy measure of the effectiveness of healthcare and the diabetic foot care systems. Survival rates and quality of life for patients following a major diabetic lower-limb amputation can often be poor. Unlike a major amputation, a minor amputation can be considered a preventative treatment. For example, the removal of dead tissue with the expectation that healing will follow.
Specific rationale:
Clinical advice was sought on which demographic factors would be relevant to control for in the standardisation analysis. It was suggested that, in particular, efforts should be made to standardise for ethnicity and age. The reasons for standardising for ethnicity were twofold:
1.<span style="white-space: pre;"> Data from the 2015/16 NDA suggests there is considerable variation in the distribution of ethnicity between the registered population with diabetes at a commissioning level.
2.<span style="white-space: pre;"> The risk of adverse end outcomes of diabetes (including amputation) differ by ethnicity. There are UK data reporting that the relative risk of amputation was three times lower in black men (but not women) in London - risk reduction was reduced to two times lower after adjustment for smoking (1). The risk of amputation in South Asians was found to be four times lower than in Europeans in Manchester and South Lancs (2). A paper from New Zealand confirms the low incidence of amputation in East and South Asians when compared to Europeans (3). A paper from 2005 found “South Asians with diabetes in the U.K. have about one-third the risk of foot ulcers of Europeans (4). The lower levels of PAD, neuropathy, insulin usage, and foot deformities of the Asians account for approximately half of this reduced foot ulcer risk. Lower neuropathy is the main contributor to the reduced African-Caribbean ulcer rate, particularly in men”. Findings from the National Diabetes Foot Care Audit Report 2014-2016 suggest that after 12 weeks patients with Black or Asian ethnicity are more likely to be alive and ulcer-free than those with White ethnicity (5).
Therefore, controlling for the age and ethnicity of the patients with diabetes allows for more robust comparisons of the rate of amputations being carried out between areas.

(2) Chaturvedi N Diabetic Med 2002; 19: 99-104.
(3) Robinson TE et al Diabet Med 2016; 33: 55-61.
(4) Abbott, et al Diabetes Care 2005. 28:1869–1875.
(5) The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership. 2017. National Diabetes Audit - National Diabetes Foot Care Audit Report 2014-2016.
Definition: Directly age and ethnicity standardised rate of minor diabetic lower-limb amputation procedures per 10,000 population-years, over a three year period for those aged 17 and over.
Data source: NHS England, multiple sources
Indicator source: National Cardiovascular Intelligence Network (NCVIN)
Definition of numerator: Count of minor amputation procedures for patients diagnosed with diabetes aged 17 and over within the three year period.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)
Definition of denominator: QOF registered population with diabetes aged 17 and over stratified by ethnicity and age, as inferred by applying proportions from the National Diabetes Audit registration data. This is a sum of 3 years of registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA) and Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Methodology:
Episodes of care within the specified three year period, which meet the criteria for minor diabetic lower-limb amputation, are identified.
The full technical definition of a diabetic lower limb procedure is as follows:
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> At least one diagnosis code (in any position) of: E10, E11, E12, E13 or E14.
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> A procedure code (in any position) of 'X10' - Amputation of leg OR 'X11' - Amputation of toe

A sum of major amputation procedures is calculated. Procedures are assigned to the commissioning organisation of responsibility of that patient at the time.
Patients under 17 were removed. Patients with no STARTAGE assigned there ADMIAGE, otherwise they were removed. Patients with no commissioning organisation of responsibility assigned (coded ‘59999’) or assigned to non-English health geography were removed. Excluded those that were regular attenders or if the patient classification was unknown. Patients who were the responsibility of a commissioning hub were removed.
Where patients had been coded as belonging to a commissioning organisation that subsequently changed, they were assigned to the most recently available organisation code based on the changes that have taken place.
Procedures were collapsed into spells of care in hospital. These were assigned to a financial year based on the FYEAR field of the admission episode of the spell. Note: in some cases, the actual amputation procedure may have taken place in a different financial year if the operation episode took place later in the spell. The sum of minor amputation procedures is stratified by age (<65, 65-79, 80+) and ethnicity (white/non-white) based on the patient’s HES records.
In each three-year period a small number of HES records did not have a valid ethnicity code assigned to the amputation spell. In these cases, patient’s past HES records (from inpatient and outpatient and emergency department records) were searched for episodes where a valid ethnicity code had been assigned. The most recent, valid ethnicity code was then assigned to the patient. Where we were still unable to identify a valid ethnicity code for a patient their ethnicity was imputed based on the known distribution of white/non-white diabetic patients in that area.
To calculate the at-risk population for the denominator, QOF registered population with diabetes were stratified by ethnicity and age, as inferred by applying proportions from the NDA registration data for the appropriate years. The denominator used in this indicator is a sum of 3 years of registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.

Category-specific rates of amputation are then calculated. These category specific rates are weighted against a standard population. The weighted category specific rates are summed to form a directly standardised rate and then mutlipled by 10,000.
Standard population/values:
An important consideration in the choice of a standard population is that the population should “not be considered abnormal or unnatural relative to the populations under study”. In our case this means the population should be representative of the population with diabetes in England. Therefore, data from the 2015/16 National Diabetes Audit was used to infer a standard population.
The NDA is an audit of the (mostly) primary care records of the registered population with diabetes. The audit collects information on the demographic characteristics of these patients. In 2015/16 81.4% of all GP practices in England took part in the audit – this equates to a collation of demographic information on 2,646,701 patients with diabetes from primary care records (information on 74,591 additional patients was also taken from secondary care records). For comparison, the entire registered population with diabetes in the Quality Outcomes Framework in 2015/16 was 3,033,529 patients. As such, the NDA offers a large, reliable, improving sample to make statistical inferences from regarding the characteristics of the English population with diabetes. The proportion of NDA registrations by age and ethnicity were calculated from the NDA. A hypothetical total population of 3,000,000 was used as a basis for creating our standard population.
Disclosure control: To avoid disclosive counts that could risk patient identification at any geography and through differencing, numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Rates have not been calculated for numerators of 7 or below.
Rounding: Numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Counts of 7 or less have been suppressed. Values were not calculated from these rounded values.
Caveats:
Rates are calculated for a pooled three years of data to allow for large enough counts of procedures to robustly standardise by age and ethnicity at a local level. When considering trends in amputation rates over time, this should be considered due to the impact a change in a single year of data can have over multiple data points. For example, during Spring 2020, there was a substantial drop in hospital activity due to the COVID-19 pandemic which impacted the number of amputation procedures taking place. This drop will impact the subsequent three data points where data for 2020/21 is included in the three year period.
Patients under 17 were removed as this indicator is also used to produce rates per 10,000 patients with diabetes and the denominator for this purpose (QOF diabetes register) does not include patients under 17.
To inform the use of HES ethnicity data for this analysis a scoping literature review was conducted and the findings suggested a white/ non-white dichotomy would be robust for the purposed of this analysis. The completeness of HES ethnicity coding has improved over time – from around 70% in 2001 to 91% in 2011. There are limited studies on the accuracy of HES ethnicity coding, but those that have addressed the question have found that:
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> Patients coded as white in HES also self-identify (or are identified in other data sources elsewhere) as white (98% concordance).
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> For those coded as non-white in HES there is considerably more discrepancy with self-reported ethnicity (and self-reported or primary care data sources). However, in general when there is a discrepancy patients have their ethnicity assigned to another non-white group. Meaning if the categorisation of HES data used is white/non-white then this would not be an issue. 
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> Estimating practice ethnicity using hospital attendance data is in closer agreement with practice recording of self-reported ethnicity than using census methods.
o<span style="white-space: pre;"> Of those with multiple HES inpatient records 94% have consistently identical ethnicities assigned to them over time.  
Furthermore, an analysis of ethnicity in HES data for major amputations in people with diabetes found no evidence of biases at CCG level that would be expected to be present if significant miscoding of ethnicity was present in those data.

Indicator: Hospital spells for foot disease for people with diabetes
Rationale:
The prevalence of diabetes is increasing, with nearly 3.5 million people registered as having the disease with general practices in England. Lower-limb complications, such as ulceration or amputation, are common among the population with diabetes and have a substantial human cost due to the impact they can have on how an individual can live their life. Health care expenditure related to foot disease in people with diabetes is a substantial cost to the NHS. The impacts to individual’s income and welfare and the wider impact on the economy may also be significant.
Many foot-related complications are preventable if identified and treated early. The guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) suggests this can be achieved in several ways:
- Improving and speeding up the care pathways, including minimising the delay for the first expert assessment within a dedicated foot protection service
- Annual foot checks are made available and encouraged for adults
- Educating patients and their family members or carers on foot problems and care pathways

Higher rates of hospital spells for foot disease can be evidence of an existing issue with one or more of these or a population at greater risk of complications. This is a holistic measure of the secondary care service use that covers the wide range of lower-limb complications that people with diabetes experience.
Definition: Crude rate of hospital spells, where the spell has been identified as containing episodes of care classified as ‘predominantly inpatient management of diabetes related foot disease’, per 10,000 population with diabetes.
Data source: NHS England, multiple sources
Indicator source: National Cardiovascular Intelligence Network (NCVIN)
Definition of numerator:
Count of spells identified as containing episodes of care classified as ‘predominantly inpatient management of diabetes related foot disease’ among patients aged 17 and over within the three year period. One spell of care was taken as a proxy for a single admission for foot disease. Only spells with a diagnosis code for diabetes were included. Spells included were those that have one or more of the following procedures/conditions:

Debridement of a foot/leg wound
Amputation
Peripheral circulatory complications
Ulcer of the lower limb
Decubitus ulcer
Cellulitis
Osteomyelitis
Gangrene
Atherosclerosis
Bacteraemia/septicaemia/septic shock/sepsis syndrome
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)
Definition of denominator: QOF registered population with diabetes aged 17 and over. This is a sum of 3 years of registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Methodology:
Finished consultant episodes of care within the specified three year period, which meet the criteria for diabetic foot disease, are identified and combined into spells of care. Patients under 17 were removed. Patients with no STARTAGE assigned there ADMIAGE, otherwise they were removed. Patients with no commissioning organisation of responsibility assigned (coded ‘59999’) or assigned to non-English health geography were removed. Excluded those that were regular attenders or if the patient classification was unknown. Patients who were the responsibility of a commissioning hub were removed.
Where patients had been coded as belonging to a commissioning organisation that subsequently changed, they were assigned to the most recently available organisation code based on the changes that have taken place.
Spells were assigned to a financial year based on the FYEAR field of the admission episode of the spell.
The denominator used in this indicator is a sum of 3 years of QOF registered population with diabetes. It is likely that the majority of patients summed together over three years will be the same individuals (excepting new diagnoses and deaths). Therefore, a more accurate interpretation of the denominator would be seeing it as a proxy measure for person-years at risk.
These spells are counted for the three year period and divided by the QOF registered population with diabetes, multiplied by 10,000.
The rates have not been standardised due to the heterogeneous nature of the conditions included under the definition of foot disease, meaning the demographic profiles across different conditions are not necessarily uniform.

Rounding: Numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Counts of 7 or less have been suppressed. Values were calculated from these rounded values.
Caveats:
Rates are calculated for a pooled three years of data to allow for large enough counts of spells to allow for a more consistent trend. When considering trends in hospital spell rates over time, this should be considered due to the impact a change in a single year of data can have over multiple data points. For example, during Spring 2020, there was a substantial drop in hospital activity due to the COVID-19 pandemic which impacted the number of admissions. This drop will impact the subsequent three data points where data for 2020/21 is included in the three year period.

Indicator: Access to Healthy Assets & Hazards Index
Rationale: The Access to Healthy Assets and Hazards (AHAH) index is designed to allow policy/decision makers to understand which areas have poor environments for health, and to help move away from treating features of the environment in isolation. The index captures multidimensional features of the built environment including accessibility to retail services (e.g., fast food outlets, pubs, gambling stores), health services, green and blue spaces, and overall air quality. These features are potentially harmful to health and the overall index captures unhealthy environments.The AHAH index is comprised of four domains: access to retail services (fast food outlets, gambling outlets, pubs/bars/nightclubs, off licences, tobacconists), access to health services (GP surgeries, A&E hospitals, pharmacies, dentists and leisure centres), green and blue spaces (access to green spaces, blue spaces, and total greenness) and air quality (pollution levels for NO2 level, PM10 level, SO2 level). The AHAH index provides a summary of an area's relative performance on these indicators (the second and third domains conceptualised as health promoting and the first (access to retail) as health demoting). It therefore provides information on how conducive to good health an area is relative to other areas, for the specific indicators.The indicator is intended to support interventions to improve the health promoting qualities of the environment, and is primarily aimed at those working in public health roles in local authorities.The AHAH index is originally produced at LSOA level as an average of values for constituent postcodes, but is required at local authority and higher geographical levels in this profile. Using the percentage of the population living in LSOAs in the worst quintile as the indicator focusses on the people exposed to the most health demoting environments. An alternative measure, to average the AHAH index value of constituent LSOAs for each higher geographical unit, becomes increasingly less useful as the size of the unit increases: an LSOA average can be thought to apply more or less to those living in that LSOA (for the majority of LSOAs), whereas an average across a local authority has a more difficult interpretation.Some of indicators in the AHAH index overlap partially with individual indicators already in the natural and built environment domain (Number of premises licensed to sell alcohol per square km, Density of fast food outlets, and Air pollution: particulate matter). In contrast to the individual indicators that provide detail on specific measures which are considered important to bring attention to, the AHAH index provides an easily accessible summary of these features of the built environment.
Definition: Percentage of the population who live in LSOAs which score in the poorest performing 20% on the Access to Healthy Assets & Hazards (AHAH) index
Data source: Geographic Data Service (GeoDS), Access to Healthy Assets and Hazards (AHAH)
Indicator source:
The overall index collates data from a variety of datasets provided by the Office of National Statistics (ONS), NHS England, NHS Scotland, NHS Wales, OpenStreetMap, Sentinel Satellite, Scottish Government, Local Data Company (LDC), Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) Data are supplied by the Geographic Data Service for Great Britain and University of Liverpool, UK.
For further information see  https://data.geods.ac.uk/dataset/access-to-healthy-assets-hazards-ahah
Definition of numerator: Total population residing in Lower Super Output Areas defined as in the bottom 20% of all areas on the Access to Healthy Assets & Hazards Index.For further details see the  https://data.geods.ac.uk/dataset/access-to-healthy-assets-hazards-ahah/resource/bf90a67b-d12a-488f-bc87-eb4523c7ac7c
Source of numerator: Geographic Data Service (GeoDS), Access to Healthy Assets and Hazards (AHAH) Geographic Data Service (GeoDS), Access to Healthy Assets and Hazards (AHAH)
Definition of denominator: Total population of area (Office for National Statistics mid year population estimates)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The Fingertips indicator is calculated by dividing the total population within a Local Authority who reside in the bottom 20% worst areas as defined by the Access to Healthy Assets & Hazards Index, as a proportion of the total resident population. The index is created by weighting together a range of indicators. All accessibility inputs are generated using road network distances. Where access is not used, estimate average values are used. Indicators are created for Lower Super Output Areas and then an overall index score is calculated by following the method for the Index of Multiple Deprivation. More detail can be found here  https://data.geods.ac.uk/dataset/access-to-healthy-assets-hazards-ahah  Numerator:For each area under each area type, the numerator was calculated as the sum of the population for LSOAs in the worst quintile.Denominator:For each area under each area type, the denominator was calculated as the sum of the population for all LSOAs.Indicator:For each area under each area type the indicator (percentage of the population who live in LSOAs which score in the poorest performing 20%) was calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and multiplying by 100.
Confidence interval details: No confidence intervals are produced for this indicator.
Caveats: Data qualityThe data quality of the AHAH index is limited to the quality of its component parts. The data is complete and variation in recording is not considered to be an issue. However, the nature of the component datasets is such that the accuracy is unknown.Air pollution data from Defra is subject to annual variation that can arise from multiple sources. One source is the ongoing improvements in methodology used in their production. As such, change in the AHAH index rank position may arise from methodological change rather than change in air pollution experienced in a given area.Access to health services (excluding leisure centres) is based on data from NHS Digital and Information Services Division (ISD). The retail services domain measures, plus the leisure centre measure in the health services domain, is based on postcode data from the Local Data Company. Though these are considered robust data sources for the measures, the accuracy of these data sets is unknown. Users should be aware there will inevitably be changes to the location and prevalence of some health and retail services after the point of being recorded. The ONS mid-year estimates at LSOA level are considered suitable for use as they are consistent with higher level population estimates.InterpretationThese caveats relate to interpretation issues for use of this indicator, not each underlying dataset used to construct the AHAH index. In general, the AHAH index on which the indicator is based should be interpreted as a relative summary of the health promoting/demoting characteristics of LSOAs based on access to health services, retail services and the physical environment. Users should remain mindful of the indicators used to produce it (access to retail services domain: fast food outlets, gambling outlets, pubs/bars/nightclubs, off licences, tobacconists; access to health services domain: GP surgeries, A&E hospitals, pharmacies, dentists and leisure centres; and physical environment domain: access to green spaces, NO2 level, PM10 level, SO2 level). For more specific uses of the index, it is recommended that users familiarise themselves with the methodological detail used to develop it, available here:  https://data.geods.ac.uk/dataset/access-to-healthy-assets-hazards-ahah  The indicator focuses on the concentration of the most health demoting LSOAs in an area (those in the worst 20%). It does not provide information on how the LSOAs not in the worst 20% are distributed across the range for a given area. For full information users should access the original AHAH index (source above).The AHAH index is constructed with each of the three domains having equal weight and each measure having an equal weight within each domain. It is therefore designed as a balanced description of an area with regard to these domains, and not as a summary of the health impacts on the population.Data on green space is from Ordnance Survey Open GreenSpace Layer and is limited to publically accessible green space in the following categories: cemetery, common, dog park, scrub, fell, forest, garden, greenfield, golf course, grass, grassland, heath, meadow, nature reserve, orchard, park, pitch, recreation ground, village green, vineyard and wood. Green spaces not in these categories may not be recognised in the measure.

Indicator: Proportion of the population meeting the recommended '5 a day' on a 'usual day' (adults) (old method)
Rationale: Note that this indicator has now been superceded by a new indicator: C15 - Percentage of adults aged 16 and over meeting the '5-a-day' fruit and vegetable consumption recommendations (new method)Questions on self reported fruit and vegetable consumption are included in Active Lives to provide data for monitoring '5 a day' consumption in adults at local authority level for the Public Health Outcomes Framework (PHOF). In England, two thirds of adults are overweight or obese. Poor diet and obesity are leading causes of premature death and mortality (Global Burden of Disease, 2017), and are associated with a wide range of diseases including cardiovascular disease and some cancers, which can have a significant impact on an individual’s physical and mental health and wellbeing.The costs of diet related chronic diseases to the NHS and more broadly to society are considerable. Average intakes of saturated fat, sugar, and salt are above recommendations while intakes of fruit and vegetables, oily fish, fibre and some vitamins and minerals in some groups are below recommendations. Average intake of trans fatty acids are within recommendations.
Definition: Proportion of the population who, when surveyed, reported that they had eaten the recommended 5 portions of fruit and vegetables on a usual day.
Data source: OHID, based on Sport England data
Indicator source: https://www.sportengland.org/research/active-lives-survey/
Definition of numerator: Weighted number of respondents aged 16 and over, with valid responses to questions on fruit and vegetable consumption, eating at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables in the previous day.Responses to the fruit and vegetables questions were summed together to provide a total number of fruit and vegetable portions eaten in the previous day.Respondents were asked:How many portions of fruit did you eat yesterday? Please include all fruit, including fresh, frozen, dried or tinned fruit, stewed fruit or fruit juices and smoothies. Indicator: Smoking status at time of delivery (old method)
Rationale:
Smoking in pregnancy has well known detrimental effects for the growth and development of the baby and health of the mother. On average, smokers have more complications during pregnancy and labour, including bleeding during pregnancy, placental abruption and premature rupture of membranes.
Encouraging pregnant women to stop smoking during pregnancy may also help them kick the habit for good, and thus provide health benefits for the mother and reduce exposure to secondhand smoke by the infant.
Smoking during pregnancy can cause serious pregnancy-related health problems. These include complications during labour and an increased risk of miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, low birth-weight and sudden unexpected death in infancy.
The  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/towards-a-smoke-free-generation-tobacco-control-plan-for-england contains a national ambition to reduce the rate of smoking throughout pregnancy to 6% or less by the end of 2022 (measured at time of giving birth). The inclusion of this indicator will ensure that the local tobacco control activity is appropriately focused on pregnant women, in order to try to achieve this national ambition.
Inclusion of this indicator will also encourage the continued prioritisation of action to reduce smoking at delivery. Decreases in smoking during pregnancy will result in health benefits for the infant and mother, as well as cost savings to the NHS.
Definition: The number of mothers known to be smokers at the time of delivery as a percentage of all maternities with known smoking status. A maternity is defined as a pregnant woman who gives birth to one or more live or stillborn babies of at least 24 weeks gestation, where the baby is delivered by either a midwife or doctor at home or in a NHS hospital
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: NHS England  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-women-s-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england <a href="https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-women-s-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england/statistics-on-womens-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england-quarter-4-january-2019-to-march-2019">

Former SubICB mergers in 2019 mean that more LAs from then on appear with the same prevalence estimate. Where local authorities cross sub-ICB location boundaries, the local authority estimate is a weighted average of the sub-ICB location indicator values. Where a local authority is within a single sub-ICB location's boundary, the local authority value presented is the value from the sub-ICB location.
There has been a change of method for reporting this information from April 2017, removing those whose smoking status is unknown from the calculation. Excluding women with unknown smoking status from the calculation will provide a more accurate representation of the true proportion of women smoking at time of delivery. In the previous definition, women with unknown smoking status were effectively categorised as non-smokers. However, a number of these would be smokers and this therefore served to deflate the indicator value. The overall impact of this change at England level is small, although the impact will be greater for those sub-ICB locations who have a high proportion of unknowns. Work is already underway to encourage and support Trusts/sub-ICB locationsto collect and record accurate information. IT issues are reported as the main reason for high levels of unknowns, which should be resolved as systems embed and improve.

Indicator: Back pain prevalence in people of all ages
Rationale:
This indicator is designed to measure back pain prevalence in England.
The Global Burden of Disease 2010 Study, ranked back pain as the biggest single cause of years lived with disability (YLD)in the world and the 6th biggest disability adjusted life years (DALY).Years lived with disability (YLD) is a measure that summarises levels of poor health and disability in a given population. It combines the prevalence of each disease with a rating of how disabling the disease state is.
Back pain prevalence increased 17% between 1990 and 2015 and with an ageing population in the UK, there is an urgent need for further research to better understand back pain.
Lower back pain is very common in working-age adults, particularly between 40 and 60 years. A loss of production due to back pain costs the UK economy an estimated £3500 million/year as well as resulting in impaired quality of life, reduced mobility, long-term morbidity, higher risk of social exclusion and reduced income.<span style="font-family: Times New Roman; font-size: medium;" size="3" face="Times New Roman"><span style="font-family: Calibri;" face="Calibri"><span style="font-size: small;" size="2">1
This indicator should be particularly useful for those planning and managing musculoskeletal services for the benefit of patients, for example local authorities, and community and specialist services.
1.  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg88/documents/low-back-pain-final-scope2
Definition: Estimated prevalence of back pain using a regression model based on data from the Health Survey for England (HSE).
Data source: Versus Arthritis and University College London UCL data
Indicator source: Musculoskeletal (MSK) Calculator produced by Imperial College London, commissioned by Versus Arthritis.
Definition of numerator:
A survey respondent was classified as having back pain if they answered YES to the following questions in the HSE:Any Pain: "Whether currently troubled by pain or discomfort?"More3m: "Pain or discomfort for more than 3 months?"Site Pain= "Where is this pain or discomfort?"
If Any Pain="YES" AND More3m="YES" and Site Pain= "Back pain" then Back pain="YES"
The values calculated in this tool are estimates based on regressionstatistical models.
After analysis, survey information contained in HSE was combined with known local data about the different risk factors to produce the model.
The following variables were used:· age , gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, body mass index (BMI), physical activity, smoking status, depression and sedentary lifestyle
The steps in applying the prevalence estimates are as follows:
· Use the regression coefficients to generate log odds (since they are from a logistic regression model) for each risk factor subcategory· Generate a similar table of odds by exponentiation· Generate a similar table of prevalence in each risk factor subcategory using the epidemiologic formula· Produce a matching table of small population subcategories. If there are no corresponding local data with a sufficiently granular breakdown e.g. ethnicity by age by sex, this requires deciding how each risk factor should be attributed across other risk factor categories. For example, we used the national age/sex/ethnicity breakdown from the Census and age/smoking breakdowns from the HSE to attribute this data at small population levels. The actual breakdown will be somewhat different and needs to be borne in mind as another source of potential error.· Multiply the population cells by the corresponding prevalence to estimate the number of people in each cell with the diseaseThe numerators for wards have been estimated from the MSOA level prevalence values. Each MSOA is made up of a number of constituent Output Areas (OAs), and each of these has been assumed to have the same prevalence as the parent MSOA. For each OA, an estimated numerator has been estimated by distributing the numerator of the MSOA according to the OA populations. The OA numerators were then aggregated to wards.
Source of numerator: Versus Arthritis and University College London (UCL), based on Health Survey for England (HSE)
Definition of denominator: For LAs and MSOAs the denominators are the ONS mid-year population estimates for all ages, based on aggregating single year of age estimates at LSOA level. For wards the denominator populations are estimated from the MSOA data. Each MSOA is made up of a number of constituent Output Areas (OAs). For each OA, a denominator has been estimated by distributing the denominator of the MSOA according to the OA populations. The OA denominators were then aggregated to wards.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Prevalence (%)=[Numerator/denominator]*100
Confidence interval details: For local authorities the confidence intervals were calculated by bootstrapping. The detailed methodology is not available.CIs were calculated for MSOA and ward level prevalence values based on those for the LAs. For each MSOA and ward the width of the confidence interval for the parent LA (e.g. +/–10%) was multiplied by √(1/p) (where p is the proportion of the LA population that is in that MSOA/ward) to get an estimate of the width of the confidence interval for the MSOA/ward.
Caveats: The indicator likely underestimates back pain, particularly in younger age groups, due to the participants having to have had back pain for more the 3months. Acute bouts of back pain can be resolved during a 3 month period, particularly in younger respondents where healing times tend to be quicker.
Notes: These are modelled prevalence estimates and are not a GP extract of the exactnumber of people in England with back pain, rather the estimates are based on self-reported back pain diagnosis.

Indicator: Overweight (including obesity) prevalence in adults, (using adjusted self-reported height and weight)
Rationale:
Obesity is a global and complex public health concern. It is associated with https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/obesity/ for a range of chronic diseases, including https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2458-9-88 ,at least 12 kinds of cancer,liver, andrespiratorydisease,and can also impact onmental health. The risk and severity of these diseases increases with a higher body mass index (BMI).

The proportion of adults in England living with obesity has seen large increases in the last four decades. Analysis of data from the https://beta.ukdataservice.ac.uk/datacatalogue/studies/study?id=2046 estimates that the prevalence of obesity in England stood at 6% of men and 9% of women aged 16 and over with 0.1% of men and 0.4% of women living with severe obesity. In 1993 the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/health-survey-for-england reported that the prevalence of obesity among men and women in this age group was 13% and 16% respectively which has increased to 29% of men and 31% of women in 2024.Under the Health Mission, the Government is committed to prevention and to tackling obesity, creating a fairer, healthier food environment. This will contribute to the Mission goals of fewer lives lost to the biggest killers and a fairer Britain where everyone lives well for longer.

Understanding the data, the trends and patterns enables us to make the case for national and local action, which includes policy and approaches to create health promoting environments, healthier food and activity options, social marketing campaigns to support behaviour change and to work with partners to design and tailor approaches to meet needs of particular groups of people.

This overweight (including obesity) indicator presents local authority estimates from Sport England's Active Lives Adult Survey data to help inform local action in preventing obesity and supporting people who are overweight or living with obesity. This indicator is linked to the https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/national-child-measurement-programme/data#page/3/gid/1938133368/pat/15/par/E92000001/ati/6/are/E12000004/iid/93881/age/168/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1 indicator. These indicators should be used in conjunction to provide a greater understanding of those who are overweight or living with obesity. It is important to track the population's movement between BMI groups andto understand whether a high prevalence of overweight (including obesity) is driven by greater numbers of people living with obesity or severe obesity, or greater numbers in the overweight category.
Definition: Percentage of adults aged 18 and over classified as overweight or obese (BMI greater than or equal to 25kg/m²)
Data source: OHID, based on Sport England data
Indicator source:
https://www.sportengland.org/research/active-lives-survey/

Justification of data source

The Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS) has been chosen as the data source for this indicator as it provides routine, robust data for Body Mass Index (BMI) calculations at local authority level which will support local monitoring of obesity estimates for the appropriate ages.

The survey provides self reported height and weight, which can be used to produce BMI estimates. The data collected also allows for adjustments to be applied to the self reported height and weight measurements at an individual level to give likely actual height and weight.

The Health Survey for England (HSE) is used by central government to monitor trends in the prevalence of overweight and obesity among adults and children in England. HSE data are available at regional level but do not allow for local authority estimates to be produced. To support local monitoring of overweight and obesity prevalence, OHID have produced overweight (including obese) and obesity indicators for each local authority in England based on ALAS data.

HSE reports overweight and obesity estimates based on nurse measured height and weight, rather than self reported height and weight. HSE also classify adults as those aged 16 and over, whereas adult BMI classifications are designed for those aged 18 and over, which is the age range for this indicator based on ALAS data.

Although there are methodological differences between ALAS and HSE, both sets of estimates display similar trends across age groups and levels of deprivation.

Definition of numerator:
Number of adults aged 18 and over with a BMI classified as overwight (including obesity), calculated from the adjusted height and weight variables. Adults are defined as obese if their body mass index (BMI) is greater than or equal to 25kg/m².

Those not recorded as male or female are excluded from the analysis. This is because the adjustment calculations are developed for males and females separately.

Respondents with a recorded height less than 1m or >=greater than or equal to 2.3m are excluded, as they are outside of the accepted range.

Respondents with no recorded height or weight are excluded.

Those aged under 18 years are excluded, as the BMI classifications have been developed for those aged 18 and over and are not the correct classification for those aged under 18 years.

Respondents that are recorded as pregnant are excluded as pregnancy will affect a woman’s BMI result. The NHS BMI calculator advises that pregnant women should use their pre pregnancy weight when calculating their BMI.

Methodology: The age standardised proportions presented are directly age standardised rates per 100 people, represented as a percentage. This is the weighted number of respondents aged 18 and over with a body mass index (BMI) classified as overweight (including obese), calculated from the adjusted height and weight variables divided by the weighted number of respondents aged 18 and over with a BMI classification, standardised to the European Standard Population, multiplied by 100. Questions on self reported height and weight are included in Active Lives Adult Survey to provide data for monitoring excess weight in adults at local authority level for the Public Health Outcomes Framework (PHOF).
Confidence interval details:
An approximate 95 percent and 99.8 percent confidence interval was derived from 10,000 simulations of excess weight prevalence for each age group within each area. Each prevalence simulation was calculated by

1 drawing a number of ‘successes’ randomly from a binomial distribution ~Bin(n,p) when n is the unweighted total population estimate and p is the weighted prevalence of excess weight.

2 dividing the number of ‘successes’ by the unweighted total respondents

The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of these prevalence estimates were then found to give the 95 percent and 99.8 percent confidence intervals respectively.

Caveats:
As outlined in theMethodology section, this indicator uses prediction equations to adjust the self reported height and weight of respondents. Prediction equations are specific to time, place, target population and methods of data collection. As such, these may not be applicable to surveys with more recent data, or different sociodemographic, health and self reported anthropometric profiles.

The NHS Digital https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/areas-of-interest/public-health/health-survey-for-england-predicting-height-weight-and-body-mass-index-from-self-reported-data found that the usefulness of prediction equations has been demonstrated by the ability to reduce considerably, although not eliminate, the differences between self-reported and measured anthropometrics across a few, easily gathered sociodemographic and health-related variables.

Indicator: Severe back pain prevalence in people of all ages
Rationale:
This indicator is designed to measure back pain prevalence in England.
The Global Burden of Disease 2010 Study, ranked back pain as the biggest single cause of years lived with disability (YLD)in the world and the 6th biggest disability adjusted life years (DALY).Years lived with disability (YLD) is a measure that summarises levels of poor health and disability in a given population. It combines the prevalence of each disease with a rating of how disabling the disease state is.Back pain prevalence increased 17% between 1990 and 2015 and with an ageing population in the UK, there is an urgent need for further research to better understand back pain.
Lower back pain is very common in working-age adults, particularly between 40 and 60 years. A loss of production due to back pain costs the UK economy an estimated £3500 million/year as well as resulting in impaired quality of life, reduced mobility, long-term morbidity, higher risk of social exclusion and reduced income.
This indicator should be particularly useful for those planning and managing musculoskeletal services for the benefit of patients, for example local authorities, and community and specialist services.
1.  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg88/documents/low-back-pain-final-scope2

Data source: Versus Arthritis and University College London UCL data
Indicator source: Musculoskeletal (MSK) Calculator produced by Imperial College London, commissioned by Versus Arthritis.
Definition of numerator:
A survey respondent was classified as having back pain if they answered YES to the following questions in the HSE:Any Pain: "Whether currently troubled by pain or discomfort?"More3m: "Pain or discomfort for more than 3 months?"Site Pain= "Where is this pain or discomfort?"
If Any Pain="YES" AND More3m="YES" and Site Pain= "Back pain" then Back pain="YES"
The values calculated in this tool are estimates based on regressionstatistical models.
After analysis, survey information contained in HSE was combined with known local data about the different risk factors to produce the model.
The following variables were used:· age , gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, body mass index (BMI), physical activity, smoking status, depression and sedentary lifestyle
The steps in applying the prevalence estimates are as follows:
· Use the regression coefficients to generate log odds (since they are from a logistic regression model) for each risk factor subcategory· Generate a similar table of odds by exponentiation· Generate a similar table of prevalence in each risk factor subcategory using the epidemiologic formula· Produce a matching table of small population subcategories. If there are no corresponding local data with a sufficiently granular breakdown e.g. ethnicity by age by sex, this requires deciding how each risk factor should be attributed across other risk factor categories. For example, we used the national age/sex/ethnicity breakdown from the Census and age/smoking breakdowns from the HSE to attribute this data at small population levels. The actual breakdown will be somewhat different and needs to be borne in mind as another source of potential error.· Multiply the population cells by the corresponding prevalence to estimate the number of people in each cell with the diseaseThe numerators for wards have been estimated from the MSOA level prevalence values. Each MSOA is made up of a number of constituent Output Areas (OAs), and each of these has been assumed to have the same prevalence as the parent MSOA. For each OA, an estimated numerator has been estimated by distributing the numerator of the MSOA according to the OA populations. The OA numerators were then aggregated to wards.
Source of numerator: Versus Arthritis and University College London (UCL), based on Health Survey for England (HSE)
Definition of denominator: For LAs and MSOAs the denominators are the ONS mid-year population estimates for all ages, based on aggregating single year of age estimates at LSOA level. For wards the denominator populations are estimated from the MSOA data. Each MSOA is made up of a number of constituent Output Areas (OAs). For each OA, a denominator has been estimated by distributing the denominator of the MSOA according to the OA populations. The OA denominators were then aggregated to wards.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Prevalence (%)=[Numerator/denominator]*100
Confidence interval details: For local authorities the confidence intervals were calculated by bootstrapping. The detailed methodology is not available.CIs were calculated for MSOA and ward level prevalence values based on those for the LAs. For each MSOA and ward the width of the confidence interval for the parent LA (e.g. +/–10%) was multiplied by √(1/p) (where p is the proportion of the LA population that is in that MSOA/ward) to get an estimate of the width of the confidence interval for the MSOA/ward.

Acute bouts of back pain can be resolved during a 3 month period, particularly in younger respondents where healing times tend to be quicker.

Indicator: Prevalence of severe hip osteoarthritis in people aged  45 and over
Rationale:
Severe osteoarthritis of the hip is a debilitating condition causing advanced pain while moving and at rest. It causes significant reduction in mobility and everyday tasks. It is the most common cause for hip replacement surgery and increases the risk of falls and hip fractures. Trends demonstrate that rates of severe hip osteoarthritis are increasing resulting in reduced quality of life as well as increasing the economic burden on health care services.There are currently no routinely collected data local data on the prevalence of this condition so the data provided here are small area modelled estimates. The estimates are based on a statistical model commissioned by Arthritis Research UK from Imperial College London using the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA)
The severe hip osteoarthritis indicator should be particularly useful for those planning and managing musculoskeletal services for the benefit of patients, it gives an indication of those requiring additional service use and surgical intervention. Local authorities, and community specialist services may use this indicator to inform work intended to optimise health benefit and patient experience, while minimising waste and remaining within budget.

By adding this additional information there is a small risk that personal data relating to living persons may be unlawfully disclosed.

In order to prevent this the following steps have been taken in line with the published ONS policy

Steps taken to protect personal information:
1. Small counts: primary suppression. All area where there were counts of zeros, 1 and 2 are supressed.
2. Pooled data over 5 years. To improve the robustness of small area data the process of pooling data over a longer timeframe is used. This has the added advantage that it protects personal data and makes identification of any individual unlikely.
