Indicator: Life expectancy at birth
Rationale: Life expectancy at birth is a useful summary measure of all cause mortality as it quantifies the differences between areas in units (years of life) that are more readily understood and meaningful to the audience than those of other measures. All cause mortality is a fundamental and probably the oldest measure of the health status of a population. It represents the cumulative effect of the prevalence of risk factors, the prevalence and severity of disease, and the effectiveness of interventions and treatment. Differences in levels of all cause mortality reflect health inequalities between different population groups, e.g. between genders, social classes, and ethnic groups.
Definition: Life expectancy is the average number of years a person would expect to live based on contemporary mortality rates. For a particular area and time period, it is an estimate of the average number of years a newborn baby would survive if he or she experienced the age specific mortality rates for that area and time period throughout his or her life. Figures reflect mortality among those living in an area in each time period, rather than mortality among those born in the area. The figures are not therefore the number of years a baby born in the area could actually expect to live, both because the mortality rates of the area are likely to change in the future and because many of those born in the area will live elsewhere for at least some part of their lives.
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts
Methodology:
Life expectancy calculations were based on abridged life table approach. Mortality data by sex and age group were extracted from annual files supplied to OHID by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Deaths were allocated to the deceased's lower super output area using the latest version of the National Statistics Postcode Lookup and aggregated to England, 'middle layer super output areas' (MSOAs), local authorities and counties.
Population data are mid-year population estimates for the geographical areas described.
Counts by single year of age were aggregated into the age groups required for the calculation of life expectancy (less than 1, 1 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, then in 5 year age bands through to 80 to 84, 90 and over).
What are output areas? The ONS produces mid-year small area population estimates by Output Areas (OA). Output areas are the lowest level of geographic area specifically designed for census data. These standardised geographic areas are designed to have equal numbers of households or populations within them making it easier to compare output areas.
They are used primarily in statistical administrative data outputs such as the census and population estimates. Output areas are "nested" within larger geographic areas that can be summed or aggregated to provide data at these larger areas.
Confidence interval details:
Confidence intervals were calculated using the method developed by Chiang, which was adjusted according to the method described by Silcocks to account for the variance in the upper age band. 

Chiang CL. The Life Table and its Construction. Introduction to Stochastic Processes in Biostatistics. New York, John Wiley and Sons, 1968, 189 to 214.
Silcocks PBS, Jenner DA, Reza R. Life expectancy as a summary of mortality in a population: statistical considerations and suitability for use by health authorities. J Epidemiology Community Health 2001; 55: 38 to 43

Using an upper age band of 90 and over is consistent with subnational life expectancy figures published by ONS, and included in the Public Health Outcomes Framework. This change was made because an increasing proportion of deaths are at ages 85 and over.In some areas, the majority of deaths at age 85 and over may be in the 85 to 89 years age band, while in other areas a large proportion of deaths may be after age 90. Splitting deaths at the oldest ages into two groups (85 to 89 years and 90 years and over) means that the latest life expectancy calculations now take account of such differences in the age structure of populations between areas. Rationale: The Department of Health’s Framework for Sexual Health Improvement in England’ (2013) (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-framework-for-sexual-health-improvement-in-england) includes the ambition toimprove sexual health outcomes for young adults. Indicator: STEC  (Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli) serogroup O157 5-year incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) serogroup O157. STEC is a zoonotic gastrointestinal infection for which animals (particularly ruminants such as cattle and sheep) are the main reservoir. Transmission occurs either due to direct contact with infected animal faeces, ingestion of food contaminated with infected animal or human faeces or via contact with the infected faeces of another person. STEC causes moderate to severe disease in humans. Most cases will present with mild (diarrhoea) to moderate (bloody diarrhoea) gastrointestinal symptoms but a proportion (~ 5%) will go on to develop more severe complications such as haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS). Some complications may require long-term care or result in permanent disability (e.g. kidney failure). Infants, young children and the elderly are particularly vulnerable to such complications.This indicator will allow local authorities to monitor the burden of disease in their area and focus more resources for interventions where this burden is high.
Definition: Crude incidence rate of laboratory confirmed Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) serogroup O157 cases (as defined in the Official Journal of the European Union) in residents of England , per 100,000 population over a 5 year period.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: 5 year count of STEC confirmed by national reference laboratory for England (Gastrointestinal Bacterial Reference Unit) as: stool that is culture positive for Escherichia coli, reactive to serogroup O (somatic antigen) 157 lipopolysaccharides and positive for stx1, stx2 or both toxin genes by PCR and/or identified as serogroup O157 by multi-locus sequence typing and postive for stx1, stx2 or both toxin genes derived from whole genome sequencing results. Data linkage (between laboratory results and enhanced surveillance questionnaires) is done within NESSSy using a probabalistic matching algorithm that is automated and run on a daily basis. Multiple isolates of related STEC in the same inidividual will be included as a single case. Cases will be assigned a year according to the date of onset, if available, or otherwise first specimen collection date.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), National Enhanced Shiga toxin-producing Eschericha coli (STEC) Surveillance Programme
Definition of denominator: Sum of annual population over a 5 year period
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Mean 5 year rate per 100,000 population. The sum of the count for 5 years is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Confidence interval method:Exact Poisson. A confidence interval is a range of values used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of the results caused by random variation of the indicator. A wider confidence interval suggests that the estimated indicator value is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true value. Exact confidence intervals are calculated in the statistical software package R using the pois.exact function from the epitools package (see  https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/epitools/versions/0.09/topics/pois.exact  for details).
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: The data provided is based on the number of confirmed STEC O157 cases resident in England reported by the Gastrointestinal Bacteria Reference Unit to NESSSy. Cases resident in other parts of the UK (Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) are not included as these cases are reported to separate systems. There may be under-reporting as not all people with STEC O157 may present to a healthcare professional and if they do present, a stool sample may not be taken. Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. Therefore, where an area has a relatively high rate of STEC, further investigation may be required to determine whether this was due to a single outbreak or multiple smaller outbreaks or sporadic cases.

Definition of numerator: STEC confirmed by national reference laboratory for England (Gastrointestinal Bacterial Reference Unit) as: stool that is culture positive for Escherichia coli, reactive to serogroup O (somatic antigen) 157 lipopolysaccharides and positive for stx1, stx2 or both toxin genes by PCR and/or identified as serogroup O157 by multi-locus sequence typing and postive for stx1, stx2 or both toxin genes derived from whole genome sequencing results. Data linkage (between laboratory results and enhanced surveillance questionnaires) is done within NESSSy using a probabalistic matching algorithm that is automated and run on a daily basis. Multiple isolates of related STEC in the same inidividual will be included as a single case. Cases will be assigned a year according to the date of onset, if available, or otherwise first specimen collection date.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), National Enhanced Shiga toxin-producing Eschericha coli (STEC) Surveillance Programme
Definition of denominator: Total population
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Confidence interval method:Exact Poisson. A confidence interval is a range of values used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of the results caused by random variation of the indicator. A wider confidence interval suggests that the estimated indicator value is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true value. Exact confidence intervals are calculated in the statistical software package R using the pois.exact function from the epitools package (see  https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/epitools/versions/0.09/topics/pois.exact  for details).
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats:
The data provided is based on the number of confirmed STEC O157 cases resident in England reported by the Gastrointestinal Bacteria Reference Unit to NESSSy. Cases resident in other parts of the UK (Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) are not included as these cases are reported to separate systems. There may be under-reporting as not all people with STEC O157 may present to a healthcare professional and if they do present, a stool sample may not be taken. Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. Therefore, where an area has a relatively high rate of STEC, further investigation may be required to determine whether this was due to a single outbreak or multiple smaller outbreaks or sporadic cases.
Local detection rates may be influenced by which laboratory tests are used to test for STEC, as the sensitivity of tests to detect the presence of infection differ. Furthermore, the increased adoption of PCR testing for multiple gastrointestinal pathogens at once may result in better ascertainment and a rise in laboratory reports.To note that ONS statistical regions differ from UKHSA regions with respect to the local authorities they contain e.g. Milton Keynes is in East of England UKHSA region but is in South East ONS statistical region.

Indicator: Estimated diabetes diagnosis rate
Rationale: For clinical commissioning groups and local health and well-being boards to understand the scope for prevention and make headway in tackling the rising numbers of people with or at risk of diabetes, they need to understand not only how many people have diabetes (recorded diabetes as currently collected) but also the estimated number of people expected to have diabetes given the characteristics of their populations. This will enable them to have a better idea of the scale of the challenge in terms of numbers and costs in developing diabetes identification and prevention programmes. It will also help them monitor the progress that they are making towards closing the gap (i.e. meeting previously unmet need) between observed prevalence (number of cases of diabetes recorded) and actual prevalence in identifying people at high risk or with hitherto undiagnosed diabetes.Diabetic complications (including cardiovascular, kidney, foot and eye diseases) result in considerable morbidity and have a detrimental impact on quality of life. Type 2 diabetes (approximately 90 percent of diagnosed cases) is partially preventable, it can be prevented or delayed by lifestyle changes (exercise, weight loss, healthy eating). Earlier detection of Type 2 diabetes followed by effective treatment reduces the risk of developing diabetic complications. NICE guidelines for diabetes include those for children and young people, pregnancy, type 1 diabetes,type 2 diabetes, prevention of type 2 diabetes. All aim to improve the prevention, identification and management of those people at risk of developing diabetes and those with the condition.  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/conditions-and-diseases/diabetes-and-other-endocrinal--nutritional-and-metabolic-conditions/diabetes
Definition: The estimated diabetes diagnosis rate, expressed as a percentage defined as the observed number of people with a formal diagnosis of diabetes as a proportion of the estimated number with diabetes
Data source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Indicator source: OHID
Definition of numerator: Total number of patients registered with GP practices, aged 17 and over at midnight on the 31st March in a particular year that have been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. In order to produce estimates for LAs, numerator counts were estimated by aggregating general practice level data. Each general practice was allocated to a located authority within which its main surgery is located, using the NHS Postcode Directory. General practice postcodes can be downloaded from  https://data.england.nhs.uk/dataset/ods-gps-gp-practices-nurses-and-pharmacies/resource/6eb9d0cc-32d0-4bfd-b7e6-a8a7018cbe1c?inner_span=True .
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)
Definition of denominator: Estimated prevalence of diabetes in adults aged 17 years and over. The full definition can be found ../../../../../../../../../../../documents/2.17_denom_definition_May18.docx
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Health Survey for England (HSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) and Patients registered at a GP practice
Methodology: Numerator divided by denominator multiplied by 100
Frequency: The expected prevalence will be updated every 2 years.  The diagnosed prevalence will be updated every year.
Confidence interval details: The expected number of people with diabetes was calculated as a sum of age-sex-ethnicity specific expected numbers, each of which was calculated by applying estimated prevalence to the estimated local age-sex-ethnicity specific population. These estimates have uncertainty around them (confidence intervals) and these were used to estimate the standard error for each subgroup. This error needs to be reflected in the overall prevalence estimates for specific populations, as well as the random variation in the observed count.Simulation allows us to capture all these separate elements and calculate approximate confidence intervals for the overall indicator: the indicator is calculated 100,000 times. On each repetition, each of the age-sex-ethnicity specific expected (binomial) distributions, and the observed (Poisson) count distribution, are randomly sampled and the indicator is calculated based on those sampled values. Hence a distribution of 100,000 random samples from the overall indicator distribution is obtained. From this distribution we can take the 2500th smallest and the 2500th largest values as robust estimates of the 95%percentlower and upper confidence limits respectively.100,000 repetitions is sufficient to ensure that, to one decimal place, the estimates of the upper and lower confidence limits are robust.The full description of the method can be found  /documents/Estimated%20Diabetes Diagnosis Rate Methodology.docx .
Disclosure control: Not applicable
Rounding: No rounding
Caveats: The prevalence estimates of diabetes are generated by the results of a model and do not represent actual prevalence. The estimates are unable to take into account any additional data that may impact on the estimate.
Notes: This indicator has replaced the original 2.17 Recorded diabetes indicator. The original indicator was found to be difficult to interpret since it could not be judged whether a high value was good or bad. The updated indicator, 2.17 Estimated diabetes diagnosis rate, is easier to interpret. A value close to 100 percent indicates a small gap between the observed prevalence and estimated prevalence and indicates that a system is good at proactively identifying people with hitherto undiagnosed diabetes.

Indicator: Gender pay gap (by workplace location)
Rationale: Social inequality translates in health inequality by systematically distributing different resources to different members of society. Gender pay inequality has been reducing over the past few decades, but remains substantial. This indicator is designed to measure the difference in pay between men and women who work in a given area. The aim is to support local practitioners understanding how employment within their local area contributes to unequal financial resources between men and women. Research has shown that income is related to life expectancy and disability free life expectancy[1], as well as self-reported health and a range of biomarkers.[2] Financial resources can determine the extent to which a person can invest in goods and services which improve health, and purchase of goods and services which are can be actively bad for health. Low incomes can also prevent active participation in social life and the following of social norms affecting feelings of self-worth and status.[3]The gender pay gap is presented here by workplace location instead of resident location to provide users with a workplace-centred view of the pay gap. It reflects less the different financial resources of residents, and more the role of local businesses in generating those differences (and may therefore support local campaigns to reduce the pay gap). This indicator complements the 'Average weekly earnings' indicator which, in contrast, does give insight into the different financial resources of men and women living in the local authority, having a more direct link to health outcomes.The definition used for this indicator -the difference between median gross hourly earnings for men and women as a proportion of median gross hourly earnings for men -is the headline definition used by the ONS[4] and so is comparable to figures which regularly appear in the press due to the introduction of reporting for larger workplaces. Median average earnings are used as the basis for this indicator to mitigate the impact of the skewed earnings distribution, in which there are a larger numbers of low earners and fewer very high earners. However, it has been noted that the use of the median may underestimate the pay gap to some extent as the majority of high earners who skew the distribution are men[5].The gender pay gap represents differences that emerge due to all factors that differentiate earnings for men and women (except differences in the amount of work done). It therefore encourages users to think about the many and varied reasons that men are on average paid more than women, be it gendered career trajectories which see more women than men reduce employment to care for children, or discrimination in the form of unequal pay for equal work or being looked over for promotion. Analytical techniques to decompose the pay gap have been used to explore the factors which drive the pay gap, providing insight into how the gap may be reduced.[6]This gender pay gap indicator uses workplace-based data instead of the resident-based indicator used in gender pay equality. The idea is that the gender pay gap emphasises social-structural inequality. Presenting the gender pay gap based on workplace location can inform locality based interventions at a workplace level, which is where the pay gap operates. This information can be viewed together with the 'average weekly earnings' indicator split by gender, also presented in this profile. Average weekly earnings highlights differences in financial resources by sex, which also takes into account differences derived from part-time work. Average weekly earnings is a direct measure of financial resource and so is more closely aligned to the health implications of variation in income, and as such is best presented at the resident level. The two measures therefore complement each other.1. Marmot MG, Allen J, Goldblatt P, Boyce T, McNeish D, Grady M, Geddes I. ASHE also benefits from a large sample size (1% of the employee workforce on PAYE schemes). However, there are a number of quality issues highlighted by the ONS:"There are known coverage issues with data on bonus and incentive payments relating to the reference period. Primarily, this is because the information is not always available to respondents at the time when they are required to provide the information to ONS.ASHE estimates may be affected by non-response bias. This is likely to be a downward bias on earnings estimates since non-response is known to affect high-paying occupations more than low-paying occupations.ASHE statistics are also subject to non-sampling bias. Jobs that are not registered on PAYE schemes are not surveyed. These jobs are known to be different from the PAYE population in the sense that they typically have low levels of pay. Imputation is also used to reduce non-response bias. Indicator: Average weekly earnings
Rationale: The Average Weekly Earnings indicator is designed to give insight into the variation of economic resources across areas and between subgroups (men and women, income decile). The indicator is a key component of the Income and Vulnerability domain in this profile as earnings are the primary source of income.Research has shown that income is related to life expectancy and disability free life expectancy[1], as well as self-reported health and a range of biomarkers.[2] Financial resources can determine the extent to which a person can invest in goods and services which improve health, and purchase of goods and services which are actively bad for health. Low incomes can also prevent active participation in social life and the following social norms affecting feelings of self-worth and status.[3] The relationship can also operate in the reverse direction, where poor health limits a person's ability to earn money.Though low income in particular is an important focus (and is reflected in the range of income indicators in the domain) the relationship between income and health outcomes operates across the income gradient[2], warranting an indicator which gives insight into earnings across the population distribution.Median average earnings is used instead of the mean to mitigate the impact of the skewed earnings distribution, in which there are a larger number of low earners and fewer very high earners. This measure of earnings includes full and part-time workers because the aim of the indicator is to provide insight into the economic resources available to people, not to compare wage rates per se (for which comparing full-time wages may be more appropriate). The measure excludes overtime payments because such earnings are potentially more erratic. Though other sources of earnings data exist, the  https://www.ons.gov.uk/surveys/informationforbusinesses/businesssurveys/annualsurveyofhoursandearningsashe  is considered to be a more accurate source of information on earnings at the local authority level due to the large sample size and given that the information is provided by employers through the PAYE system rather than being self-reported by employees.1. Confidence interval details:
The confidence intervals are based on standard errors estimated by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) using a Generalised Estimation System method for percentile estimates. The data are provided at source with a 'confidence %',this is the standard error as a percentage of the median estimate. The 'confidence %' is used to calculate the standard error in pounds (£). The standard error (SE) is then used to calculate the 95% confidence interval as follows:Lower limit: estimate - (SE x 1.96)Upper limit: estimate + (SE x 1.96)The following summary of the method used to calculate the standard errors was provided by the ONS:There are a number of steps in calculating the standard error of the quantile value.

 Using GES [Generalised Estimation System] set an indicator variable that shows whether an employees response is lower or equal to the quantile estimate [q]. If the employee has a value that is less than or equal to the quantile estimate then this indicator is set to 1 otherwise it is 0. 
 We then calculate the weighted total of these indicator variables through GES and take the standard error that it produces, we'll call this s.
 Multiply the standard error by a constant, say n. It should be noted that normal practice for estimating a 95% confidence interval is to add and subtract 1.96 x the standard error from the quantile estimate. 
 Add this number to the value of the cumulative frequency distribution that the quantile represents i.e. 0.5 for the median, 0.25 for the lower quartile etc. to get an upper bound and subtract it for a lower bound. So, the lower bound is given by ql = q-ns and the upper bound is qu =q+ns.
 Use the method to calculate the initial quantile value to estimate the response values that correspond to these boundary values; ql and qu

Estimate the standard error of the quantile estimate, q by dividing the range of response values corresponding to the boundaries by twice the amount you multiplied the standard error of the mean indicator variable by i.e. SE(q)=(qu-ql)/2n.

Indicator: Households with problem debt
Rationale: The indicator is designed to measure the prevalence of more serious debt that has the potential to impact on people's health directly through stress related channels and by consuming financial resources that could have otherwise gone towards health promoting goods and services. The ONS describe problem debt as situations where debt has become more than just a burden to households.Research has found an association between debt and health outcomes such as health satisfaction, mental health [1], ability to self-care, problems performing usual activities, pain problems and psychological health [2], and mortality risk [3]. The measure of problem debt used by the ONS in this indicator includes elements of subjective assessment of debt, which have been found to be important predictors of health effects [2]. In addition, debt can negatively affect other wider determinants of health such as housing, employment, education and access to healthcare [4].The indicator is aimed at practitioners working locally or nationally and is intended to highlight the level of problem debt across the country and to frame this as a public health issue. The issue is addressed from a public health perspective with policy recommendations by the Royal Society of Public Health [4].1. Keese M, Schmitz H. The number of households in problem debt, where problem debt is defined by the ONS as follows: living in a household that has liquidity problems only, solvency problems only or both liquidity and solvency problems. These terms are defined as follows:- Liquidity problemsWhere household debt repayments represent at least 25% of net monthly income and at least one adult in the household reports falling behind with bills or credit commitments; or where at least one adult in the household is currently in two or more consecutive months arrears on bills or credit commitments and at least one adult in the household reports falling behind with bills or credit commitments.- Solvency problemsWhere household debt represents at least 20% of net annual income and at least one adult considers their debt a heavy burden.
Student loans are excluded from the calculation of debt. Further details can be found in a methodological note on the derivation of problem debt ( https://eur01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ons.gov.uk%2Fpeoplepopulationandcommunity%2Fpersonalandhouseholdfinances%2Fincomeandwealth%2Fbulletins%2Fwealthingreatbritainwave5%2F2014to2016%23household-debt&data=04%7C01%7CCaroline.X.Tudor%40phe.gov.uk%7C3de5d5f58299457c892608d9fabb1e1b%7Cee4e14994a354b2ead475f3cf9de8666%7C0%7C0%7C637816503892226724%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000&sdata=9ZV2cyUdrfsrx%2BwO2tZqRZjfXdX6kvVZPQry60wtg%2B4%3D&reserved=0 ).
Definition of denominator: Total number of households
Methodology: The percentage of households in problem debt is calculated (by the ONS and provided at source) as follows: Number of households in problem debt divided by the total number of households, multiplied by 100.
Confidence interval details: Not available
Rounding: Regional and England figures are rounded before publication by ONS. Totals may not add.
Caveats: The measure of problem debt is a construct derived from available data. The measure is constructed in a way that includes only households that have indicated their debt is a problem in addition to objective measures of debt. However, there may be households who feel their debt is a problem that are not captured if they do not meet the objective thresholds.The ONS produce other descriptions of household debt which may support users in interpreting this indicator of problem debt. In line with many large national surveys the response rate is around 50% for new household contacts. Weights are used to gross-up estimates to national populations and to reduce bias due to sampling design. Imputation is also used to reduce non-response bias. These methods improve the overall quality of the estimates, though often at the expense of precision (i.e. standard errors will increase). No particular data quality issues are highlighted that affect interpretation at the regional level.To minimise problems associated with missing data, deductive and statistical imputation is carried out by the ONS. Indicator: Non-typhoidal Salmonella incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of non-typhoidal Salmonella. Salmonella is a bacteria that lives in the guts of domestic and wild animals including poultry, cattle, pigs, hedgehogs, snakes and lizards. Salmonella infection can cause gastrointestinal illness, typhoid fever, paratyphoid fever and in rare cases lead to complications such as sepsis. This indicator relates to the Salmonella causing food poisoning i.e. non-typhoidal Salmonella (not those causing typhoid or paratyphoid fever).
Definition: Crude incidence rate of episodes of laboratory reported non-typhoidal Salmonella in human residents of England, per 100,000 population
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: Laboratory confirmed episodes of non-typhoidal Salmonella. Positive laboratory isolates of the same type of Salmonella from the same patient within a 13 week period are defined as a single episode.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS)
Definition of denominator: Total population
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Exact poisson. A confidence interval is a range of values used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of the results caused by random variation of the indicator. A wider confidence interval suggests that the estimated indicator value is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true value. Exact confidence intervals are calculated in the statistical software package R using the pois.exact function from the epitools package (see https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/epitools/versions/0.09/topics/pois.exact for details)
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: a) Misclassification of residence: Residence is assigned based on available patient postcode (In 2015, 81% of people were assigned residence by their postcode). Where this is not available the case will be assigned to the location of the GP of the case (<1%) or the location of the laboratory (18%). As not all cases will have a patient postcode then those LAs with laboratories contained within may have a higher rate due to misclassification of residence. To note that ONS statistical regions differ from UKHSA regions with respect to the local authorities they contain e.g. Milton Keynes is in East of England UKHSA region but is in South East ONS statistical region.b) Under-reporting: There is under-reporting of Salmonella as not all people will present to healthcare, and if they do present to health care then a specimen may not be requested. The Second Study of Infectious Intestinal Disease in the Community (IID2 Study) indicated that for every case reported to national surveillance - nearly 5 cases of disease occurred in the community (Tam CC, et al. Longitudinal study of infectious intestinal disease in the UK (IID2 study): incidence in the community and presenting to general practice (2012) Gut Jan; 61(1):69-77). Although there is a statutory duty to report, the completeness of laboratory reporting varies which will influence the reported rates of infection. c) Outbreaks:Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. Therefore, where an area has a relatively high rate of Salmonella in a particular time period, further investigation may be required to determine whether this can be explained by a particular outbreak(s) or whether there are other contributory factors resulting in persistent high rates of infection. d) Failure of removal of duplicates: Data in SGSS are de-duplicated so that multiple isolates that relate to the same episode of infection are merged. - Episode length. Sample dates within 13 weeks of one another are counted as one episode of infection. Records that are identical with sample dates 14 or more weeks apart will both be reported; records with 13 or fewer weeks between sample dates will be merged into one record.- Matching patient identifiable information (PII) -Information such as name, date of birth, NHS number and postcode are used to determine whether records are duplicates; cases with matching or very similar information will have their records merged. Records that are missing most of this information cannot be merged.- Differing species, subspecies and serovars isolated. If one sample was produced where one test detected one type of salmonella and another sample detected another type of salmonella, these will not be merged.- Isolates from the same case and/or sample with differing antimicrobial resistance results are counted as two separate records.- Instances where intermediate results are provided by the frontline laboratory that include interim results for antimicrobial resistance cannot be merged with final results where that information has been filled out; where this happens the cases will not merge.e) Information presented at UKHSA regionlevel will be different from that presented using different boundaries, e.g. ONS regions.f) SGSS is a live laboratory reporting system therefore numbers may vary if data is extracted on a different dateg) Local detection rates may be influenced by which laboratory tests are used to test for Salmonella, as the sensitivity of tests to detect the presence of infection differ.

Indicator: Shigella incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of infection with Shigella spp. Shigellosis, also known as bacillary dysentery, is caused by four species:• Shigella flexneri• Shigella sonnei• Shigella dysenteriae• Shigella boydiiShigella flexneri and Shigella sonnei are endemic in the UK while infections with Shigella dysenteriae and Shigella boydii are usually imported.Shigella generally causes a relatively mild illness, however recent research has shown that 1 in 5 cases may progress to more severe disease1. This includes cases requiring hospitalisation due to bloody diarrhoea, persistent gastroenteritis or more severe complications such as bacteraemia. Patients with Shigella dysenteriae can also develop a very severe condition known as haemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) related to the presence of an exotoxin. Infection is readily transmitted from person to person, via the oro faecal route. In the past, shigellosis has primarily been associated with travel to countries with poor sanitation or transmission between young children and their care-givers in household, nursery or school settings. More recently, the case burden has increased amongst adult males relative to all other demographic groups and outbreaks of Shigella sonnei and Shigella flexneri have been linked to person-to-person spread among men who have sex with men (MSM)2,3. MSM infected with Shigella have high rates of co-infection with HIV4 and other sexually transmitted infections, may be immunocompromised and more often require hospitalisation. Plasmid-mediated multi-drug resistant strains of Shigella are of increasing concern. Outbreaks require public health management and individual public health follow-up is required to prevent further transmission (for more information see public health guidelines for shigellosis5). Definition: Crude incidence rate of episodes of laboratory confirmed Shigella in human residents of England, per 100,000 population per year
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: Laboratory confirmed episodes of Shigella spp. infection summarised by year of laboratory report for England, UKHSACentre, upper tier local authorities and lower tier local authorities. Isolates of the same species of Shigella from the same patient within a 14 day period are defined as a single episode.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS)
Definition of denominator: Office of National Statistics mid-year population estimates for the year of laboratory reporting or the preceding year if population estimates for the laboratory report year are not available at the time of publication.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: A confidence interval is a range of values used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of the results caused by random variation of the indicator. A wider confidence interval suggests that the estimated indicator value is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true value. Exact confidence intervals are calculated in the statistical software package R using the pois.exact function from the epitools package (see https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/epitools/versions/0.09/topics/pois.exact for details)
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: a) Misclassification of residence: Patients are geolocated based on their postcode of residence. In 2015, 81% of people were assigned residence by their postcode. Where this is not available, the patient's GP postcode is used (<1%) or the postcode of the primary diagnostic laboratory that processed their Shigella isolate (18%). Patients missing a residential postcode may be geographically misclassified (allocated to a local authority or region in which they are not a resident i.e. those areas with large laboratories within them may have artificially high rates). To note that ONS statistical regions differ from PHE Centres with respect to the local authorities they contain e.g. Milton Keynes is in East of England PHE Centre but is in South East ONS statistical region.b) Underascertainment: The true incidence of Shigella is underestimated by these methods as: - not all cases will present to a healthcare facility;- not all cases that do present to a healthcare facility will provide a specimen for laboratory analysis;- not all primary diagnostic laboratories provide their data to SGSS (121 laboratories routinely report to SGSS - public laboratories: > 95% coverage, private laboratories: coverage unknown);- not all primary diagnostic laboratory Shigella results pass the minimum data quality checks for uploading to SGSS (on average 0.03% of records are quarantined or have translation errors);- although there is a statutory duty to report, completeness and timeliness of reporting may vary by laboratory (and therefore region).All of these factors influence the reported incidence of infection. c) Outbreaks: Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. Therefore, where an area has a relatively high rate of Shigella in a particular time period, further investigation may be required to determine whether this can be explained by a particular outbreak(s) or whether there are other contributory factors resulting in persistent high rates of infection.d) Deduplication failures: i. Episode of infection: data in SGSS are de-duplicated so that multiple isolates that relate to the same episode of infection are merged, based on episode length. Specimen dates for isolates of an identical strain from the same patient within 13 days of one another are merged and counted as a single episode of infection. Specimen dates for isolates of an identical strain from the same patient that are 14 or more days apart are counted as separate episodes of infection. This may result in an overestimate of incidence in some cases, as Shigella is shed in stools for up to six weeks after onset of symptoms. Microbiological clearance is currently required for non-sonnei Shigella infections; in addition some patients experience persistent gastroenteritis and may provide further specimens for testing beyond the 14-day period used for deduplication.ii. Probabalistic matching: multiple records for the same patient are deduplicated based on probabalistic matching of patient identifiable information (name, date of birth, NHS number and postcode); consequently cases with matching or very similar information will have their records merged. This may lead to under estimation of incidence where separate patients are incorrectly merged. Records that are missing most of this information cannot be merged; this may lead to over estimation of incidence where isolates from the same patient, for the same strain and episode of illness are not merged due to incomplete or incorrect patient identifying information. iii. Incomplete speciation: isolates from from the same patient episode are not merged unless all isolates have been speciated and are the same species. Some clearance specimens may not be speciated, in which case the results will not be merged with the initial diagnostic result. This may lead to an over estimation of incidence.iv. Different antimicrobial resistance test results: Isolates from the same case and/or sample with differing antimicrobial resistance results are counted as two separate records. Intermediate results with missing data in the antimicrobial resistance section cannot be merged with results from the same patient episode that have a complete antimicrobial resistance profile. In these scenarios, incidence may be over estimated as antimicrobial resistance profiles in a single patient episode can change during the course of their infection, particularly if antimicrobials are prescribed for their Shigella infection or other co-infections.e) Extraction from a live database:Data for this health profile are extracted from SGSS, which is a live database and therefore numbers may vary if data is extracted on a different date. This may lead to under or over estimation of incidence due to:- batch uploading of laboratory results for the preceding year, after the date of extraction (under estimation);- correction of personal identifying information, antimicrobial resistance test results or other data used for deduplication for records from the preceding year, after the date of extraction (under or over estimation depending on how deduplication is affected by the corrected data).In addition, data presented on this health profile may not be directly comparable to data presented in other reports, where the date of extraction differs or where different geographic boundary versions have been used to summarise the results.f) Local detection rates may be influenced by which laboratory tests are used to test for Shigella, as the sensitivity of tests to detect the presence of infection differ.Furthermore, the increased adoption of PCR testing for multiple gastrointestinal pathogens at once may result in better ascertainment and a rise in laboratory reports.

Indicator: MRSA bacteraemia 12-month rolling case counts and rates of hospital-onset, by Sub ICB Location (SICBL) and month
Rationale:
A long running voluntary surveillance scheme of laboratory reported cases ofStaphylococcus aureusbacteraemia showed increasing incidence of meticillin resistantS. aureus(MRSA) infections in England, Wales and Northern Ireland in the 1990s. This generated both media and public interest. In response, the Department of Health (DH) in England introduced a mandatory surveillance scheme forS. aureusbacteraemias in April 2001, which included data on the number of cases that were due to MRSA. In October 2005 the mandatory surveillance scheme for MRSA bacteraemias was enhanced to collect patient-level data.
Additionally, all NHS organisations reporting cases of MRSA bacteraemia from the 1 April 2013, are required to complete a Post Infection Review (PIR). This process was commenced to support the delivery of zero tolerance on MRSA bacteraemia, as set out by NHS England in the Planning Guidance<a href="https://www.england.nhs.uk/everyonecounts/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Everyone counts: Planning for Patients 2013/14. A PIR is undertaken after all MRSA bacteraemias with the purpose of identifying how a case occurred, to identify actions by local healthcare teams which will prevent a reoccurrence and to identify the organisation best placed to ensure improvements are made (this is known as “assigning” a case to an organisation).A low value is indicative of a low count ofMRSA.
Definition:
Laboratory-confirmed cases ofStaphylococcus aureusbacteraemia detected by blood culture confirmed resistant to any of:

Meticillin
Oxacillin
Cefoxitin
Flucloxacillin
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/staphylococcus-aureus-guidance-data-and-analysis
Definition of numerator:
All cases ofMRSA meeting the 'Definition' section above occurring for thepast 11 months are summed with the current month to give arolling 12-month total. For the calculation of rates, the past 11 months are summed with the current month and the denominator is the sum of the bed-days (for trusts) or population (for CCGs) for the current month and preceding 11 months.

The rate for a month is then calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and multiplying by 100,000 to give a manageable value.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Healthcare Associated Infection Data Capture System (HCAI DCS) Mandatory Surveillance
Definition of denominator: Denominator values are calculated as an annual rolling sum. For any given month, the denominator includes the value for the defined geography in the given month and the 11 preceeding months.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The rate gives the annual rolling rate for a given month. In this calculation, the numerator is the sum of the cases for the current month and the 11 preceeding months. The denominator is the sum of the bed days for the current month and the 11 preceeding months. The rate for a month is then calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and multiplying by 100,000 to give a manageable value.
Confidence interval details: Confidence intervals are not calculated as the population value is known.
Caveats: These data do not provide a basis for decisions on the clinical effectiveness of infection control interventions in individual Trusts: further investigations considering potential confounders would need to be undertaken before this could be done.Nor do these data provide a basis for comparisons between acute Trust or Sub ICB Location (SICBL). Rate information, using rate calculations as currently defined, is not appropriate for comparison. The counts of infections have not been adjusted to give a standardised rate considering factors such as organisational demographics or case mix. Rate information is of use for comparison of an individual organisation over time.‘All reported cases’ refers to all MRSA-positive blood cultures reported by the Trust whose laboratory processes the specimen. It is important to note that this does not necessarily imply that the infection was acquired there.Cases that the UKHSA's HCAI Data Capture System attributes to a commissioning hub (such as the national commissioning hub, 13Q, or one of the regional Health & Justice commissioning hubs) are not featured in sub ICB Location dashboards but they do still contribute to the highest spatial level—the England national total. This means the England case total may be slightly higher than the sum of all sub ICB Location cases.

Indicator: % reporting a long term MSK problem who also report depression or anxiety
Rationale: Depression and anxiety is four times more common among people in persistent pain compared to those without pain[1]. People with chronic low back pain have been shown to have a significantly higher frequency of musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain conditions and common sequelae of pain such as depression (13.0% vs. 6.1%), anxiety (8.0% vs. 3.4%) and sleep disorders (10.0% vs. 3.4%), compared to people without low back pain [2]. The odds of back pain in people with symptoms of depression have been shown to be 50% higher than in those without symptoms of depression [3].This indicator measures the prevalence of anxiety/depression in adults with a musculoskeletal condition. It will raise awareness of the association between musculoskeletal conditions and mental health and may stimulate better pain management strategies among those with MSK conditions.[1] Lepine, J., & Briley, M. (2004). The epidemiology of pain in depression. Human Psychopharmacology: Clinical and Experimental, 19(S1). doi:10.1002/ hup.618.[2] Gore, M., Sadosky, A., Stacey, B., Tai, K. and Leslie, D. (2012). The Burden of Chronic Low Back Pain. Spine, 37(11), pp.E668–E677.[3] Pinheiro, M. B., Ferreira, M. L., Refshauge, K., Ordonana, J. R., Machado, G. C., Prado, L. R. Ferreira, P. H. (2015). Symptoms of Depression and Risk of New Episodes of Low Back Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta–Analysis. Arthritis Care & Research, 67(11), 1591–1603. doi:10.1002/acr.22619
Definition: The percentage of people aged 18+ reporting an MSK condition, either long term back pain or long term joint pain, who also report feeling depressed or anxious.
Data source: NHS England, GP Patient Survey
Indicator source: GP Patient Survey
Definition of numerator: Weighted count of those who answered "long term back pain" or "long term joint pain" to Q31 ("Do you have any of the following conditions?") and answered Q34e ("State of your health today, what is your level of anxiety/depression?") with one of the folowing responses: "Extremely anxious/depressed," or "moderately anxious/depressed," or "severely anxious/depressed."
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: Weighted count of those who answered "long term back pain" or "long term joint pain" to Q31 ("Do you have a long term health conditions?") and gave a valid answer to Q34e ("State of your health today, what is your level of anxiety/depression?")
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology: The prevalence is calculated by dividing the weighted count of the numerator by the weighted count of the denominator (with a valid answer), expressed as a percentage.Full details on weighting within the GP Patient Survey can be found at https://www.gp-patient.co.uk/surveysandreports
Disclosure control: This indicator contains no small counts. If counts below 5 were present discloure control would be applied.
Caveats: This indicator is a self reported prevalence from the GP Patient Survey it is not a diagnosed prevalence rate. There is no definition in the survey to what "long term" means so this is interpreted by the participant. Numerators and denominators are weighted so they are standardised to the local authorities population.Where local authority data is shown we have collated data for all those patients registered at GP practices within a given local authority. This may mean in a limited number of cases a patient may live outside a local authority but still be counted as within the local authority as the GP practice they attend is registered as within the given local authority. The reverse is also true that a patient may live within a local authority but attend a GP practice outside the local authority and may be missed from the count.Some demographic groups within the GP Patient Survey have lower response rates, and there are some variations in regional response rates. The data is weighted to account for non-response by gender, age and practice.

Indicator: Average health related quality of life score for adults who reported having a long term MSK problem.
Rationale: Musculoskeletal conditions, such as osteoarthritis and back pain, are the leading cause of disability in adults in England [1] and studies also show that depression and anxiety is four times more common among people in persistent pain compared to those without pain [2]. Reduced mobility, pain or discomfort and anxiety/depression are all factors which can reduce quality of life scores. The average health related quality of life score for adults in England, aged 18+, with no long term condition was 0.91 in 2016/17, when filtered to those with a long term MSK condition this score was significantly worse at 0.58 in 2016/17, indicating that adults who reporting have a long term MSK condition also reported a worse quality of life [3]. This indicator will provide a greater focus on improving overall quality of life by preserving independence and promoting well-being in people with an MSK condition - this is key to keeping systems functioning and to ensure that the needs of this large group of users are addressed.Routinely collected and collated health related quality of life scores can be used to understand if the healthcare they receive is effective in improving musculoskeletal health outcomes. This indicator could therefore be used as an outcome measure for musculoskeletal health within local and national outcomes frameworks, including at individual service level.1. Global, regional, and national incidence, prevalence, and years lived with disability for 310 diseases and injuries, 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015. (2016)2. Lepine, J., & Briley, M. (2004). The epidemiology of pain in depression. Human Psychopharmacology: Clinical and Experimental, 19(S1). doi:10.1002/ hup.618.3. GP Patient Survey analysis by Public Health England 2016/17
Definition: Average health status score for adults aged 18+years who reported having a long term MSK problem, either long term back pain or long term joint pain, as measured using the EQ-5D scale.
Data source: NHS England, GP Patient Survey
Indicator source: GP Patient Survey
Definition of numerator: The sum of EQ-5D index scores for people who answered 'yes' to either long term back or long term joint pain.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: Unweighted count of people completing the GP Patient Survey who answered yes to either long term back pain or long term joint pain.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology: Health status is converted to an index score by GP Patient Survey team from responses to Q34 on the GP Patient's Survey, which asks respondents to describe their health status using the five dimensions of the EuroQuol 5D (EQ-5D) survey instrument:MobilitySelf CareUsual ActivitiesPain/discomfortAnxiety/depressionEQ-5D assesses whether health-related quality of life is changing over time, while controlling for potential measurable confounders (age, sex, long-term conditions, caring responsibility, etc...).EQ-5D has been filtered to those who answered "long term back pain" or "long term joint pain" to Q31 ("Do you have any of the following conditions?")The result of the patient survey have been calculated for the different geographies and inequalities dimensions by using an average of the EQ-5D score where there was a valid response for Q34 and Q31. The England value excludes results where the geographical area is unknown.
Confidence interval details: T-distribution is the standard method for calculating confidence intervals when using a mean and a normal distribution. While the distribution of this indicators individual scores may be skewed, the verylarge sample size means the chosen method is robust to deviations from normality.
Disclosure control: This indicator contains no small counts. If counts below 5 were present discloure control would be applied.
Caveats: Where local authority data is shown we have collated data for all those patients registered at GP practices within a given local authority. This may mean in a limited number of cases a patient may live outside a local authority but still be counted as within the local authority as the GP practice they attend is registered as within the given local authority. The reverse is also true that a patient may live within a local authority but attend a GP practice outside the local authority and may be missed from the count.There is no definition in the survey to what "long term" means so this is interpreted by the participant. Indicator: Giardia incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of Giardia. Giardiasis can be transmitted by direct contact with infected animals or humans, or by consumption of water, food or beverages contaminated by the faeces of infected animals or humans. People may also be infected by swimming in contaminated water (for example in lakes or rivers). Many cases are associated with foreign travel. Persistently significantly high rates of Giardia in the absence of known outbreaks would indicate the need to investigate the underlying reasons and reinforce prevention activity as appropriate e.g. advice regarding contact with animals.
Definition: Crude incidence rate of episodes of laboratory reported Giardia in human residents of England, per 100,000 population
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: Laboratory confirmed episodes of Giardia. Positive laboratory isolates of the same type of Giardia from the same patient within a 2 week period are defined as a single episode.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS)
Definition of denominator: Total population
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Exact poisson. A confidence interval is a range of values used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of the results caused by random variation of the indicator. A wider confidence interval suggests that the estimated indicator value is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true value. Exact confidence intervals are calculated in the statistical software package R using the pois.exact function from the epitools package (see https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/epitools/versions/0.09/topics/pois.exact for details)
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: a) Misclassification of residence: Residence is assigned based on available patient postcode (In 2015, 81% of people in SGSS overall (not specifically Giardia) were assigned residence by their postcode). Where this is not available the case will be assigned to the location of the GP of the case (<1%) or the location of the laboratory (18%). As not all cases will have a patient postcode then those LAs with laboratories contained within may have a higher rate due to misclassification of residence. b) Under-reporting: There is underreporting of Giardia as not all people will present to healthcare, and if they do present to health care then a specimen may not be requested. The Second Study of Infectious Intestinal Disease in the Community (IID2 Study) indicated that for every case reported to national surveillance - 14 cases of disease occurred in the community (Tam CC, et al. Longitudinal study of infectious intestinal disease in the UK (IID2 study): incidence in the community and presenting to general practice (2012) Gut Jan; 61(1):69-77). Although there is a statutory duty to report, the completeness of laborting reporting varies which will therefore influence the reported rates of infection. c) Outbreaks:Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. Therefore, where an area has a relatively high rate of Giardia in a particular time period, further investigation may be required to determine whether this can be explained by a particular outbreak(s) or whether there are other contributory factors resulting in persistent high rates of infection.d) Failure of removal of duplicates: Data in SGSS are de-duplicated so that multiple isolates that relate to the same episode of infection are merged. • Episode length. Sample dates within 2 weeks of one another are counted as one episode of infection. Records that are identical with sample dates 2 or more weeks apart will both be reported; records with 2 or fewer weeks between sample dates will be merged into one record. Matching patient identifiable information (PII) -Information such as name, date of birth, NHS number and postcode are used to determine whether records are duplicates; cases with matching or very similar information will have their records merged. Records that are missing most of this information cannot be merged.• Differing species. If one sample was produced where one test detected one type of Giardia and another sample detected another type of Giardia, these will not be merged.e) Local detection rates may be influenced by which laboratory tests are used to test for Giardia, as the sensitivity of tests to detect the presence of infection differ. Furthermore, the increased adoption of PCR testing for multiple gastrointestinal pathogens at once may result in better ascertainment and a rise in laboratory reports.

Indicator: Odds of smoking for those with a routine and manual occupation compared to the odds of smoking for those with other occupations
Rationale: Smoking is the most important cause of preventable ill health and premature mortality in the UK. Smoking is a major risk factor for many diseases, such as lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart disease. It is also associated with cancers in other organs, including lip, mouth, throat, bladder, kidney, stomach, liver and cervix.Smoking is a modifiable behavioural risk factor; effective tobacco control measures can reduce the prevalence of smoking in the population.The Government’s Tobacco Control Plan (Towards a Smokefree Generation: A Tobacco Control Plan for England, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/towards-a-smoke-free-generation-tobacco-control-plan-for-england ) published in July 2017 sets out the Government’s strategy to reduce smoking prevalence among adults and young people, and to reduce smoking during pregnancy. Another of the main targets is to "reduce the inequality gap in smoking prevalence, between those in routine and manual occupations and the general population".  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/towards-a-smoke-free-generation-tobacco-control-plan-for-england . This indicator is designed to help local authorities monitor the extent of the difference in smoking prevalence between their residents with routine and manual occupations compared with other occupations.
Definition: The odds of current smoking among working age adults (aged 18 to 64) with a routine and manual occupation divided by the odds of current smoking among those with other occupations expressed as an odds ratio.This is a renamed version of the previously published ‘Smoking prevalence in adults – socioeconomic gap in current smokers’. The underlying odds ratio calculation remains the same.

Methodology:
The value is presented as an odds ratio. An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an event. The OR represents the odds that an event will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the event occurring in the absence of that exposure.
This is calculated as:
Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d)which can be simplified toOdds Ratio = ad/bc
This odds ratio represents the odds of those with a routine or manual occupation smoking compared with those with another occupation.
The odds ratio for this indicator represents the odds that an event (smoking) will occur in the presence of a certain exposure (having a routine or manual occupation), compared to the odds of the same event (smoking) occurring in the absence of the exposure (having a routine or manual occupation).
The odds of the event in the exposed group is:
The number of people who reported having a routine and manual occupation and smoking (a) divided by the number of people who did not report having a routine and manual occupation but did report smoking (b).
The odds in the event in non-exposed group is:
The number of people who reported having a routine and manual occupation but did not report smoking (c) divided by the number of people who did not report having a routine and manual occupation or smoking (d).

Indicator: Oesophageal cancer registrations
Rationale: This indicator is a measure for the incidence of oesophageal cancer in England. The relative risks of cancers that could be caused by smoking list oesophageal cancer as the third after lung cancer and head & neck cancers. In England, around 7,829 people were diagnosed with cancer of the oesophagus in 2018 (1) and the age-standardised one-year survival for patients diagnosed with oesophageal cancer between 2013 and 2017 was 47% for men and 46% for women. The five-year survival was at 16.3% for men and 18.7% for women (2).References:(1) Cancer registration statistics: England 2018 final release, May 2020; https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/cancer-registration-statistics-england-2018-final-release (2) Cancer survival in England: Adults diagnosed between 2013 and 2017 and followed up to 2018, August 2019; https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/datasets/cancersurvivalratescancersurvivalinenglandadultsdiagnosed
Definition: Directly age-standardised registration rate for oesophageal cancer (ICD-10 C15), in persons of all ages, per 100,000 2013 European Standard Population
Data source: NHS England
Indicator source: National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service retrieved from the Cancer Analysis System (CAS), NHS Digital
Definition of numerator: Cancer registrations for oesophageal cancer (ICD-10, C15) in the calendar years 2007-09 to 2017-2019. The National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service collects data relating to each new diagnosis of cancer that occurs in England. This does not include secondary cancers. Data are reported according to the calendar year in which the cancer was diagnosed.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service (NCRAS)
Definition of denominator: Population-years (ONS mid-year population estimates aggregated for the respective years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0-4, 5-9,…, 85-89, 90+).
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The directly age-sex-standardised rates are calculated by taking the age and sex specific crude rates and applying them to the age distribution of a hypothetical population (in this case, the 2013 European Standard Population).For both males and females, numerator data for each five year age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific cancer registration rates for the area and sex.These age-specific rates are multiplied by the European standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age-adjusted rate of cancer registrations for the area. This age-adjusted rate of registrations is divided by the total European standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age-standardised registration rate for the area. The age-sex-standardised rates for persons follows the same process for each sex and sums across the age-specific rates for each sex.
Confidence interval details: A confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically, it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value. The 95% confidence intervals for the age-sex-standardised rates were calculated by National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service using an adaptation of the method described by Tiwari et al. (1).Tiwari’s method calculates a confidence interval for the directly standardised rates based on the assumption of a gamma distribution. It gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for rates and is particularly accurate for when rates are small in any specific cell and when there is large variability in the weights used to standardise the rate. This is particularly relevant when assessing age-standardised rates across multiple populations. (1) Tiwari RC1, Clegg LX, Zou Z. Efficient interval estimation for age-adjusted cancer rates. Stat Methods Med Res. 2006 Dec;15(6):547-69.
Disclosure control: The data are subject to standard NHS disclosure control methods.Count suppression has been applied to any geographical area with a count of 1-5. Suppression acheived by combining small count areas with neighboring geographies.
Caveats:
Reviews of the quality of UK cancer registry data  1, 2  have concluded that registrations are largely complete, accurate and reliable. The data on cancer registration ‘quality indicators’ (mortality to incidence ratios, zero survival cases and unspecified site) demonstrate that although there is some variability, overall ascertainment and reliability is good. However cancer registrations are continuously being updated, so the number of registrations for each year may not be complete, as there is a small but steady stream of late registrations, some of which only come to light through death certification.
1. Huggett C (1995). Review of the Quality and Comparability of Data held by Regional Cancer Registries. Bristol: Bristol Cancer Epidemiology Unit incorporating the South West Cancer Registry. 2. Seddon DJ, Williams EMI (1997). Data quality in population based cancer registration. British Journal of Cancer 76: 667-674.

Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: Flu (2 to 3 years old)
Rationale: Influenza (also known as Flu) is a highly infections viral illness spread by droplet infection. The flu vaccination is offered to people who are at greater risk of developing serious complications if they catch flu. The seasonal influenza programme for England is set out in the Annual Flu Letter ( https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/annual-flu-programme ). Both the flu letter and the flu plan have the support of the Chief Medical Officer (CMO), Chief Pharmaceutical Officer (CPhO) and Director of Nursing. Vaccination coverage is the best indicator of the level of protection a population will have against vaccine preventable communicable diseases. Immunisation is one of the most effective healthcare interventions available and flu vaccines can prevent illness and hospital admissions among these groups of people. Increasing the uptake of flu vaccine among these high risk groups should also contribute to easing winter pressure on primary care services and hospital admissions. Coverage is closely related to levels of disease. Monitoring coverage identifies possible drops in immunity before levels of disease rise.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />UKHSA will continue to provide a centre of expert advice and monitoring of public health, including immunisation. NHS England now has responsibility for commissioning the flu programme and GPs continue to play a key role. NHS England teams will ensure that robust plans are in place locally and that high vaccination uptake levels are reached in the clinical risk groups. For more information see the Green Book chapter 19 on "Influenza" ( https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/influenza-the-green-book-chapter-19 ).

Indicator: E. coli bacteraemia case counts and rates of community-onset, by sub ICB location (SICBL) and financial year
Rationale: Escherichia coli(E. coli) is a Gram-negative bacterium and has been the predominant cause of bacteraemia in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, overtaking those caused byS. aureus(a Gram-positive bacterium), since 2003. Laboratory confirmed cases ofE. colibacteraemia.
Community-onset cases are all those that are not hospital-onset cases.

Rationale:
A long running voluntary surveillance scheme of laboratory reported cases ofStaphylococcus aureusbacteraemia showed increasing incidence of meticillin resistantS. aureus(MRSA) infections in England, Wales and Northern Ireland in the 1990s. This generated both media and public interest. In response, the Department of Health (DH) in England introduced a mandatory surveillance scheme forS. aureusbacteraemias in April 2001, which included data on the number of cases that were due to MRSA. In October 2005 the mandatory surveillance scheme for MRSA bacteraemias was enhanced to collect patient-level data.
Additionally, all NHS organisations reporting cases of MRSA bacteraemia from the 1 April 2013, were required to complete a Post Infection Review (PIR). This process was commenced to support the delivery of zero tolerance on MRSA bacteraemia, as set out by NHS England in the Planning Guidance<a href="https://www.england.nhs.uk/everyonecounts/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Everyone counts: Planning for Patients 2013/14. A PIR is undertaken after all MRSA bacteraemias with the purpose of identifying how a case occurred, to identify actions by local healthcare teams which will prevent a reoccurrence and to identify the organisation best placed to ensure improvements are made (this is known as “assigning” a case to an organisation).From 1 April 2018, the PIR process changed from being applied by all trusts to trusts identified as having high rates of MRSA. For more information, please see https://improvement.nhs.uk/resources/mrsa-guidance-post-infection-review/ .A low value is indicative of a low rate of MRSA.
Definition:
Laboratory confirmed cases ofMRSAbacteraemia.
Community-onset cases are all those that are not hospital-onset cases.
Hospital-onsetis determined on patient location, date of admission, date of specimen and patient category. Hospital onset is only indicative for cases where NHS patient specimens are taken on the third day of admission onwards (eg day three when day one equals day of admission) at an acute trust (including cases with unspecified specimen location) for inpatients, day patients, emergency assessment or unspecified patient category.
Records with a missing admission date (where the specimen location is acute trust or missing and the patient category is inpatient, day patient, emergency assessment or unspecified) are also included. Other cases may have hospital onset, but not in acute trusts.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/escherichia-coli-e-coli-guidance-data-and-analysis

The relevant rate per 100,000 population was calculated as follows:
rate = (cases for given period/CCG-level population estimate)*100,000

As such some SICBLs may experience higher or lower rates than expected due to this change.
