Indicator: Child development: percentage of children achieving the expected level in communication skills at 2 to 2 and a half years
Rationale:
Disparities in child development are recognisable in the second year of life and have an impact by the time children enter school. If left unsupported, these children are more likely to fail to achieve their full potential.
From 2015 all children in England became eligible for a Healthy Child Programme development review, delivered as part of the universal health visitor service, around their second birthday.
The Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ 3) was identified to be suitable for generating data for a population measure of child development outcomes. Health visiting teams should have been using ASQ 3 as part of a child's two year reviews from April 2015. There are a range of ASQ 3 questionnaires, with the one to be applied depending on the child's exact age in months. At the 2 to 2 and a half year review, the 24 month questionnaire should be applied if the child is aged between 23 months 0 days and 25 months 15 days; the 27 month questionnaire should be applied if the child is aged between 25 months 16 days and 28 months 15 days, and the 30 month questionnaire should be applied if the child is 28 months 16 days or older.
ASQ 3 provides an objective measure of development and allows comparisons to be made helping to identify children who are not developing as expected and supporting decisions on closer monitoring of progress or early intervention services. Domains of development which are tested include communication, gross motor, fine motor, problem solving and personal-social skills. The expected levels of development are dependent on the questionnaire used and the domain.
There are inequalities in the number of children who achieve the expected level in their development, with children living in more deprived areas and boys less likely to be at the expected levels.
The indicators of child development at 2 to 2 and a half years calculated from the ASQ 3 scores are outcomes indicators, allowing OHID to measure trends and improvements in child development outcomes which will drive school readiness and longer-term outcomes in later life such as education, employment and life chances.
The proportion of children at or above the expected level in all five domains gives an indicator of the proportion of children who are developing as expected at age 2, with individual domains helping to gain a clearer picture of levels and inequalities in other areas, including communication skills.
<div style="box-sizing: border-box;">The Department of Health is developing an outcome measure of child development at age 2 to 2½ years. The measure will help monitor child development across England in order to observe changes in population health from year to year, and potentially also use the data to track children’s outcomes as they grow up. It is very important that the indicator of child development at age 2 to 2½ is included in the PHOF. The indicator will help to build a picture of child development at age 2 to 2½ at national and local level. It will support local areas in assessing the effectiveness and impact of services for 0 to 2 year olds and with planning services for children age 2 and beyond. The data will also help to assess the effectiveness and impact of services for 0 to 2 year olds and support future planning. Data for the measure will be collected during the Healthy Child Programme (HCP) two year review or integrated review, where in place. The Ages and Stages Questionnaire-3 (ASQ-3) covers five domains of child development: communication, gross motor skills, fine motor skills, problem solving and personal-social development. Health visiting teams should have been using ASQ-3 as part of HCP two year reviews from April 2015. This indicator shows the proportion of 2 to 2½ reviews which use the ASQ-3 and have achieved the expected level in communication skills. Understanding and publishing coverage statistics will inform the decision to publish the outcomes indicators that can be derived from the ASQ-3. Please see <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/healthy-child-programme-0-to-19-health-visitor-and-school-nurse-commissioning" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/healthy-child-programme-0-to-19-health-visitor-and-school-nurse-commissioning
Definition: Percentage of children who received a 2 to 2 and a half year review who were at or above the expected level in the Ages and Stages Questionnaire 3 (ASQ 3) communication skills domain.
Data source: OHID, based on interim reporting data for universal health visiting services
Definition of numerator: All 2 to 2.5 year reviews which have a score within the domain, where the scores are at or above the domain and questionnaire specific threshold. These thresholds are used when assessing the child to establish whether development is as expected, or if further support is needed.
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), Child and maternal health statistics - Child development outcomes at 2 to 2 and a half years (via interim national reporting process)
Definition of denominator: All 2 to2 and a half year reviews which have a score within the domain.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), Child and maternal health statistics - Child development outcomes at 2 to 2 and a half years (via interim national reporting process)
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100. A process of estimation was applied to any local authority data where a return was submitted for only 3 quarters or data failed validation for a single quarter. An estimated numerator for the missing quarter was calculated as an average of the numerators of the other 3 quarters, and the same for an estimated denominator. Where a numerator or denominator has been submitted as 0, no estimation has been performed. An annual numerator and denominator have been calculated based on the estimated numerator and denominator and the known numerators and denominators.
Caveats:
Child development is assessed using ASQ-3 as part of the mandated 2 to 2 and a half year health visitor review.

This may be indicative of reviews and assessments being targeted to more vulnerable communities, and a subsequent low level of children achieving the expected level of development.

Values requiring caution have been flagged with a value note.

Indicator: Percentage of adults walking for travel at least three days per week
Rationale: Creating an environment where people actively choose to walk and cycle as part of everyday life can have a significant impact on public health and may reduce inequalities in health. (1) Public Health England has a stated aim to support work across government on sustainable travel to promote increased levels of physical activity through walking and cycling and contribute to the implementation of the government’s sports strategy.These active travel indicators are designed to help support the work of organisations in promoting active travel. The promotion of active travel is also encouraged in the CMO’s Health Impacts of All Pollution – what do we know report (2).As well as reducing polluting emissions, encouragement of active travel (walking or cycling on journeys for which a car would previously have been used) will also have wider public health benefits associated with increased physical activity.For most people, the easiest and most acceptable forms of physical activity are those that can be built into everyday life. Examples include walking or cycling instead of travelling by car, and using stairs instead of lifts. ‘Active travel’ (or active transportation or mobility) means walking or cycling as an alternative to motorised transport (notably cars, motorbikes/mopeds etc) for the purpose of making everyday journeys.Although this active travel indicator doesn’t take into account intensity, any substitution of sedentary time for physical activity, even if it just results in low intensity activity, will increase energy expenditure. Minimising the amount of time spent being sedentary for extended periods is part of the CMOs’ physical activity guidelines. Sedentary behaviour can be reduced throughout the day, including at work, when travelling and at home. This can include replacing motorised travel with active travel such as cycling and walking.(3)(1) NICE Guidance, 2012. Physical activity: walking and cycling. Definition: The number of respondents aged 16 and over, with valid responses to questions on walking, walking for travel in bouts of 10 minutes or more on at least twelve days in the previous 28 days expressed as a percentage of the total number of respondents aged 16 and over.
Data source: Department for Transport
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/walking-and-cycling-statistics
Definition of numerator: Weighted number of valid respondents aged 16 and over, walking for travel in bouts of 10 minutes or more on at least twelve days in the previous four weeks.Active Lives Adult Survey data is collected November-November.
Source of numerator: Sport England (SE), Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS)
Definition of denominator: Weighted number of respondents aged 16 and over, with valid responses to questions on walking for travel.Active Lives survey data is collected November-November.
Source of denominator: Sport England (SE), Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS)
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100. The survey uses a 28-day reference period to record the number of days of walking for travel (of at least 10 minutes) and then divides the number of days by four to calculate a weekly average.At least 3 times per week is equal to at least 12 days in 28. The counts are weighted to be representative of the national population.
Confidence interval details: DfT published confidence intervals have been applied.The confidence intervals have been calculated using the Complex Samples module in SPSS. A sample plan was created for each of the weights, stratified to Local Authority. This plan was used to create tables of confidence intervals for each measure by analysis variable. This approach ensures that the confidence intervals accurately represent theeffectivesample size, rather than simply calculating them based on the achieved sample. This is needed because we have disproportionately sampled respondents by LA, which introduces selection bias. If we did not apply this correction our stated confidence intervals would be inaccurate (too narrow).
Caveats: The indicator reports the number of days on which walking for travel occurred. Due to the survey design, the number of trips and length of those trips is not available.DfT’s walking and cycling estimates do not use the intensity information, this means walking activity may not be at a high enough intensity to achieve benefits of physical activity.Results are grouped according to the area where respondents live, which may not be the same as the area where they walk or cycle.The values are calculated from the self-report Active Lives Adult Survey, which is subjective and is influenced by the respondent's ability to recall and assess their physical activity levels. Self-reported data may also be affected by respondent desire to confirm to expectations and social norms (e.g. smoking under-estimated and physical activity over-estimated). However, although this might affect the absolute values, this should not affect comparisons if the bias is consistent across populations.
Notes: The data is produced by the Department for Transport (DfT). DfT are  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/walking-and-cycling-statistics .Inequalities data has been published without confidence intervals. The lack of confidence intervals limits the ability to compare values and means that the significance RAG rating is unable to be applied within Fingertips.The source data, Active Lives Adult Survey, is a 'push-to-web' survey. It involves four postal mailouts designed to encourage participants to complete the survey online. A letter is sent to a household inviting up to two people per household to take part in the survey, either online or by requesting a paper version of the questionnaire.There is also the option to take part via telephone for those whose first language is not English, and for those who may find online or paper completion difficult, for example those who are visually impaired.The survey is ‘device-agnostic’ and can be completed on mobile or desktop devices. At the third mailing a paper questionnaire is sent out to maximise response rates. This flexibility means an easier, more convenient way for people to access the survey.The overall sample size will be around 190,000 people each year. The Active Lives Adult Survey provides around 500 interviews in most of the Local Authorities in England, though some key areas will involve surveying a bigger number of people. The achieved sample sizes for the Isles and Scilly and the City of London are around 250. These are far smaller than for other areas and therefore results for these areas may not be statistically robust. The unusually small populations of Isles of Scilly and City of London also mean that they are not directly comparable with other authorities. Therefore caution is needed when interpreting the results for these two areas. The survey sample is randomly selected from the Royal Mail’s Postal Address File (generally regarded as the “Gold Standard” for population surveys), which is a list of addresses in the UK that is maintained by the Royal Mail and has a very high coverage of private residential addresses.Data has been weighted to ONS population measures for geography and key demographics.For the Active Lives Adult Survey the weights correct for the disproportionate selection of addresses across local authorities and for the selection of adults and youths within households. They also adjust the achieved sample by month to control for seasonality. In addition, by weighting to population estimates and national estimates from the Annual Population Survey (2015-16), the weights should also reduce bias in the survey estimates. There were five stages to the weighting strategy: 1) calculation of an individual (within household) selection weight; 2) initial calibration to local authority and age/sex population estimates and month counts assuming a proportionate sample; 3) a second stage of calibration to the same measures as well as national estimates from the Annual Population Survey; 4) trimming of the second stage of calibration; and 5) a final adjustment to regional counts.

Indicator: Percentage reporting at least two long-term conditions, at least one of which is MSK related
Rationale: Musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions, such as osteoarthritis and back pain, are the leading cause of disability in adults in England[1]. People with a musculoskeletal condition are also likely to have another long-term condition. Four out of five people with osteoarthritis have at least one other long-term condition such as hypertension or cardiovascular disease[2]. This is partly because the prevalence of long-term conditions increases with rising age, and also because osteoarthritis shares common risk factors such as obesity with other long-term conditions. Among people living with multiple conditions, musculoskeletal conditions have been reported to cause the greatest impact on overall wellness, independence and quality of life due to increased pain and limited movement[3]. This indicator measures the prevalence of adult survey respondents who have a musculoskeletal condition and at least one additional long term health condition. It will enable public health advisors to determine the prevalence of multimorbidities in those suffering a musculoskeletal condition. Prevention and improvement of musculoskeletal health problems underpins living well and independently with multimorbidities. 1. Global, regional, and national incidence, prevalence, and years lived with disability for 310 diseases and injuries, 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015. (2016) 2. Breedveld FC (2004). Osteoarthritis – the impact of a serious disease. Rheumatology (Oxford) 43 Suppl 1: i4–i8. 3. Arthritis Research UK (2016). Musculoskeletal Conditions and Multimorbidity
Definition: The percentage of survey respondents aged 16+ reporting an MSK condition (arthritis or ongoing problem with back or joints) who also reported an additional long term condition.
Data source: NHS England, GP Patient Survey
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (based on GP Patient Survey data)
Definition of numerator:
Weighted count of those who answered "Arthritis or ongoing problem with back or joints" to the question "Which, if any, of the following long-term conditions do you have?" and who also responded that they had an additional long term condition (Q35 2018-2020, Q33 2021). The response “I do not have any long-term conditions” is ignored when counting the number of long-term conditions.

Participants were excluded if their local authority of residence was invalid or outside of England.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: Weighted count of survey participants who gave a valid response to GP Patient Survey question "Which, if any, of the following long-term conditions do you have?"(Q35 2018-2020, Q33 2021).Participants were excluded if their local authority of residence was invalid or outside of England.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology:
The prevalence is calculated by dividing the weighted count of the numerator by the weighted count of the denominator (with a valid answer), expressed as a percentage.

The denominator presented in the data download is the unweighted count of the number survey respondents who were included in the calculation of the statistic.

The number of respondents has been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights consider survey design and non-response rates. Weights are calibrated to population counts by GP practice as well as population counts by age and gender by CCG.

Full details on weighting within the GP Patient Survey can be found athttps://www.gp-patient.co.uk/surveysandreports
Confidence interval details:
An approximate 95% and 99.8% confidence interval was derived from 10,000 simulations of weighted prevalence for each area. Each prevalence simulation was calculated by

1 drawing a number of ‘successes’ randomly from a binomial distribution ~Bin(n,p) when n is the unweighted total population estimate and p is the weighted prevalence.

2 dividing the number of ‘successes’ by the unweighted total respondents

The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of these prevalence estimates were then found to give the 95% and 99.8% confidence intervals respectively.
Disclosure control: Values calculated with an unweighted or weighted numerator or denominator under 10 have been suppressed.
Caveats: This indicator is a self-reported prevalence from the GP Patient Survey it is not a diagnosed prevalence rate. The definition of "long term" is a condition lasting or expected to last 12 months or more.

Both responses are treated in the same way for identifying the number of long-term conditions.

April 2022 Revisions

Previous versions of this indicator definition incorrectly stated that the patient’s age needed to be valid for them to be included.

A minor error was identified with the calculation of the previously reported value for all persons, 16+ years, England in 2018. This has now been corrected. The has increased the estimated prevalence rate from 13.40% to 13.41%.

Indicator: Smoking prevalence in adults with a long-term mental health condition (aged 18 and over) - current smokers (GPPS) (old method)
Rationale: Smoking is the most important cause of preventable ill health and premature mortality in the UK. Smoking is a major risk factor for many diseases, such as lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart disease. It is also associated with cancers in other organs, including lip, mouth, throat, bladder, kidney, stomach, liver and cervix.Smoking is a modifiablebehavioural risk factor; effective tobacco control measures can reduce the prevalence of smoking in the population. Studies have shown that people with mental health conditions are more likely to smoke than the general public and that smoking rates increase with the severity of illness1. Indicator: Listeria incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of Listeria monocytogenes. Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis, a rare but potentially life-threatening disease. Healthy adults are unlikely to experience infection, however, Listeria infection (listeriosis) is dangerous to pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. Listeria is typically spread by contaminated foods. Listeria is an unusual bacterium because it can grow at low temperatures, including refrigeration temperatures of below 5°C. It is, however, killed by cooking food thoroughly and by pasteurisation. Local variation in numbers may reflect poor food management, variation in the numbers of people with weakened immune systems or different uptake of food safety messages in pregnant women. Areas with persistent significantly high rates in the absence of known outbreaks should investigate the cause and should enhance prevention advice as appropriate

Indicator: Scarlet fever notification rate/100,000 aged 0-9 yrs
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of scarlet fever cases. Scarlet fever is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or group A streptococci (GAS) bacteria. This infection is of public health importance because it is highly contagious and occasionally the GAS can cause serious and life threatening disease. Those most at risk of infection are children between the ages of two and eight years. Variation in incidence rate may reflect differences in underlying population.
Definition: Crude incidence rate of scarlet fever notifications in residents of England aged 0-9 years, per 100,000 population
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: UKHSA
Definition of numerator: A statutory notification of scarlet fever.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Notifications of Infectious Diseases (NOIDs)
Definition of denominator: Children 0-9 years old.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population.The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Byar's Method, benchmarking significance level is 95%. Byar’s method [1] gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for counts based on the assumption of a Poisson distribution. It is sufficiently accurate for counts as low as 5 (below 5, an exact method should be used, based on Poisson tables or the Chi-squared distribution). Byar’s method is the preferred method for calculating confidence intervals for counts, crude rates, indirectly standardised rates and indirectly standardised ratios, but it can also be used for proportions, as long as the proportions are small (much closer to zero than to one) as the Poisson distribution is a very good approximation to the Binomial distribution when the proportion being measured is small. The method is described in detail in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals. [2]1 Breslow NE, Day NE. Statistical methods in cancer research, volume II: The design and analysis of cohort studies. Lyon: International Agency for Research on Cancer, World Health Organization; 1987:69.2 Eayres D. Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals. York: APHO; 2008. http://www.apho.org.uk/resource/item.aspx?RID=48457

Therefore observed variation in rates may in part reflect variation in reporting, in addition to the variation in incidence of infection. A notification may be based on clinical symptoms and signs only, and therefore lacks specificity (e.g. a notification of a case of scarlet fever may be another illness).

Indicator: Alcohol-related conditions: admission episodes (all primary and secondary diagnoses)
Rationale:
Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.
The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol. This indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.

The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (1) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (2). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).

The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.

Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence. The methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

Mumps is a vaccine preventable viral infection which can occasionally cause severe complications, including swelling of the ovaries (oophoritis), swelling of the testes (orchitis), aspetic meningitis and deafness. Variation in incidence rate may reflect differences in underlying population including variation in uptake of vaccination. High rates of mumps should prompt a review of routine immunisation uptake and vaccination of high risk groups.

Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Mumps Enhanced Surveillance Programme

Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates

All infants and their families are eligible to receive a visit led by a health visitor within the first two weeks from birth, which is known as the New Birth Visit (NBV). This metric is designed to measure what proportion of infants receive a timely NBV. This visit forms part of the Healthy Child Programme (HCP), and is important to ensure a continuum of support following on from visits by a midwife, which usually end at day 10. This visit is also important in identifying any development issues with the infant (including early referral to a specialist team where needed), to promote sensitive parenting, to provide safe sleeping advice, to support feeding and to discuss concerns and worries, including maternal mental health.
More information on the 'Healthy Child Programme' can be found here:  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/healthy-child-programme-0-to-19-health-visitor-and-school-nurse-commissioning  , and information on the 'Rapid Review to Update Evidence for the Healthy Child Programme 0 to 5' can be found here:  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/healthy-child-programme-rapid-review-to-update-evidence 
Carrying out the new birth visit within 14 days means that any problems can be identified early, and interventions may be more successful the earlier they are put in place. For example, women may exclusively breastfeed for longer, if appropriate advice is given early enough to enable breastfeeding to be successfully established.
The health visitor service delivery metrics for local authorities are currently published in ODS data tables:  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/child-and-maternal-health-statistics#health-visitor-service-delivery  . Local authorities have asked the Child and Maternal Health Intelligence team (via their Centre Leads) to put the metrics into Fingertips so that they can see the automated colour coding for benchmarking purposes and so that Fingertips will automatically show trends over time. This visualisation functionality of Fingertips will help commissioners and health professionals to track how many families in their local area have received the New Birth Visit on time, and assist with planning, commissioning and improving local services.
Definition: The proportion of infants receiving a new birth visit (NBV) by a Health Visitor within 14 days (two weeks) of birth.
Data source: OHID, based on interim reporting data for universal health visiting services
Definition of numerator: The number of infants that receive a face to face New Birth Visit (NBV) within 14 days by a Health Visitor
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), Child and maternal health statistics - Health visitor service delivery (via interim national reporting process)
Definition of denominator: The total number of infants who turned 30 days in the reference period (financial year), at a resident population level. The denominator is 30 days and not 14 days because a new birth visit is valid up to 30 days. This metric shows visits carried out by 14 days. Visits carried out between 15 and 30 days are reported separately here:  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/child-and-maternal-health-statistics#health-visitor-service-delivery .
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), Child and maternal health statistics - Health visitor service delivery (via interim national reporting process)
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100. A process of estimation was applied to any local authority data where a return was submitted for only 3 quarters or data failed validation for a single quarter. An estimated numerator for the missing quarter was calculated as an average of the numerators of the other 3 quarters, and the same for an estimated denominator. Where a numerator or denominator has been submitted as 0, no estimation has been performed. An annual numerator and denominator have been calculated based on the estimated numerator and denominator and the known numerators and denominators.
Caveats:
Two stages of validation are carried out
The number of infants due a New Birth Visit should be greater than or equal to the number of infants who received a New Birth Visit
The number of infants due a New Birth Visit must be within +20% / -20% of the resident population of children aged 0 of that particular area.
Notes: Hammersmith & Fulham Council has identified an error when reporting the proportion of New Birth Visits completed within 14 days for 2024/25. The data has therefore been removed. No other changes have been made.Hackney & City of London and Cornwall & Isles of Scilly make joint data submissions. The move to residence-based reporting has necessitated joint working of neighbouring local authorities to ensure children on authority borders are included in the correct return, however it is not known how successfully this is being implemented in every area.
Impact of COVID-19: Virtual contacts were counted as valid, mandated service delivery for all data for 2020 to 2021 during the period of the pandemic response

Indicator: Proportion of infants receiving a 6 to 8 week review
Rationale:
The 6 to 8 week review is an opportunity for support with breastfeeding if required, and allows an assessment of the mother's mental health, as well as reinforcing the discussions and messages from the new birth visit. It is an opportunity to ensure the mother has had a six-week postnatal check, and that the infant has received the infant physical examination, as well as a reminder of the importance of the vaccinations that take place in the first few months. Any difficulties the mother has had in receiving benefits she is entitled to can be discussed and support offered.

Indicator: Proportion of children receiving a 12-month review
Rationale:
All children should receive a review by a health visitor led team shortly before they turn one year. This allows for assessment of the baby's physical, emotional and social needs in the context of their family, including predictive risk factors, and provides an opportunity for both parents to talk about any concerns that they may have about their baby's health, as well as a reminder of the importance of the vaccinations at around one year. It also allows monitoring of the baby's growth, and discussions on weaning, oral health and home safety (particularly relevant as babies are now sitting independently, rolling over, and may be starting to walk). In addition, it presents an opportunity to discuss preconception health before any future pregnancy. A review between 9 and 12 months ensures any issues can be identified early and referrals made as appropriate. However it is accepted that for many reasons these reviews may be a little late and the content is still of value. This metric therefore shows the proportion of children who have a 12-month review on time or slightly late (by 15 months).

Indicator: Hospital admissions for dental caries (0 to 5 years)
Rationale: Dental caries (tooth decay) and periodontal (gum) disease are the most common dental pathologies in the UK. Tooth decay has become less common over the past two decades, but is still a significant health and social problem. It results in destruction of the crowns of teeth and frequently leads to pain and infection. Dental disease is more common in deprived areas compared to affluent communities. The indicator is a good direct measure of dental health and an indirect, proxy measure of child health and diet.
Definition: Finished consultant episodes for dental caries among children aged 0 to 5, rate per 100,000.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Population Health Analysis, Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Finished consultant episodes for all persons aged 0 to5 years with primary operation F09 or F10 and primary diagnosis codesK021, K025, K028, K029, K040, K045, K046 or K047.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Definition of denominator: Local authority figures: Mid-year population estimates: Single year of age and sex for local authorities in England and Wales; estimated resident population (0 to 5 years of age).
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate per 100,000 population aged 0 to 5 years
Confidence interval details: 95% confidence intervals are calculated using the Byar's method
Disclosure control:
From 2016/17-2018/19 onwards, all sub-national counts are rounded to the nearest 5, and counts of 1-7 are suppressed. Rates are calculated using rounded counts, and confidence intervals are calculated using unrounded counts. Values relating to City of London and Isles of Scilly have been combined with Hackney and Cornwall.
For time points prior to 2016/17-2018/19, values relating to City of London and Isles of Scilly have been combined with Hackney and Cornwall.All values between 1 and 5 have been suppressed and, where necessary, other LAs and comparators have also been suppressed in order to prevent possible disclosure and disclosure by differencing.
Caveats:
NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust in 2023 to 2024. The Trust reported a large proportion of missing values in the sex field between October 2023 and March 2024. NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust in 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025. The Trust reported a large proportion of missing values in the sex field, affecting approximately 40% of Admitted Patient Care (APC) records in 2023 to 2024 and 56% of APC records in 2024 to 2025. As a result, sex breakdowns based on Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) data have not been published for areas where more than 10% of records had missing sex values. Areas where between 1% and 10% of records had missing sex values have been flagged and should be interpreted with caution.No assumptions can be made about the method of anaesthesia provided for these procedures but it is likely that the majority of episodes involved general anaesthetic. It is possible that different coding protocols are applied in some sites and this could explain some of the variation. In some instances the data are an underestimate of the number of episodes, as the Community Dental Service may provide the extraction service in hospital premises but the episodes may not be included in hospital data recording. NHS England has identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust (RXC) in 2018/19 only. Approximately 85,000 records erroneously had all diagnosis and procedure codes removed. Therefore, PHE did not publish values for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 10% of patients from that area with missing codes from RXC in the current year (2018/19). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients with missing codes from RXC have been flagged to be treated with caution. For more details of the issue, see https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/hospital-episode-statistics/the-processing-cycle-and-hes-data-quality#hes-data-quality-notes

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Frimley Health Foundation Trust in 2022 to 2023. Frimley Health Foundation Trust did not submit HES data for June 2022 to March 2023. Therefore, values have not been published based on HES data for areas that had over 10% of hospital patients from an area treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022) have been flagged to be treated with caution.In 2023, NHS England announced a https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdigital.nhs.uk%2Fdata-and-information%2Ffind-data-and-publications%2Fstatement-of-administrative-sources%2Fmethodological-changes%2Fimpact-of-changes-to-recording-of-same-day-emergency-care-activity-to-hospital-episode-statistics-hes-data&data=05%7C02%7CZachary.Gleisner%40dhsc.gov.uk%7C4c6b429dca6744c7978908dc38602955%7C61278c3091a84c318c1fef4de8973a1c%7C1%7C0%7C638447232861632065%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=OekajVwhFKS5YNnlA%2BBjY%2FXTplZUBIqWIfJFUeWr7Jw%3D&reserved=0 to require Trusts to report Same Day Emergency Care (SDEC) to the Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) by July 2024. Early adopter sites began to report SDEC to ECDS from 2021/22, with other Trusts changing their reporting in 2022/23 or 2023/24. Some Trusts had previously reported this activity as part of the Admitted Patient Care data set, and moving to report to ECDS may reduce the number of admissions reported for this indicator. NHSE have advised it is not possible accurately to identify SDEC in current data flows, but the impact of the change is expected to vary by diagnosis, with indicators related to injuries and external causes potentially most affected.

When considering if SDEC recording practice has reduced the number of admissions reported for this indicator at local level, please refer to the https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdigital.nhs.uk%2Fdata-and-information%2Fdata-collections-and-data-sets%2Fdata-sets%2Femergency-care-data-set-ecds%2Fsame-day-emergency-care&data=05%7C02%7CZachary.Gleisner%40dhsc.gov.uk%7C4c6b429dca6744c7978908dc38602955%7C61278c3091a84c318c1fef4de8973a1c%7C1%7C0%7C638447232861644348%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=5YyDnaEGpaNWyj4veJBvLHXpCGa55KhwqPgYiUceVDI%3D&reserved=0 of sites who have reported when they began to report SDEC to ECDS.
Notes: OHID and NHS England, through the NHS Outcomes Framework, both publish data on the extraction of teeth for children (resulting from tooth decay, as well other reasons) in an acute setting. To provide greater consistency and coherence, the respective organisations have agreed to use common age groupings across the two releases and agree a common set of procedure and caries diagnosis codes in their definitions for future publications. These new age groups are being used for the first time in the 2017-18 data, but unfortunately can't be applied to earlier years due to potential disclosure issues with previously published data.Following Census 2021, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) carried out reconciliation and rebasing of the mid year population estimates (MYE) it produces. This process happens every 10 years following the census. The official population estimates for mid 2012 to mid 2020 have been revised, to incorporate the data now available from Census 2021. The data for this indicator has been revised to use the rebased population estimates from 2012 onwards.
Impact of COVID-19:

Indicator: Mortality from causes considered preventable (aged under 75)
Rationale:
The basic concept of preventable mortality is that deaths are considered preventable if, in the light of the understanding of the determinants of health at the time of death, all or most deaths from the underlying cause could potentially be avoided by public health and primary prevention interventions (that is, before the onset of diseases or injuries, to reduce incidence).
Preventable mortality overlaps with, but is not the same as treatable mortality, which includes causes of deaths that can be mainly avoided through timely and effective healthcare interventions, including secondary prevention and treatment (that is, after the onset of disease, to reduce case-fatality). Preventable mortality and treatable mortality are the two components of avoidable mortality, as defined by the Office for National Statistics. The inclusion of this indicator sends out a clear signal of the importance of prevention as well as treatment in reducing avoidable deaths.
Definition: Standardised mortality ratio (SMR) for deaths from causes considered preventable, aged under 75
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: The total number of deaths from causes considered preventable among persons aged under 75 years.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract
Definition of denominator: The sum of the age-specific (aggregated into five year age bands 0 to 4, 5 to 9 through to 70 to 74) number of deaths from causes considered preventable that would be expected if the local area experienced the same age-specific mortality rates as for England
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Mortality data by five year age group were extracted from annual files supplied to Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). These were deaths registered in the calendar years 2019 to 2023 from causes considered preventable for persons aged under 75 years. Deaths from causes considered preventable were classified by underlying cause of death recorded as ICD codes A00 to A09, A35, A36, A80, A37, A39, A40.3, A41.3, A49.2, A50 to A60, A63, A64, B01, B05, B06, B15 to B19, B20 to B24, B50 to B54, G00.0, G00.1, A15 to A19 (at 50% of total count), B90 (at 50% of total count), J65 (at 50% of total count), C00 to C16, C22, C33 to C34, C45, C43, C67, C53 (at 50% of total count), D50 to D53, E10 to E14 (at 50% of total count), I71, (at 50% of total count), I10 to I13 (at 50% of total count), I15 (at 50% of total count), I20 to I25 (at 50% of total count), I60 to I69 (at 50% of total count), I70 (at 50% of total count), I73.9 (at 50% of total count), J09 to J11, J13 to J14, J40 to J44, J60 to J64, J66 to J70, J82, J92, A33, A34, Q00, Q01, Q05, V01 to V99, W00 to X39, X46 to X59, X66 to X84, Y16 to Y34, X86 to Y09, U50.9, E24.4, F10, G31.2, G62.1, G72.1, I42.6, K29.2, K70, K85.2, K86.0, Q86.0, R78.0, X45, X65, Y15, K73, K74.0 to K74.2, K74.6, F11 to F16, F18, F19, X40 to X44, X85, Y10 to Y14, X60 to X64, U07.1 to U07.2, registered in the respective calendar years, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, through to 70 to 74). For England and local authoritiesDeaths were allocated to the deceased's lower tier local authority (LTLA) of usual residence using the May 2024 version of the National Statistics Postcode Lookup. Population data are mid-year population estimates for LTLAs, by quinary age group, supplied by ONS for 2019 to 2023. LTLA deaths and population estimates were aggregated to higher geographies using standard geographical lookup tables obtained from ONS Geography.For MSOAsDeaths were allocated to the deceased's lower layer super output area (LSOA) of usual residence using the May 2024 version of the National Statistics Postcode Lookup. Population data are mid-year population estimates for LSOAs, by quinary age group, supplied by ONS for 2019 to 2022, and using mid-2023 LSOA population estimates calculated by OHID. These are based on mid-year estimates for LSOAs for 2022, published by ONS. These have been aged on a year and then constrained to mid-year population estimates for 2023 local authorities, published by ONS. LSOA deaths and population estimates were aggregated to MSOA using standard geographical lookup tables obtained from ONS Geography.Expected deaths were calculated by applying age-specific death rates for England in 2019 to 2023 to each area's population. SMRs were calculated by dividing the observed total deaths in the area by the expected deaths and multiplying by 100.
Standard population/values: Age-specific mortality rates in England for the 5 year period
Confidence interval details: 95 percent confidence limits were calculated using the Byar's method for rates. For more details, please refer to the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Standardisation/ISRatios.html .

Rounding: Counts and denominators have been rounded to 2 decimal places, with values and confidence intervals rounded to 5 decimal places.
Impact of COVID-19: As this indicator includes the year 2020, deaths due to COVID-19 will be included. For other underlying causes, these may include deaths where COVID-19 was also involved and mentioned on the death certificate.

Indicator: Listeria 5-year incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of Listeria monocytogenes. Listeria monocytogenes causes listeriosis, a rare but potentially life-threatening disease. Healthy adults are unlikely to experience infection, however, Listeria infection (listeriosis) is dangerous to pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. Listeria is typically spread by contaminated foods. Listeria is an unusual bacterium because it can grow at low temperatures, including refrigeration temperatures of below 5°C. It is, however, killed by cooking food thoroughly and by pasteurisation. Local variation in numbers may reflect poor food management, variation in the numbers of people with weakened immune systems or different uptake of food safety messages in pregnant women. Areas with persistent significantly high rates in the absence of known outbreaks should investigate the cause and should enhance prevention advice as appropriate
Definition: Crude incidence rate of confirmed Listeria monocytogenes reported in residents of England, per 100,000 population over a 5 year period
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: National Enhanced Surveillance for Listeria in residents of England and Wales, UKHSA
Definition of numerator: 5 year count of laboratory confirmed cases of Listeria monocytogenes
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), National Enhanced Listeria Surveillance Programme
Definition of denominator: Sum of annual population over a 5 year period
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: 5-year count of laboratory confirmed case of measles divided by the sum of the 5-year denominator, multipled by 100,000. Confidence intervals calculated using exact poisson.
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: National surveillance data includes cases identified by laboratory reports or those reported by Health Protection Teams where it is assumed that the HPT has been alerted by a laboratory report, but where national surveillance does not have access to the original report.

Indicator: School readiness: percentage of children achieving at least the expected level in communication and language skills at the end of Reception
Rationale: The 2018 to 2019 remit letter states that it expects the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities to drive improvements in outcomes at scale with a particular focus on child health speech, language and communication needs and school readiness.Disparities in child language capabilities are recognisable in the second year of life and are clearly having an impact by the time children enter school. If left unsupported, these children are more likely to fail to achieve their full potential. The Office for Health Improvement and Disparities has been allocated funding to train Health Visitors in the use of a new communication and language assessment tool to identify problems at 2 to 2 and a half years, and to arrange interventions where children are below expected level of development in this area. As part of the Department for Education (DfE) plan for improving social mobility through education, their ambition to close the ‘word gap’ focusses on the development of key early language and literacy skills for pupils who are disadvantaged or not achieving their full potential.The Early Years Foundation Stage Profile is used each year to inform plans for child development, informing Key Stage 1 teachers and parents about each child's development and needs. Data from the communication and language early learning goal check gives teachers and service planners information on children’s ability to communicate effectively, and whether additional intervention is required to enable them to meet the standard. This is an outcome indicator used to measure the impact of early years services (including the universal and non universal aspects of health visiting) and also regarded as an important social determinant of longer term health, education and life chances.
Specific rationale: School Readiness: The percentage of children achieving at least an expected level of development within both communication and language early learning goals (listening, attention and understanding ELG and speaking ELG).
Definition: Children defined as having reached at least the expected level of development in communication and language skills at the end of the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) as a percentage of all eligible children. For children to have achieved at least the expected level means that they achieved ‘expected’ or ‘exceeded’ levels of development within all three communication and language early learning goals (listening and attention, understanding, speaking).
Data source: Department for Education
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/statistics-early-years-foundation-stage-profile
Definition of numerator: Number of children defined as having reached at least the expected level of development in communication and language skills at the end of the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS). For children to have achieved at least the expected level means that they achieved ‘expected’ or ‘exceeded’ levels of development within both communication and language early learning goals (listening, attention and understanding ELG and speaking ELG).
Source of numerator: Department for Education (DfE), Early years foundation stage (EYFS) profile results
Definition of denominator: Number of children eligible for the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) Profile
Source of denominator: Department for Education (DfE), Early years foundation stage (EYFS) profile results
Methodology: Crude percentage: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 100.
Confidence interval details: Wilson Score method used
Disclosure control: Data is publicly available via  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/statistics-early-years-foundation-stage-profile
Notes: EYFS reforms were introduced in September 2021, as part of those reforms, the EYFS profile was significantly revised. It is therefore not possible to directly compare 2021 to 2022 assessment outcomes with earlier years. The 2019 to 2020 and 2020 to 2021 data collections were cancelled due to coronavirus (COVID19). For further information please refer to the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/statistics-early-years-foundation-stage-profile

Indicator: Estimated prevalence of common mental disorders: % of population aged 16 & over
Specific rationale: This indicator gives local health and care systems an estimate of the prevalence of common mental disorders in their area to support planning of preventative mental health interventions and mental health care and services, including access to psychological therapies (IAPT). NHS England has a set a target for CCGs of treating 25% of all persons with CMD in IAPT services. This indicator replaces the existing indicator 90853: Estimated prevalence of common mental disorders: % of population aged 16-74. 90853 provides a prevalence estimate for 2014/15 based on 2000 survey results (Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey - APMS). APMS now provides data on mental disorders in persons aged 75 and over (previously up to 75 years) and additionally the population of interest for IAPT services includes older people. The new indicator therefore provides a more current and practical prevalence estimate. Although there are some estimates of specific CMD at a local level (see below), there are no other validated estimates of the prevalence of all CMD.The indicator is designed to estimate local prevalence of CMD using national survey estimates applied to local demography.The indicator is aimed at local health and care policymakers, practitioners and intelligence specialists providing, planning and commissioning services aiming to reduce mental illness and improve the mental health care for people with CMD. It does this by giving an estimate of the absolute and relative need. It will also be used by national IAPT leads to aid in future IAPT planning cycles. The indicator is intended to support action to improve the mental health and life opportunities of those living with CMD by enabling local policy makers, service providers and commissioners to understand the numbers of people with CMD. Further details regarding IAPT can be found https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/common-mental-disorders/supporting-information/IAPT and a glossary of terms is provided https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/common-mental-disorders/supporting-information/Glossary .Links to further mental health related resources are provided  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/healthy-ageing/supporting-information/mental-health .
Definition: The estimated proportion of the population aged 16 & over who have a common mental disorder (CMD), where CMD is defined as any type of depression or anxiety.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Indicator computed by PHE (based on 2014 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (APMS) source data owned by NatCen and NHS Digital)
Definition of numerator: For each LTLA, UTLA, CCG & STP, the numerator is the estimate of the total number of people (aged 16 and over) expected to have a CMD. This is calculated by aggregating the numbers of people (aged 16 and over) expected to have a CMD in LSOAs within each CCG/STP/LTLA/UTLA.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (APMS)
Definition of denominator: For each LTLA, UTLA, CCG & STP, the denominator is the number of people aged 16 & over.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator to give a percentage.
Confidence interval details: Assume each deprivation/age/sex prevalence proportion follows a binomial distribution. Simulate prevalence proportions using the sampled CMD prevalence and 95% CIs from 2014 APMS to determine distribution parameters. On each simulation, the prevalence proportions are randomly sampled from the assumed binomial distributions and the indicator is calculated based on the randomly sampled values. Perform 10,000 iterations. The indicator is calculated 10,000 times forming a distribution of random samples of the indicator. From this we can take the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles to be estimates of the lower and upper limits, respectively of the 95% confidence interval for the indicator.
Caveats: This indicator gives an estimate of how many people aged 16 and over in the general population are expected to have CMD in a given area. A CMD is defined as any type of depression or anxiety.  This is an estimate of the true prevalence and is also likely an under-estimate: (1) estimates are calculated using CMD prevalence proportions based on individuals living in private households, which excludes those who are homeless and those living in institutional settings (e.g. care homes, prisons) who are likely to have poorer mental health; (2) the method uses the latest APMS, 2014, to calculate reference prevalence proportions which are applied to current local populations and it is likely that prevalence proportions have increased since 2014.  The 2014 APMS national survey used to estimate initial CMD prevalence proportions was of 7,500 individuals, where a larger sample would have provided more robust and precise estimates. This is most applicable for estimates in local areas that are more deprived with younger populations, as this was an under-sampled demographic in APMS. Further details on survey methodology can be found in the APMS documentation on the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/adult-psychiatric-morbidity-survey/adult-psychiatric-morbidity-survey-survey-of-mental-health-and-wellbeing-england-2014 .  This indicator is calculated using a simple method based on age, sex and deprivation. There may be other local factors which mean that true prevalence is different from the indicator value. NHS Digital publish CMD prevalence estimates by Government Office Region as part of the APMS analysis.These are estimated directly from the survey results and are available on the  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/adult-psychiatric-morbidity-survey/adult-psychiatric-morbidity-survey-survey-of-mental-health-and-wellbeing-england-2014 . PHE Government Office Region CMD estimates broadly give a similar picture to those estimated directly from the APMS, however there are some differences particularly for the South West region. These differences are expected, as the PHE method is simple and adjusts for few factors and therefore does not capture all the variation in CMD prevalence.The indicator is not standardised for age. Age is an input variable in the construction of the metric and accounts for a proportion of the variation between areas. Standardising for age would tend to make all CCGs, STPs, UTLs and LTLAs revert to the national rate.The indicator improves when the indicator value decreases.

Indicator: Healthy life expectancy at 65
Rationale: This indicator provides an important summary measure of the mortality and morbidity in those aged 65 years and over. Healthy life expectancy shows the years a person can expect to live in good health (rather than in poor health).
Definition:
A measure of the average number of years people aged 65 years can expect to live in ‘good’ general health. For a given area and time period, it estimates how long a person aged 65 years would be expected to live in good general health, if current mortality rates and levels of good health remained constant throughout their remaining life.
Figures are calculated from deaths from all causes, mid year population estimates, and self-reported general health status, based on data aggregated over a 3-year period. Estimates reflect the prevalence of good health and mortality among those living in an area in each time period.
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectanciesuk/between2011to2013and2022to2024 ; Office for National Statistics (ONS), https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthinequalities/datasets/healthylifeexpectancybynationalareadeprivationenglandtimeseries
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths registered in the respective calendar years for ages 65 and over and the prevalence of people aged 65 and over reporting good or very good health.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract, Annual Population Survey (APS) and English Census (2011 and 2021) data
Definition of denominator: ONS mid year population estimates for ages 65 years and over for the respective calendar years, Annual Population Survey and 2011 and 2021 English censuses
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates, Annual Population Survey (APS) and English Census (2011 and 2021) data
Methodology:
Healthy life expectancy is calculated by abridged Sullivan life tables, for males and females separately using 5-year age bands. A Sullivan life table extends the traditional life table by partitioning years lived into favourable and unfavourable health states to provide an estimate of healthy life expectancy for males and females at birth and each geographical unit. In addition to the number of deaths and mid year population estimates used in a traditional life table, the Sullivan life table also incorporates the proportion of people reporting their general health as good or very good. In response to the question “How is your health in general; would you say it was…” responses “Very good” and “Good” are categorised as ‘Good’ health and “Fair”, “Bad” or “Very bad” as ‘Not Good’ health. A life table template which illustrates the method used to calculate healthy life expectancy (and 95 percent confidence intervals) can be found on the  https://www.ons.gov.uk/file?uri=/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/datasets/healthstatelifeexpectancytemplate/current/healthstatelifeexpectanciestemplate.xls 

Estimates of health status are primarily based on self-reported data from the Annual Population Survey, supplemented with data from the 2011 and 2021 Censuses. Modelling and imputation are used to improve estimates for age groups where survey data are limited, particularly for those over 85.

Further details on the methodology can be found via the  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectanciesuk/between2011to2013and2022to2024
Frequency: Annual. ONS typically release local authority data in December and national deprivation deciles data in March.
Confidence interval details: The method used has been documented by  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/methodologies/healthstatelifeexpectanciesukqmi2020to2022
Disclosure control: Disclosure control not applied as the estimates do not reveal any information about individuals.
Caveats: The Annual Population Survey excludes residents of communal establishments such as care homes but does include NHS housing and students in halls of residence where inclusion takes place at their parents’ address.

Indicator: Reoffending levels: percentage of offenders who reoffend
Rationale: Tackling a persons offending behaviour is often intrinsically linked to their physical and mental health, and in particular any substance misuse issues. This outcome therefore cannot be addressed in isolation. Offenders often also experience significant health inequalities that will need to be identified, examined and addressed locally in partnership with organisations across the criminal justice system. Furthermore, a large proportion of families with multiple needs are managed through the criminal justice system, and their issues are inter-generational. Reoffending therefore has a wide impact on the health and well being of individuals, their children and families, and the communities they live in.The consequences of tackling offending and reoffending will benefit a wide range of service agencies and enhance their outcomes. Public health is a crucial part of a multi-agency approach to reducing reoffending, which includes police, courts, prisons, probation, community safety partners, social services, housing and education at a local level.
Definition: The percentage of offenders who reoffend. Annual figures are formed by taking a weighted average of the four preceding three month offender cohorts.
Data source: OHID, based on Ministry of Justice data

Definition of numerator: The number of reoffenders.A reoffender is an offender who, after entering the cohort in a three month period, commits a reoffence that leads to a court conviction, caution, reprimand or warning within the one year followup period , or within a further six months to allow the offence to be proven in court.This annual figure is formed by combining the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. I.e. for the year 2016 to 2017, the number of reoffenders is gathered from the following quarterly cohorts; Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017.The annual figure is provided by Ministry of Justice in their https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics collection, available on GOV.UK.
Source of numerator: Ministry of Justice (MoJ), Proven reoffending statistics
Definition of denominator: The number of offenders.This annual figure is formed by combining the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. I.e. for the year 2016 to 2017, the number of offenders is gathered from the following quarterly cohorts; Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017.The annual figure is provided by Ministry of Justice in their https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics collection, available on GOV.UK.
Source of denominator: Ministry of Justice (MoJ), Proven reoffending statistics
Methodology: Percentage: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 100. The percentage is calculated by taking the sum of the number of reoffenders in the four quarter cohorts that make up the respective year, divided by the sum of the number of offenders in each of those quarterly cohorts.The calculation is provided by Ministry of Justice in their https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics collection, available on GOV.UK.The proven reoffending statistics, in which this indicator is based on, had a methodology change, as announced in ‘ https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/519644/proven-reoffending-consultation-response.pdf ’. The main changes to the methodology were: •Changing to a three month cohort instead of the previous twelve month cohort. •A change from calendar year to financial year for annual results.In addition, the data source used to compile the statistics has changed from October 2015 following probation services reforms. For more information on the impact of these changes, please see:  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/658380/how-the-measure-of-reoffending-has-changed-and-the-effect-of-these-changes.pdf .
Frequency: Annual.Data for this indicator are calculated by summing up the counts for the number of offenders and the number of reoffenders that are recorded in the four quarterly cohorts that take place within the financial year. As an example, for the year 2016 to 2017, the four quarterly cohorts that are included are Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017.Ministry of Justice advise to use annual data as a method of proven reoffending rather than using quarterly data, as quarterly data would not be possible to produce for some areas due to small cohort sizes. Annual data is also preferred to allow comparisons across years without the variability of the quarterly data.
Disclosure control: Isles of Scilly data are suppressed due to low numbers. However, numerator and denominator data for Isles of Scilly are published by Ministry of Justice.In keeping with the disclosure control techniques employed by Ministry of Justice, proportions and averages based on less than 30 offenders are removed as they make data unreliable for interpretation.
Caveats:
Data for ICBs are estimated from local authority data. In most cases ICBs are coterminous with local authorities, so the ICB figures are precise. In cases where local authorities cross ICB boundaries, the local authority data are proportionally split between ICBs, based on population located in each ICB.

The affected ICBs are:

    • Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire;
    • Bedfordshire, Luton and Milton Keynes;
    • Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West;
    • Cambridgeshire and Peterborough;
    • Frimley;
    • Hampshire and Isle of Wight;
    • Hertfordshire and West Essex;
    • Humber and North Yorkshire;
    • Lancashire and South Cumbria;
    • Norfolk and Waveney;
    • North East and North Cumbria;
    • Suffolk and North East Essex;
    • Surrey Heartlands;
    • Sussex;
    • West Yorkshire. Previously, proven reoffending statistics were produced based on a 12 month cohort. However, following a https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/519644/proven-reoffending-consultation-response.pdf , it was decided to switch to a 3 month cohort.Since the change from a 12 month to a three month cohort, annual cohorts are formed by combining the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. An individual offender, and their offences, can therefore appear up to four times within a single annual cohort (one from each quarter). This can lead to an increase of reoffending rates for the annual cohort compared to the old methodology based on a 12 month cohort, since prolific offenders and their offences may be counted multiple times. Additionally, since any individual three month cohort contains fewer offenders than a 12 month cohort would, three month cohorts are subject to greater statistical fluctuations. Therefore, their results are likely to vary more than those of 12 month cohorts.The group of offenders whose offending behaviour is proven are likely to be a subgroup of all active offenders. The Offending, Crime and Justice Survey (2003) estimated that around one in ten people in England and Wales aged between 10 and 65 had committed an offence in the previous 12 months, which translates into approximately 3.8 million people. This compares to around 629,000 offenders in the April 2005 to March 2006 cohort used to measure proven reoffending, underlining that the offenders whose proven reoffending behaviour is presented in the Proven Reoffending Statistics Quarterly Bulletin are a small and probably unrepresentative sample of the population of all active offenders.For information, offences are counted as proven reoffences if they meet all of the following criteria:• They are recordable. Not all offences are on the PNC, and more recordable offences than non-recordable offences are entered. Analysis comparing offences proven at court with offences recorded on the PNC suggests the most common offences that are not recorded relate to motor vehicles, e.g. using a motor vehicle whilst uninsured against third-party risks, speeding offences or keeping a vehicle on the highway without a driving licence, or television licence fee evasion.• They were committed in England or Wales.• They are offences that were prosecuted by the police. PNC data are collected and entered by the police, and offences prosecuted by the police are likely to be recorded more comprehensively on the PNC than offences prosecuted by other organisations. For example, benefit fraud is prosecuted by the Department for Work and Pensions. Therefore, benefit fraud offences may be poorly represented on the PNC.• Offences are only counted if they are proven through caution, reprimands or final warnings (for juveniles) and court convictions. Offences that are not proven, or which are met with other responses from the Criminal Justice System, are not counted.• The offence is not a breach offence, i.e. breach of a court order, since we are only interested in new offences. If an offender commits multiple offences on the same day, each offence will be counted separately. For example, if an offender commits three offences on the same day, this will count as three reoffences.The data required for measuring proven reoffending are based on a range of sources (prison data, probation data, young offenders in secure accommodation and criminal records from the Police National Computer) from a range of agencies (Her Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service, the Youth Justice Board, local authorities and the National Police Improvement Agency). These figures have been derived from administrative IT systems that, as with any large scale recording system, are subject to possible errors with data entry and processing.For more information on data quality, please see the Data Quality section in the https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1071735/Guide-to-proven-reoffending-Apr22.pdf .

Indicator: Pertussis incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of pertussis (Whooping cough) cases. Pertussis is a vaccine preventable bacterial infection which can cause serious and life threatening complications. At highest risk are infants under 6 months of age. However, the majority of cases occur in individuals aged 15 years and over. Variation in incidence rate may reflect differences in uptake of vaccination. High rates of pertussis should prompt a review of routine immunisation uptake and vaccination of high risk groups.
Definition: Crude incidence rate of laboratory confirmed pertussis cases per 100,000 population
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: New cases of laboratory confirmed pertussis infection
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Respiratory and Vaccine Preventable Bacteria Reference Unit (RVPBRU)
Definition of denominator: Population who reside in area
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Confidence intervals have been calculated by UKHSA using R and are based on the exact Poisson method (cil denominator count, poisson per (100000)) (for more information go to www.stata.com)
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: Every effort is made to ensure accuracy and completeness of the data. UKHSA Pertussis Enhanced Surveillance Programme sources information from the UKHSA Second Generation Surveillance System and National and Reference Laboratories. a) Underreporting: Clinical cases of pertussis may not be tested and if they are tested and test positive, may not be reported to PHE. b) Misclassification of residence. Cases may be assigned incorrectly to a LA if postcode information is missing. If postcode of residency is not available, residency will be assigned according to GP practice or requesting laboratory if GP is not known. c) Outbreaks: Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. d) The data presented here may differ from data from other sources, including from NOIDS (Notification of Infectious Diseases) and CIMS (UKHSA public health management system). e) The sum of the local authority data may not equal the regional and overall England data because for some individuals only the region or country of residence is available.
