Indicator: Disability-free life expectancy at 65
Rationale: DFLE at age 65 years is an important summary measure of health and has implications for: quality of life; fitness for work given increases in the State Pension age; personal finances; social connections and contributions; health and care services; and the wider economy. This indicator complements the proposed indicator of healthy life expectancy at age 65 to measure progress on the government's 'Ageing Grand Challenge' mission to "ensure that people can enjoy at least 5 extra healthy, independent years of life by 2035, while narrowing the gap between the experience of the richest and poorest." (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/industrial-strategy-the-grand-challenges/industrial-strategy-the-grand-challenges#ageing-society).It is also a key measure to monitor progress on PHE's productive healthy ageing policy based on the World Health Organisation's healthy ageing framework ( http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/186463/9789240694811_eng.pdf;jsessionid=A23EAC34980DC7F2B797BDF882EEF975?sequence=1 ).It has also informed the 'Work, health and disability green paper: improving lives' joint strategy between the Department of Work and Pensions and the Department of Healt and Social Care ( https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/work-health-and-disability-improving-lives/work-health-and-disability-green-paper-improving-lives ), and can be used to inform follow-up initiatives at national, regional and local level.
Definition: Disability free life expectancy (DFLE) at 65 is an estimate of the number of years a person aged 65 years would expect to live without a long lasting physical or mental health condition or disability limiting their ability to carry out day to day activities. This is based on contemporary mortality rates and prevalence of self-reported disability free state. The prevalence of disability free state is derived from responses to a survey question on general health. For a particular area and time period, it is an estimate of the average number of years a person aged 65 years would live without disability if he or she experienced the age specific mortality rates and prevalence of disability free state for that area and time period throughout his or her remaining life. Figures are calculated from deaths from all causes, mid year population estimates, and self reported disability free state, based on data aggregated over a three year period.
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectanciesuk/previousReleases
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths registered in the respective calendar years for ages 65 years and over and the weighted prevalence of people reporting in the Annual Population Survey that they do not have a physical or mental health condition or illness that has or is expected to last 12 months or more and has reduced an individual's ability to undertake activities of daily living. The weighting is based on Census 2011 health data.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS), Census based Health state adjustment factors
Definition of denominator: ONS mid year population estimates for ages 65 years and over for the respective calendar years and Annual Population Survey sample weighted to local authority population totals.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS), Census based Health state adjustment factors
Methodology: Disability free life expectancy is calculated by abridged Sullivan life tables, for males and females separately using 5 year age bands. A Sullivan life table extends the traditional life table by partitioning years lived into favourable and unfavourable health states to provide an estimate of disability free life expectancy for males and females at birth and by age group for each geographical unit. In addition to the number of deaths and mid year population estimates used in a traditional life table, the Sullivan life table also incorporates the proportion of people reporting in the Annual Population Survey that they do not have a persistent illness or disability that reduces their ability to carry out day to day activities. Note that the survey questions used to estimate disability in the Annual Population Survey (APS) changed in 2013 so comparable source data is only available from 2014 to 2016 onwards. The current questions are: Do you have any physical or mental health conditions or illnesses that have lasted or are expected to last 12months or more? Response options: Yes; No. If “Yes” the respondent is then asked: Does your condition or illness, any of your conditions or illnesses reduce your ability to carry out normal day to day activities? Response options: Yes, a lot; Yes, a little; Not at all.In December 2018, ONS implemented a revision based on stakeholder feedback. Adjustments have been made to the Annual Population Survey data using Census 2011 health data to smooth subnational fluctuations and to impute plausable prevalence for younger and older ages. A detailed explanation of this revision is provided in the Quality and Methodology Information report  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/methodologies/healthstatelifeexpectanciesukqmi National deciles of area deprivation are created through ranking small geographical populations known as 'Lower layer Super Output Areas' (LSOAs) by ranking them according to their deprivation score and grouping them into 10 divisions. Each decile represents approximately 10% of the national population, with decile one containing the 10 per cent most deprived LSOAs and decile 10 the 10 per cent least deprived.Note that ONS have not reported on trends in DFLE because of changes in the survey questions used to estimate disability in the Annual Population Survey (APS) between 2009 to 2011 and 2015 to 2017.
Frequency: Annual. ONS typically release local authority data in December and national deprivation deciles data in March.
Confidence interval details: The 95 percent confidence intervals calculated around the disability-free life expectancy estimates for each area follow the methodology outlined in "Health Expectancy Calculations by the Sullivan Method: A Practical Guide" (Jagger, Van Oyen, Robine 2014)  http://www.eurohex.eu/pdf/Sullivan_guide_pre%20final_oct%202014.pdf . This methodology assumes that if the sample size of the survey producing the prevalence rates is not very large compared to the population on which the mortality data are based, then the variance from the mortality rates is negligible. Therefore only the variance of the disability free prevalence rates is used when calculating the confidence intervals for disability free life expectancy in this output. The Annual Population Survey used for estimating the disability free prevalence has a complex design; this is taken account of in the confidence interval calculation.
Disclosure control: Disclosure control not required as mortality data used in the calculation are classified as 'discoverable' by ONS, i.e. they can be obtained from individual death certificates and individual survey responses cannot be derived from the published statistics.
Caveats: The Annual Population Survey excludes residents of communal establishments except NHS housing and students in halls of residence where inclusion takes place at their parents' address. The Census 2011 health data weighting helps to an extent by adjusting for older populations.This measure is based on self-reported health status so will be affected by subjective perception of health. Users of the indicator should also note the change in methodology adopted by ONS as described in the methodology section.

Indicator: C. difficile infection case counts and rates of community onset-healthcare associated, by Sub ICB Location (SICBL) and financial year
Rationale: Surveillance of C. difficile laboratory faecal samples in England and Wales was introduced in 1990 as part of the Public Health Laboratory Service’s voluntary monitoring of infectious diseases. Between 1990 and 2004 there was a rise in the number of C. difficile infections, from less than 3,000 in 1990 to more than 45,000 in 2004. Rates of C. difficile infections also rose over this time period in all age groups ≥40 years old. Due to the increasing incidence of C. difficile infections, the mandatory reporting of C. difficile infection in people aged ≥65 years was introduced in England in January 2004, this was a quarterly aggregate data return reported by NHS acute Trusts comprising data on the number of toxin-positive C. difficile faecal samples. Due to the continued rise of C. difficile infections among the population aged ≥65 years, the C. difficile mandatory surveillance scheme was enhanced in April 2007, to be patient-level and to cover all C. difficile infections in patients aged 2 years and over.Prior healthcare interactions was introduced in Apr 2017 as a means to determine any prior healthcare interactions from the same Trust.A low value is indicative of a low rate ofC. difficile community-onset healthcare associated cases.
Definition:
C. difficile infection C. difficile infection in patients with a positive specimen taken on day 2 or less of admission (with day 1 as day of admission), and a prior healthcare interaction at the same Trust within the last 28 days. Including all patients aged 2 years and above, diagnosed by one of the following five methods: 1.Diarrhoeal stools (Bristol Stool types 5-7) where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive*
2.Toxic megacolon or ileostomy where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive*
3.Pseudomembranous colitis revealed by lower gastro-intestinal endoscopy or Computed Tomography
4.Colonic histopathology characteristic of C. difficile infection (with or without diarrhoea or toxin detection) on a specimen obtained during endoscopy or colectomy
5.Faecal specimens collected post-mortem where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive or tissue specimens collected post-mortem where pseudomembranous colitis is revealed or colonic histopathology is characteristic of C. difficile infection
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/clostridium-difficile-guidance-data-and-analysis
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Healthcare Associated Infection Data Capture System (HCAI DCS) Mandatory Surveillance
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Standard population/values:
Sub ICB location (SICBL) population values are based upon Office for National Statistics (ONS) Mid-Year Population Estimates (2011 Census based).

The relevant rate per 100,000 population was calculated as follows:
rate = (cases for given period/SICBL-level population estimate)*100,000
Confidence interval details: Confidence intervals not calculated as the population value is known.
Caveats: These data do not provide a basis for decisions on the clinical effectiveness of infection control interventions in individual Trusts: further investigations considering potential confounders would need to be undertaken before this could be done.Nor do these data provide a basis for comparisons between acute Trust or SICBLs. Rate information, using rate calculations as currently defined, is not appropriate for comparison. The counts of infections have not been adjusted to give a standardised rate considering factors such as organisational demographics or case mix. Rate information is of use for comparison of an individual organisation over time.‘All reported cases’ refers to all toxin positive results for C. difficile infections that are detected by the Trust whose laboratory processed the specimen. This means the England case total & rates may be slightly higher than the sum of all sub ICB Location cases & rates.<span class="ui-provider gp b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z ab ac ae af ag ah ai aj ak" dir="ltr">IMPORTANT NOTE: CCG calculations for the period between January 2021 and January 2022 have been based on SICBL boundaries. As such some SICBLs may experience higher or lower rates than expected due to this change. Rationale: Surveillance of C. difficile laboratory faecal samples in England and Wales was introduced in 1990 as part of the Public Health Laboratory Service’s voluntary monitoring of infectious diseases. Between 1990 and 2004 there was a rise in the number of C. difficile infections, from less than 3,000 in 1990 to more than 45,000 in 2004. Definition:
C. difficile infection C. difficile infection in patients with a positive specimen taken on day 3 or greater of admission (with day 1 as day of admission). Including all patients aged 2 years and above, diagnosed by one of the following five methods: 1.Diarrhoeal stools (Bristol Stool types 5-7) where the specimen is C. difficile toxin positive*

This is important, as it reflects how well people living undiagnosed late stage HIV are identified by HIV testing in England, and what portion of new diagnoses they constitute. Indicator: Deprivation score (IMD 2019)
Rationale: Deprivation covers a broad range of issues and refers to unmet needs caused by a lack of resources of all kinds, not just financial. The English Indices of Deprivation attempt to measure a broader concept of multiple deprivation, made up of several distinct dimensions, or domains, of deprivation.The English Indices of Deprivation 2019 are measures of multiple deprivation at the small area level. The model of multiple deprivation which underpins the indices of Deprivation 2019 is based on the idea of distinct domains of deprivation which can be recognised and measured separately. These domains are experienced by individuals living in an area. People may be counted in one or more of the domains, depending on the number and the types of deprivation that they experience. Each domain represents a specific form of deprivation experienced by people and each can be measured individually using a number of indicators. Seven distinct domains have been identified in the English Indices of Deprivation; Income Deprivation, Employment Deprivation, Health Deprivation and Disability, Education, Skills and Training Deprivation, Barriers to Housing and services, Living Environment Deprivation and Crime. Individual domains can be used in isolation as measures of each specific form of deprivation. They can also be combined, using appropriate weights, into a single overall Index of Multiple Deprivation which can be used to rank every small area in England according to the deprivation experienced by the people living there. Along with two supplementary indices, Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index and Income Index Affecting Older People Index, they form the English Indices of Deprivation. These statistics allow the most, and least, deprived areas of the country to be identified as well as providing information about the issues faced by people living in different parts of the country.
Definition: The English Indices of Deprivation 2019 use 39 separate indicators, organised across seven distinct domains of deprivation which can be combined, using appropriate weights, to calculate the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019 (IMD 2019). This is an overall measure of multiple deprivation experienced by people living in an area.
Data source: OHID, based on Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government data

Methodology: For GP deprivation scores, the population weighting is based on NHS Digital,  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice/april-2019  https://files.digital.nhs.uk/16/740C9E/gp-reg-pat-prac-lsoa-male-female-apr-19.zip  (persons).For more information, please see the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2019-technical-report
Caveats: The Indices of Deprivation 2019 are relative measures of deprivation. This means it can tell you if one area is more deprived than another, but not by how much.The Indices of Deprivation 2019 is not a measure of affluence; all of the indicators used in the index are designed to identify aspects of deprivation, not affluence. Therefore the area ranked as the least deprived is not necessarily the most affluent.

Indicator: Disability free life expectancy at birth
Rationale: This indicator will provide more information on healthy ageing to complement the existing PHOF indicator on healthy life expectancy.  The government ‘grand challenge’ for our ageing society [1], has a mission to ensure that people can enjoy at least 5 extra healthy, independent years of life by 2035, while narrowing the gap between the experience of the richest and poorest. DFLE at birth has been proposed as the metric to measure progress towards achieving this ambition.  [1] Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (2018) Policy paper: The Grand Challenge mission.
Definition: A measure of the average number of years a person would expect to live without a long lasting physical or mental health condition or disability that limits daily activities.The measure uses a prevalence of those living without a disability derived from responses to a survey question. For a particular area and time period, it is an estimate of the average number of years a newborn baby would live without a disability if he or she experienced the age specific mortality rates and disability free prevalence for that area and time period throughout his or her life. Figures are calculated from deaths from all causes, mid year population estimates, and self reported disability, based on data aggregated over a three year period. Figures reflect the prevalence of those living without a disability and mortality among those living in an area in each time period, rather than what will be experienced throughout life among those born in the area. The figures are not therefore the number of years a baby born in the area could actually expect to live disability free, both because the prevalence and mortality rates of the area are likely to change in the future and because many of those born in the area will live elsewhere for at least some part of their lives.
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectanciesuk/previousReleases
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS), Census based Health state adjustment factors
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS), Census based Health state adjustment factors
Methodology:
Disability free life expectancy is calculated by ONS using abridged Sullivan life tables, for males and females separately using 5 year age bands. A Sullivan life table extends the traditional life table by partitioning years lived into those lived with and without disability to provide an estimate of disability free life expectancy for males and females at birth and each geographical unit. The traditional life table uses ONS death registration data, and ONS mid year population estimates aggregated for the relevant years. In addition to these, the Sullivan life table also incorporates the weighted proportion of people reporting being free from disability,from the Annual Population Survey. The proportion of people reporting being free of disability is determined by responses to the following two questions:"Do you have any physical or mental health conditions or illnesses that have lasted or are expected to last 12 months or more?" -> "No" respondents are included.If "Yes" the respondent is asked "Does your condition or illness/any of your conditions or illnesses reduce your ability to carry out normal day to day acitvities?" -> "Not at all" respondents are included.

To prepare the Annual Population Survey data for the Sullivan method, a set of adjustments are applied to the dataset. These adjustments use data from the 2011 Census to smooth fluctuations in subnational disability free prevalence, and impute a plausible disability free prevalence at both younger and older ages. Further explanation of these adjustments can be found here: https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ons.gov.uk%2Fpeoplepopulationandcommunity%2Fhealthandsocialcare%2Fhealthandlifeexpectancies%2Fmethodologies%2Fhealthstatelifeexpectanciesukqmi&data=05%7C01%7CAshu.Sehgal%40dhsc.gov.uk%7Cae295f1407ab4330f57108da22adaa38%7C61278c3091a84c318c1fef4de8973a1c%7C1%7C0%7C637860426556618667%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=VGZP0R78gofKKcviNU6B%2BBtxSHt%2FOZNPVL4%2BtlxK6Kg%3D&reserved=0 A life table template which illustrates the method used to calculate disability free life expectancy (and 95 percent confidence intervals) can be found on the ONS website: https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/datasets/healthstatelifeexpectancytemplate
Confidence interval details: The 95 percent confidence intervals calculated around the healthy life expectancy estimates for each area follow the methodology outlined in "Health Expectancy Calculations by the Sullivan Method: A Practical Guide" (Jagger, Van Oyen, Robine 2014)  http://www.eurohex.eu/pdf/Sullivan_guide_pre%20final_oct%202014.pdf This methodology assumes that if the sample size of the survey producing the prevalence rates is not very large compared to the population on which the mortality data are based, then the variance from the mortality rates is negligible. Therefore only the variance of the health prevalence rates is used when calculating the confidence intervals for healthy life expectancy in this output. The Annual Population Survey used for estimating the health prevalence has a complex design; this is taken account of in the confidence interval calculation.
Disclosure control: Disclosure control not required as mortality data used in the calculation are classified as 'discoverable' by ONS, i.e. they can be obtained from individual death certificates and individual survey responses cannot be derived from the published statistics.
Rounding: Data are published to 5 decimal places by ONS. Data will be displayed to 1 decimal place in PHOF.
Caveats: The disability free life expectancy figures exclude residents of communal establishments except NHS housing and students in halls of residence where inclusion takes place at their parents' address.

Indicator: Percentage of 5 year olds with experience of visually obvious dental decay
Rationale: Oral health is an integral part of overall health; when children are not healthy this affects their ability to learn, thrive and develop. This indicator therefore links to a key policy: Getting the Best Start in Life. Poor oral health is a priority under Best Start in Life, it was also a topic of a Health Select Committee inquiry, and the most common cause of hospital admission for 5 to 9 year olds. This indicator allows benchmarking of oral health of young children across England, and is an excellent proxy measure of assessing the impact of the commissioning of oral health improvement programmes on the local community. Dental caries is a synonymous term for tooth decay.
Definition: Percentage of 5 year olds with dental decay extending to the dentine layer which can be detected by visual observation alone
Data source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, National Dental Epidemiology Programme
Indicator source: Dental Public Health Epidemiology Programme for England: oral health survey of five year old children (Biennial publication: latest report 2024)
Definition of numerator: Number of 5 year olds in a given area with at least one tooth decayed, missing or filled
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), National Dental Epidemiology Programme (NDEP)
Definition of denominator: Number of 5 year olds examined for a given area
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), National Dental Epidemiology Programme (NDEP)
Methodology: For this indicator, the numerator was divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100 to obtain the unweighted percentage. The sampling methodology used for this survey was school based and therefore not truly representative of the population of five year old children by Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) quintile. Thus, the sample was treated as a stratified random sample, that is, children were selected randomly from each IMD quintile but the sampling probability varied between IMD quintiles. For this reason, IMD weighted estimates were produced to provide more robust estimates of overall decay prevalence. Weighting of the sample data allows a closer match to the actual distribution of deprivation quintiles in the source population.

Indicator: Rate of prescriptions for nicotine replacement products per 100,000 smokers
Rationale: Local Stop Smoking Services data is currently the only published data on prescriptions for smoking cessation, and although it contains some data on nicotine replacement products, it does not contain information on all patients being prescribed nicotine replacement products. The ePact2 dataset contains details of all prescriptions in England by the prescribing GP practice and therefore does not have the same limitations.This indicator will help local authorities to monitor trends in prescribing nicotine replacement products to their smoking population and will sit alongside Stop Smoking Services data to add additional context.
Definition: Number of nicotine replacement products prescribed as a rate per 100,000 smokers
Data source: OHID, based on NHS Business Services Authority and Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: ePact2 dataset - NHS Business Services Authorityhttps://www.nhsbsa.nhs.uk/epact2 (account required)
Definition of numerator: Number of nicotine replacement products prescribed
Source of numerator: NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), Prescription data (ePACT2)
Definition of denominator: Population who currently smoke. Smoking prevalence estimates at local authority level were multiplied by the corresponding ONS mid-year population estimates to calculate the smoking population.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Methodology: Data are extracted from the ePact2 database at practice level and aggregated to LA.
Confidence interval details: A simulation method is used to calculate 95% confidence intervals surrounding the estimates by the following process:Prior to the simulation: 1)The prevalence is logit-transformed logit (prev) = (ln (prev / (1 – prev))2)The standard deviation (SD) of the logit-transformed prevalence is calculated. This is done by first calculating the Wilson Score confidence intervals for the prevalence, using n as the denominator and (prev × n / 100) as the numerator3)These confidence limits are then logit-transformed, and the difference between the logit-transformed upper and lower limits is divided by (2 × 1.96) to give an estimate of the SD of the logit-transformed prevalenceSimulation: for each iteration: 4)A random number between 0 and 1 is generated using the Mersenne Twister algorithm, and used to provide a random value from a normal distribution with mean = logit (prev) and SD = the SD of logit (prev)5)This random sampled value is transformed to a prevalence using the inverse of the logit function, and multiplied by the population to give a randomised estimated number of smokers in the LA (the denominator of the randomised indicator)6)A second random number is generated and used to provide a random value from a normal distribution with mean = num (eg the number of smokers who have set a quit date in the LA) and SD = sqrt (num) – this is the randomised numerator value7)The randomised indicator value is calculated by dividing the randomised numerator by the randomised denominator8)The randomised indicator value is added to an array of randomised indicator valuesAfter the simulation: 9)From the array of randomised indicator values, the (1–α/2)th centile smallest and largest values are identified and returned as the lower and upper confidence limits respectively (where α is the confidence level specified for the confidence intervals, eg 0.95)
Caveats: The practice of prescribing nicotine replacement products varies between localities, for example local stop smoking service A may require their clients to return every 2 weeks to receive their next prescription whereas local stop smoking service B may require this every 4 weeks. In this instance service A would be prescribing two prescriptions for every one prescribed by service B.Also some areas may only fund a 12 week programme whereas others may have made a strategic decision to offer a shorter course due to budgetary constraints. In this case the value would be higher in the service which offers the longer course of treatment as the patient would receive more prescriptions over the 12 week period than say someone on a 4 week programme.Differences in practice are reflected in the indicator value and higher values may indicate more frequent prescriptions being issued rather than more smokers receiving smoking cessation medication. Therefore small differences between rates are likely to reflect local differences in operation rather than indicate that the services in one LA are better than another. However, large differences can be used as an indication of variation in smoking cessation prescribing practice.The data does not include NRT provided through incentive schemes where vouchers may be issues by stop smoking practitioners.
Notes: Data are collected on the basis of the LA of the practice providing the prescription rather than the LA of residence of the patient. Patients are not restricted to attending a GP in the LA with which they are resident. This means that the number of prescriptions is not necessarily that in the LA’s own population. However, for this indicator prescriptions are expressed per 100,000 resident smoking population. Smoking prevalence as measured by the APS is self-reported and as such, prone to response bias. In addition the prevalence data is not age standardised . All issues of accuracy and completeness highlighted for smoking prevalence will also affect this indicator.

Indicator: Reoffending levels: average number of reoffences per reoffender
Rationale: Tackling a persons offending behaviour is often intrinsically linked to their physical and mental health, and in particular any substance misuse issues. This outcome therefore cannot be addressed in isolation. Offenders often also experience significant health inequalities that will need to be identified, examined and addressed locally in partnership with organisations across the criminal justice system. Furthermore, a large proportion of families with multiple needs are managed through the criminal justice system, and their issues are inter-generational. Re-offending therefore has a wide impact on the health and well being of individuals, their children and families, and the communities they live in.The consequences of tackling offending and re-offending will benefit a wide range of service agencies and enhance their outcomes. Public health is a crucial part of a multi agency approach to reducing re-offending, which includes police, courts, prisons, probation, community safety partners, social services, housing and education at a local level.
Definition: The average number of reoffences per reoffender.
Data source: OHID, based on Ministry of Justice data
Indicator source: Ministry of Justice Proven Reoffending Statistics January to March https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.gov.uk%2Fgovernment%2Fcollections%2Fproven-reoffending-statistics&data=05%7C01%7Cashu.sehgal%40dhsc.gov.uk%7C214498bacd224958902a08db815584b9%7C61278c3091a84c318c1fef4de8973a1c%7C1%7C0%7C638245976516411593%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=6feRqMw4DRMEnB0kYJ0uV3kPmRtkjg4AT1ra7BFuHOk%3D&reserved=0
Definition of numerator: The number of proven reoffences committed. A proven reoffence is defined as any offence committed in a one year follow up period and receiving a court conviction, caution, reprimand or warning in the one year follow-up or a further six months waiting period. The waiting period is the additional time beyond the follow-up period to allow for offences which are committed towards the end of the follow-up period to be proven by court, resulting in a conviction, caution, reprimand or final warning. This annual figure is formed by combining the number of reoffences commited in the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. I.e. for the year 2016 to 2017, the number of reoffences is gathered from the following quarterly cohorts: Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017. The annual figure is provided by Ministry of Justice in their  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics  collection, available on GOV.UK.
Source of numerator: Ministry of Justice (MoJ), Proven reoffending statistics
Definition of denominator: The number of reoffenders. A reoffender is an offender who, after entering the cohort in a three-month period, commits a reoffence that leads to a court conviction, caution, reprimand or warning within the one year follow up period , or within a further six months to allow the offence to be proven in court. This annual figure is formed by combining the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. i.e. for the year 2016 to 2017, the number of reoffenders is gathered from the following quarterly cohorts; Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017.The annual figure is provided by Ministry of Justice in their  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics  collection, available on GOV.UK.
Source of denominator: Ministry of Justice (MoJ), Proven reoffending statistics
Methodology: The average number of re-offences committed per reoffender is calculated by taking the sum of the number of reoffences in the four quarter cohorts that make up the respective year, divided by the sum of the number of reoffenders in each of those quarterly cohorts. In effect, this method is presenting an average of the averages and, as a result, it allows for both re-offenders and reoffences to be counted more than once in the annual figures.The calculation is provided by Ministry of Justice in their  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/proven-reoffending-statistics  collection, available on GOV.UK.
Frequency: Annual. Data for this indicator are calculated by summing up the counts for the number of reoffenders and the number of reoffences that are recorded in the four quarterly cohorts that take place within the financial year. As an example, for the year 2016 to 2017, the four quarterly cohorts that are included are Apr 2016 to Jun 2016, Jul 2016 to Sep 2016, Oct 2016 to Dec 2016 and Jan 2017 to Mar 2017.Ministry of Justice advise to use annual data as a method of proven reoffending rather than using quarterly data, as quarterly data would not be possible to produce for some areas due to small cohort sizes. Annual data is also preferred to allow comparisons across years without the variability of the quarterly data.
Disclosure control: Isles of Scilly data are suppressed due to low numbers. However, numerator and denominator data for Isles of Scilly are published by Ministry of Justice.In keeping with the disclosure control techniques employed by Ministry of Justice, proportions and averages based on less than 30 offenders are removed as they make data unreliable for interpretation.
Caveats: Previously, proven reoffending statistics were produced based on a 12 month cohort. However, following a  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/519644/proven-reoffending-consultation-response.pdf , it was decided to switch to a 3 month cohort. Since the change from a 12 month to a three-month cohort, annual cohorts are formed by combining the four quarterly cohorts of the relevant year. An individual offender, and their offences, can therefore appear up to four times within a single annual cohort (one from each quarter). This can lead to an increase of reoffending rates for the annual cohort compared to the old methodology based on a 12 month cohort, since prolific offenders and their offences may be counted multiple times. Additionally, since any individual three month cohort contains fewer offenders than a 12 month cohort would, three month cohorts are subject to greater statistical fluctuations. Therefore, their results are likely to vary more than those of 12 month cohorts.The group of offenders whose offending behaviour is proven are likely to be a subgroup of all active offenders. The Offending, Crime and Justice Survey (2003) estimated that around one in ten people in England and Wales aged between 10 and 65 had committed an offence in the previous 12 months, which translates into approximately 3.8 million people. This compares to around 629,000 offenders in the April 2005 to March 2006 cohort used to measure proven reoffending, underlining that the offenders whose proven reoffending behaviour is presented in the Proven Reoffending Statistics Quarterly Bulletin are a small and probably unrepresentative sample of the population of all active offenders.For information, offences are counted as proven reoffences if they meet all of the following criteria:• They are recordable. Not all offences are on the PNC, and more recordable offences than non recordable offences are entered. Analysis comparing offences proven at court with offences recorded on the PNC suggests the most common offences that are not recorded relate to motor vehicles, e.g. using a motor vehicle whilst uninsured against third party risks, speeding offences or keeping a vehicle on the highway without a driving licence, or television licence fee evasion.• They were committed in England or Wales.• They are offences that were prosecuted by the police. PNC data are collected and entered by the police, and offences prosecuted by the police are likely to be recorded more comprehensively on the PNC than offences prosecuted by other organisations. For example, benefit fraud is prosecuted by the Department for Work and Pensions. Therefore, benefit fraud offences may be poorly represented on the PNC.• Offences are only counted if they are proven through caution, reprimands or final warnings (for juveniles) and court convictions. Offences that are not proven, or which are met with other responses from the Criminal Justice System, are not counted.• The offence is not a breach offence, i.e. breach of a court order, since we are only interested in new offences. If an offender commits multiple offences on the same day, each offence will be counted separately. For example, if an offender commits three offences on the same day, this will count as three reoffences.The data required for measuring proven reoffending are based on a range of sources (prison data, probation data, young offenders in secure accommodation and criminal records from the Police National Computer) from a range of agencies (Her Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service, the Youth Justice Board, local authorities and the National Police Improvement Agency). These figures have been derived from administrative IT systems that, as with any large scale recording system, are subject to possible errors with data entry and processing. For more information on data quality, please see the Data Quality section in the  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1071735/Guide-to-proven-reoffending-Apr22.pdf .
Notes: This indicator is to replace PHOF indicator 1.13ii average number of reoffences per offender. It has been necessary to alter this indicator to the one being described in this form, to reflect the following changes: •The changed denominator (going from offenders to reoffenders). The average number of proven reoffences per reoffender is detailed by the MoJ as a measure of proven reoffending. This change was detailed in the recent  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/778214/PHOF_refresh_proposal.pdf .•The changed methodology used to aggregate the yearly counts and rates.•The change from producing annual data for every calendar year to every financial year, decided following the consultation on proven reoffending statistics.Due to these changes, we are not able to produce confidence intervals for this indicator.

Indicator: Emergency hospital admissions for asthma in adults (aged 19 years and over)
Rationale:
The 2018 Health Survey for England indicated that amonst adults 11% of wormen and 9% of men had asthma, and 10% of children aged under 15 had asthma. Most of the care for people with asthma is provided in primary care. The national guidelines [1] for the management of asthma state that people with asthma should not need emergency treatment if appropriate routine care is given.
This hospital admissions indicator will help identify areas where diagnosis and monitoring of asthma in primary care could be improved.
[1] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2017)  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80  [Accessed 29 July 2019]
Definition: Emergency admissions to hospital in persons (aged 19 years and over) where the primary diagnosis is asthma (ICD-10 codes J45 to J46). Directly age standardised rate per 100,000 population (standardised to the European standard population).
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: Calculated by Office for Health Improvement and Disparities: Health and Social Care using data from NHS Digital - Hospital Episode Statistics Admitted Patient Care (HES APC) and Patients registered at a GP Practice.
Definition of numerator:
Sum of the emergency admissions for patients with asthma as a primary diagnosis (ICD10 codes J45 to J46).
Emergency admissions defined as unpredictable and at short notice (method of admission codes beginning with '2'). Finished admission episodes of the first episode were counted (episode order = 1, episode status = 3 ). No filter was applied for sex.
Sub ICB location of responsibility using the latest sub ICB location configuration across all time periods. Sub ICB location configuration taken from NHS Digital's "Numbers of Patients Registered at a GP Practice" publication and looking up the sub ICB location in the April of the most recently published year. Patients are allocated to a sub ICB location based on the registered practice code on the HES episode. Where the code indicates the responsibility is to a practice outside England, this record is excluded. All records without a practice code, and those with a practice code that is not recognised but does not indicate that responsibility is outside England, are allocated using the patient postcode, to the sub ICB location within whose geographical boundary they live. Specialist commissioning codes are excluded. Only valid fields used.
England values created from the sum of all sub ICB locations.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Definition of denominator:
Sub ICB location populations are aggregated from GP practice population snapshots, from NHS Digital's  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice  publication and looking up the sub ICB location in the April of the most recently published year.
In 2013/14 and 2014/15, only five year age bands were published, in these cases the populations have been divided by five to estimate a single year of age population. Subsequent publications have presented populations by single year of age and sex.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Patients registered at a GP practice
Methodology: Directly standardised rates per 100,000 population, age-standardised to the 2013 European Standard Population.
Confidence interval details:
Dobson & Byar's methods with adjusted variance for repeat admissionsA confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically, it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.
Dobson & Byar's method is used for calculating confidence intervals for directly standardised rates. Where there are repeat admissions to hospital during the year the Dobson & Byar's method has been used with an adjustment to the variance to take this into account.
A confidence interval is calculated for the observed total count of events using Byar's method,1 which gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for counts based on the assumption of a Poisson distribution and is sufficiently accurate for counts as low as 10, the minimum count recommended for DSRs. This interval is then weighted and scaled to give the interval for the standardised rate using the method described by Dobson.2 The method is described in detail in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.3Full technical details of the new methodology will be made available soon and can be requested from  mailto:healthcare.variation@dhsc.gov.uk 
1 Breslow NE, Day NE. Statistical methods in cancer research, volume II: The design and analysis of cohort studies. Lyon: International Agency for Research on Cancer, World Health Organization; 1987: 69.2 Dobson A et al. Confidence intervals for weighted sums of Poisson parameters. Stat Med 1991;10: 457-62.3 Eayres D.  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/documents/APHO%20Tech%20Briefing%203%20Common%20PH%20Stats%20and%20CIs.pdf  York: APHO; 2008.
Disclosure control:
All sub-national counts are rounded to the nearest 5, and counts of 1-7 are suppressed in accordance with HES disclosure control guidelines. Rates and confidence intervals are calculated using unrounded counts.
DSR's have not been calculated for any numerator values below 10. The  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/guidance/supporting-information/PH-methods  provides further details
Caveats:
This indicator is based on the number of patients registered at a GP based on the sub ICB location of responsibility. England counts are aggregated from all known lower geography values. Values may not match those previously produced as these will be based on the most recent GP practice to sub ICB location lookup. Any changes to the lookup will alter the total count and population of a sub ICB location and so values may differ from those previously shown for the same area and time period.
It is important to note that an equivalent LA based indicator (which uses resident population) would have different values for coterminous LAs and sub ICB locations and the England value would also differ. The England denominator for this indicator is based on aggregating patients registered at GPs. The  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice/data-quality-statement  provides further information.
Patients are assigned to a sub ICB location based on the registered practice code in their HES episode. If the code belongs to a practice outside England, the record is excluded. Records without a practice code use the patient’s postcode to determine the sub ICB location. Practice codes are sourced from the most recent April GP practice code list size dataset. Small changes in counts and rates can occur when a new GP practice code lookup is used as their admissions may be reclassified.
Values may be different to those previously published due to NHS digital implementing an improved method of matching of patients across all national patient-level datasets. The  https://digital.nhs.uk/services/personal-demographics-service/master-person-service provides further details.
NHS Digital has identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust (RXC) in 2018/19. Approximately 85,000 records erroneously had all diagnosis codes removed. Therefore, OHID have not published values for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 10% of patients from that area with missing diagnosis codes from RXC in the current year (2018/19). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients with missing diagnosis codes from RXC have been flagged to be treated with caution.
NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Frimley Health Foundation Trust in 2022 to 2023. Frimley Health Foundation Trust did not submit HES data for June 2022 to March 2023. Therefore, areas have been suppressed where many patients were likely to have been treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust and neighbouring areas have been flagged to be treated with caution.
NHS Digital identify data quality issues affecting HES data. For more details please see  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/hospital-episode-statistics/the-processing-cycle-and-hes-data-quality 
In 2023, NHS England announced a methodological change to require Trusts to report Same Day Emergency Care (SDEC) to the Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) by July 2025. Early adopter sites began to report SDEC to ECDS from 2021/22. Some Trusts had previously reported this activity as part of the Admitted Patient Care data set and moving to report to ECDS may reduce the number of admissions reported for this/these indicator/s. NHSE have advised it is not possible accurately to identify SDEC in current data flows, but the impact of the change is expected to vary by diagnosis, with indicators related to injuries and external causes potentially most affected.
When considering if SDEC recording practice has reduced the number of admissions reported for this indicator at local level, please refer to the published list of sites who have reported when they began to report SDEC to ECDS.

Simple Name: Emergency hospital admissions for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Simple Definition: Rate of emergency hospital admissions for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

Indicator: Mortality for people referred to secondary mental health services (aged 18 to 74)
Rationale:
As part of the 10 Year Health Plan for England [1], the government has committed to a new approach to mental health. Neighbourhood healthcare services [2] are a core element of the 10 Year Health Plan, aiming to improve support for people with complex needs. These services build on existing approaches to reducing health inequalities, including Core20PLUS5 framework [3].
From 2026 to 2027 the government is making available funding over 4 years to invest in new models of care, including community-based mental health centres, mental health emergency departments and eliminating out-of-area placements [4].
Alongside this investment, a new modern service framework (MSF) for people with severe mental illness (SMI) is being developed. This MSF is to set consistency in clinical standards across England so that patients and families get the best quality, evidence-based treatment and support. The forthcoming MSF is to consider and outline opportunities for improving the physical health outcomes of people with severe and enduring mental problems [5].
People living with SMI experience some of the widest health inequalities in England. Their life expectancy is 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population [6]. They also have a much higher risk of developing preventable physical conditions [7].
Compared with the general patient population, patients with SMI are at substantially higher risk [7] of obesity, asthma, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cardiovascular disease. They make more use of secondary urgent and emergency care for their physical health conditions [8].
This indicator is part of measuring this inequality in people severe and enduring mental illness and will support on delivery of government’s commitments on improving outcomes for this population.
This indicator uses people with an open referral to secondary mental health services in the 5 years before their death as a proxy for ‘people with a severe and enduring mental problems’.

Definition: Directly age standardised rate of deaths of people aged 18 to 74, referred to secondary mental health services, per 100,000 population. Referrals to mental health services in the five years preceding death are included with or without contact or inpatient stay.
Data source: NHS England and Office for National Statistics
Definition of numerator:
Counts, by five year age bands (plus 18-19 year olds), of people aged 18 to 74 whose death was registered in the years in question, and who had a referral to secondary mental health services (excluding Learning Disabilities and Autism (LDA) only activity) in the 5 years preceding death.
The mental health data sets are searched for evidence of referral to secondary mental health services back until April 2009. Therefore, any deaths before April 2014 will not have a full 5 years of mental health data searched. Analysis has shown that this is 0.2% of deaths registered in 2015-17 and that proportion is expected to decrease for later time periods
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Civil Registrations of Death linked to the following datasets: Mental Health Services Dataset (MHSDS), Mental Health and Learning Disabilities Dataset (MHLDS) and Mental Health Minimum Dataset (MHMDS)
Definition of denominator: ONS mid-year population estimates, aggregated
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Directly age standardised rate
Disclosure control:
Values have not been calculated for areas where the number of deaths was fewer than 10, and the counts have been suppressed for these areas
This has been approved by NHS England’s Disclosure Control Board
Rounding:
Counts for areas below England level have been rounded to nearest 5 following the calculation of the rate

This is the subject of a paper before NHS Digital’s Disclosure Control Board for approval
Caveats:
Variations in access to secondary mental health services and referral practice across different local authorities will affect the indicator. Areas where few adults are referred to secondary mental health services might have lower mortality for this population group. This is because fewer deaths in adults will be in people referred to secondary mental health services in the 5 years before their death. Indicator: Estimated number of children and young people with mental disorders  – aged 5 to 17
Rationale: This indicator provides local health and care systems with an estimated number of children and young people (CYP) aged 5 to 17 years (inclusive) with mental health disorders in their area. It is to support planning of mental health interventions, including Children and Young People’s Improving Access to Psychological Therapies Programme and Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS).
Specific rationale: This indicator helps to deliver an essential part of the profile's purpose – i.e. to quantify need. In doing so it supports implementation of various priority government policies, including Future In Mind (2015), The Five Year Forward View for Mental Health (2016) and the NHS Long Term Plan (2019). In addition, it can inform the Department for Education’s (DfE) introduction of new guidance for schools on relationships, sex and health education; which includes mental health.
Definition: The estimated number of children and young people (CYP) aged 5 to 17 who have a mental disorder (MD). This includes emotional disorders, behavioural disorders, hyperactivity disorders, and autism spectrum, eating and other less common disorders.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: This indicator gives an estimate of how many children and young people aged 5 to 17 years in the general population are expected to have had a mental disorder in a given area in 2017. MDs are defined as: emotional disorders (anxiety disorders, depressive disorders and bipolar affective disorder), behavioural disorders (oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder confined to family, unsocialised conduct disorder, socialised conduct disorder, and other conduct disorder), hyperactivity disorders, and autism spectrum, eating and other less common disorders (tics, selective mutism and psychosis).The indicator has no denominator, and so the numerator and the indicator are synonymous. The indicator is broken down by Clinical Commissioning Group and Local Authorities.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Mental Health of Children and Young People Survey (MHCYPS)
Definition of denominator: The indicator is a count so it does not have a denominator.
Source of denominator: Not applicable (N/A)
Methodology: Prevalence proportion figures by age category (5-10, 11-16, 17-19) and sex (male, female) at England level are taken from The Mental Health of Children and Young People in England, 2017 survey. These are then applied to the CCG and Local Authority populations by age category and sex to give an estimated number of children with MD in each local area.The prevalence proportion figure for 17-19 year olds was applied to the population of 17 year olds. 18 and 19 year olds are not included in this indicator.
Frequency: The count will be recalculated every 3 years to account for CCG and LA boundary changes.
Confidence interval details:
Like the value, confidence intervals are presented as counts.Assume each age/sex prevalence proportion follows a binomial distribution. Simulate prevalence proportions using the sampled prevalence and 95% CIs from The Mental Health of Children and Young People in England, 2017 survey to determine distribution parameters. On each simulation, the prevalence proportions are randomly sampled from the assumed binomial distributions and the count indicator is calculated based on these randomly sampled proportion values. Perform 150,000 iterations.
The indicator is calculated 150,000 times forming a distribution of random samples of the indicator. From this we take the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles to be estimates of the lower and upper limits respectively of the 95% confidence interval for the indicator.
Disclosure control: The count estimatesare not based on real individuals at a local level. They are estimates based on national rates and local demography, so there is no issue of disclosure.
Caveats: This indicator is calculated using a simple method based on age and sex. There may be other factors that influence the prevalence of mental illness in children, but we have not been able to incorporate them into this indicator. The main reason for this is a lack of population data at local level, disaggregated by the variables that are significantly related to the observed prevalence proportion (such as relationships at school, for example).The resulting local prevalence proportions (based on age and sex) show no significant variation between LADs or CCGs. Because of this,it is considered more useful (by stakeholders) that we publish local counts alongside national prevalence proportions (which can be accessed here: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/mental-health-of-children-and-young-people-in-england/2017/2017 )<a href="https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/mental-health-of-children-and-young-people-in-england/2017/2017">.Counts are not a valid input to comparison of prevalence within local populations but do quantify absolute burden of need across geographies, as well as being valid inputs to service planning, management and commissioning. Currently there is no other dataset that will allow calculation of up to date local burden of mental health problems within the CYP population.There are (at least) two potential data quality issues associated with the main data source for this indicator (The Mental Health of Children and Young People in England, 2017 survey). (1) It used the NHS Patient Register to identify potential participants, which excludes some groups and may under/over estimate others; (2) Where a participant’s spoken English was not good enough to adequately respond to the survey, they were not included. Again, this may lead to an under/over estimation of the true prevalence. The survey sample was 9,117 children aged 2 to 19, with 50.4% boys and 49.6% girls. A larger sample overall and within specific age/sex groups sample would have provided more robust and precise estimates.
Data re-use: The data may be used referencing Public Health England.

Indicator: The percentage of zero and one day emergency admissions to hospital for pneumonia
Rationale:
Pneumonia continues to place a huge burden on the NHS. Community acquired pneumonia is a leading cause of admission to hospital, despite being avoidable in many cases.
The NHS Long Term Plan [1] is committed to reducing the burden from pneumonia. Most people with pneumonia have low severity illness and are managed at home. About 1 in 5 require hospital management. 
Pneumonia accounts for about half of all cases of severe sepsis managed on intensive care units. Length of hospital stay is associated with the severity of illness on admission to hospital. Admissions with a shorter length of stay may represent those patients who are suitable for Same Day Emergency Care (SDEC), (also known as ambulatory emergency care), where emergency treatment is carried out on the same day without need for admission to a hospital bed. The NHS long term plan argues for increasing the use of SDECs to reduce avoidable emergency admissions.
[1] NHS (2019)  https://www.longtermplan.nhs.uk/publication/nhs-long-term-plan/  [Accessed 23 January 2019]
Definition: The percentage of zero and one day emergency admissions to hospital with the diagnosis of pneumonia, based on sub ICB location of responsibility.

Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)

Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Methodology:
Numerator divided by denominator expressed as a percentage.
Calculated using the HES database fields for:

Emergency admissions (admimeth) defined as unpredictable and at short notice (method of admission codes beginning with'2')
Finished Discharge Episodes (FDE=1) A FDE indicates whether the patient was discharged at the end of the last episode in a spell. This finished admission episode field has not been used as this only counts the first episode and as we are looking at length of stay we want to look at only spells where patients have been discharged from hospital.
Spell duration (SPELDUR) Where each spell is defined as a continuous period of time spent as a patient within a trust and gives the duration of spell in days derived from the difference between the patients admission date and discharge date when the spell has finished.
Diagnosis (Diag_01) Data has been categorised by the primary diagnosis on the record where the ICD 10 code was between J12 and J18 (pnemonia diagnosis codes). The diagnosis field is based on what the patient was diagnosed with on admission.
Sex - No filter was applied for sex.
ICB sub-location responsibility using the latest sub ICB location configuration across all time periods. sub ICB location configuration taken from NHS Digital's "Numbers of Patients Registered at a GP Practice" publication and looking up the sub ICB location in the April of the most recently published year. Patients are allocated to an sub ICB location based on the registered practice code on the HES episode. Where the code indicates the responsibility is to a practice outside England, this record is excluded. All records without a practice code, and those with a practice code that is not recognised but does not indicate that responsibility is outside England, are allocated using the patient postcode, to the sub ICB location within whose geographical boundary they live. Values may not match those previously produced as these will be based on the most recent GP practice to sub ICB location lookup. Any changes to the lookup will alter the total count and population of a sub ICB location and so values may differ from those previously shown for the same area and time period.

Patients are assigned to a sub ICB location based on the registered practice code in their HES episode. If the code belongs to a practice outside England, the record is excluded. Records without a practice code use the patient’s postcode to determine the sub ICB location. Practice codes are sourced from the most recent April GP practice code list size dataset. Therefore, areas have been suppressed where many patients were likely to have been treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust and neighbouring areas have been flagged to be treated with caution. Indicator: Dementia: Proportion of people with dementia prescribed anti-psychotic medication in the last six weeks
Rationale: The purpose of this indicator is to measure the prescribing of anti-psychotic medication to people with dementia. This indicator is aimed at CCGs and service providers to help monitor good quality of care for people with dementia. Ensuring dementia patients receive a high quality of care is one of the targets outlined in the Prime Minister’s ‘Challenge on Dementia 2020’ and dementia wellness pathway. The use of anti-psychotics as a way of managing dementia symptoms is viewed as poor practice and discouraged due to the negative impact on a patient’s wellbeing: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/challenge-on-dementia-2020-implementation-plan  People with dementia may develop behavioural and psychological symptoms (BPSD) including agitation, aggression, distress, and psychosis and are often prescribed anti-psychotic medication, and in some cases inappropriately.NICE guidance recommends prescription of anti-psychotics should be undertaken with serious consideration and to only offer anti-psychotic medication as a first-line treatment if there is a risk of the patient harming themselves or others if the patient is severely distressed. Alternative psychosocial and environmental interventions should initially be offered.In the case when anti-psychotics are required, Risperidone is the only licensed anti-psychotic of choice for short-term use which is licensed for 6 weeks use, after which a review should follow.<a href="https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/risperidone.html">
Definition: The proportion of people with dementia and in receipt of anti-psychotic medication in the last six weeks.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/recorded-dementia-diagnoses

Definition of denominator: All people with a diagnosis of dementia recorded on the primary register in England(all ages).
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Recorded Dementia Diagnoses (RDD)
Methodology: Numerator/denominator * 100

Indicator: Invasive Meningococcal Disease (IMD) confirmed cases rate/100,000
Rationale: This indicator is designed to measure the local burden of invasive meningococcal disease (IMD). IMD is an important health protection issue due to the severity of the disease, especially in young children and teenagers. Meningoccoal infection is vaccine preventable, with the routine immunisation schedule indicating infant and teenage immunisation against different strains of Neisseria Meningitidis. High rates of invasive meningococcal disease should prompt review of the causes e.g. an outbreak, poor uptake of vaccination among risk groups.
Definition: Crude incidence rate of new cases of laboratory confirmed IMD infection per 100,000 population
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: New cases of laboratory confirmed IMD.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Meningococcal Reference Unit (MRU)
Definition of denominator: Population who reside in area
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: count of laboratory confirmed cases of IMD divided by the denominator, multipled by 100,000. Confidence intervals calculated using exact poisson.
Confidence interval details: Confidence intervals have been calculated by UKHSA using R and are based on the exact Poisson method (cil denominator count, poisson per (100000)) (for more information go to www.stata.com)
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats: Every effort is made to ensure accuracy and completeness of the data. UKHSA Invasive Meningococcal Surveillance Programme only includes laboratory confirmations from MRU. A) Underreporting: IMD samples confirmed at local NHS / private laboratories may not be sent to MRU for confirmation. b) Misclassification of residence. Cases may be assigned incorrectly to a LA if postcode information is missing. If postcode of residency is not available, residency will be assigned according to requesting laboratory. c) Outbreaks: Outbreaks may lead to localised increases in infection due to specific events. d) The data presented here may differ from data from other sources, including from NOIDS (Notification of Infectious Diseases) and CIMS (UKHSA public health management system). e) The sum of the local authority data may not equal the regional and overall England data because for some individuals only the region or country of residence is available.<span data-teams="true">To note that numbers may differ from other published reports which assign region based on the laboratory of testing.<span data-teams="true">To note that numbers may differ from other published reports which assign region based on the laboratory of testing.

Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: MenB booster (2 years)
Rationale: The MenB vaccine protects against invasive meningococcal disease capsule group B most commonly presenting as either septicaemia or meningitis, or a combination of both. The vaccine was introduced into the routine childhood immunisation programme in September 2015 for babies at 8 and 16 weeks of age, with a booster dose after the first birthday. Vaccination coverage is the best indicator of the level of protection a population will have against vaccine preventable communicable diseases. Coverage is closely correlated with levels of disease. Monitoring coverage identifies possible drops in immunity before levels of disease rise. The MenB vaccine is given to all children under two years old as part of the childhood vaccination programme. Previous evidence shows that highlighting vaccination programmes encourages improvements in uptake levels and may also have relevance for NICE guidance PH21: Reducing differences in the uptake of immunisations (The guidance aims to increase immunisation uptake among those aged under 19 years from groups where uptake is low).
Definition: Children for whom the local authority is responsible who completed a booster course of Meningococcal group B (MenB) vaccine at any time by their second birthday as a percentage of all children whose second birthday falls within the time period.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency, Coverage of Vaccinations Evaluated Rapidly Programme
Indicator source: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/cover-of-vaccination-evaluated-rapidly-cover-programme-annual-data
Definition of numerator: Total number of children whose second birthday falls within the time period who received a MenB booster at any time before their second birthday.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Cover of Vaccination Evaluated Rapidly Programme (COVER)
Definition of denominator: Total number of children whose second birthday falls within the time period.
Source of denominator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Cover of Vaccination Evaluated Rapidly Programme (COVER)
Methodology: Crude percentage: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 100.
Disclosure control: The Isles of Scilly has been aggregated with Cornwall, City of London with Hackney and Rutland with Leicestershire.
Caveats:
ICB dataGP-level coverage data is collected by the NHS Digital strategic data collection service, as provided by Child Health Information Service (CHIS) providers. Completeness of practices and data quality may vary, and so validations may need to be made if using this data for analyses.Full GP postcodes are used to aggregate data to ICB published by NHS Digital. These may not be consistent with the local authority geographies used by the CHIS providers in the local authority level report. Unregistered children are allocated to a ICB based on residence.
ICB data do not form part of the core annual COVER programme official statistics because we do not have full assurance that they meet the quality pillar of the Code of Practice for Statistics.
Caution should be exercised when comparing coverage figures over time due to occasional data quality issues reported by some data suppliers. Apparent trends could reflect changes in the quality of data reported as well as real changes in vaccination coverage. Indicator: Percentage of deaths with three or more emergency admissions in the last 90 days of life.
Rationale:
The purpose of this indicator is to encourage improvement in the quality of end of life care in the following ways:

Anticipatory planning and end of life care being addressed in a co-ordinated and timely way.
Key information about the person's condition needs and preferences being shared across the local health and care system.
Local community services should be configured so that they can be responsive to patient's urgent end of life care needs.

This indicator is also published by NHS in the NHS Oversight Framework. Our aim in publishing this indicator in the profiles is to make this national NHS indicator available to stake holders in the context of the other indicators relevant to end of life care, and to provide a more specific breakdown of the indicator for age at death (75 years or older and under 75). It is actively monitored by Sustainability and Transformation Partnerships (STPs) and Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs), and the demand for breakdowns of this information can be shown in stakeholder surveys and enquiries to PHE.
Definition: Number of people with three or more emergency admissions in their last 90 days of life as a percentage of all deaths.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
Count of individual people who had 3 or more emergency admissions in their last 90 days of life. People are counted in the numerator if they have 3 or more emergency admissions meeting the following criteria:

(HES) classpat = 1, 2 or 5
(HES) epistat = 3
(HES) admimeth = 2* (i.e. starts with a "2")
(ONS) dod - (HES) admidate < 91
(ONS) age_at_death [used only for the subsidary indicators for age bands 75 years and older and under 75]
(ONS) cause_of_death_neonatal_1 is empty
(ONS) subsequent_activity_flag is empty

The criteria are based on field names as per the data dictionaries of the Hospital Episode Statistics database (HES) and the HES_ONS linked mortality database (ONS).
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) linked to Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Mortality Extract data
Definition of denominator: All deaths of people aged over 28 days.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Methodology: The indicator is calculated as 100 *(numerator/denominator).
Disclosure control:
In accordance with NHS Digital Guidance, Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) Analysis Guide.

Zeros are unchanged
Numerators 1-7 are suppressed
Numerators 8 or over are rounded to the nearest 5
Rounding: Subnational geographies with numerators of between 1 and 7 admissions have been suppressed. At a subnational level, counts greater than 7 are rounded to the nearest 5. These are in accordance with HES analysis guidelines.
Caveats:
n 2023, NHS England announced a https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/find-data-and-publications/statement-of-administrative-sources/methodological-changes/impact-of-changes-to-recording-of-same-day-emergency-care-activity-to-hospital-episode-statistics-hes-data to require Trusts to report Same Day Emergency Care (SDEC) to the Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) by July 2024. The rate of attended contacts provides local health and care systems with an important measure of demand. It will help to assess how the demand reflects the mental health needs of the local population and if the demand can be met by current service provisions. Therefore, the data may not represent the activity being delivered, but my be more indicitive of the level of recording.For the up-to-date data quality reports, see https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/mental-health-data-hub/mental-health-services-data-quality Contacts are not a mandatory requirement so some trusts may submit referrals without associated contacts. If the value seems out of alignment with local prevalence estimates and what is known about local primary care capacity to manage mental illness, action may be taken to improve data quality. If the values align with the other local indicators then action may be taken to increase the rate of attended contacts by improving access to services. Conversely, action may be taken to reduce the rate of attended contacts by interventions to improve the mental health of the population, or by improving the capacity of primary care services. Ultimately, each local system is unique and any action should be based on a thorough understanding of the balance of these influences in the local system.

Data Indicator values and counts have not been published when the count missingness is assessed as greater than 10%, and a note has been applied when the count missingness is assessed as between 5 and 10%. Note that occasionally issues with a provider’s data quality may impact unusually on missingness calculations resulting in values and counts for an area being removed or flagged where the impact is less clear.
