Methodology:
These rates are directly age standardised using European Standard Population 2013 per 100,000.This improves the comparability of rates for different areas, or between different time periods, by taking into account differences in the age structures of the populations being compared.The directly age standardised rate is the rate of events that would occur in a standard population if that population were to experience the age specific rates of the subject population. The standard population used for the direct method is the European Standard Population.The methodology is based on that provided in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly Used Public Health Statistics and their Confidence Intervals.
<a href="https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/guidance">https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/guidanceFigures were calculated using the PHEIndicatormethods R package available from https://github.com/PublicHealthEngland/PHEindicatormethods Directly standardised rates have also been calculated for each sex, for a variety of age groups, and for each deprivation quintile. Caveats:
MHSDS is a complex data set of 50+ tables in a relational database. However, only the tables containing patient details and referrals are mandatory. The level of completion for other tables varies between providers and is improving. Therefore, the data may not represent the activity being delivered, but may be more indicative of the level of recording.

For the up-to-date data quality reports, see  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/mental-health-data-hub/mental-health-services-data-quality .

The rate of inpatient stays will be influenced by a range of factors and an admission can be the most appropriate support for some individuals.

For people admitted to an acute mental health unit, a therapeutic environment provides the best opportunity for recovery. Purposeful, patient-orientated and recovery-focused care is the goal from the outset. Units operating beyond capacity may struggle to offer such care and cannot admit new patients, who are then looked after further away from home or in non-specialist settings.

The NHS Long Term Plan builds on the Five Year Forward View for Mental Health commitment to eliminate inappropriate adult Out of Area Placements (OAPs) by 2020/21, and maintain this position going forward. OAPs currently remain relatively widespread.

An inappropriate OAP for acute mental health in-patient care is defined as when a person with assessed acute mental health needs who requires adult mental health acute inpatient care, is admitted to a unit that does not form part of their usual local network of services. This means an inpatient unit that does not usually admit people living in the catchment of the person’s local community mental health service, and where the person cannot be visited regularly by their care co-ordinator to ensure continuity of care and effective discharge planning.

Some inpatient stays are the result of out of area placements (OAPs) but not all OAPs are recorded in MHSDS. Therefore some rates of inpatient stays reported in this metric will be lower than if all OAPs were included. There may be benefit in considering the separate bespoke data collection on all OAPs (from  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/out-of-area-placements-in-mental-health-services ) alongside this metric.

Indicator: Proportion of total antibiotic prescribing from the "Reserve" category of the nationally adapted WHO AWaRe index
Rationale: The consumption of antibiotics is a major driver for the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.In 2017 the World Health Organisation (WHO) updated the Essential Medicines List (EML) and classified key antibiotics into  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29303731  to improve access (Access), to monitor important antibiotics (Watch) and preserve effectiveness of ‘last resort’ antibiotics (Reserve). These  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31361000/  through expert elicitation with the Department of Health and Social Care advisory committee on antibiotic prescribing, resistance and healthcare-associated infection (APRHAI) for use in English antimicrobial stewardship.
Definition: This indicator displays what proportion of total antibiotic prescribing within NHS acute Trusts is from within the "Reserve" category of the WHO Essential Medicines List AWaRe index amended for use in English antimicrobial stewardship policy by expert elicitation.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency, based on Rx-info data
Indicator source: UKHSA calculated from data supplied by RxInfo ©.
Definition of numerator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD)count of antibiotics within the "Reserve" category of the WHO AWaRe index (as amended for use in English antibiotic stewardship) for the quarter specified.
Source of numerator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Definition of denominator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD)count of total antibiotic prescribing for the quarter specified using the WHO 2019 DDDs.
Source of denominator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100 (percentage)
Standard population/values: No standard population has been used.
Frequency: This indicator will be updated with quarterly data on a quarterly basis.
Disclosure control: The source data contains no personal or identifiable information and so statistical disclosure control has not been applied.
Rounding: No rounding has been used.
Caveats: Drugs are only included in the numerator and denominator if they have a British National Formulae (BNF) 5.1 code and Defined Daily Dose (DDD) values provided by the World Health Organisation. Anti-TB, Anti-Parasitic and topical antibiotics are excluded to align with requirements for the NHS Standard Contract and previous NHS England antibiotic resistance CQUINs.The figures produced in this indicator are raw and unadjusted for the confounding effects of both the age and sex mix of patient populations served by hospitals, or for other factors such as deprivation and complexity of care that can drive hospital antibiotic prescribing. Therefore Trusts may appear outliers for this measure byfulfilling valid care of the specific population that they serve.Further considerationis required to adapt the AWaRe index for use in specialisthealthcare settings, including an improved understanding ofcase-mix. However, until routine electronic prescribing of antibiotics is available nationally, there is limited work that can beperformed in this area.For these reasons comparison between different organisations should be treated with caution. Nonetheless, as NHS national quality improvement schemes require each hospital to improve from its own baseline levels this is consistent with improving the quality of antibiotic prescribing in each hospital. The data for any new quarter are provisional and will be updated with more accurate admissions and prescribing data in the subsequent quarter’s data release. The proportions for past quarters may therefore change to reflect this.
Notes: The Defined Daily Dose (DDD) is the assumed average maintenance dose per day for a medicine used for its main indication in adults. In general, the DDDs for antibiotics are based on their use in moderately severe infections. The DDD is the internationally recognised unit of measurement of medicine consumption, recommended by the World Health Organisation (WHO). DDDs allow comparison of medicine use over time hence its use in this context.

Indicator: Mortality rate from asthma, all ages
Rationale: Every asthma death represents a failure of management of a reversible condition. Although advances in treatments, increased research and the development of evidence-based clinical guidelines have contributed to a reduction in deaths from asthma over the past 50 years, mortality rates within the UK are among the highest in Europe, and numbers have tended to increase over recent years although deaths are falling in younger people. Asthma is a complex disease, and it is not just those with severe asthma who die. The National Review of Asthma Deaths (NRAD) was the first national investigation of asthma deaths in the UK and examined data from a cohort for whom asthma was the cause of death between February 2012 and January 2013. 1 A number of recommendations were made in order to reduce the number of asthma deaths, but there is little evidence of a systematic approach nationally to the implementation of these recommendations. There are still a significant number of deaths from asthma every year. Nationally, asthma mortality varies between sex and age groups. Mortality rates significantly increase with age and are higher in female patients(1,2). The NRAD report suggests that in the majority of cases there were factors, which if addressed, would have reduced the risk of death.1 Royal College of Physicians (2014) National Review of Asthma Deaths - Why asthma still kills, https://www.rcplondon.ac.uk/projects/outputs/why-asthma-still-kills [Accessed 30 July 2019] 2 Watson L, Turk F, James P and others (2007) Factors associated with mortality after an asthma admission: A national United Kingdom database analysis Respiratory Medicine 101(8):1659-64 doi: 10.1016/j.rmed.2007.03.006  https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0954611107001266 [Accessed 30 July 2019]

More information on comparability ratios is available in the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Mortality/Comparability_ratios.html .
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: For single years: Population for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+) For three-year rolling averages: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+)

Methodology: Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: Meningococcal ACWY conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) (14 to 15 years)
Rationale: The MenACWY vaccination was introduced into the national immunisation programme in autumn 2015 to respond to a rapid and accelerating increase in cases of invasive meningococcal group W (MenW) disease, which was declared a national incident. The MenACWY conjugate vaccine provides direct protection to the vaccinated cohort and, by reducing MenW carriage, will also provide indirect protection to unvaccinated children and adults. This follows advice from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI). It is routinely offered through schools in academic school Years 9 and 10 (rising 14 and rising 15 year olds). The indicator measures local authority level MenACWY vaccine coverage for students at the end of school Yr 10. Vaccination coverage is the best indicator of the level of protection a population will have against vaccine preventable communicable diseases. Coverage is closely correlated with levels of disease. Monitoring coverage identifies possible drops in immunity before levels of disease rise.Previous evidence shows that highlighting vaccination programmes encourages improvements in uptake levels. May also have relevance for NICE guidance PH21: Reducing differences in the uptake of immunisations (The guidance aims to increase immunisation uptake among those aged under 19 years from groups where uptake is low).
Definition: Local authority level vaccine coverage estimates for the school-based meningococcal ACWY adolescent vaccination programme for 14 to 15 year olds
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/meningococcal-acwy-immunisation-programme-vaccine-coverage-estimates">https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/meningococcal-acwy-immunisation-programme-vaccine-coverage-estimates
Definition of numerator: Total number of adolescents in LA responsible population whose 15th birthday falls within the time period who have ever received MenACWY vaccine.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Local Screening and Immunisation Teams
Definition of denominator: Total number of adolescents attending school in LA plus adolescents resident in the LA not linked to any school whose 15th birthday falls within the time period.
Source of denominator: Department for Education (DfE), Schools, pupils and their characteristics
Methodology: Crude percentage: numerator is divided by denominator and then multiplied by 100
Disclosure control: Small numbers less than 5 are suppressed
Caveats:
On 23 March 2020, all educational settings in England were advised to close by the UK Government as part of COVID19 pandemic measures. Although the importance of maintaining good vaccine uptake was impressed, operational delivery of all school aged immunisation programmes was paused for a short period of time as a consequence of school closures limiting access to venues for providers and children who were eligible for vaccination and to ensure that lock down regulations where not breached.

The NHSEI central public health commissioning and operations team rapidly established an Immunisation Task and Finish Group, with regional NHSEI and UKHSA representation. The group was established to:

• assess the impact of COVID19 on all immunisation programmes, including school aged programmes
• develop technical guidance and a plan for restoration and recovery of school aged programmes, once education settings were re opened

From 1 June 2020 some schools partially re opened for some year groups for a mini summer term. NHSEI published clinical guidance for healthcare professionals on maintaining immunisation programmes during COVID19 (3), and the Department of Education published further guidance (4) which led to schools allowing vaccination sessions to resume on site.

NHSEI commissioned, school-aged immunisation providers were able to implement their restoration and recovery plans to commence catch-up during the summer of 2020. This included delivery of programmes in school and community settings following a robust risk assessment and in line with UK Government Public Health COVID19 guidance.

In September 2020, schools across the UK reopened for general in person attendance. During the 2020 to 2021 academic year, students were required to stay at home and learn remotely if they tested positive for COVID19 or if they were a contact of a confirmed COVID19 case and so school attendance rates in England were lower than normal (1), especially in areas with very high COVID19 incidence rates. In England, as part of a wider national lockdown in January 2021, schools were closed to all except children of keyworkers and vulnerable children. From early March 2021, primary schools reopened, with a phased reopening of secondary schools.

Although this led to some disruption of school based elements of programme delivery in the 2020 to 2021 academic year, NHSEI Regional Public Health Commissioning teams worked with NHSEI commissioned school-aged immunisation providers to maintain the delivery of the routine programme and catch-up. As the routine programme is commissioned for a school aged cohort rather than a school based cohort, providers were able to build on existing arrangements such as community based clinics in place for children not in mainstream education. A wide variety of local arrangements were established to ensure programme delivery continued effectively and safely in the school and community premises, during the term time and schoolbreaks.

Indicator: Percentage of COPD deaths that occur in care homes
Rationale:
Patients with advanced respiratory diseases have a very high symptom burden near the end of life, with a particularly high prevalence of breathlessness, fatigue, anxiety and depression [1,2]. For all patients with advanced respiratory disease, good quality palliative care should be initiated early and address the holistic needs of patients and their families. There is considerable evidence that despite their higher symptom burden, and the recommendations in national and international guidelines [3,4], patients with COPD have much poorer access to palliative care [2,5,6].
There is limited data at national level on access to palliative care and good quality end of life care for patients with advanced respiratory diseases. A commonly used indicator of choice at end of life is place of death [7], with evidence that with good advanced care planning patients are more likely to die in their preferred place [8]. Although place of death is only one factor of importance to patients and their families, and not necessarily the most important one [9,10], the fact that it is routinely recorded for all deaths provides useful insights into variations in end of life care.
This indicator is intended to be used in conjunction with two other COPD place of death indicators to highlight variation in end of life care.

Indicator: Percentage of COPD deaths that occur in hospital
Rationale:
Patients with advanced respiratory diseases have a very high symptom burden near the end of life, with a particularly high prevalence of breathlessness, fatigue, anxiety and depression [1,2]. Good quality palliative care should be initiated early and address the holistic needs of patients and their families. There is evidence that despite their higher symptom burden, and the recommendations in guidelines [3,4], patients with COPD have poorer access to palliative care [2,5,6].

There is limited data at a national level on access to palliative care. A commonly used proxy indicator of choice at end of life is place of death [7], with evidence that with good advanced care planning patients are more likely to die in their preferred place [8]. Although place of death is only one factor of importance to patients and their families, and not necessarily the most important one [9,10], the fact that it is routinely recorded for all deaths provides useful insights into variations in end of life care.

This indicator is intended to be used in conjunction with two other COPD place of death indicators to highlight variation in end of life care.

Indicator: Odds of smoking with a long-term mental health condition compared to the odds of smoking without (old method)
Rationale: Smoking is the most important cause of preventable ill health and premature mortality in the UK. Smoking is a major risk factor for many diseases, such as lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart disease. It is also associated with cancers in other organs, including lip, mouth, throat, bladder, kidney, stomach, liver and cervix.Smoking is a modifiablebehavioural risk factor; effective tobacco control measures can reduce the prevalence of smoking in the population. Studies have shown that people with mental health conditions are more likely to smoke than the general public and that smoking rates increase with the severity of illness(1). In addition studies have shown that those smoking more than 15 cigarettes a day are more likely to experience a common mental health disorder than those who smoke fewer cigarettes or do not smoke at all(2), and 40% of cigarettes smoked in England are smoked by people with a mental health problem(3).The Government’s Tobacco Control Plan(4) published in July 2017 sets out the Government’s strategy to reduce smoking prevalence among adults and young people, to reduce smoking during pregnancy and to reduce the gap between routine and manual occupations and the general population. It also identified the need for improved data on smoking and mental health, and this indicator aims to address this.1. Royal College of Physicians smoking and mental health leaflet https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/usefulresources/publications/collegereports/cr/cr178.aspx 4. Towards a Smokefree Generation: A Tobacco Control Plan for England, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/towards-a-smoke-free-generation-tobacco-control-plan-for-england
Definition: <span style="line-height: 107%; mso-fareast-font-family: Calibri; mso-fareast-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-ansi-language: EN-GB; mso-fareast-language: EN-US; mso-bidi-language: AR-SA;">The odds of current smoking among adults (aged 18 and over) with a long-term mental health condition divided by the odds of current smoking without a long-term health condition expressed as an odds ratio.
Data source: NHS England
Indicator source: Calculated by OHID from GPPS data
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: Sample size with a valid response to both of the following questions in the GP Patient Survey for the chosen area type:-"Which of the following long-term health conditions do you have...A mental health condition?"- "Which of the following best describes your smoking habits?"
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology:
The value is presented as an odds ratio. An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an event. The OR represents the odds that an event will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the event occurring in the absence of that exposure.

This odds ratio represents the odds of those with a long-term mental health condition smoking compared with those with no long-term mental health condition.Specifically, an odds ratio compares the oddsthat an event (smoking) will occur in the presence of a certain exposure (having a long-term mental health condition) to the odds of the same event (smoking) occurring in the absence of the exposure (having a long-term mental health condition).

The odds of the event in the exposed group is:

(a) The number of people who reported smoking and having a long-term mental health condition

(b) The number of people who reported not smoking and had a long-term mental health condition

The odds in the event in non-exposed group is:

(c) The number of people who reported smoking and not having a long-term mental health condition

(d) The number of people who reported not smoking and not having a long-term mental health condition

The Odds Ratio was calculated by:

Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d)= ad/bc

The sample is restricted to respondents age 18+ years, with a valid response to the question "Which of the following long-term health conditions do you have...A mental health condition?". The number of respondents has been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights consider survey design and non-response.

The number of respondents have been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weigths consider survey design and non-response rates.Full details on weighting within the GPPS can be found in the Technical Annex https://gp-patient.co.uk/technical-annex-introduction-2025
Confidence interval details: Confidence intervals are calculated as follows:lower 95% CI = e^( ln(OR) - 1.96 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d))upper 95% CI = e^( ln(OR) + 1.96 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d))whereOR = odds ratioa = current smokers in the group with a long-term mental health conditionb = non-smokers in the group with a long-term mental health conditionc = current smokers not in the group with a long-term mental health conditiond = non-smokers not in the group with a long-term mental health condition
Disclosure control: Values have been suppressed where small counts produced very large confidence intervals.
Rounding: Odds displayed to 2 decimal places but no further rounding is applied during the calculation
Caveats:
Previously the GPPS fieldwork was carried out in two waves across the financial year. From 2016/17 there was only one wave of fieldwork from January to March, however due to the trend the indicator remains reported by financial year.
Various changes were made to the questionnaire in 2017/18 including the inclusion of 16-17 year old respondents. For the purposes of continuity, the calculation of this indicator does not include responses from 16-17 year olds and therefore may differ from figures published elsewhere. For full details of the changes made to the questionnaire, please see the GPPS website https://www.gp-patient.co.uk/surveysandreports For the 2019/20 data anumber of checks were undertaken at key stages of the survey, including during the sample preparation and data cleaning stages. These help to identify obvious errors in the sample and response data, such as the inclusion of ineligible patients or incorrect coding. During reporting it was noted that there was a higher proportion of people who had not answered a selection of questions, including the questions on sex and age when compared with the average for the previous two years. This was investigated further and it was concluded that it was an issue with scanning sensitivity in relation to these questions. The missing values were randomly spread throughout the data set, the scale of the missing values represented a small proportion of overall responses and were shown not to have impacted trends. For these reasons it was concluded that this had not significantly impacted on the survey results.
Notes:
An odds ratio of 1 represents no difference between smoking prevalence rates in the two groups. If the confidence intervals overlap 1, we can say with 95% confidence that there is no significant difference in the prevalence of mental health conditions between the groups.

An odds ratio higher than 1 signifies the group with a long-term mental health condition are more likely to smoke than their counterparts. For example, if the odds ratio is 2, they have twice the odds of smoking. On the other hand, an odds ratio between 0 and 1 signifies that they are less likely to smoke. For example, if the odds ratio is 0.5, they have half the odds of smoking.

These data have not been age-standardised and, therefore, variation between area values may be a result of differences in population structure.

Small sample sizes may cause fluctuations for smaller geographical areas, which should be interpreted with caution.

Indicator: Percentage of cancers diagnosed at stages 1 and 2
Rationale: Stage at diagnosis is a measure of how much a cancer has grown and spread, with advanced stages meaning the cancer is bigger or has spread to other parts of the body (metastasis)and consequentially patient outcomes are worse for later stages. The data can be used to provide information to a wide range of patient and professional groups; plan services aimed at early detection and diagnosis of cancer, and inform cancer research. Additionally, as there are often different treatment options at an advanced stage at diagnosis these data can inform understanding of cancer treatment services.
Definition: New cases of cancer diagnosed at stages 1 and 2 as a percentage of all new cases of cancer diagnosed at any known stage (1, 2, 3, and 4) for the following cancer sites: invasive malignancies of lung, oesophagus, colon, rectum, pancreas, invasive melanomas of the skin, breast, uterus, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, Hodgkin Lymphoma, larynx, oropharynx, oral cavity, and non Hodgkin lymphoma.
Data source: NHS England, National Disease Registration Service
Definition of numerator: Cases of cancer diagnosed at stages 1 and 2 for the following cancer sites: invasive malignancies of lung, oesophagus, colon, rectum, pancreas, invasive melanomas of the skin, breast, uterus, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, Hodgkin Lymphoma, larynx, oropharynx, oral cavity, and non Hodgkin lymphoma.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Disease Registration Service (NDRS)
Definition of denominator: Cases of cancer diagnosed at any known stage (1, 2, 3, and 4) for the following cancer sites: invasive malignancies of lung, oesophagus, colon, rectum, pancreas, invasive melanomas of the skin, breast, uterus, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, Hodgkin Lymphoma, larynx, oropharynx, oral cavity, and non Hodgkin lymphoma.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Disease Registration Service (NDRS)
Methodology: Tumour level data from the National Cancer Registry database maintained by NHS Digital's National Disease Registration Service is aggregated by patient postcode at diagnosis to each geography. The proportion of new cases of cancer diagnosed at stages 1 and 2 are calculated as a percentage of all new cases of cancer diagnosed at any known stage (1, 2, 3, and 4) for the following cancer sites: invasive malignancies of lung, oesophagus, colon, rectum, pancreas, invasive melanomas of the skin, breast, uterus, ovary, prostate, testis, kidney, bladder, Hodgkin Lymphoma, larynx, oropharynx, oral cavity, and non Hodgkin lymphoma. Site specific staging systems have also been included. Please refer to the technical document on case-mix adjusted percentage of cancers diagnosed at stages 1 and 2 by CCG in England for details here:  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/find-data-and-publications/statement-of-administrative-sources/methodological-changes#cancer-statistics
Confidence interval details: Crude measure: Wilson Score method
Disclosure control: Isles of Scilly's totals have been combined with Cornwall UA to prevent potential disclosure of individuals. Cancer groups with a stage completeness of less than 70% over the last 3 years (2020-2022) are not included as they are considered unreliable.
Rounding: Percentages and supporting confidence intervals will be presented to one decimal place.
Caveats:
This indicator is not case-mix adjusted. A case-mix adjusted indicator (calculated within a regression model framework) is available at ICB level (see notes section). This approach was not followed here due to the number of different geographic breakdowns, and issues of statistical stability for smaller geographies.

The primary impact of case-mix adjustment is to reduce differences between geographies by adjusting for differences in cancer group (in addition to sex, age, and deprivation). For example, more affluent areas tend to have a higher comparative incidence of breast and prostate cancer (which tend toward early stage at diagnosis) and a lower incidence of lung cancer (which tends toward late stage at diagnosis).

Indicator: Smoking prevalence in adults (aged 18 and over) admitted to treatment for substance misuse (NDTMS) - all opiates
Rationale:
Smoking is the most important cause of preventable ill health and premature mortality in the UK. Smoking is a major risk factor for many diseases, such as lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart disease. It is also associated with cancers in other organs, including lip, mouth, throat, bladder, kidney, stomach, liver and cervix.
Smoking is a modifiablebehavioural risk factor; effective tobacco control measures can reduce the prevalence of smoking in the population.
The Government’s Tobacco Control Plan (1) published in July 2017 sets out the Government’s strategy to reduce smoking prevalence among adults and young people, and to reduce smoking during pregnancy.
Other studies have shown that whilst “high smoking prevalence has been observed among those misusing other substances” there is little smoking cessation support available to this vulnerable population (2,3). The latest PHE publication on the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System (NDTMS) reported that nearly 49,000 people said they had smoked tobacco in the 28 days before starting treatment yet only around 3% were recorded as having been offered referrals for smoking cessation interventions (4). Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: Flu (primary school aged children)
Rationale: Influenza (also known as Flu) is a highly infectious viral illness spread by droplet infection. The flu vaccination is offered to people who are at greater risk of developing serious complications if they catch flu.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />However, it is hoped that in extending the childhood influenza vaccination programme to healthy children will provide direct protection for those immunised as well as indirectly protecting the remaining population by reducing transmission. See recommendations from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) for the childhood flu programme.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /> http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20120907090205/http:/www.dh.gov.uk/prod_consum_dh/groups/dh_digitalassets/@dh/@ab/documents/digitalasset/dh_133598.pdf <br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />Vaccination coverage is the best indicator of the level of protection a population will have against vaccine preventable communicable diseases. Immunisation is one of the most effective healthcare interventions available and flu vaccines can prevent illness and hospital admissions among these groups of people. Increasing the uptake of flu vaccine among these high risk groups should also contribute to easing winter pressure on primary care services and hospital admissions. Coverage is closely related to levels of disease. Monitoring coverage identifies possible drops in immunity before levels of disease rise.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />UKHSA will continue to provide a centre of expert advice and monitoring of public health, including immunisation. NHS England now has responsibility for commissioning the flu programme and GPs continue to play a key role. NHS England teams will ensure that robust plans are in place locally and that high vaccination uptake levels are reached in the clinical risk groups. For more information see the Green Book chapter 19 on "Influenza" ( https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/influenza-the-green-book-chapter-19 ).

Methodology: Vaccine uptake data will be collected via the ImmForm website on vaccinations administered from 1 September to end January inclusive. All data is cumulative (i.e., total vaccinations administered from 1 September to the end of the month or week in question) and is provided by local authorities submitting their data manually each month.<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />1. Data is final and represents a percentage of all Local Authorities (LAs) in England responding to the final survey. Denominators are the provisional number of eligible children in schools in the LA geography AND children educated out of school in the LA geography, defined by child age on the 1st of September 2021. GP delivery was commissioned in Isles of Scilly Local Authority. Therefore, figures have been extracted from GP systems and are based on the number of patients registered with a GP practice located within the LA geographical boundary as defined by child age on 1 September 2021 (GP delivery).<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />4. Percent vaccine uptake of number of children vaccinated with influenza vaccine includes both LAIV (Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine) and IIV (Inactivated Influenza Vaccine).<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />The data collection will comprise of all eligible children as outlined in the annual flu letter. Although eligibility includes secondary school aged children, only those in of primary school age are included in this collection i.e., Reception to Year 6 (aged 4 to 11).<br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" /><br style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; border: none; outline: none;" />Coverage data reflects, to the best of providers’ ability, all eligible children in school years Reception to year 6 that have been vaccinated in school, including children who may have been vaccinated by GPs or pharmacies. Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: Shingles vaccination coverage (71 years)
Rationale:
The shingles vaccination programme was introduced to reduce the incidence and severity of shingles in those targeted by the programme by boosting individuals’ pre existing VZV immunity (1). The shingles vaccine stimulates individual pre existing immunity which cannot be acquired, therefore immunisation is required for protection.
In 2010, the UK’s Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) recommended that a herpes zoster (shingles) vaccination programme should be introduced for adults aged 70 years, with a catch up programme for those aged 71 to 79 years.
<div style="box-sizing: border-box;">In April 2017, eligibility criteria for the shingles vaccination was revised so that adults become eligible for the routine programme on their 70th birthday and remained eligible until their 80th birthday. Following this change, from 2018 to 2019, vaccine coverage is measured in those aged 71 and is calculated as the total number of patients who turned 71 between 1 April and 31 March, and were vaccinated by the end of June, as a proportion of the number of patients that turned 71 years old between 1 April and 31 March.
Prior to this (2013 to 2014 to 2017 to 2018), the vaccine was routinely offered to adults aged 70 years on 1 September of the programme year. Vaccine coverage was calculated as the total number of patients aged 70 on 1 September who had ever received the vaccination (numerator) as a proportion of the number of patients registered aged 70 years on 1 September (denominator) as of the following August.
Due to the changes in the vaccination coverage collection described, data for this indicator are not comparable to the previous shingles indicator D06c: shingles vaccination coverage among 70 year olds, available from 2013 to 2014 to 2017 to 2018.

Definition:
Percentage of children (aged under 16 years) living in relative low income families.

Relative low income is defined as a family in low income before housing costs (BHC) in the reference year. This indicator concentrates on those with household incomes below 60% of the average. A family must have claimed Child Benefit and at least one other household benefit (Universal Credit, tax credits, or Housing Benefit) at any point in the year to be classed as low income in these statistics.
Data source: OHID, based on Department for Work and Pensions and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
Number of children aged under 16 years in relative low income families, before housing costs, by financial year.

Confidence intervals and associated benchmarking should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Statistical disclosure control has been applied by DWP which guards against the identification of an individual claimant.

Indicator: Last BP reading of patients (<80 yrs, with CHD) in the last 12 months is <= 140/90 mmHg (denominator incl. PCAs)
Rationale: This indicator measures the intermediate health outcome of a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or less in patients with CHD. Its intent is to promote the secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD) through satisfactory blood pressure control. This intermediate outcome can be achieved through lifestyle advice and the use of drug therapy.The NICE clinical guideline on Hypertension recommends a target clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in patients aged under 80 years with treated hypertension and a clinic blood pressure below 150/90 mmHg in patients aged 80 years and over, with treated hypertension.A major overview of randomised trials showed that a reduction of 5 - 6 mmHg in blood pressure sustained over five years reduces coronary events by 20 - 25 per cent in patients with CHD.As of 1st April 2019, exception reporting was replaced with Personalised Care Adjustments (PCAs). PCAs can be applied to patients for a number of specified reasons and are usually the result of a patient or a GP decision at a personal level. Examples of PCAs could be patient or carer refusal of treatment, a patient cancels or does not attend a consultation appointment, or a GP’s advice that two types of medication or treatment methodology should not be administered simultaneously.The percentage of patients receiving the intervention (means: the denominator includes Personalised Care Adjustments (PCAs), i.e. all patients on the register) gives a more accurate indication of the rate of the provision of interventions as the denominator for this measure covers all patients the indicator applies to, regardless of PCA status and is therefore from a public health perspective the more relevant measure. For more details on PCAs please consult the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/quality-and-outcomes-framework-achievement-prevalence-and-exceptions-data/2019-20/technical-annex#qof-pca-data for QOF on NHS Digital.

Indicator: Under 75 mortality rate from liver disease considered preventable
Rationale: Liver disease is one of the top causes of death in England and people are dying from it at younger ages. Most liver disease is preventable and much is influenced by alcohol consumption and obesity prevalence, which are both preventable through public health interventions. The basic concept of preventable mortality is that deaths are considered preventable if, in the light of the understanding of the determinants of health at the time of death, all or most deaths from the underlying cause (subject to age limits if appropriate) could mainly be avoided through effective public health and primary prevention interventions.Preventable mortality overlaps with, but is not the same as ‘treatable’ mortality, which includes causes of deaths which could potentially be avoided through effective healthcare interventions, including secondary prevention and treatment.Preventable mortality and treatable mortality are the two components of ‘avoidable’ mortality.The inclusion of this indicator (alongside others in the Public Health and NHS Outcomes Frameworks) reinforces the Government’s commitment to reducing avoidable deaths through public health policy and interventions and sends out a clear signal that prevention of liver disease is just as important as treatment.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate from liver diseases considered preventable, per 100,000 population, in those aged under 75 years
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths that are considered preventable from liver disease (classified by underlying cause of death recorded as ICD-10 codes B15 to B19, C22, K70, K73, K74.0 to K74.2, K74.6 registered in the respective calendar years, in people aged under 75, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9,…, 70 to 74).Numbers of deaths may have been adjusted using comparability ratios. More information on comparability ratios is available in the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Mortality/Comparability_ratios.html .

Definition of denominator: For single years: Population for people under 75 years of age, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 70 to 74) For three-year rolling averages: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people under 75 years of age, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 70 to 74)

Indicator: Mortality due to cardiovascular disease for people referred to secondary mental health services (aged 18 to 74)
Rationale:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the major causes of death in under 75s in England and people with severe mental health problems are at higher risk of CVD. There have been huge gains over the past decades in terms of better treatment for CVD and improvements in lifestyle, but to ensure that there continues to be a reduction in the rate of under 75 mortality from CVD, there needs to be concerted action in both prevention and treatment. This is necessary across all sectors of society, including people with severe mental health problems
As part of the 10 Year Health Plan for England [1], the government has committed to a new approach to mental health. Neighbourhood healthcare services [2] are a core element of the 10 Year Health Plan, aiming to improve support for people with complex needs. These services build on existing approaches to reducing health inequalities, including Core20PLUS5 framework [3].
From 2026 to 2027 the government is making available funding over 4 years to invest in new models of care, including community-based mental health centres, mental health emergency departments and eliminating out-of-area placements [4].
Alongside this investment, a new modern service framework (MSF) for people with severe mental illness (SMI) is being developed. This MSF is to set consistency in clinical standards across England so that patients and families get the best quality, evidence-based treatment and support. The forthcoming MSF is to consider and outline opportunities for improving the physical health outcomes of people with severe and enduring mental problems [5].
People living with SMI experience some of the widest health inequalities in England. Their life expectancy is 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population [6]. They also have a much higher risk of developing preventable physical conditions [7].
Compared with the general patient population, patients with SMI are at substantially higher risk [7] of obesity, asthma, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cardiovascular disease. They make more use of secondary urgent and emergency care for their physical health conditions [8].
This indicator is part of measuring this inequality in people severe and enduring mental illness and will support on delivery of government’s commitments on improving outcomes for this population.
This indicator uses people with an open referral to secondary mental health services in the 5 years before their death as a proxy for ‘people with a severe and enduring mental problems’.

Definition: Directly age standardised rate of deaths due to all cardiovascular diseases (including heart disease and stroke) in people aged 18 to 74, referred to secondary mental health services, per 100,000 population. Referrals to mental health services in the five years preceding death are included with or without contact or inpatient stay.
Data source: NHS England and Office for National Statistics
Definition of numerator: Counts, by five year age bands (plus 18-19 year olds), of people aged 18 to 74 whose death was registered in the years in question and was from cardiovascular diseases (classified by underlying cause of death recorded as ICD codes I00-I99) , and who had a referral to secondary mental health services (excluding Learning Disabilities and Autism (LDA) only activity) in the 5 years preceding death. The mental health data sets are searched for evidence of referral to secondary mental health services back until April 2009. Therefore, any deaths before April 2014 will not have a full 5 years of mental health data searched. Analysis has shown that this is 0.2% of deaths registered in 2015-2017 and that proportion is expected to decrease for later time periods.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Civil Registrations of Death linked to the following datasets: Mental Health Services Dataset (MHSDS), Mental Health and Learning Disabilities Dataset (MHLDS) and Mental Health Minimum Dataset (MHMDS)
Definition of denominator: ONS mid-year population estimates, aggregated
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Directly age standardised rate.There has been a software change resulting in the way cause of death is recorded on the ONS deaths dataset ( https://eur03.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ons.gov.uk%2Fpeoplepopulationandcommunity%2Fbirthsdeathsandmarriages%2Fdeaths%2Farticles%2Fcauseofdeathcodinginmortalitystatisticssoftwarechanges%2Fjanuary2022&data=05%7C01%7CStephanie.Webb%40dhsc.gov.uk%7C30b884b5ba01420109a908da2842a5fd%7C61278c3091a84c318c1fef4de8973a1c%7C1%7C0%7C637866563951242005%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=EThJ8eI%2FIBxr1e%2FBxKD%2F5upnsOjQLyXa%2Fxy2lJNcewE%3D&reserved=0  and, with NHS England, we have been investigating the impact of this change and whether comparability ratios should be applied to data pre 2020. The application of comparability ratios for these indicators will be revisited when the next version of the diagnosis recording is implemented.

Values have not been calculated for areas where the number of deaths was fewer than 10, and the counts have been suppressed for these areas
This has been approved by NHS England's Disclosure Control Board
Rounding: Counts for areas below England level have been rounded to nearest 5 following the calculation of the rate
Caveats:
Variations in access to secondary mental health services and referral practice across different local authorities will affect the indicator. Areas where few adults are referred to secondary mental health services might have lower mortality for this population group. This is because fewer deaths in adults will be in people referred to secondary mental health services in the 5 years before their death. Conversely, areas where many adults are referred to secondary mental health services, mortality might be higher. This is because more deaths in adults will be in the group referred to secondary mental health services. Use of this indicator should be combined with local knowledge and consideration of other indicators in the Adult mental health and wellbeing profile.
This indicator omits patients with severe mental health problems receiving only care from NHS Talking Therapies, primary care or voluntary sector services that do not submit to MHSDS.
No secondary mental health services data was collected in December 2015, and the quality of the data collected in January - March 2016 could not be assessed. Therefore, this period has not been included when searching for evidence of an open referral with secondary mental health services for deceased people. Furthermore, any referrals to secondary mental health services open at the end of November 2015 are assumed to have remained open until at least the end of March 2016.
Children and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) have only submitted data to the Mental Health data sets since April 2016. Therefore, for some people it has not been possible to search the mental health data for the full 5 years before death.
The number of providers submitting to the Mental Health Data Sets has increased over time, and the amount of data submitted by each provider has also increased. Therefore, the larger the time period between death and a patient's last referral to services being closed, the more likely it is that the evidence of that referral was not found.
As evidenced by NHS England data, the population referred to secondary mental health services increased since 2015. This increase may reflect changes in the level of mental health need and demand, clinical characteristics of population accessing services, referral patterns and service availability. It is important to consider growth and change in the mental health population when assessing trends over time.

People with severe mental health problems have similar rates of cancer to the rest of the population. However, case fatality rates are higher and survival rates are lower for the cohort with referrals to secondary mental health services. This contributes to high mortality from cancer in people aged 18 to 74 referred to secondary mental health services.

As part of the 10 Year Health Plan for England [1], the government has committed to a new approach to mental health. Neighbourhood healthcare services [2] are a core element of the 10 Year Health Plan, aiming to improve support for people with complex needs. These services build on existing approaches to reducing health inequalities, including Core20PLUS5 framework [3].

From 2026 to 2027 the government is making available funding over 4 years to invest in new models of care, including community-based mental health centres, mental health emergency departments and eliminating out-of-area placements [4].

Alongside this investment, a new modern service framework (MSF) for people with severe mental illness (SMI) is being developed. This MSF is to set consistency in clinical standards across England so that patients and families get the best quality, evidence-based treatment and support. The forthcoming MSF is to consider and outline opportunities for improving the physical health outcomes of people with severe and enduring mental problems [5].

People living with SMI experience some of the widest health inequalities in England. Their life expectancy is 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population [6]. They also have a much higher risk of developing preventable physical conditions [7].

Compared with the general patient population, patients with SMI are at substantially higher risk [7] of obesity, asthma, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cardiovascular disease. They make more use of secondary urgent and emergency care for their physical health conditions [8].

This indicator is part of measuring this inequality in people severe and enduring mental illness and will support on delivery of government’s commitments on improving outcomes for this population.

Caveats:
Variations in access to secondary mental health services and referral practice across different local authorities will affect the indicator. It is important to consider growth and change in the mental health population when assessing trends over time.

Indicator: Excess mortality due to cancer for people referred to secondary mental health services (aged 18 to 74)
Rationale:
Cancer is the highest cause of death in England in under 75s. To ensure that there continues to be a reduction in the rate of mortality from cancer, there needs to be concerted action in both prevention and treatment. People referred to secondary mental health services have similar rates of cancer to the rest of the population. However, case fatality rates are higher and survival rates are lower for the group with severe mental health problems. This contributes to higher mortality from cancer in adults with severe mental health problems.
As part of the 10 Year Health Plan for England [1], the government has committed to a new approach to mental health. Neighbourhood healthcare services [2] are a core element of the 10 Year Health Plan, aiming to improve support for people with complex needs. These services build on existing approaches to reducing health inequalities, including Core20PLUS5 framework [3].
From 2026 to 2027 the government is making available funding over 4 years to invest in new models of care, including community-based mental health centres, mental health emergency departments and eliminating out-of-area placements [4].
Alongside this investment, a new modern service framework (MSF) for people with severe mental illness (SMI) is being developed. This MSF is to set consistency in clinical standards across England so that patients and families get the best quality, evidence-based treatment and support. The forthcoming MSF is to consider and outline opportunities for improving the physical health outcomes of people with severe and enduring mental problems [5].
People living with SMI experience some of the widest health inequalities in England. Their life expectancy is 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population [6]. They also have a much higher risk of developing preventable physical conditions [7].
Compared with the general patient population, patients with SMI are at substantially higher risk [7] of obesity, asthma, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cardiovascular disease. They make more use of secondary urgent and emergency care for their physical health conditions [8].
This indicator is part of measuring this inequality in people severe and enduring mental illness and will support on delivery of government’s commitments on improving outcomes for this population.
This indicator uses people with an open referral to secondary mental health services in the 5 years before their death as a proxy for ‘people with a severe and enduring mental problems’.

Indicator: Odds ratio of reporting a mental health condition among people with and without an MSK condition
Rationale:
In the UK, musculoskeletal conditions are the leading cause of disability accounting for 30.5% of all years lived with disability [1]. 26% of adults report having been diagnosed with at least one mental illness over their lifetime [2]. A 2012 paper estimated that in England approximately 4.6 million people had both a long-term physical health condition and a mental health problem [3]. There is often co-existence and a complex interaction between mental health and musculoskeletal conditions. Living with a musculoskeletal condition can lead to depression and anxiety and conversely, poor mental health can exacerbate or potentially lead to musculoskeletal condition [4]. Co-morbid mental health and musculoskeletal disorders have serious implications, affecting people’s motivation and ability to self-manage and adapt healthy behaviours, such as exercising. For example, depression can make pain feel worse, the person is less likely to self-manage resulting in poorer health behaviours such as reduced physical activity, and some medications taken for mental health conditions can have impact on weight gain and the development of musculoskeletal conditions. Delivery of care is still often built around the individual conditions, rather than the way the person experiences them collectively. As a result, care is often fragmented with lower outcomes and may not consider the combined impact of the conditions and their treatments on a person’s quality of life. All too often, when people experience care, they experience ‘silo’ care that is not integrated across conditions or specialisms and that does not account for the wider needs of the person. This indicator has been produced to raise awareness of the association between musculoskeletal conditions and mental health conditions and to stimulate better pain management strategies.

2. http://healthsurvey.hscic.gov.uk/support-guidance/public-health/health-survey-for-england2014/mental-health-problems.aspx

3. Naylor, C., Parsonage, M., McDaid, D., Knapp, M., Fossey, M., & Galea, A. (2012). Long term conditions and mental health. The cost of co-morbidities London: The King’s Fund- Centre for Mental Health. https://www.kingsfund.org.uk/sites/default/files/field/field_publication_file/long-term-conditions-mental-health-cost-comorbidities-naylor-feb12.pdf

4. http://arma.uk.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/MSK-and-Mental-Health-Nov2018.pdf
Definition:
The odds ratio of those with a long-term musculoskeletal condition also having a mental health condition compared with those with no musculoskeletal condition.
The definition of "long-term" is a condition lasting or expected to last 12 months or more.

Methodology:
The value is presented as an odds ratio. An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an event. The OR represents the odds that an event will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the event occurring in the absence of that exposure. This is calculated as:
Event Yes No Exposure Yes a b No c d Odds Ratio = odds of the event in the exposed group / odds of the event in the non-exposed group Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d) which can be simplified to Odds Ratio = ad/bc This odds ratio represents the likelihood of those with a long-term musculoskeletal condition also having a mental health condition compared with those with no musculoskeletal condition. The odds ratio for this indicator represents the odds that an event (having a mental health condition) will occur in the presence of a certain exposure (having a musculoskeletal health condition), compared to the odds of the same event (having a mental health condition) occurring in the absence of the exposure (not having a musculoskeletal health condition). The odds of the event in the exposed group is: The number of people who reported having a mental health condition and a musculoskeletal health condition (a) divided by the number of people who did not report having a mental health condition but did report having a musculoskeletal health condition (b). The odds in the event in non-exposed group is: The number of people who reported having a mental health condition but did not report having a musculoskeletal condition (c) divided by the number of people who did not report having a mental health condition or musculoskeletal healthcondition (d). This is illustrated by:
Mental health condition Yes No Musculoskeletal health condition Yes a b No c d

Patients were asked the following question regarding long-term conditions:

Which, if any, of the following long-term conditions do you have? This was Q33 in the 2021 survey and Q35 in 2018 to 2020.

A long-term musculoskeletal condition was indicated by the response – “Arthritis or ongoing problem with back or joints”.

A long-term mental health condition was indicated by the response – “A mental health condition”. The Odds Ratio was calculated by: Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc The sample is restricted to respondents age 16+ years, with a valid response to the question "Which of the following long-term health conditions do you have...". Participants were excluded if their local authority of residence was invalid or outside of England. The number of respondents has been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights consider survey design and non-responserates. Weights are calibrated to population counts by GP practice as well as population counts by age and gender by CCG. Full details on weighting within the GP Patient Survey can be found at https://www.gp-patient.co.uk/surveysandreports

Indicator: Population density: people per square kilometre
Rationale: Knowing the population density of an area contributes to an overall social demographic description of an area. The close proximity of populations is important in the spread of infectious diseases. Along with other social demographic information it can help towards planning for the health and social care needs of a particular population.
Definition: Population density is the total population per square kilometre
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics
Definition of numerator: Total population for a given area. Includes all ages.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Definition of denominator: Total geographic area by kilometre squared
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
Population density is calculated as the population estimate for each area divided by its land area in square kilometres. Land area is measured to the mean high water mark for costal areas and excluded areas of inland water. This is the Eurostat recommended method for compiling population density figures. A guide on how SAM are used is available from the ONS  https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/documents/f6717e32fb9c4304988c2c30bf063b1b/explore 
What are output areas? The Office for National Statistics (ONS) produces mid year small area population estimates by Output Areas (OA). Output areas are the lowest level of geographic area specifically designed for census data. These standardised geographic areas are designed to have equal numbers of households or populations within them making it easier to compare output areas.They are used primarily in statistical administrative data outputs such as the census and population estimates. Output areas are "nested" within larger geographic areas that can be summed or aggregated to provide data at these larger areas.
The Local Health profile provides small area data at Middle Layer Super Output Areas (MSOA). Using geographic lookups, also provided by ONS, we can sum the numerator and denominator for each LSOA up to MSOA and Local Authority.
The LSOA population data and the land area data are provided by the ONS and are then summed or aggregated to the larger geographic areas.

Definition of denominator: ONS mid-year population estimates
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area. This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.

The smoking-attributable fractions (SAFs), i.e. the proportion of disease attributable to smoking, are calculated using the formula below:

SAF = [current_p (current_rr-1) + ex_p (ex_rr-1)] / [1+current_p (current_rr-1) + ex_p (ex_rr-1)]

where:

current_p = proportion of current smokers

ex_p = proportion of ex-smokers

current_rr = relative risk for current smokers

ex_rr = relative risk for ex smokers

The estimated number of smoking-attributable deaths is then calculated by multiplying the observed number of deaths by the SAFs.

The need for safer roads is also linked to public health strategy, and existing government backed initiatives, to increase "active travel" and physical activity. The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents have issued a guide to Road Safety and Public Health (2014), which explores the relationship between road safety and public health aims. The guide recommends that public health and road safety teams identify areas for collaborative working and potential benefits of road safety initiatives on other health issues, and share data and evidence to identify effective actions and evaluate their impact.

Confidence interval details: A confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.Byar’s method1 gives very accurate approximate confidence intervals for counts based on the assumption of a Poisson distribution. It is sufficiently accurate for counts as low as 10 (below 10, an exact method should be used, based on Poisson tables or the Chi squared distribution). Byar’s method is the preferred method for calculating confidence intervals for counts, crude rates, indirectly standardised rates and indirectly standardised ratios, but it can also be used for proportions, as long as the proportions are small (much closer to zero than to one) as the Poisson distribution is a very good approximation to the Binomial distribution when the proportion being measured is small. The method is described in detail in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals.2For this indicator, some areas have a confidence interval reported despite the count being adjusted upwards slightly as a result of a statistical model, while areas with larger adjustments have no confidence interval reported. Indicator: Alcohol-related mortality
Rationale:
In England, among people aged 15 to 49 years, alcohol is the leading cause of ill-health, disability and death (1) (2). Alcohol misuse is a significant public health problem with major health, social and economic consequences, estimated at between £21 and £52 billion a year (3).

The UK Chief Medical Officers (CMOs) advise that to keep the risk from alcohol low, adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol per week. Alcohol adversely affects health in a range of ways and there is no definitively ‘safe’ lower limit - no level of regular alcohol consumption improves health. Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol has a wide range of health impacts including cardiovascular disease, cancers (breast, bowel, throat and mouth), and drinking during pregnancy can lead to long-term harm to the baby (3).

The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. Alcohol-related deaths can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm. The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. All mortality records are extracted that contain an attributable disease and the age and sex specific fraction applied. The results are summed into quinary age bands for the numerator and a directly standardised rate calculated using the European Standard Population. This revised indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (4) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (5). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the indicators was quantified and explored (6). The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made. Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged. Definition: Deaths from alcohol-related conditions, all ages, directly age-standardised rate per 100,000 population (standardised to the European standard population).
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
Deaths from alcohol-related conditions based on underlying cause of death, registered in the calendar year for all ages. Each alcohol related death is assigned an alcohol attributable fraction based on underlying cause of death (and all cause of deaths fields for the conditions: ethanol poisoning, methanol poisoning, toxic effect of alcohol). Alcohol-attributable fractions were not available for children. Mortality data includes all deaths registered in the calendar year where the local authority of usual residence of the deceased is one of the English geographies and an alcohol attributable diagnosis is given as the underlying cause of death.For full list of alcohol-attributable ICD-10 codes see Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update (4).References:(4) PHE (2020) Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update

https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/alcohol-attributable-fractions-for-england-an-update
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: ONS mid-year population estimates aggregated into quinary age bands.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area.These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area.This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
The methodology for calculating the alcohol attributable fractions is published by PHE in ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (4). This report also includes a detailed list of all alcohol attributable diseases, including ICD 10 codes and relative risks. Excluding all diseases with a negative fraction, as the indicator is designed to quantify only the level of harm caused by alcohol, the corresponding fractions are appended to the ONS mortality file by age and sex and these are summed as the numerator rather than the sum of records extracted. Directly age-standardised rates are then calculated per 100,000 standardised to the European Standard Population.

There is the potential for the underlying cause of death to be incorrectly attributed on the death certificate and the cause of death misclassified. Rationale:
Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.
The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.
The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (1) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (2). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).
The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.
Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).

The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.
