Rationale:
Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.
The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.
The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (1) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (2). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).
The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.
Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.

For each episode identified, an alcohol-attributable fraction is applied based on the diagnostic codes, age group, and sex of the patient. Where there is more than one alcohol-related ICD10 code among the 20 possible diagnostic codes the codes with the largest positive alcohol attributable fraction is selected; in the event of there being two or more codes with the same alcohol-attributable fraction within the same episode, the one from the lowest diagnostic position is selected. NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for Nottingham University Hospitals Trust (NUH) in 2016 to 2017. Over 30% of records from this trust did not have a valid geography of residence assigned. Therefore values have not published for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 20% of patients from that area treated at NUH in the previous year (2015 to 2016). Areas where 10% to 20% of the previous year’s patients were treated at NUH have been flagged and should be treated with caution.

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust (RXC) in 2018 to 2019. Approximately 85,000 records erroneously had all diagnosis codes removed. Therefore, values have not been published for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 10% of patients from that area with missing diagnosis codes from RXC in the current year (2018 to 2019). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients with missing diagnosis codes from RXC have been flagged to be treated with caution.

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Frimley Health Foundation Trust in 2022 to 2023. Frimley Health Foundation Trust did not submit HES data for June 2022 to March 2023. Therefore, values have not been published based on HES data for areas that had over 10% of hospital patients from an area treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022) have been flagged to be treated with caution.

Following the conclusion of the consultation (6) the trend will only go back to 2016/17.

This indicator is based on admission episodes to hospital for alcohol related conditions. This counts the number of times that a person has been admitted to hospital in the year with an alcohol related condition, and not the person themselves.

Where the observed total number of admissions is less than 10, the rates have been suppressed as there are too few admissions to calculate directly standardised rates reliably. The cut-off has been reduced from 25, following research commissioned by PHE and in preparation for publication which shows DSRs and their confidence intervals are robust whenever the count is at least 10.

The COVID-19 pandemic had a large impact on hospital activity with a reduction in admissions in 2020 to 2021. Indicator: Admission episodes for alcoholic liver disease (Broad)
Rationale:
Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.
The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.
The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (1) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (2). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).
The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.
Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

Definition:

Rationale:
Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.
The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.
The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (1) published by PHE in 2020. A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (3).
The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.
Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

Direct standardisation improves the comparability of rates for different areas, or between different time periods, by taking into account differences in the age and sex structures of the populations being compared. The directly age standardised rate is the rate of events that would occur in a standard population if that population were to experience the age specific rates of the subject population. Explicitly: DSR = Σi wi ri / Σi wi)x100,000 (expressed per 100,000 population) where: wi is the number, or proportion, of individuals in the standard population in age group i. ri is the crude age-specific rate in the subject population in age group i, given by: ri = Oi/ni where: Oi is the observed number of events in the subject population in age group i. ni is the number of individuals in the subject population in age group i. The standard population used for the direct method is the European Standard Population 2013. The methodology for calculating the alcohol attributable fractions is published in ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (5). This report also includes a detailed list of all alcohol attributable diseases, including ICD 10 codes and relative risks. Excluding all diseases with a negative fraction, as the indicator is designed to quantify only the level of harm caused by alcohol, the corresponding fractions are appended to the Hospital Episodes Statistics (HES) file by age and sex and these are summed as the numerator rather than the sum of records extracted.Confidence Intervals for DSRs were calculated according to the APHO methodology (6) which uses the Dobson and Byars methods.

(5) PHE (2020) Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update
 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/alcohol-attributable-fractions-for-england-an-update 
(6) APHO (2011) Commonly used public health statistics and their confidence intervals https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/documents/APHO%20Tech%20Briefing%203%20Common%20PH%20stats%20and%20CIs.pdf
Disclosure control: The Isles of Scilly and City of London data have been aggregated with Cornwall and Hackney respectively. Disclosure control has not been applied to this data as it would be very difficult to identify individuals in areas at lower or upper tier local authority level.
Rounding: All sub national counts are rounded to the nearest 5. Rates and confidence intervals are calculated using unrounded counts.
Caveats:
In 2023, NHS England announced a methodological change to require Trusts to report Same Day Emergency Care (SDEC) to the Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) by July 2024. Early adopter sites began to report SDEC to ECDS from 2021/22, with other Trusts changing their reporting in 2022/23 or 2023/24. Some Trusts had previously reported this activity as part of the Admitted Patient Care data set, and moving to report to ECDS may reduce the number of admissions reported for this/these indicator/s. NHSE have advised it is not possible accurately to identify SDEC in current data flows, but the impact of the change is expected to vary by diagnosis, with indicators related to injuries and external causes potentially most affected.

When considering if SDEC recording practice has reduced the number of admissions reported for this indicator at local level, please refer to the published list of sites who have reported when they began to report SDEC to ECDS.

It must be noted that the numerator is based on financial year and the denominator on calendar mid-year population estimates e.g. 2019/20 admission rates are constructed from admission counts for the 2019/20 financial year and mid-year population estimates for the 2019 calendar year.

Data for England includes records with geography 'No fixed abode'. Alcohol-attributable fractions were not available for children. Conditions where low levels of alcohol consumption are protective (have a negative alcohol-attributable fraction) are not included in the calculation of the indicator. Does not include attendance at Accident and Emergency departments.

The confidence intervals do not take into account the uncertainty involved in the calculation of the AAFs – that is, the proportion of admissions that are caused by alcohol and the alcohol consumption prevalence that are included in the AAF formula are only an estimate and so include uncertainty. The confidence intervals published here are based only on the observed number of admissions and do not account for this uncertainty in the calculation of attributable fraction - as such the intervals may be too narrow.

Analysis has revealed significant differences across the country in the coding of cancer patients in the Hospital Episode Statistics. In particular, in some areas, regular attenders at hospital for treatments like chemotherapy and radiotherapy are being incorrectly recorded as admissions. Since cancer admissions form part of the overarching alcohol-related admission national indicators, the inconsistent recording across the country for cancer patients has some implication for these headline measures.

Cancer admissions make up approximately a quarter of the total number of alcohol-related admissions on the narrow definition. Analysis suggests that, although most Local Authorities would remain within the same RAG group compared with the England average if cancer admissions were removed, the ranking of Local Authorities within RAG groups would be altered. We are continuing to monitor the impact of this issue and to consider ways of improving the consistency between areas.

In order to allow comparison of groups with different age structures it is common to present “age standardised” rates. These are calculated by summing the product of age specific rates for each age band in the group by the number in that age band in the standard population. The sum is then divided by the total number in all age bands in the standard population to obtain the age standardised rate. This improves the comparability of rates for different areas, or between different time periods, by taking into account differences in the age structure of the populations being compared. Any difference between groups in age standardised rates is then not due to difference in age structure since the same standard population was used to calculate all age standardised rates. The method does however assume that minor differences in age structure within age bands are unimportant and in general this is true.
Notes:
Following Census 2021, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) carried out reconciliation and rebasing of the mid year population estimates (MYE) it produces. This process happens every 10 years following the census. The official population estimates for mid 2012 to mid 2020 have been revised, to incorporate the data now available from Census 2021. The data for this indicator has been revised to use the rebased population estimates from 2012 onwards.

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for Nottingham University Hospitals Trust (NUH) in 2016 to 2017. Over 30% of records from this trust did not have a valid geography of residence assigned. Therefore values have not published for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 20% of patients from that area treated at NUH in the previous year (2015 to 2016). Areas where 10% to 20% of the previous year’s patients were treated at NUH have been flagged and should be treated with caution.

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting HES data for East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust (RXC) in 2018 to 2019. Approximately 85,000 records erroneously had all diagnosis codes removed. Therefore, values have not been published for indicators based on HES data for areas that had more than 10% of patients from that area with missing diagnosis codes from RXC in the current year (2018 to 2019). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients with missing diagnosis codes from RXC have been flagged to be treated with caution.

NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Frimley Health Foundation Trust in 2022 to 2023. Frimley Health Foundation Trust did not submit HES data for June 2022 to March 2023. Therefore, values have not been published based on HES data for areas that had over 10% of hospital patients from an area treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022). Areas with between 1 to 10% of patients treated at Frimley Health Foundation Trust in the previous year (2021 to 2022) have been flagged to be treated with caution.

Following the conclusion of the consultation (6) the trend will only go back to 2016/17.

This indicator is based on admission episodes to hospital for alcohol related conditions. This counts the number of times that a person has been admitted to hospital in the year with an alcohol related condition, and not the person themselves.

Where the observed total number of admissions is less than 10, the rates have been suppressed as there are too few admissions to calculate directly standardised rates reliably. The cut-off has been reduced from 25, following research commissioned by PHE and in preparation for publication which shows DSRs and their confidence intervals are robust whenever the count is at least 10.

Because of this, NHS Digital have been unable to analyse coverage (measured as the difference between expected and actual records submitted by NHS Trusts) in the normal way. Indicator: Vision outpatient attendances

This indicator provides areas with comparable population-based rates that have not been previously available.The  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/atlas-of-variation  showed during 2019/20 there were approximately 9.0 million outpatient attendances (all ages) for the treatment specialty codes relating to hospital-based ophthalmic services. Clinical commissioning group (CCG) values ranged from 9,821 to 24,131 per 100,000 population, a 2.5-fold difference between CCGs.
Definition: Attended outpatient appointments for all vision treatment specialties. Directly age standardised rate per 100,000 population (standardised to the European standard population).
Data source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Attended outpatient appointments (HES outpatient data field 'ATTENDED' = 5 - Seen, having attended on time or, if late, before the relevant care professional was ready to see the patient OR 6 - Arrived late, after the relevant care professional was ready to see the patient, but was seen) for all vision treatment specialties (HES outpatient data field 'TRETSPEF' 130 = Ophthalmology , 216 = Paediatric Ophthalmology, 460 = Medical Ophthalmology, 655= Orthoptics and 662 = Optometry).There is no additional filtering made on diagnosis or procedure codes.ICB sub-location assigned using GP practice code (available from NHS Digital). When GP practice code is missing, residence (LSOA) used to assign ICB sub-location. GP Practice codes beginning with 'W' and 'S' (Wales and Scotland) excluded. GP Practice codes beginning with 'X', 'Y' and 'Z' (unclassified or not applicable - prisons, specialist commissioning etc) excluded. GP Practice codes beginning with 'V' excluded with the exception of 'V81997' and 'V81999' ('patient not registered but eligible to' and 'not possible to determine'). Definition of denominator: Registered population all ages. Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Patients registered at a GP practice
Methodology: Directly standardised rate for all persons using the 2013 European Standard Population as the reference standard. Numerator data for each age band group are divided by the denominator population data for each age band group respectively to give age-specific rates for the area. These age-specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each group respectively and summed across all groups to give the age-adjusted count for the area. The age-adjusted count is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age-standardised rate for the area.

Indicator: Patients with Asthma: review in the last 12 months (denominator incl. PCAs)
Rationale: The aim of this indicator is to encourage the use of validated asthma questionnaires, recording of the number of exacerbations and written action plans in annual asthma reviews. PCAs can be applied to patients for a number of specified reasons and are usually the result of a patient or GP decision at a personal level. Examples of PCAs could be patient or carer refusal of treatment, a patient cancels or does not attend a consultation appointment or a GP’s advice that two types of medication or treatment should not be administered simultaneously. Indicator: Patients' heart failure diagnosis confirmed by an ECG or specialist assessment (denominator incl. PCAs)
Rationale: The aim of this indicator is to encourage practices to confirm diagnosis and establish the underlying causes of heart failure. Symptoms and signs suggestive of heartfailure are not always sufficient to make a definitive diagnosis and further investigation is usually required to confirm cardiac dysfunction and to identify causes. Serum natriuretic peptide tests can beused to determine whether people with suspected heart failure should be referred onwards. Time to ECG and/or specialist assessment depends on serum natriuretic peptide levels. People with high levels should have their diagnosis confirmed within 6 weeks. Diagnosis for people with very high natriuretic peptide levels or a history of myocardial myocardial infarction (MI) should be confirmed more urgently (within 2 weeks), due to their poor prognosis.Individuals with suspected acute heart failure and raised natriuretic peptide levels should have echocardiography within 48 hours of admission to hospital. Indicator: Patients with heart failure who had a review in the last 12 months, including the assessment of functional capacity (denominator incl. PCAs)
Rationale: The aim of this indicator is to encourage the recording of functional capacity as well as the optimisation of medicines for people diagnosed with heart failure. Regular review is associated with improvement in quality of life and a reduction in the need for urgent hospitalisation. In patients whose clinical condition or medication has changed, short monitoring intervals are recommended. Heart failure patients in stable condition can be monitored at longer intervals.As of 1st April 2019, exception reporting was replaced with Personalised Care Adjustments (PCAs). PCAs can be applied to patients for a number of specified reasons and are usually the result of a patient or a GP decision at a personal level. Examples of PCAs could be patient or carer refusal of treatment, a patient cancels or does not attend a consultation appointment, or a GP’s advice that two types of medication or treatment methodology should not be administered simultaneously.The percentage of patients receiving the intervention (means: the denominator includes Personalised Care Adjustments (PCAs), i.e. all patients on the register) gives a more accurate indication of the rate of the provision of interventions as the denominator for this measure covers all patients the indicator applies to, regardless of PCA status and is therefore from a public health perspective the more relevant measure. For more details on PCAs please consult the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/quality-and-outcomes-framework-achievement-prevalence-and-exceptions-data/2019-20/technical-annex#qof-pca-data for QOF on NHS Digital.

Rationale: The aim of this indicator is to promote early identification of Non-Diabetic Hyperglycaemia (NDH). Indicator: Mortality rate from all causes, all ages
Rationale: All-cause mortality is a fundamental measure of the health status of a population. It represents the cumulative effect of the prevalence of risk factors, the prevalence and severity of disease, and the effectiveness of interventions and treatment. Differences in levels of all-cause mortality reflect health inequalities between different population groups, e.g. between genders, social classes and ethnic groups.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate for all deaths, per 100,000, for all ages
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths registered in the respective calendar years, in people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9,…, 90+)Mortality counts for 2025 come from provisional mortality data, provided by the ONS.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: For single years: Population for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+) For three-year rolling averages: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+)Population estimates for 2025 come from 2022-based population projections (migration category variant on 2023 local authority geographies edition of the dataset), provided by the ONS.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area. This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
Frequency: The data will be updated annually
Caveats: Please note data may not match published Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures due to differences in the version of postcode lookup used

The resultant revisions to rates are very small and do not introduce any meaningful changes to results previously presented. Data for LSOA deprivation deciles will be revised in a future profile update.Data have been presented as single years and also three-year rolling averages. This is to allow users to monitor effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.Where the observed total number of deaths is less than 10, the rates have been suppressed as there are too few deaths to calculate directly standardised rates reliably.

Indicator: Proportion of total antibiotic prescribing from the "Watch" and "Reserve" categories of the nationally adapted WHO AWaRe index
Rationale: The consumption of antibiotics is a major driver for the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.In 2017 the World Health Organization (WHO) updated the Essential Medicines List (EML) and classified key antibiotics into  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29303731  to improve access (Access), to monitor important antibiotics (Watch) and preserve effectiveness of ‘last resort’ antibiotics (Reserve). These classifications have been further refined through expert elicitation with the Department of Health advisory committee on antibiotic prescribing, resistance and healthcare-associated infection (APRHAI) for use in English antimicrobial stewardship.
Definition: This indicator displays what proportion of total antibiotic prescribing within NHS Acute Trusts is from within the "Watch" and "Reserve" categories of the WHO AWaRe index amended for use in English antimicrobial stewardship policy by expert elicitation.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency, based on Rx-info data
Indicator source: UKHSA calculated from data supplied by RxInfo ©.
Definition of numerator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD) count for the antibiotics within the "Watch" and "Reserve" categories of the WHO AWaRe index (as amended for use in English antibiotic stewardship) for the quarter specified.
Source of numerator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Definition of denominator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD)count of total antibiotic prescribing for the quarter specified using the WHO 2019 DDDs.
Source of denominator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100 (percentage)
Standard population/values: No standard population has been used.
Frequency: This indicator will be updated with quarterly data on a quarterly basis.
Disclosure control: The source data contains no personal or identifiable information and so statistical disclosure control has not been applied.
Rounding: No rounding has been used.
Caveats: Drugs are only included in the numerator and denominator if they have a British National Formulae (BNF) 5.1 code and Defined Daily Dose (DDD) values provided by the World Health Organization.Anti-TB, Anti-Parasitic and topical antibiotics are excluded to align with requirements for the NHS Standard Contract and previous NHS England antibiotic resistance CQUINs.The figures produced in this indicator are raw and unadjusted for the confounding effects of both the age and sex mix of patient populations served by hospitals, or for other factors such as deprivation and complexity of care that can drive hospital antibiotic prescribing. Therefore, Trusts may appear outliers for this measure by fulfilling valid care of the specific population that they serve.Further considerationis required to adapt the AWaRe index for use in specialisthealthcare settings, including an improved understanding ofcase-mix. However, until routine electronic prescribing of antibiotics is available nationally, there is limited work that can beperformed in this area.For these reasons comparison between different organisations should be treated with caution. Nonetheless, as NHS national quality improvement schemes require each hospital to improve from its own baseline levels this is consistent with improving the quality of antibiotic prescribing in each hospital.The data for any new quarter are provisional and will be updated with more accurate admissions and prescribing data in the subsequent quarter’s data release. The proportions for past quarters may therefore change to reflect this.
Notes: The Defined Daily Dose (DDD) is the assumed average maintenance dose per day for a medicine used for its main indication in adults. In general, the DDDs for antibiotics are based on their use in moderately severe infections.The DDD is the internationally recognised unit of measurement of medicine consumption, recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). DDDs allow comparison of medicine use over time hence its use in this context.
Data re-use: These data may be used referencing UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA)

Indicator: % people aged 16+ who agree that people in their neighbourhood can be trusted
Rationale: This indicator is part of a new Local Wellbeing Indicator framework for local authorities and public health leaders in government. In 2011, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) introduced a Measuring National Wellbeing programme, to inform national decision-making. This indicator forms part of a new indicator framework, which is intended to meet the need for a practical local translation of that programme, helping to inform local decision-makers so they can better understand the wellbeing of their constituents, and how they can act to improve it. The framework and indicator set are the product of a six-month scoping project funded by the Health Foundation, and co-commissioned by the ONS and Public Health England (PHE), in collaboration with the What Works Centre for Wellbeing and Centre for Thriving Places. The framework consists of 26 indicators designed to measure local wellbeing across 7 domains [1]. This indicator focuses on general social trust in others, which is a key cross-national predictor of subjective wellbeing [1].1.  https://whatworkswellbeing.org/resources/understanding-local-needs-for-wellbeing-data/
Definition: The percentage of individual interviewees aged 16+ who responded 'agree' or 'strongly agree' to the statement "People in this neighbourhood can be trusted". This question is in the local neighbourhood module of the main survey of the Understanding Society Survey. In the Understanding Society Survey Wave 6 (2014-15, published 2016), of 37,445 individual interviewees who were asked to respond to this statement, 36,435 (97.3%) responded ‘strongly agree’, ‘agree’, ‘neither agree/disagree’, ‘disagree’, or ‘strongly disagree’.
Data source: Centre for Thriving Places, based on Understanding Society Survey data
Indicator source: Provided to OHID by the Centre for Thriving Places (CTP),  https://www.centreforthrivingplaces.org/
Definition of numerator: Count of all the ‘agree’ and ‘strongly agree’ responses to the statement "People in this neighbourhood can be trusted". This is calculated using the variable nbrcoh3 from the local neighbourhood module of the Understanding Society main survey. The numerator is calculated from a single wave of the survey, from interviews collected across a two-calendar year period. Variable nbrcoh3 is described here:  https://www.understandingsociety.ac.uk/documentation/mainstage/dataset-documentation/variable/nbrcoh3
Source of numerator: University of Essex, Institute for Social and Economic Research, Understanding Society Survey
Definition of denominator: Count of all the valid responses to the statement "People in this neighbourhood can be trusted": ‘strongly agree’ , ‘agree’, ‘neither agree/disagree’, ‘disagree’, and ‘strongly disagree’. This is calculated using the variable nbrcoh3 from the local neighbourhood module of the Understanding Society main survey. The denominator is calculated from a single wave of the survey, from interviews collected across a two-calendar year period. Variable nbrcoh3 is described here:  https://www.understandingsociety.ac.uk/documentation/mainstage/dataset-documentation/variable/nbrcoh3
Source of denominator: University of Essex, Institute for Social and Economic Research, Understanding Society Survey
Methodology: This indicator was produced by the Centre for Thriving Places (CTP). The CTP method is outlined in the CTP documentation ‘TPI_2021_Indicator Calculations’ and is described as:“The variable ‘f_nbrcoh3’ from the local neighbourhood module of Wave 6 of the USS was used to produce this indicator. This variable captures agreement with the statement “People in this neighbourhood can be trusted”. The USS data was weighted using weights provided within the dataset. A local authority lookup obtained via special license was used to match participants to local authorities. To calculate an indicator value per LA, the number of participants who responded ‘agree’ or ‘strongly agree’ was taken as a percentage of the total number of participants per LA.” https://www.thrivingplacesindex.org/docs/TPI_2021_Indicator_Calculations.pdf
Frequency: Two waves of Understanding Society have contained variable nbrcoh3. Wave 3, 2011-12, and wave 6, 2014-15. This indicator uses wave 6. The Centre for Thriving Places estimated that the indicator may be calculated every 6 years.
Disclosure control: The Centre for Thriving Places reported that values where the denominator is less than fifty have been suppressed to avoid reporting values based on very small denominators: Hartlepool; Rutland; Kensington and Chelsea. https://www.thrivingplacesindex.org/docs/TPI_2021_Methodology.pdf  , Section 2.7, page 18.
Caveats: This indicator uses the April 2020 - March 2021 English local authority structure. The wave 6 dataset (from the Understanding Society Survey) used for this indicator is from 2014-15. Some indicator values were calculated by combining data for defunct local authorities - for example aggregating data from old districts to calculate a value for a new unitary authority. This involved taking a weighted average of the district values, weighting them based on their overall population.The wave 6 dataset didn't include data for Christchurch district local authority. The wave 6-based figures given in this indicator for Bournemouth, Christchurch & Poole UA use data for the pre-April 2019 Bournemouth and Poole UAs and don't include data for Christchurch district. The wave 6-based figures given for Dorset UA use data for the pre-April 2019 Dorset County, which included Christchurch district.No data are included for Isles of Scilly or City of London. Data for these local authorities have not been combined with data for other local authorities.
Notes: The indicator values, denominators and confidence intervals were provided to OHID by the Centre for Thriving Places,  https://www.centreforthrivingplaces.org/

Indicator: Air pollution: estimated fraction of mortality attributable to particulate air pollution
Rationale:
Poor air quality is a significant public health issue. There is strong evidence that air pollution causes the development of coronary heart disease, stroke, respiratory disease, and lung cancer, exacerbates asthma and has a contributory role in mortality (Air Pollution Evidence Review from Public Health England, 2019 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/improving-outdoor-air-quality-and-health-review-of-interventions). The annual burden of long-term exposure to air pollution in the UK has been estimated to be an effect equivalent to 29,000 to 43,000 deaths at typical ages ( UKHSA Chemical Hazards and Poisons Report, 2022).

Although air pollution can be harmful to everyone, it particularly affects people living in polluted areas, those who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution in their day to day lives, and those who are more susceptible to health problems caused by air pollution, widening health inequalities (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-matters-air-pollution).

The annual average metric is a summary of typical environmental conditions and the population weighting accounts for human exposure. In addition to this indicator, other air pollutants (such as NO2), as well as indoor air pollutants, are also considered important. However, methodological considerations make it impractical to include these in a health outcomes indicator at present.
Specific rationale: Inclusion of this indicator in the Public Health Outcomes Framework enables Directors of Public Health to prioritise action on air quality in their local area to help reduce the health burden from air pollution.

Methodology:
An increase of 10 µg/m3 in population-weighted annual average background concentration of PM2.5* is assumed to increase all cause mortality rates by 8% - a relative risk (RR) of 1.08 per 10 µg/m3 (COMEAP, 2022). For a population weighted modelled annual average background PM2.5 concentration x, RR is calculated as (1.08)(x/10) (as explained in PHE, 2014). The fraction of deaths attributable to PM2.5 is expressed as a percentage, calculated as 100*(RR-1)/RR.

For example for the the year 2021 England air pollution was 7.4 µg/m3

To calculate the RR for England you use the following formula:

RR = 1.08^(7.4/10)

RR = 1.059

To calculate the attributable fraction:

AF = (1.059 - 1)/1.059 * 100

AF = 5.54%
Population weighted annual average concentrations of PM2.5 were provided by Ricardo for all lower tier and unitary local authorities within England, as well as combined at upper tier, regional and national level along with NHS regions. Attributable fractions can be calculated at all these scales.

Indicator: Food Insecurity - percentage of households experiencing food insecurity
Rationale:
The Food Standards Agency define Food Security as ‘having access at all times to enough food that is both sufficiently varied and culturally appropriate to sustain an active and healthy life [1]’. Poor diet is one of the largest contributors to the burden of non-communicable disease in the UK [2]. The impact of living in a state of food insecurity is associated with a number of negative physical, mental and social health outcomes in adults and children [3],[4]. Studies have shown some groups are affected by food insecurity more than others [5] and single adults with multiple children areparticularly at risk [6]

Data on food bank usage has been monitored for some time but is not an appropriate proxy for food insecurity [7]. Some evidence suggests that fewer people use food banks than are vulnerable to food insecurity [8], [9]. Location of food banks is often based on community resources and local social networks. Food insecurity is a major challenge for the government's levelling up agenda [10] and is particularly pertinent with the rising cost of living.
Definition: <span style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; outline: none; border: medium none currentcolor;">The percentage of households that are experiencing food <span style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; outline: none; border: medium none currentcolor;">insecurity at regional and England level as <span style="box-sizing: border-box; padding: 0px; margin: 0px; outline: none; border: medium none currentcolor;">measured by the food security questions in the Family Resources Survey (FRS).
Data source: Department for Work and Pensions
Indicator source: Pre-calculated values from the https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/family-resources-survey--2
Definition of numerator: The numerator is the estimated number of food insecure households at regional and England level.This can be found in the Household food insecurity tables spreadsheet in the Family Resoruces survey collection. The numerator is in available in table 9.1 under the column 'Food insecure'.
Source of numerator: Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Family Resources Survey (FRS)
Definition of denominator: The denominator is the estimated number of households at regional and England level.This can be found in the Household food insecurity tables spreadsheet in the Family Resources survey collection.
Source of denominator: Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Family Resources Survey (FRS)
Methodology: The indicator is calculated at source as the estimated number of food insecure households divided by the estimated total number of households. The estimates are based on sample counts that have been adjusted using multi-purpose grossing factors (see Notes section). Once grossed, sample estimates are representative of the population.
Confidence interval details: Wilson score method. These confidence intervals are calculated by OHID and provide conservative estimates of uncertainty around the percentages of households experiencing food insecurity. These confidence intervals indicate significant differences between regions.
Disclosure control: Regional level data available only
Caveats:
The Family Resources Survey (FRS) is an annual survey of around 20,000 households across the UK. There is some uncertainty around estimates derived from it because not every household in the country is interviewed as part of the survey.

It is also important to note that food insecurity is only measured over a 30-day window meaning the annual prevalence of how many people experience problems accessing food in the population will remain unknown.

The questions do not directly ask about the food security status of children. A young child’s experience in a food insecure household may be very different from their parents. It is also excludes shared household such as those shared by a group of professionals.
Notes:
The Family Resources Survey (FRS) has a sampling design which captures robust estimates at regional level about income and living circumstances of household and families. The survey design takes into account factors of working-age adults and unemployment via a stratified clustered probability sample. The data is grossed up to regional level [13].

The number of food insecure households are based on survey responses where:

·High food security (score = 0): The household has no problem, or anxiety about, consistently accessing adequate food

·Marginal food security (score = 1 or 2): The household had problems at times, or anxiety about, accessing adequate food, but the quality, variety, and quantity of their food intake were not substantially reduced

·Low food security (score = 3 to 5): The household reduced the quality, variety, and desirability of their diets, but the quantity of food intake and normal eating patterns were not substantially disrupted

·Very low food security (score = 6 to 10): At times during the last 30 days, eating patterns of one or more household members were disrupted and food intake reduced because the household lacked money and other resources for food

Households with low or very low food security are “food insecure”. Food insecure households have a risk of, or lack of access to, sufficient, varied food.Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic: For the whole of the 2020 to 2021 survey year, data collection was by telephone instead of face-to-face. This shift in mode of interview has been accompanied by a substantial reduction in the number of interviews achieved: just over 10,000 interviews were achieved this year, compared with 19,000 to 20,000 in a typical FRS year. Whilst these statistics have undergone extensive quality assurance prior to publication, it is recommended that users exercise additional caution when using the data for 2020 to 2021. For more information see the Guidance tab of the Household Food Security tables at link: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/family-resources-survey-financial-year-2020-to-2021

Indicator: Acute Lyme disease laboratory confirmed incidence rate/100,000
Rationale: These data will enable local authorities, health protection teams and other services to provide appropriate health promotion advice locally, including tick awareness and the provision of disease management guidance. The rates of acute Lyme disease by local authority are likely to be an underestimate of the true incidence of acute Lyme disease in England as cases may be diagnosed clinically and treated without laboratory confirmation, as per NICE guidelines. Additionally, cases diagnosed at local NHS or private laboratories but not sent to the Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory (RIPL) for confirmation, are not included in this dataset. Awareness of tick bites and Lyme disease may vary across the country. In areas where there is greater awareness of the potential risks, individuals may be more likely to seek medical attention for symptoms following a tick bite and clinicians may be more likely to suggest Lyme disease as a differential. This may lead to differences in laboratory-confirmed Lyme disease case rates in different local authorities.
Definition: Incidence rate of laboratory confirmed acute Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) cases in England per 100,000 population.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: New acute cases of laboratory confirmed Lyme disease.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory (RIPL)
Definition of denominator: Total population.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000. Confidence intervals calculated using exact Poisson.
Confidence interval details: <span data-teams="true">Confidence intervals have been calculated using R-4.5.2 and are based on the exact Poisson method [cil denominator count, poisson per (100000)]
Disclosure control: Counts for Isles of Scilly and City of London are combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.
Caveats:
Cases of Lyme disease are not statutorily notifiable by medical practitioners and cases may be diagnosed clinically and treated without laboratory diagnostics being performed as per NICE guidelines. Laboratory confirmed Lyme disease cases may also be under-reported as patient samples diagnosed at local NHS laboratories or private laboratories may not be sent to RIPL for diagnosis or confirmation.

This data presents the number and incidence rate per 100,000 population of laboratory confirmed cases of acute Lyme disease in England by local authority between 2017 and 2025. This data includes cases who are resident in England or, where a valid residence postcode is unknown, the postcode of the hospital and/or laboratory where diagnosis was made is used to determine locality in England. This data may therefore differ from that in other sources, including CIMS (UKHSA’s public health case management system) and data presented in the annual One Health Vector-Borne Disease (VBD) report.

For a small number of cases a valid residence or the hospital/laboratory postcode was not available for geographic lookup. In this instance, these cases were included in the total number of cases for England total but may not appear in the breakdown by smaller areas (LTLA and UTLA), therefore the total number of cases outlined by smaller areas will not match the total number for England.

The place of residence or hospital of diagnosis of a case does not necessarily reflect the geographic area where the tick bite occurred. They may have contracted it in another local authority area or another country.

Rates are presented from 2017 to 2025 with overall acute Lyme disease rates per 100,000 population, as well as those by area of reporting, calculated using the mid-year population estimates provided by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Population estimates for 2024 were used to calculate rates for 2025 as a proxy, as estimates for 2025 were not available at the time of publication.

Data reported from 2025 onwards are subject to a revised surveillance process (now including a one-year episode window, one record is retained per individual within a 365-day period); this update in methodology may affect case numbers and should be considered when interpreting trends in diagnoses prior to, and after, 2025. These numbers were last updated on 30 September 2026.

Indicator: Food Insecurity (INDIRECT measure) – percentage of local authority population living in areas at highest risk of food insecurity
Rationale:
The Food Standards Agency define Food Security as ‘having access at all times to enough food that is both sufficiently varied and culturally appropriate to sustain an active and healthy life [1]’. Poor diet is one of the largest contributors to the burden of non-communicable disease in the UK [2]. The impact of living in a state of food insecurity is associated with a number of negative physical, mental and social health outcomes in adults and children [3],[4]. Studies have shown some groups are affected by food insecurity more than others [5] and single adults with multiple children are particularly at risk [6].

Data on food bank usage has been monitored for some time but is not an appropriate proxy for food insecurity. Some evidence suggests that fewer people use food banks than are vulnerable to food insecurity [7], [8], [9]. Location of food banks is often based on community resources and local social networks. Food insecurity is a major challenge for the government's levelling up agenda [10] and is particularly pertinent with the rising cost of living.

Food insecurity is commonly assessed using specific questionnaires as in the Food Standards Agency food tracker survey and the Family Resources Survey. However, these data sources do not provide estimates of food insecurity below regional level. The data in this indicator attempts to bridge that gap by providing local authority estimates of population at risk from food insecurity. This indicator allows policy makers and researchers to identify areas with populations at higher risk of food insecurity to enable effective interventions to be put into place.
Definition: Percentage of the lower tier local authority (LTLA) population who live in Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs) which score in the 20% at highest risk nationally on the Food Insecurity Risk Index.
Data source: Department for Work and Pensions
Indicator source: Source data from the University of Southampton.
Definition of numerator: The sum of the population for the LSOAs in the (20%) two deciles at highest risk nationally on the Food Insecurity Risk Index, within each LTLA.
Source of numerator: Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Family Resources Survey (FRS)
Definition of denominator: The sum of the LSOA mid-year population estimates, in each LTLA.
Source of denominator: Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Family Resources Survey (FRS)
Methodology:
The Food Insecurity INDIRECT indicator is a synthetic indicator based on the University of Southampton’s Food Insecurity Risk Index [11]. It is based on the demographic profiles of households and individuals at greatest risk of food insecurity – see notes section.

Calculation:

  • LSOAs in England are ranked according to the Food Insecurity Risk Index;
    • Those LSOAs which rank in the 20% at highest risk are identified;
      • The LSOA population in the 20% at highest risk are summed to LTLA level and divided by the LTLA population.

        The indicator is the number of persons living in areas at highest risk of food insecurity at LTLA level divided by the total number of persons at LTLA level. The 20% at highest risk was used to demonstrate maximum variability in the data, whilst also identifying those LSOAs most at risk, as identified via a sensitivity analysis.
Confidence interval details: The index is provided by the University of Southampton without uncertainty attached. Confidence intervals are not applied to the percentage of population at risk as they would not take into account the underlying uncertainty in the index itself.
Disclosure control: Not applicable, aggregate information with no small values.
Rounding: Not applicable.
Caveats:
This indicator is an indirect measure as robust data does not exist at low level of geographies which directly identify food insecure households or individuals. Therefore, it should be interpreted as the percentage of population living in areas which are at highest risk of food insecurity, relative to all other areas in England. It does not mean that everybody living in these areas is at highest risk. It does not mean that everybody who is at risk will experience food insecurity. The University of Southampton provide the Food Insecurity Risk Index values and OHID have no control over the domains for inclusion of the calculation of the index values.

The indirect measure provides the relative position of a local area with respect to others. It cannot be compared over time as the index it is based on is updated annually as the evidence on food insecurity changes.

The https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/wider-determinants/data#page/4/gid/1938133045/pat/159/par/K02000001/ati/15/are/E92000001/iid/93862/age/1/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1 ) 93862 is a complementary indicator providing a direct assessment of households experiencing food insecurity at regional and England levels. The direct measure is based on data from the Family Resources Survey. The indirect indicator as presented here includes data about people and households. It does not include all structural factors available in the source data such as bus stops, download speeds etc because these are less relevant in urban settings and can skew the indicator towards rural areas having higher risk of food insecurity. Separate data on structural risk factors that can be used alongside this indicator are available at mylocalmap.org.uk
Notes:
TheUniversity of Southampton Food Insecurity Risk Indexlooks at the proportion of households or individuals in an LSOA who are in the following groups: Claimants of benefits, age 16+ (%), Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), 2020/21 Persons on low income and either living alone, or living in a household with dependent children, all ages (%), Census 2021 Persons with no educational qualifications, age 16+ (%), Census 2021 Mental ill health, composite, IMD 2019 Mood & Anxiety indicator Distance (Euclidean km) to nearest medium and large grocery stores (1,400m2+), Geolytix Retail Points 2021.

These indicators are weighted equally and combined into a single Food Insecurity Risk Index at LSOA level. The exception is the distance based measure which is weighted at 0.25 to the other four variables. This addition and weighting are based on fieldwork undertaken by researchers where store access was a key concept in workshops with service providers and clients of food aid. The reduced weighting avoids over-correction for access issues, particularly in rural areas.

The index was designed for use by local government for locality-based targeting of resources. It is updated on an annual basis taking into account evidence on risk factors for food insecurity and thus cannot be compared over time. The Food Insecurity Risk Index is described in the briefing paper on the local map website available at:https://mylocalmap.org.uk/iaahealth/

Note the University of Sheffield also produce estimates of food insecurity [12] at local authority level. Their data is based on a survey commissioned by the Food Foundation that was conducted in Jan 2021 by YouGov.Measures include those experiencing hunger, those struggling to access food, and those who worry about food insecurity.

Indicator: Average Attainment 8 Score among children eligible for Free School Meals (FSM)
Rationale:
Children’s education and development of skills are important for their own wellbeing and for that of the nation as a whole.

Learning ensures that children develop the knowledge and understanding, skills, capabilities and attributes that they need for mental, emotional, social and physical wellbeing now and in the future.Children with poorer mental health are more likely to have lower educational attainment and there is some evidence to suggest that the highest level of educational qualifications is a significant predictor of wellbeing in adult life; educational qualifications are a determinant of an individual's labour market position, which in turn influences income, housing and other material resources.Educational attainment is influenced by both the quality of education children receive and their family socio-economic circumstances. Being on FSM isconsidered to be a good indicator of socio-economic disadvantage in the UK [1]. Young people in the UK are usually eligible for free school meals (FSM) if their parents or carers are on a low income or in receipt of certain benefits.Children on FSM perform relatively poorly compared to counterparts without FSM [2].

This indicator shows attainment for children eligible for free school meals. Attainment is measured via the Average Attainment 8 measure which is calculated by adding together a student’s highest scores across eight government approved qualifications (including GCSEs and EBacc). Pupils are at the end of Key Stage 4 (KS4) aged 15-16 and attending state-funded schools in England.

This indicator can be compared to the general Average Attainment 8 Score indicator https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/search/average%20attainment%208#page/3/gid/1/pat/15/par/E92000001/ati/6/are/E12000004/iid/93378/age/175/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1 . Indicator: Air pollution: fine particulate matter (new method - concentrations of total PM2.5)
Rationale:
Poor air quality is a significant public health issue. There is strong evidence that air pollution causes the development of coronary heart disease, stroke, respiratory disease, and lung cancer, exacerbates asthma and has a contributory role in mortality (Air Pollution Evidence Review from Public Health England, 2019 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/improving-outdoor-air-quality-and-health-review-of-interventions). The annual burden of long-term exposure to air pollution in the UK has been estimated to be an effect equivalent to 29,000 to 43,000 deaths at typical ages (UKHSA Chemical Hazards and Poisons Report, 2022).

Although air pollution can be harmful to everyone, it particularly affects people living in polluted areas, those who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution in their day to day lives, and those who are more susceptible to health problems caused by air pollution, widening health inequalities (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-matters-air-pollution).

The annual average metric is a summary of typical environmental conditions and the population weighting accounts for human exposure. In addition to this indicator, other air pollutants (such as NO2), as well as indoor air pollutants, are also considered important. However, methodological considerations make it impractical to include these in a health outcomes indicator at present.

The inclusion of this indicator aims to support local areas to prioritise action on air quality to help reduce the health burden from air pollution.The data used for this indicator is the same as that which underlies the PHOF indicator - https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/public-health-outcomes-framework/data#page/6/gid/1000043/pat/15/par/E92000001/ati/6/are/E12000004/iid/93861/age/230/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1/page-options/car-do-0 . The method is based on total concentrations of PM2.5 rather than just the anthropogenic component.
Specific rationale: For the Wider Determinants tool, the environmental condition itself, as opposed to the estimated health impact, was considered a more direct measure of a wider determinant.

PM2.5 is also known as fine particulate matter.<!-- [if !supportLineBreakNewLine]--><!--[endif]-->

Indicator: Antibiotic prescribing from the “Watch” and “Reserve” categories of the nationally adapted WHO AWaRE index; DDDs per 1000 admissions by quarter and trust
Rationale:
The consumption of antibiotics is a major driver for the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

In 2017 the World Health Organization (WHO) updated the Essential Medicines List (EML) and classified key antibiotics into https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29303731 to improve access (Access), to monitor important antibiotics (Watch) and preserve effectiveness of ‘last resort’ antibiotics (Reserve). These https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31361000/ through expert elicitation with the Department of Health advisory committee on antibiotic prescribing, resistance and healthcare-associated infection (APRHAI) for use in English antimicrobial stewardship.

This indicator provides a standardised way to look at prescribing of “Watch” and “Reserve” antibiotics as defined by the nationally adapted WHO AWaRE index.For this indicator, a lower value is indicative of lower prescribing.
Definition: The rate shows how many "Watch" and "Reserve" antibiotic defined daily doses (DDDs) have been prescribed in each Trust per 1000 admissions per quarter.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency, based on Rx-info data
Indicator source: UKHSA calculated from data supplied by RxInfo ©.
Definition of numerator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD) count for the antibiotics within the "Watch" and "Reserve" categories of the WHO AWaRe index (as amended for use in English antibiotic stewardship) for the quarter specified for each participating Trust.
Source of numerator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Definition of denominator: Hospital admissions for the quarter reported.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Methodology: We calculate acute Trust prescribing rates using HES admissions data as follows:(DDD count for the quarter / Admissions for the quarter)*1000
Standard population/values: No standard population has been used
Frequency: This indicator will be updated quarterly with quarterly data
Disclosure control: The source data contains no personal or identifiable information and so statistical disclosure control has not been applied
Rounding: No rounding has been used
Caveats: Drugs are only included in the numerator if they have a British National Formulae (BNF) 5.1 code and Defined Daily Dose (DDD) values provided by the World Health Organization. Anti-TB, Anti-Parasitic and topical antibiotics are excluded to align with requirements for the NHS Standard Contract and previous NHS England antibiotic resistance CQUINs.The data for any new quarter are provisional and will be updated with more accurate admissions and prescribing data in the subsequent quarter’s data release. The rates of consumption for past quarters may therefore change to reflect this.Admissions data retrieved from hospital episode statistics (HES) supplied by NHS digital. Provisional admissions data are used for each quarter to be more representative of Trust activity. As a result, quarterly data will be updated 4 months after the end of the quarter to account for the lag in HES admissions data quality and allow for more accurate reporting. Admissions data will be updated as finalised data becomes available.The figures produced in this indicator are raw and unadjusted for the confounding effects of both the age and sex mix of patient populations served by hospitals, or for other factors such as deprivation and complexity of care that can drive hospital antibiotic prescribing. Therefore Trusts may appear outliers for this measure byfulfilling valid care of the specific population that they serve.Further considerationis required to adapt the AWaRe index for use in specialisthealthcare settings, including an improved understanding ofcase-mix. However, until routine electronic prescribing of antibiotics is available nationally, there is limited work that can beperformed in this area.For these reasons comparison between different organisations should be treated with caution. Nonetheless, as NHS national quality improvement schemes require each hospital to improve from its own baseline levels this is consistent with improving the quality of antibiotic prescribing in each hospital.The case mix of patients attending hospitals during the COVID surge period (Q1 2020/21) is likely to differ significantly from their “normal” demographics. Therefore, comparisons of rates before and during the pandemic should be treated with caution.
Notes: The Defined Daily Dose (DDD) is the assumed average maintenance dose per day for a medicine used for its main indication in adults. In general, the DDDs for antibiotics are based on their use in moderately severe infections.The DDD is the internationally recognised unit of measurement of medicine consumption, recommended by the World Health Organisation (WHO). DDDs allow comparison of medicine use over time hence its use in this context.

Indicator: Potential years of life lost (PYLL) due to alcohol-related conditions
Rationale: Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. Alcohol misuse is estimated to cost the NHS about £3.5 billion per year and society as a whole £21 billion annually.The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related deaths can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.Potential years of life lost (PYLL) is a measure of the potential number of years lost when a person dies prematurely. The basic concept of PYLL is that deaths at younger ages are weighted more heavily than those at older ages. The advantage in doing this is that deaths at younger ages may be seen as less important if cause-specific death rates were just used on their own in highlighting the burden of disease and injury, since conditions such as cancer and heart disease usually occur at older ages and have relatively high mortality rates.To enable comparisons between areas and over time, PYLL rates are age-standardised to represent the PYLL if each area had the same population structure as the 2013 European Standard Population (ESP). PYLL rates are presented as years of life lost per 100,000 population.
Definition: Potential years of life lost (PYLL) due to alcohol-related conditions, all ages, directly age-standardised per 100,000 population (standardised to the ESP).
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: The number of age-specific alcohol-related deaths multiplied by the national life expectancy for each age group and summed to give the total potential years of life lost due to alcohol-related conditions.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extracts and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Single Year Life Tables
Definition of denominator: ONS Mid-Year Population Estimates aggregated into quinary age bands.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
Deaths from alcohol-related conditions are extracted and assigned an alcohol attributable fraction based on underlying cause of death (and all cause of deaths fields for the conditions: ethanol poisoning, methanol poisoning, toxic effect of alcohol). Mortality data includes all deaths registered in the calendar year where the local authority of usual residence of the deceased is one of the English geographies and an alcohol attributable diagnosis is given as the underlying cause of death.National life expectancy figures are taken from the 2016 ONS life tables. A population weighted average life expectancy is calculated for each age band. The number of age-specific deaths are then multiplied by the average national life expectancy for each age group. Therefore, PYLL is calculated as the sum of the mortality rate in each age group weighted by the potential number of years of life lost as indicated by remaining life expectancy for each age group. This report also includes a detailed list of all alcohol attributable diseases, including ICD 10 codes and relative risks. Excluding all diseases with a negative fraction, as the indicator is designed to quantify only the level of harm caused by alcohol, the corresponding fractions are appended to the ONS mortality file by age and sex and these are summed as the numerator rather than the sum of records extracted.References:(1) ONS (2022) User guide to mortality statistics https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/methodologies/userguidetomortalitystatisticsjuly2017 (2) PHE (2020) Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an updatehttps://www.gov.uk/government/publications/alcohol-attributable-fractions-for-england-an-update
Confidence interval details:
Dobson & Byar's (PYLL variation).The standard Dobson & Byar's method used for DSRs has been adapted to reflect the fact that the numerator for this indicator is years of life lost, not deaths, and that the indicator is PYLL rather than a typical DSR. It is important to note that the variation used does not treat the number of years of life lost as the count of deaths because one event (death) results in several or many years of life lost and as such years of life lost cannot be treated as independent Poisson-distributed events. Rather, the basic method (Dobson & Byar's) is correct and for PYLL must still be based on the counts of deaths as these are the events observed. The variation in the calculation to adapt to PYLL is a change in the weighting parameter, not the count of events. For DSRs, the weighting given to each age group is derived from the standard population (typically, the European Standard Population). PYLL is still a weighted average of mortality rates but the weighting reflects the years of life lost as well as the standard popualtion. Caveats: There is the potential for the underlying cause of death to be incorrectly attributed on the death certificate and the cause of death misclassified. Alcohol-attributable fractions were not available for children. Conditions where low levels of alcohol consumption are protective (have a negative alcohol-attributable fraction) are not included in the calculation of the indicator.The national life expectancies for England have been used for all sub-national geographies to illustrate the disparaties in the burden caused by alcohol between local areas and the national average.The confidence intervals do not take into account the uncertainty involved in the calculation of the AAFs – that is, the proportion of deaths that are caused by alcohol and the alcohol consumption prevalence that are included in the AAF formula are only an estimate and so include uncertainty. The confidence intervals published here are based only on the observed number of deaths and do not account for this uncertainty in the calculation of attributable fraction - as such the intervals may be too narrow.

The data for this indicator has been revised to use the rebased population estimates from 2012 onwards.The data point covering the period from March 2020 will include any effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. All mortality records are extracted that contain an attributable disease and the age and sex specific fraction applied. The results are summed into quinary age bands for the numerator and a directly standardised rate calculated using the European Standard Population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (2) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (3). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (4).
