Indicator: Intravenous antibiotic prescribing; DDDs per 1000 admissions by month and NHS Acute Trust
Rationale: The consumption of antibiotics is a major driver for the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria. The UK Government National Action Plan (NAP) for antmicrobial resistance (AMR) has set an ambition to reduce antimicrobial use in humans by 15% by 2024, and specifically a 10% reduction in broad-spectrum prescribing in hospitals.Intravenous-to-oral switch (IVOS) is an important antimicrobial stewardship intervention. Research evidence confirms several IVOS benefits, including decreased risk of bloodstream and catheter-related infections, reduced equipment costs, carbon footprint and hospital length-of-stay, increased patient mobility and comfort, and released nursing time to care for patients.The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and partners have developed national guidelines for https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/antimicrobial-intravenous-to-oral-switch-criteria-for-early-switch . Adherence to these guidelines is the focus of a 2023/24 NHS England Commissioning for Quality and Innovation (CQUIN). Compliance with the 2023/24 IVOS CQUIN is also published as an AMR local indicator (LINK WHEN LIVE) on Public Health Profiles (Fingertips). This Indicator presents the use of IV antibiotics in relation to the number of patients admitted to a particular NHS acute Trust. An additional indicator (93984) demonstrates the proportion of total antibiotic use that is administered by the IV route for each Trust. This provides additional context as for example large NHS acute Trusts may have high rates of IV antibiotic use but this may be a low proportion of it's total antibiotic use.For this indicator, a lower value is indicative of lower prescribing
Definition: The rate shows how many intravenous antibiotic defined daily doses (DDDs) have been prescribed in each Trust per 1000 admissions per month.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency, based on Rx-info data
Definition of numerator: Defined Daily Dose (DDD) count for intravenous antibiotics for the month specified for each NHS Acute Trust.
Source of numerator: Rx-info (Define), DDDs based on trust-submitted prescribing data
Definition of denominator: Hospital admissions for the month reported.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Methodology: We calculate acute Trust prescribing rates using HES admissions data as follows:(DDD count for the month / Admissions for the month)*1000
Frequency: This indicator will be updated with monthly data on a quarterly basis.
Disclosure control: The source data contains no personal or identifiable information and so statistical disclosure control has not been applied
Rounding: HES admissions have been rounded to the nearest 5 in adherence with NHS Digital disclosure control methodology
Caveats: Drugs are only included in the numerator if they have a British National Formulae (BNF) 5.1 code and Defined Daily Dose (DDD) values provided by the World Health Organization. Anti-TB, Anti-Parasitic and topical antibiotics are excluded to align with requirements for the NHS Standard Contract and previous NHS England antibiotic resistance CQUINs.The data for any new quarter are provisional and will be updated with more accurate admissions and prescribing data in the subsequent quarter’s data release. The rates of consumption for past quarters may therefore change to reflect this.Admissions data retrieved from hospital episode statistics (HES) supplied by NHS digital. Provisional admissions data are used for each quarter to be more representative of Trust activity. As a result, quarterly data will be updated 4 months after the end of the quarter to account for the lag in HES admissions data quality and allow for more accurate reporting. Admissions data will be updated as finalised data becomes available.The figures produced in this indicator are raw and unadjusted for the confounding effects of both the age and sex mix of patient populations served by hospitals, or for other factors such as deprivation and complexity of care that can drive hospital antibiotic prescribing. Therefore Trusts may appear outliers for this measure byfulfilling valid care of the specific population that they serve.Further considerationis required to adapt the AWaRe index for use in specialisthealthcare settings, including an improved understanding ofcase-mix. However, until routine electronic prescribing of antibiotics is available nationally, there is limited work that can beperformed in this area.For these reasons comparison between different organisations should be treated with caution. Nonetheless, as NHS national quality improvement schemes require each hospital to improve from its own baseline levels this is consistent with improving the quality of antibiotic prescribing in each hospital.
Notes: The Defined Daily Dose (DDD) is the assumed average maintenance dose per day for a medicine used for its main indication in adults. In general, the DDDs for antibiotics are based on their use in moderately severe infections.The DDD is the internationally recognised unit of measurement of medicine consumption, recommended by the World Health Organisation (WHO). DDDs allow comparison of medicine use over time hence its use in this context.

Indicator: Sexually transmitted Shigella spp. diagnostic rate per 100,000 adult male population
Rationale:
Shigellosis, also known as bacillary dysentery, is caused by infection with Shigella bacteria. It can cause severe illness, requiring admission to hospital for treatment.

Transmission is via the faeco-oral route and is associated with i) travel to countries with poor sanitation ii) transmission between young children and their care-givers in household, nursery or school settings iii) close sexual contact amongst gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM). Infections amongst GBMSM have been increasing over the past decade and circulating strains are becoming multi or extensively resistant to antibiotics.

Shigella is a notifiable infection reported through laboratory surveillance. As information on sexual orientation is not collected within laboratory surveillance data, reports of infections among adult males with no recent history of foreign travel are used as a proxy for domestically acquired infections in GBMSM. Previous research has validated the use of this proxy[1].This is a subset of the shigella incidence rate indicator that has been published on the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/health-protection . This new indicator selects the portion of infections that are likely sexually transmitted in order to present these alongside other STIs, with a similar epidemiological pattern and geographical distribution, to inform infection prevention and control. The overall increasing number and widening geographical spread makes occurrences of this infection similar to other STIs that are included on the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/sexualhealth  to inform local health awareness and monitoring, public health planning and health promotion.[1]Mitchell HD and others. ‘ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6927305/ .’ Microbiology society 2019: volume 5, issue 11
Specific rationale: This is a subset of the shigella incidence rate indicator that has been published on the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/health-protection . This new indicator selects the portion of infections that are likely sexually transmitted in order to present these alongside other STIs, with a similar epidemiological pattern and geographical distribution, to inform infection prevention and control. The overall increasing number and widening geographical spread makes occurrences of this infection similar to other STIs that are included on the https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/sexualhealth  to inform local health awareness and monitoring, public health planning and health promotion.
Definition: Shigella spp. diagnoses among men who have sex with men (defined as adult men without a recent history of foreign travel) as a rate per 100,000 adult male population, restricted to residents of England.
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Definition of numerator: Laboratory confirmed episodes of Shigella spp. infection among adult males without a recent history of foreign travel summarised by year of laboratory report for the following geographies: England, UKHSA region, upper tier local authorities and lower tier local authorities, and integrated care boards. Isolates of the same species of Shigella from the same patient within a 14 day period are defined as a single episode.For each year between 2016 and 2024, the numerator will be calculated as the number of Shigella spp. diagnoses among adult men aged 16 years and above without a recent history of foreign travel.
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS)
Definition of denominator: The denominators for 2016 to 2024 are sourced from Office for National Statistics (ONS). The number of adult men aged 16 years and above recorded in the ONS mid-2024 population estimates based on 2021 Census data was used for all years.Population estimates for 2025 were not available at the time of publication. Therefore, rates for 2025 are calculated using estimates from 2024 as a proxy.As there are no estimates of adult men by travel history available, the denominator selected is the best available.Further details on the ONS census are available from the  https://www.ons.gov.uk/census .
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Rate per 100,000 population. The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Where the numerator was 10 or above, Byar's method was used to calculate confidence intervals. Where numerators are small (less than 10) the Exact X2 method was used to calculate confidence intervals.
Disclosure control:
Numbers between 1 and 4 with a population less than 10,000 are suppressed. Where counts for Isles of Scilly or City of London are between 1 and 4, these are combined with Cornwall or Hackney respectively.

When disclosure control is required, further guidance is available on the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hiv-and-sti-data-sharing-policy  page.
Caveats:
a) Misclassification of residence:Patients are geolocated based on their postcode of residence.In 2015, 81% of people were assigned residence by their postcode. Where this is not available, the patient's GP postcode is used (less than 1%) or the postcode of the primary diagnostic laboratory that processed their Shigella isolate (18%).Patients missing a residential postcode may be geographically misclassified (allocated to a region in which they are not a resident).b) Case ascertainment:The current surveillance methodology underestimates the true incidence of Shigella because:
- not all cases present to a healthcare facility
- not all cases that present to a healthcare facility will provide a specimen for laboratory analysis
- not all primary diagnostic laboratories provide their data to SGSS. 121 laboratories routinely report to SGSS. Most (above 96%) public laboratories report to SGSS, however the proportion of private laboratories that report is unknown. In addition, not all primary diagnostic laboratory shigella results pass the minimum data quality checks for uploading to SGSS. On average 0.03% of records are quarantined or have translation errors
- although there is a statutory duty to report, completeness and timeliness of reporting may vary by laboratory (and therefore region)All of these factors influence the reported incidence of infection.c) Outbreaks:Outbreaks may lead to large localised increases in infection due to specific events. When a location has a relatively high rate of Shigella in a particular time period, further investigation may be required to determine whether this is the result of an outbreak(s) or other factors that could create persistent, high rates of infection.d) Deduplication failures:i. Episode of infection: data stored in SGSS are de-duplicated so that multiple isolates that relate to the same episode of infection are merged, based on episode length. Specimen dates for isolates of an identical strain from the same patient within 13 days of one another are merged and counted as a single episode of infection. Specimen dates for isolates of an identical strain from the same patient that are 14 or more days apart are counted as separate episodes of infection. This may result in an overestimate of incidence in some cases, as Shigella is shed in stools for up to 6 weeks after onset of symptoms. Microbiological clearance is currently required for non-sonnei Shigella infections; in addition, some patients experience persistent gastroenteritis and may provide further specimens for testing beyond the 14-day period used for deduplication.

ii. Probabilistic matching: multiple records for the same patient are deduplicated based on probabilistic matching of patient identifiable information (name, date of birth, NHS number and postcode); consequently, cases with matching or very similar information will have their records merged. This may lead to underestimation of incidence where separate patients are incorrectly merged. Records that are missing most of this information cannot be merged; this may lead to overestimation of incidence where isolates from the same patient, for the same strain and episode of illness are not merged due to incomplete or incorrect patient identifying information.iii. Incomplete speciation: isolates from the same patient episode are not merged unless all isolates have been speciated and are the same species. Some clearance specimens may not be speciated, in which case the results will not be merged with the initial diagnostic result. This may lead to an overestimation of incidence.
iv. Different antimicrobial resistance test results: Isolates from the same case and/or sample with differing antimicrobial resistance results are counted as two separate records. Intermediate results with missing data in the antimicrobial resistance section cannot be merged with results from the same patient episode that have a complete antimicrobial resistance profile. In these scenarios, incidence may be overestimated as antimicrobial resistance profiles in a single patient episode can change during the course of their infection, particularly if antimicrobials are prescribed for their Shigella infection or other co-infections.e) Extraction from a live database:Data for this health profile are extracted from SGSS and GDW, which are live databases and therefore numbers may vary if data is extracted on a different date.
This may lead to under or overestimation of incidence due to:
- batch uploading of laboratory results for the preceding year, after the date of extraction (underestimation)
- correction of personal identifying information, antimicrobial resistance test results or other data used for deduplication for records from the preceding year, after the date of extraction (under- or overestimation depending on how deduplication is affected by the corrected data)In addition, data presented on this health profile may not be directly comparable to data presented in other reports, where the date of extraction differs or where different geographic boundary versions have been used to summarise the results.f) Local detection rates may be influenced by which type of laboratory tests are used to test for Shigella, as the sensitivity of tests to detect the presence of infection differ.g) 'Non-travel' includes cases who reported no recent foreign travel and those where recent travel history is not known. Hence, we are assuming that in cases where travel history is not known, the case has not travelled.
h) Whilst sexually transmitted Shigella is concentrated among adult males without a recent history of foreign travel, Shigella infection among an adult male without a recent history of foreign travel may not always be sexually transmitted, as whilst less likely, other routes of transmission are possible.i. Shigella spp. diagnoses among adult men aged 16 years and above with no recent foreign travel history vary substantially between local areas. This is expected and is a feature of the epidemiology of sexually transmitted shigellosis. Transmission of sexually transmitted Shigella is focused in large, urban centres where a higher proportion of gay, bisexual and other GBMSM reside (such as London, Manchester, Brighton). In 2021, the range of diagnoses per 100,000 among lower tier local authorities was between 0 per 100,000 and 30.0 per 100,000. However, with a median of 0 diagnoses per 100,000, areas frequently reported no diagnoses in the 12-month period.j) Laboratory surveillance data used for this indicator does not collect information on sexual orientation. Therefore, an adult man without a recent history of foreign travel, diagnosed with Shigella, is assumed to be GBMSM.

Here we have used a rate to be consistent with other STI indicators on the Sexual and Reproductive Health Profiles. As part of the process of developing this indicator the relative ranking of local authorities using both the rate and the count has been compared and are shown to be similar using both methods. The quality of Shigella data within SGSS is likely to improve, and providing data within this indicator will help to drive this improvement.Shigellosis, also known as bacillary dysentery, is caused by infection with any of four species of Shigella bacteria. Two of these: Shigella flexneri and Shigella sonnei are endemic in the UK. Indicator: Mortality rate for deaths involving diabetes, all ages
Rationale:
Diabetes is a lifelong metabolic condition in which the body does not produce sufficient insulin to regulate blood glucose levels.Diabetes can lead to several long-term complications that affect blood vessels and circulation. People with diabetes are at significantly greater risk than the general population of developing other conditions such as:

heart disease
heart failure
heart attack
stroke
chronic kidney disease
retinopathy

Improvements in the care and outcomes for people with diabetes are possible. This indicator captures mortality trends for all deaths involving diabetes, as diabetes contributes to a proportion of deaths that are not selected as the underlying cause of death.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate for deaths involving diabetes, per 100,000 population, for all ages
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths involving diabetes (classified by underlying cause of death or mention of death recorded as ICD-10 codes E10 to E14), registered in the calendar year, in people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9,…, 90+)
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: For single years: Population for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+) For three-year rolling averages: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area. This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
Frequency: The data will be updated annually
Caveats: Please note data may not match published Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures due to differences in the version of postcode lookup used

Impact of COVID-19: This indicator covers the period since March 2020 and includes the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Measures put in place to control the COVID-19 pandemic have affected the transmission of influenza and other respiratory viruses during the flu seasons of 2020 to 2021, and 2021 to 2022. These measures included public health messaging, social and physical distancing measures, national lockdowns, the wearing of face coverings, hand hygiene and travel restrictions. Changes in healthcare-seeking patterns also affect some influenza indicators directly and indirectly. Although many of these restrictions and interventions were lifted by the 2022 to 2023 influenza season (some measures were reintroduced in December 2021 as Omicron-variant COVID-19 emerged, curtailing influenza transmission), these factors continue to be important to consider when interpreting this indicator, especially when comparing with previous seasons.

Indicator: Admissions to hospital for cataract surgery in people aged 65 years and over
Rationale: Cataract surgery is the treatment for symptomatic, age-related cataract and prevention of vision impairment. It is a clinically safe and effective micro-surgical procedure, associated with good functional outcomes for both first and second eye surgery. It remains a high volume NHS activity with surgery predominantly (85%) performed in adults of 65 years of age and over. Whilst cataract is a major cause of global vision impairment and blindness, it infrequently causes certifiable sight impairment in the UK.Surgical activity has steadily increased and is expected to continue to do so as demand continues to rise with the ageing population.At least a third of all procedures are consistently for second eye surgery. Periodically there have been restrictions on access to surgery (particularly second eye surgery) as a means to reduce costs to manage health budgetary restrictions. However NICE Guideline NG77 recognises the need for cataract surgery in both eyes, and its contribution to maintaining population eye health.The  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/atlas-of-variation showed during 2019/20, almost 384,000 cataract operations were performed in the NHS. Cinical commissioning group (CCG) rates ranged from 2,462 to 5,299 per 100,000 population.
Definition: Admission to hospital for cataract surgery in people aged 65 years and over. Directly age standardised rate per 100,000 population (standardised to the European standard population).
Data source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: The number of admissions to hospital for cataract surgery (operative procedure (OPERTN) C712 - Phacoemulsification of lens, OR C751 - Insertion of prosthetic replacement for lens NEC) in people aged 65 years and over. ICB sub-location assigned using GP practice code (available from NHS Digital). When GP practice code is missing, residence (LSOA) used to assign ICB sub-location. GP Practice codes beginning with 'W' and 'S' (Wales and Scotland) excluded. GP Practice codes beginning with 'X', 'Y' and 'Z' (unclassified or not applicable - prisons, specialist commissioning etc) excluded. GP Practice codes beginning with 'V' excluded with the exception of 'V81997' and 'V81999' ('patient not registered but eligible to' and 'not possible to determine'). ICB sub-location of GP practice field (CCG_GP_practice) used to exclude NHS England-commissioned armed forces (13Q). The same process was followed for ICB and NHSE region geographies.

Rationale: Intravitreal injection therapy with licensed anti-v<span class="ILfuVd" lang="en"><span class="hgKElc">ascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) drugs for ophthalmic use was first introduced in the NHS in 2008. Anti-VEGF drugs are the main treatment for the routine management of wet age related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic macular oedema (DMO) and macular oedema, the leading causes of certifiable sight impairment and sight loss in adults in England. Indicator: Admissions to hospital for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment surgery in people aged 18 years and over
Rationale: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. Retinal detachment refers to the separation of the retina from the surrounding tissues. The process results in progressive loss of vision and can lead to permanent visual loss in the affected eye. Retinal detachment is one of the most common eye emergencies in England. The most common type of retinal detachment is rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) associated with a tear or break in the retina.Patients presenting with RRD symptoms should be referred for immediate assessment by an ophthalmologist. Prompt recognition and referral may allow early surgical repair, reducing the risk of permanent impairment of visual acuity, or even preventing the full progression of retinal detachment . Symptomatic retinal detachment invariably results in lifelong loss of vision if left untreated.Risk factors for this type of retinal detachment include age, myopia, eye injuries, ophthalmic operations, and familial or genetic risk factors. From the data presented in the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/atlas-of-variation , the rate of surgery for RRD in England during 2019/20 was 23.5 per 100,000 of the adult population affecting approximately 10,600 people a year.

Indicator: Breast screening coverage: aged 53 to 70 years old
Rationale: Breast screening supports early detection of cancer and is estimated to save 1,400 lives in England each year. This indicator provides an opportunity to incentivise screening promotion and other local initiatives to increase coverage of breast screening. Improvements in coverage would mean more breast cancers are detected at earlier, more treatable stages.
Definition: 3-year screening coverage %: The number of eligible women who have had a breast screening test result recorded in the past 36 months divided by the total number of eligible women, for those registered to the practice on last day of the review period.
Data source: NHS England, Breast Screening Programme
Definition of numerator: The number of eligible women aged between 53 and 70, registered to the practice on the last day of the review period, who have had a breast screening test result recorded in the past 36 months
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Breast Screening Programme (BSP)
Definition of denominator: The number of women aged between 53 and 70 registered to the practice on the last day of the review period (number of eligible women)
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Breast Screening Programme (BSP)
Methodology: The data were taken from the National Health Application and Infrastructure Services (NHAIS) via the Open Exeter system, with suppression then applied (see Disclosure control). The data extracted represent the situation at the end of 31 March and covers the previous financial year.
Disclosure control: A Central Suppression Methodology is applied. This rounds values between 0 and 7 (inclusive) to 5, and values above 7 to the nearest 5. Additionally, practice-level data is suppressed for practices with a rounded denominator of 15 or less. Any data suppression is applied to GP practices, sub-ICBs, ICBs and England on an individual basis, using aggregated, unrounded data; this means that activity for any practices with suppressed data is included within counts derived for their respective larger geographies. Auto-aggregated data (e.g. for PCNs) will be based on pre-rounded and suppressed data.
Caveats: For some practices, this indicator may be based on a small number of patients. Caution is advised when considering such data, as small numbers mean that random variation can result in apparently large changes over time or apparently larger differences compared to other areas. This indicator gives screening coverage by GP practice (on a registered basis). This is not the same as the indicator based on Local Authorities which do not account for where patients are registered with a GP practice. This is likely to result in different England totals depending on the underlying population type (registered or resident). Specifically, it results in overall England-level data which is different to that published by the national screening programme (which is resident based).Data for England totals here include those registered to practices not attributable to ICBs, such as MoD or detained setting practices.For practices that have merged or had boundary changes, the data may not be reliable for time periods covering the practice changes. For data up to 2021/22, data is only included in the profiles, including any aggregate data, where the practice had a list size of at least 1000.
Notes: Eligible women are invited for breast screening for the first time between their 50th and 53rd birthdays and every three years thereafter up to but not including their 71st birthdays. Over this period, a women who responds to each invitation should be screened 7 times. This indicator measures the fraction of eligible women who should have been invited at least once (those aged between 53 and 70) and who have had a breast screening test result reported at least once in the 36 months/ three years up to 31 March of the data year.
Impact of COVID-19: Breast screening coverage is low for some practices in 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 as an impact of COVID-19. It is also a little lower for England for these years. A pause to breast screening services in the early stages of the pandemic has led to subsequent delays in some screening cycles, beyond the usual three-year interval. This means that, at the cut-off date when screening coverage has been measured, some eligible people would not have had the opportunity to have had breast screening within the last three-years, resulting in a lower than expected screening coverage. Where this has been seen, it is often noted that screening coverage increases shortly after the date cut-off used for this indicator, as those affected are invited and/or attend screening shortly after the cut-off date.

Indicator: Estimated cost per capita of alcohol-related hospital admissions (Broad)
Rationale:
Alcohol misuse across the UK is a significant public health problem with major health, social, and economic consequences (1).This indicator aims to highlight the impact of alcohol-related conditions on inpatient hospital services in England. High costs of alcohol-related admissions are indicative of poor population health and high alcohol consumption. This indicator highlights the resource implications of alcohol-related conditions and supports the arguments for local health promotion initiatives. Publication of this indictaor will allow national and local cost estimates to be updated and consistently monitored going forward. This measure accounts for just one aspect of the cost of alcohol to society, but there are others such as primary care, crime, ambulatory services and specialst treatment services as well as broader costs such as unemployment and loss of productivity.

The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related admissions can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.

References:(1) PHE (2020) The Burden of Disease in England compared with 22 peer countries https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/global-burden-of-disease-for-england-international-comparisons/the-burden-of-disease-in-england-compared-with-22-peer-countries-executive-summary
Definition: Crude rate of cost of admissions for alcohol-related conditions (Broad definition) per head of population.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
The total cost (£s) of alcohol-related admissions (Broad).Admissions to hospital where the primary diagnosis is an alcohol-related condition, or a secondary diagnosis is an alcohol-related external cause.

More specifically, hospital admissions records are identified where the admission is a finished episode [epistat = 3]; the admission is an ordinary admission, day case or maternity [classpat = 1, 2 or 5]; it is an admission episode [epiorder = 1]; the sex of the patient is valid [sex = 1 or 2]; there is a valid age at start of episode [startage between 0 and 150 or between 7001 and 7007]; the region of residence is one of the English regions, no fixed abode or unknown [resgor<= K or U or Y]; the episode end date [epiend] falls within the financial year, and an alcohol-attributable ICD10 code appears in the primary diagnosis field [diag_01] or an alcohol-related external cause code appears in any diagnosis field [diag_nn].

For each episode identified, an alcohol-attributable fraction is applied to the primary diagnosis field or an alcohol-attributable external cause code appears in one of the secondary codes based on the diagnostic codes, age group, and sex of the patient. Where there is more than one alcohol-related ICD10 code among the 20 possible diagnostic codes the codes with the largest alcohol attributable fraction is selected; in the event of there being two or more codes with the same alcohol-attributable fraction within the same episode, the one from the lowest diagnostic position is selected. For a detailed list of all alcohol attributable diseases, including ICD 10 codes and relative risks see‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (2).Alcohol-related hospital admission episodes were extracted from HES according to the Broad definition and admissions flagged as either elective or non elective based on the admission method field. The cost of each admission episode was calculated using https://www.england.nhs.uk/costing-in-the-nhs/national-cost-collection/ (published by NHS England) main schedule dataset for the corresponding financial year applied to elective and non-elective admission episodes. The healthcare resource group (HRG) was identified using the HES field SUSHRG [SUS Generated HRG] which is the SUS PbR derived HRG code at episode level. Healthcare Resource Groups (HRGs) are standard groupings of clinically similar treatments which use common levels of healthcare resource. The elective admissions were assigned an average of the elective and day-case costs. The non-electives were assigned an average of the non-elective long stay and non-elective short stay costs. Where the HRG was not available or did match the National Reference Costs look-up table an average elective or non-elective cost was imputed. This may result in the cost of these admissions being underestimated.For each record the AAF was multiplied by the reference cost and the resulting values were aggregated by the required output geographies to provide numerators for the cost per capita indicator. References:

(2) PHE (2020) Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update

https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/alcohol-attributable-fractions-for-england-an-update
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on NHS England (NHSE) and Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Definition of denominator: Mid-year population estimates.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: numerator is divided by denominator.
Caveats:
Not all alcohol-related conditions require inpatient services so this indicator is only one measure of the alcohol-related health problems in each local area. However, inpatient admissions are easily monitored and this indicator provides local authorities with a routine method of monitoring the health impacts of alcohol in their local populations. The Healthcare Resource Group cost assigned to each hospital admission is for the initial admission episode only and doesn’t include costs related to alcohol in any subsequent episodes in the hospital spell.Where the HRG was not available or did match the National Reference Costs look-up table an average elective or non-elective cost was imputed. This may result in the cost of these admissions being underestimated.It must be noted that the numerator is based on financial year and the denominator on calendar mid-year population estimates e.g. 2019/20 admission rates are constructed from admission counts for the 2019/20 financial year and mid-year population estimates for the 2020 calendar year.Data for England includes records with geography 'No fixed abode'. Alcohol-attributable fractions were not available for children. Conditions where low levels of alcohol consumption are protective (have a negative alcohol-attributable fraction) are not included in the calculation of the indicator. Does not include attendance at Accident and Emergency departments.Hospital Episode Statistics overall is well completed. However, year-on-year variations exist due to poor completion from a proportion of trusts.

Analysis has revealed significant differences across the country in the coding of cancer patients in the Hospital Episode Statistics. In particular, in some areas, regular attenders at hospital for treatments like chemotherapy and radiotherapy are being incorrectly recorded as ordinary or day-case admissions. Since cancer admissions form part of the overarching alcohol-related admission national indicators, the inconsistent recording across the country for cancer patients has some implication for these headline measures. Cancer admissions make up approximately a quarter of the total number of alcohol-related admissions. Analysis suggests that, although most Local Authorities would remain within the same RAG group compared with the England average if cancer admissions were removed, the ranking of Local Authorities within RAG groups would be altered. We are continuing to monitor the impact of this issue and to consider ways of improving the consistency between areas.The COVID-19 pandemic had a large impact on hospital activity with a reduction in admissions in 2020 to 2021. Because of this, NHS Digital have been unable to analyse coverage (measured as the difference between expected and actual records submitted by NHS Trusts) in the normal way. There may have been issues around coverage in some areas which were not identified as a result.
Notes:
The methodology for this indicator differs to that used by the same indicator published prior to 2023. The current methodology assigns costs to hospital admissions using the SUS generated HRG code of the admission episode and the National Reference Costs published by NHS England. National Reference Costs are the costs hospital providers incur. In contrast, the previous method used the SUS generated core Spell HRG, where available, which takes into account all the episodes in a hospital spell. It also used the standard Payment by Results methodology (PbR), which is a measure of the amount hospital trusts are reimbursed for providing care.The proportion of disease attributable to alcohol (alcohol attributable fraction) is calculated using a relative risk (a fraction between 0 and 1) specific to each disease, age group and sex combined with the prevalence of alcohol consumption in the population. This indicator uses updated alcohol attributable fractions, based on new relative risks from ‘Alcohol-attributable fractions for England: an update’ (3) published by PHE in 2020. A detailed comparison between the 2013 and 2020 alcohol attributable fractions is available in Appendix 3 of the PHE report (4). A consultation was also undertaken with stakeholders where the impact of the new methodology on the LAPE indicators was quantified and explored (5).

The calculation that underlies all alcohol-related indicators has been updated to take account of the latest academic evidence and more recent alcohol-consumption figures. The result has been that the newly published mortality and admission rates are lower than those previously published. This is due to a change in methodology, mainly because alcohol consumption across the population has reduced since 2010. Therefore, the number of deaths and hospital admissions that we attribute to alcohol has reduced because in general people are drinking less today than they were when the original calculation was made.

Figures published previously did not misrepresent the burden of alcohol based on the previous evidence – the methodology used in this update is as close as sources and data allow to the original method. Though the number of deaths and admissions attributed to alcohol each year has reduced, the direction of trend and the key inequalities due to alcohol harm remain the same. Alcohol remains a significant burden on the health of the population and the harm alcohol causes to individuals remains unchanged.

Indicator: Gambling premises per 100,000 population
Rationale:
Public Health England’s “Gambling-related harms: evidence review” found that gambling is associated with a wide range of harms for both people who gamble and those close to them,including financial, health, and relationship harms. Until recently, most gambling participationand harm research has focused on people who experience severe problems and individual-level risk factors. Less gambling research has focused on community or societal risk factorssuch as availability of gambling outlets, which are established risk factors for alcohol harm(1) and tobacco use (2) . However, one review of majority cross-sectional studies suggeststhat the density of and proximity to land-based gambling outlets is associated with increasedgambling and the latter with problem gambling rates (3, 4).Additionally, there is someevidence of an economic gradient in England for experiencing gambling harm, where peoplewho are the most socio-economically deprived or disadvantaged have lower rates ofgambling participation but the highest levels of harmful gambling and susceptibility togambling harm (4) . A relationship between the density of outlets and deprivation has beendemonstrated for other unhealthy commodities such as alcohol, tobacco, and fast food (5-8).
Available research on the relationship between gambling outlet density/proximity in anEnglish context is lacking, but a single study shows that areas where there was a highconcentration of gambling machines had a higher proportion of economically inactiveresidents than areas that didn’t, and a third of all areas considered to have a high density ofthese machines were located within one mile of the coast (9).
An indicator monitoring the number of gambling premises in an area will facilitate density/proximity comparisons with gambling participation rates and harms across areas which will be important to understanding this relatively under-researched area. From a policy perspective, licensing authorities have a wide range of powers under the 2005 Gambling Act (herein, the Act) to refuse or place conditions on applications for gambling premise licences where there is cause for concern (10). The Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport have committed in a recent white paper reviewing the Act to bring the licensing regime in line with that for alcohol by legislating to introduce a formal system of cumulative impact assessments, when Parliamentary time allows. This indicator will support this policy commitment.

Indicator: Mortality rate for deaths involving hypertensive disease, all ages
Rationale: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is when the pressure in blood vessels is too high (140/90 mmHg or higher). It is common and can be serious if not treated. Treatment for hypertension is very effective at lowering blood pressure and at improving outcomes and significantly reduces the risk of heart attacks, stroke, heart failure and all-cause mortality. This indicator captures mortality trends for all deaths where hypertension was mentioned as a contributing cause, as hypertension contributes to a proportion of deaths that are not selected as the underlying cause of death.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate for deaths involving hypertensive disease, per 100,000 population, for all ages
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities

Indicator: Potential working years of life lost (PWYLL) due to alcohol-related conditions
Rationale: Alcohol consumption is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths from a diverse range of conditions. The Government has said that everyone has a role to play in reducing the harmful use of alcohol - this indicator is one of the key contributions by the Government (and the Department of Health and Social Care) to promote measurable, evidence based prevention activities at a local level, and supports the national ambitions to reduce harm set out in the Government's Alcohol Strategy. This ambition is part of the monitoring arrangements for the Responsibility Deal Alcohol Network. Alcohol-related deaths can be reduced through local interventions to reduce alcohol misuse and harm.Years of life lost is a measure of premature mortality. The purpose of this measure is to estimate the length of time a person would have lived had they not died prematurely. As the calculation includes the age at which death occurs it is an attempt to quantify the burden on society from the specified cause of mortality. Alcohol-related deaths often occur at relatively young ages. One of the ways to consider the full impact of alcohol on both the individual and wider society is to look at how many working years are lost each year due to premature death as a result of alcohol.To enable comparisons between areas and over time, PWYLL rates are age-standardised to represent the PWYLL if each area had the same population structure as the 2013 European Standard Population (ESP). PWYLL rates are presented as years of life lost per 100,000 population.
Definition: Potential working years of life lost (PWYLL) due to alcohol-related conditions, ages 16-64, directly age-standardised per 100,000 population.

Confidence interval details:
Dobson & Byar's (PYLL variation).The standard Dobson & Byar's method used for DSRs has been adapted to reflect the fact that the numerator for this indicator is years of life lost, not deaths, and that the indicator is YLL rather than a typical DSR. It is important to note that the variation used does not treat the number of years of life lost as the count of deaths because one event (death) results in several or many years of life lost and as such years of life lost cannot be treated as independent Poisson-distributed events. Rather, the basic method (Dobson & Byar's) is correct and for WYLL must still be based on the counts of deaths as these are the events observed. The variation in the calculation to adapt to WYLL is a change in the weighting parameter, not the count of events. For DSRs, the weighting given to each age group is derived from the standard population (typically, the European Standard Population). WYLL is still a weighted average of mortality rates but the weighting reflects the years of life lost as well as the standard popualtion. Indicator: Access rate to specialist perinatal mental health services
Rationale:
The review 'The Best Start for Life. A Vision for the 1,001 Critical Days' (2021) highlighted that pregnancy and the period after birth can be an exhilarating and challenging time for new parents. For some women, new mental health conditions may develop during the pregnancy or pregnancy may exacerbate already existing mental health conditions. It can be especially so if parents have experienced trauma or an unexpected event in childbirth or their baby’s development.The antenatal and postnatal mental health NICE guidelines (2020) recognise the serious impact of undiagnosed or untreated depression and anxiety disorders on the health and wellbeing of the mother and baby during pregnancy and the postnatal period.The impact of untreated perinatal mental illness can be severe, with long lasting effects on women, their babies and families if not identified early and managed effectively. Evidence suggests that:

<li class="MsoNormal">maternal depressive illness and anxiety can affect the infant’s mental health
<li class="MsoNormal">perinatal psychiatric disorders are associated with an increased risk to both mortality and morbidity in mother and child
<li class="MsoNormal">psychotic illness in pregnancy is also known to be associated with an increased risk of pre-term delivery, stillbirth, perinatal death and neurodevelopmental disorder
<li class="MsoNormal">over the past two decades, psychiatric disorder contributed to 15% of all maternal deaths in pregnancy and six months postpartum
<li class="MsoNormal">suicide remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality in the UK
<li class="MsoNormal">parental depression has a negative impact on how parents interact with children 

'Family Hubs and Start for Life programme' (2023) committed to the availability of appropriate local specialist perinatal mental health services. The NHS Long Term Plan (2019) also committed to creating a comprehensive, joined up mental health service offer for parents. The access rate provides local health and care systems with an important measure of demand. It will help to assess how the demand reflects the perinatal mental health needs of the local population and if the demand can be met by current service provisions. It is a measure of the number of attendances with specialist perinatal mental health services that are happening in the community in the time period. This will be influenced by the prevalence of perinatal mental ill health in the community, the capacity of primary care services to manage this need, and how much activity local secondary specialist perinatal mental health services are delivering.
Definition: Directly age standardised rate of access to specialist perinatal mental health services per 1,000 females having a delivery
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, using Mental Health Services Data Set and Hospital Episode Statistics, NHS England
Definition of numerator: Pooled counts (over 3 years), by five year age bands for females aged 15 to 44 and for 45 to 54 year olds combined, for females aged 15 to 54 who had at least one attended contact (face to face or virtual, excludes telephone, SMS, email or other electronic method) with a specialist community perinatal mental health service, which is recorded in the Mental Health Services Data Set against team code C02 in a financial year.Females are assigned to geographic areas based on their location of residence.Age defined at latest mental health contact in the financial year.Females counted once in each financial year, irrespective of the number of contacts in the financial year.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Mental Health Services Dataset (MHSDS)
Definition of denominator: Pooled counts (over 3 years), by five year age bands for females aged 15 to 44 and for 45 to 54 year olds combined, of females aged 15 to 54 years who had at least one delivery episode within a financial year (episode type code 2 or 5).Females are assigned to geographic areas based on their location of residence.Age is defined as at time of delivery.Females are only counted once per financial year, irrespective of the number of deliveries they may have had during the financial year.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)
Methodology: These rates are directly age standardised using a Standard Population per 1,000. This improves the comparability of rates for different areas, or between different time periods, by taking into account differences in the age structures of the populations being compared. The directly age standardised rate is the rate of events that would occur in a standard population if that population were to experience the age specific rates of the subject population.The methodology is based on that provided in APHO Technical Briefing 3: Commonly Used Public Health Statistics and their Confidence Intervals. https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/guidance Figures were calculated using the PHEIndicatormethods R package available from https://github.com/PublicHealthEngland/PHEindicatormethods Directly standardised rates have also been calculated for a variety of age groups, and for each deprivation quintile. These use the same methodology as for the all females, 15 to 54 years indicator, and also use the above standard population. The two 5-year age groups for 45 to 49 years and 50 to 54 years have been combined due to small numbers in these age groups.Standardisation is calculated to allow comparison of access to services between areas, deprivation quintiles and age groups. Prevalence work shows that there are peaks in prevalence for females with perinatal mental health need in the younger and older age groups.Deprivation quintiles have been calculated using IMD 2019 using LSOA 2011.
Standard population/values:
Average counts for England per financial year over the period April 2014 to March 2019, by five year age bands for females aged 15 to 44 and for 45 to 54 year olds combined, of resident females aged 15 to 54 years who had at least one delivery episode within a financial year (episode type code 2 or 5). 

The source for this data was HES.
Frequency: This indicator is intended to be updated yearly.
Disclosure control: Values have not been calculated for areas where the number of females attending perinatal services was fewer than 10, and the counts fewer than 5 have been suppressed. This has been approved by NHS England's Disclosure Control Board.
Rounding: Numerator and denominator counts for areas below England level have been rounded to nearest 5 following the calculation of the rate.
Caveats: Only women or people identifying as women are included in the numerator so that the numerator and denominator are as in line as possible. It is not possible to identify demographics of partners of women having a delivery episode from HES, so they were excluded. Records without demographics or LSOA are excluded. Women who had a delivery episode outside of hospital are excluded.MHSDS is a complex data set of 50+ tables in a relational database. However, only the tables containing patient details and referrals are mandatory for providers to submit. The level of completion for other tables varies between providers and is improving. Therefore, the data may not represent the activity being delivered, but may be more indicative of the level of recording. For the up-to-date data quality reports, see https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/mental-health-data-hub/mental-health-services-data-quality Rates should be considered in context of wider local system interventions to improve the mental health of the population, system design, and wider local system support to keep people well. Ultimately, each local system is unique and any action should be based on a thorough understanding of the balance of these influences in the local system. There are now specialist perinatal services in all local NHS areas across the country, however, five years ago 40% of the country did not have a specialist community team. As services have been introduced gradually across the country during the reporting periods, geographical variation should be interpreted with caution. Particular attention should be paid to variation in rates between populations within areas.For the purposes of this indicator, gender for the numerator has been defined as as per the NHSE specialist perinatal mental health indicator access indicator https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-collections-and-data-sets/data-sets/mental-health-services-data-set/submit-data/quick-guide-to-submitting-perinatal-access-and-maternal-access-data

Indicator: Model-based estimated prevalence of perinatal mental health conditions
Rationale:
The review 'The Best Start for Life. A Vision for the 1,001 Critical Days' (2021) highlighted that pregnancy and the period after birth can be an exhilarating and challenging time for new parents. For some women, new mental health conditions may develop during the pregnancy or pregnancy may exacerbate already existing mental health conditions. It can be especially so if parents have experienced trauma or an unexpected event in childbirth or their baby’s development.The antenatal and postnatal mental health NICE guidelines (2020) recognise the serious impact of undiagnosed or untreated depression and anxiety disorders on the health and wellbeing of the mother and baby during pregnancy and the postnatal period.The impact of untreated perinatal mental illness can be severe, with long lasting effects on women, their babies and families if not identified early and managed effectively. Evidence suggests that:

  • maternal depressive illness and anxiety can affect the infant’s mental health
  • perinatal psychiatric disorders are associated with an increased risk to both mortality and morbidity in mother and child
  • psychotic illness in pregnancy is also known to be associated with an increased risk of pre-term delivery, stillbirth, perinatal death and neurodevelopmental disorder
  • over the past two decades, psychiatric disorder contributed to 15% of all maternal deaths in pregnancy and six months postpartum
  • suicide remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality in the UK
  • parental depression has a negative impact on how parents interact with children 'Family Hubs and Start for Life programme' (2023) committed to the availability of appropriate local perinatal mental health services. NHS Long Term Plan (2019) also committed to creating a comprehensive, joined up mental health service offer for parents. To support delivery on these commitments, local prevalence of perinatal mental health conditions is essential to design and commission appropriate services reflecting the level of local need and how this varies across England. This indicator estimates the level of local perinatal mental health need.
Definition: Estimated prevalence of pre-existing or newly diagnosed mental health conditions during perinatal period.
Data source: OHID, based on Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator:
The numerator is the estimate of the total number of females (aged 15 to 55) expected to have a perinatal mental health (PMH) condition based on the differences in age and deprivation structure of women giving birth (ONS maternities) for that area and weighted prevalence proportions from Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) [1].

A perinatal mental health condition is defined as: common mental disorders (CMD), including depression,anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, antenatal and postnatal depression, social anxiety Disorder, and seasonal affective disorder personality disorders eating disorders, including anorexia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and bulimia nervosa severe mental illness, including bipolar disorder, psychosis and schizophrenia perinatal mental health psychosis

Weighted prevalence proportions from CPRD by deprivation quintile (based on Index of Multiple Deprivation 2015) and age groups (5-year age groups up to 39 years, and 40 years and over) were applied to each geographical area's population by deprivation quintile and the same age groups to produce an estimated count of PMH conditions. Evidence suggest that age and deprivation are statistically significant predictors of mental health problems during perinatal period.[1] Females aged 15 to 55 years with evidence of birth event (live birth, stillbirth, and late miscarriage) in 2016 were identified in primary care electronic health records data (CPRD) using SNOMED and READ codes. Women were included in the birth cohort (a non-random sample of 128,070 women), if medical history was available for the complete perinatal period, which was defined as 1 year before and 2 years after birth event. Weighting of the birth cohort was carried out to account for regional differences in CPRD and ONS maternities.

Females were identified as having a perinatal mental health condition based on SNOMED and READ codes for 'diagnoses' or a combination of 'symptoms and medication' or historical diagnoses of severe mental illness.
Source of numerator: Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD)
Definition of denominator: Number of maternities in females aged 15 to 55 years.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual births and mortality extracts
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator to give a percentage.
Frequency:
The indicator is usually recalculated every 3 to 5 years, depending on data availability. Current updates (2016 and 2019) reflect changes in the age and deprivation structure of the area’s population rather than changes in the CPRD derived, weighted prevalence.
COVID-19 pandemic impacted on access to primary care services and therefore the update period will be longer with latest pre-pandemic update being 2019 and first post-pandemic update 2022 or 2023 (time period subject to sensitivity analysis).
Confidence interval details:
Assume each deprivation quintile and age group prevalence proportion follows a binomial distribution. Simulate prevalence proportions using the weighted prevalence proportions and 95% CIs from CPRD to determine distribution parameters. On each simulation, the prevalence proportions are randomly sampled from the assumed binomial distributions and the indicator is calculated based on these randomly sampled proportion values. Perform 10,000 iterations.

The indicator is calculated 10,000 times forming a distribution of random samples of the indicator. From this we take the 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles to be estimates of the lower and upper limits respectively of the 95% confidence interval for the indicator.
Disclosure control: The count estimates are not based on real individuals at a local level. They are estimates based on national rates and local demography, so there is no issue of disclosure.
Rounding: The indicator is rounded to 2 decimal points.
Caveats:
This indicator gives an estimate of how many females aged 15 to 55 in the general population are expected to have a perinatal mental health condition in a given area. Prevalence estimates are based on 'diagnoses' or a combination of 'symptoms and medication' or historical diagnoses of severe mental illness recorded by a medical professional in primary care records. Therefore, the estimates do not include any possible undiagnosed conditions, self-reported mental health problems or mental health conditions recorded in other care settings

Perinatal period is defined up to 2 years post birth. This definition differs to commonly used up to 1 year post birth and it aligns the indicator with the specification for specialist perinatal mental health services in England.

This indicator is an estimate based on women in contact with primary care about their perinatal mental health and is likely to be an under-estimate for some areas. It applies the weighted prevalence from CPRD to local population of females giving birth in a year by age group and deprivation quintiles. Therefore, variation is based on demographic differences of local populations. The following caveats should be considered: Not all mothers will report their mental health problems to their GPs - evidence suggest that some ethnic groups are less likely to seek support from GPs during the perinatal period and some GPs are less likely to ask about mental health problems. Recording practices in primary care of perinatal mental health problems will vary. Only females registered with GPs are considered and some populations at higher risk of mental health problems (such as homeless women or certain migrant populations) might not be included. CPRD is a large, non-random sample and not all regions are equally represented in CPRD – weighting for region was carried out to minimise the impact. As this indicator determines pre-conception and conception date (start of the perinatal period) based on birth event, for some women with early term births this might not be accurate. This indicator relies on the medical record history covering the full perinatal period and for women to remain with the same GP until end of the period - this will exclude women who are more likely to move or change GP within the perinatal period. This indicator is calculated using a simple method based on age and deprivation - there may be other local factors which mean that actual prevalence is different from the indicator value. For example, evidence suggests that women from some ethnic minorities may experience a higher level of PMH conditions. However, ethnicity was not included in the model as there is reason to believe the data on PMH by ethnic group held in primary care may be incomplete.

Although CPRD is not regionally representative, comparison to ONS births data shows that it aligns well with females giving birth in England by age groups and deprivation deciles.

The indicator is not standardised for age. Age is an input variable in the construction of the indicator and accounts for a proportion of the variation between areas.
Notes:
The prevalence proportions of perinatal mental health condition derived from CPRD are in line with published research.

This indicator uses the following key definitions: Perinatal period - this study aligns the definition with NHS Long term Plan commitments and therefore the perinatal period is defined as starting from 1 year before birth (3 months pre-conception period and up to 9 months pregnancy) and ending 2 years after birth. Birth event - is defined as either a direct or indirect birth outcome. Direct birth outcomes are medical observations that record an actual birth event/delivery. Indirect birth outcomes are medical observations that record a procedure or process indicating a birth event/delivery. Still and premature births at 24 weeks gestation or later are included. Mental health condition - is defined based on an NICE Guidance. Prevalence - in this study is defined as recorded period prevalence based on a primary care record, where a mental health condition is identified as a prevalent case during the perinatal period.

This indicator does not delineate between first occurrence of mental health issue and a repeat occurrence for each woman. This indicator does not delineate between first or any subsequent pregnancy within the woman's record.

All code lists have undergone internal and external (by academic and clinical experts) validation.

This indicator uses a combination of diagnoses, symptoms and medication to define perinatal mental health conditions. For all mental health conditions, the majority of cases were identified as having been diagnosed during the perinatal period. However, in relation to case identification of depression, around 21% of cases were identified by a combination of symptom recording with a relevant medication (prescribed within 3 months of symptom record).

Indicator: HIV testing rate per 100,000 population
Rationale: HIV testing is integral to the treatment and management of HIV. Knowledge of HIV status increases survival rates and reduces the risk of onward transmission through aiding early diagnoses and treatment.Testing and diagnosis rates are closely linked. Therefore, this testing rate indicator serves as a valuable complement to the 'HIV diagnosis rate per 100,000' indicator.
Definition: HIV testing among people who accessed sexual health services* in England, expressed per calendar year as a rate per 100,000 population.Data is presented by patient residence, including residents in England and those with an unknown residence. Data for residents outside of England are excluded. The rate is given per the total Office for National Statistics (ONS) population.This measure includes GUMCAD (STI surveillance system) data only.* Publicly funded sexual health services providing specialist level 3 and non-specialist level 2 STI related care (including online services). Further details on the levels of sexual healthcare provision are provided in the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) Standards for the Management of STIs (Appendix B).
Data source: UK Health Security Agency
Indicator source: GUMCAD STI Surveillance System
Definition of numerator: Total number of HIV tests taken per year, across all sexual health services reporting to GUMCAD, among residents in England (and for those with an unknown residence).The number of HIV tests is derived from Episode Activity codes (SNOMED or Sexual Health and HIV Activity Property Types –SHHAPT) relating to HIV testing and diagnosis.Data is de-duplicated to ensure that only one HIV test code is allowed per 6 week period.Data represents the total number of HIV tests taken, and not the number of people tested (one person may be tested multiple times in any year).
Source of numerator: UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), GUMCAD STI Surveillance System
Definition of denominator: Total number of people living within the selected geographical area.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 100,000.
Confidence interval details: Confidence interval method: Exact PoissonA confidence interval is a range of values that is used to quantify the imprecision in the estimate of a particular indicator. Specifically, it quantifies the imprecision that results from random variation in the measurement of the indicator. A wider confidence interval shows that the indicator value presented is likely to be a less precise estimate of the true underlying value.Confidence intervals have been calculated by UKHSA using RStudio and are based on the exact Poisson method (using the stats package and poisson.test function).
Disclosure control: Numbers between 1 and 4 with an underlying population less than 10,000 are suppressed.Further details are available on the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hiv-and-sti-data-sharing-policy  page.

Caveats: The England total may include those reported with an unknown residence. Therefore, the sum of residence data by region may not equal the England total.Data represents the number of HIV tests, and not the number of people tested (one person may be tested multiple times). This means that theoretically an individual testing repeatedly through multiple services within a given year could inflate the testing rate within a given geographical area. However, the impact of this is thought to be minimal due to the scale of the population denominator and services would likely only provide testing where appropriate.A single test from an individual may be reported through online and physical service providers leading to duplication. We are unable to deduplicate these because individuals do not carry through their patient ID between the two services. However, quality checks were conducted to ensure that inflation due to double counting does not exceed 5%. Any instances exceeding this threshold are accompanied by a data quality note ‘Value may be inflated due to potential duplicate reporting between online and physical services’.Numbers reported in 2023 and 2024 may be higher than expected in the South West and Yorkshire and Humber regions due to changes in clinic software providers in these areas.Every effort is made to ensure accuracy and completeness of GUMCAD data, including web-based reporting with integrated checks on data quality. However, responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of data lies with the reporting service.Data reported in 2020 and 2021 was notably lower than previous years due to the disruption to sexual health services during the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Notes: Regions shown in the profiles are with reference to regions (ONS defined) which do not match the UKHSA regions shown in the annual HIV data tables.Data is reported based on patient residence as provided by clinics, specifying the lower tier local authority of residence.
