Indicator: Estimated prevalence of undiagnosed adult hypertension
Rationale: Hypertension is based on arbitrary cut-off points within a range of blood pressurevalues, but most national and international guidelines share a common threshold for hypertension, defined as a persistently raised blood pressure greater than or equal to a measurement of 140/90mmHg. The  https://www.longtermplan.nhs.uk/online-version/chapter-3-further-progress-on-care-quality-and-outcomes/better-care-for-major-health-conditions/cardiovascular-disease/  published in 2019 included an ambition to prevent 150,000 strokes, heart attacks and dementia cases by 2029 by improving the detection and treatment of patients with hypertension and other high risk cardiovascular conditions.Hypertension is major risk factor for cardiovascular disease and high systolic blood pressure was estimated as the second highest global risk factor for all disease burden and the leading global risk factor for cardiovascular disease, as measured by disability adjusted life years. The detection of hypertension requires an understanding of hypertension in the community where it is currently undiagnosed and therefore untreated.Estimates of undiagnosed hypertension cannot be calculated from administrative services such as healthcare systems and are reliant on population sources, such as survey samples or cohort studies with local area coverage.  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/health-survey-for-england  (HSE) is an annual survey sample with a representative sample of the England population. It is designed to estimate the proportion of people in England who have health conditions, including the prevalence hypertension, both those who have a diagnosis from a doctor and those are not diagnosed. This data can be used to support the objectives of the NHS Long Term plan for the detection of hypertension. However, due to the sample size there are no published data of undiagnosed hypertension for local areas below England level produced by the HSE.Due to the lack of direct estimates of undiagnosed hypertension at local level, modelled local estimates have been created to help support local community hypertension detection activities using a consistently measured data source taken from the HSE.
Definition: Modelled estimated prevalence of undiagnosed hypertension with blood pressure >= 140/90mmHg, for adults aged 16 years or older
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics and NHS England data
Definition of numerator:
The numerator was defined as the estimated count of people in 2021 aged 16 years or older who were not diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor or nurse and their mean blood pressure was greater than or equal to 140mmHg systolic and/or 90mmHg diastolic.
The numerators were estimated using combined HSE 2017 to 2019 weighted age group and sex proportions of undiagnosed hypertension multiplied by the age group and sex mid-year 2021 populations of local geographies and summed to total counts. This was undertaken using the following steps:

Extracting the proportions of HSE survey respondents with the HSE definition of undiagnosed hypertension by sex and 5-year age groups: 16 to 19, 20 to 24, then 5-year bands through to 80 to 84 and 85 years and older). These were the proportion of survey respondents who answered 'no' to the question of whether they had 'doctor-diagnosed' hypertension and had a mean blood pressure recorded in the HSE nurse interview greater than or equal to 140/90 mmHg. Note that individuals in the survey were weighted using HSE nurse weights before proportions were calculated. Weighting is a statistical technique used to adjust survey results to make them more accurate and representative of the population. Further detail on the calculation of HSE weights can be found in the 2019 HSE  https://files.digital.nhs.uk/24/190E9D/HSE19-Methods-rep.pdf .
Multiplying each age and sex group proportion by the mid-year population estimates in 2021 for each matching age and sex group for the geography of interest to obtain a count of people with undiagnosed hypertension by age and sex group.
Summing the total count across age and sex group to obtain the final geography estimated numerator.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Health Survey for England (HSE) and Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Definition of denominator: Mid-year population estimate for people aged 16 years and older
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: The final values for each geography were calculated by estimating the numerator (see definition) then dividing the estimated numerator by mid-year population estimates for ages 16 and over and multiplying by 100 to produce a percentage value.A  /documents/Undiagnosed_Hypertension_technical_2024.html  for the method is available.
Confidence interval details:
Uncertainty limits were applied using statistical simulation. A large number of randomly generated proportions for each age and sex group were generated, using information and assumptions about the distributions underpinning the distribution in each age and sex group.
For each age and sex group, the logit transformation was applied to the prevalence estimate from HSE (equation 1). The corresponding standard errors were estimated, based on the confidence intervals of the prevalence estimates (equation 2).Equation 1: lp = log⁡(p)/log⁡(1-p)Equation 2: ls = ((log⁡(ucl/(1-ucl) )-log⁡(lcl/(1-lcl)))/z97.5)/2
For each simulation, a random number from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1 were generated (using the Mersenne Twister algorithm) for each age and sex group. These numbers were transformed to the binomial distribution with means (lp) and standard errors (ls) estimated from the HSE data as above. These transformed numbers were randomly generated logit-transformed proportions of undiagnosed patients in each age and sex group. They were then transformed back to counts and summed across the age and sex groups (equation 3).
Equation 3: ∑(i to n) (exp⁡(lpi+zRilsi)/((1+exp⁡(lpi+zRilsi ) ) ) Ni )Where:
n = Number of age and sex groups
N = Age and sex group population
p = Age and sex group prevalence estimate from HSE
lcl = Lower 95% confidence limit for the prevalence estimate
ucl = Upper 95% confidence limit for the prevalence estimate
z97.5 = 97.5th percentile point of the standard normal distribution (≈1.96)
zR = Value of the standard normal distribution for randomly generated probability (between 0 and 1)
lp = Logit of the prevalence estimate
ls = Estimated standard error of lpA total of 10,000 simulations were undertaken for each geography. The total simulated counts for each geography were ordered and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the distribution of counts were extracted. These were then divided by the population aged 16 and older and expressed as the 95% uncertainty limits around the central estimated prevalence for each geography.
Rounding: Values have been rounded to 1 decimal place.
Caveats: Undiagnosed hypertension estimates reported by the HSE rely on a measure of self-report from survey respondents where they answer a question on whether they have ever been told by a doctor or nurse whether they had hypertension. This is referred to as 'doctor diagnosed' hypertension in the HSE, referring to self-report of the survey respondent and is not a clinical recording of hypertension from a doctor or nurse.The values presented in this indicator are synthetically constructed estimates of undiagnosed hypertension. They use the England age and sex distribution taken from a sample of the England population and apply this to the local population of interest to estimate the value. There was a total of 12,620 respondents with valid blood pressure readings aged 16 years and older in the HSE sample from 2017 to 2019. The estimates do not take into consideration other local population risk factors that may influence the numbers of people who may have hypertension and have not been diagnosed by the healthcare professional.

Indicator: Mortgage home repossessions: rate per 100,000 dwellings
Rationale:
Individuals who experience home repossessions due to mortgage defaults are at a heightened risk of developing common mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression [1]. This may be associated with losing the security of owned housing and the often transitory nature of the rented housing population [1]. Monitoring mortgage repossessions is crucial for understanding the financial stress faced by homeowners and its broader impact on mental health. This indicator provides valuable insights into economic stability and helps inform targeted interventions aimed at preventing home loss and supporting those at risk.

Data source: Ministry of Justice
Definition of numerator: The number of mortgaged homes that have been repossessed within each Local Authority area defined by post code.Local authority counts are derived from the defendant's address and in some cases this is not identified. These claims have not been included in regional or local authority level data, but are include at national level. Therefore the England figure may not match aggregations of lower levels of geographies. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/mortgage-and-landlord-possession-statistics
Source of numerator: Ministry of Justice (MoJ), Mortgage and landlord possession statistics
Definition of denominator: The total number of dwellings within an area that are owned with a mortgage or loan, as defined by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This includes only those dwellings classified as owned with mortgage or loan, excluding dwellings that are owned outright or rented or shared ownership. The total number of dwellings is based on the Census 2021 estimates that classify households in England by tenure. The Census 2021 estimates have been used as the denominator for all years.Census 2021 data on tenure of household are available from the  https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/TS054/editions/2021/versions/4 .
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census
Methodology:
The indicator for mortgaged home repossessions is calculated using data sourced from administrative records maintained by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ). This data includes the number of mortgage repossession claims registered at county courts within a specified period.
The repossession rate is calculated on a quarterly basis. The numerator is the total number of mortgage repossession claims initiated in county courts during each quarter. The denominator is the total number of dwellings within an area that are owned with a mortgage or loan, as reported by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The quarterly rates are summed to derive the annual figure.
The crude rate of mortgage repossessions is then calculated using the following formula:
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml">Repossessions per 100,000 dwellings=(Number of mortgage repossession claims/Total number of mortgaged dwellings)×100,000
Disclosure control: Local Authorities with under 5 mortgage repossessions have been suppressed.
Notes: October 2024In the October 2024 release, the methodology for this indicator was updated. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) updated the method for calculating mortgage and landlord repossession rates to improve accuracy and relevance. Previously, the total number of dwellings from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government was used as the denominator.The number of dwellings by tenure within each area is now used as the denominator. This change provides a more precise reflection of repossession rates, considering the specific tenure type rather than an overall dwelling count. This approach avoids potential overcounting of dwellings and offers a clearer insight into the specific housing situations leading to repossessions. The number of dwellings by tenure also allows for better geographical comparisons by accounting for the varried distribution of dwellings by tenure across local authorities.Further information on this change and the impact on rates of home repossessions can be found in MoJ's supporting document: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/mortgage-and-landlord-possession-statistics-april-to-june-2024/mortgage-and-landlord-possession-statistics-april-to-june-supporting-document#introduction Data prior to 2021, using the previous methodology, and statisical commentary on the rates of home repossessions can be found in MoJ's collection page: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/mortgage-and-landlord-possession-statistics

Indicator: Folic acid supplements taken before pregnancy
Rationale:
Folic acid (also known as vitamin B9) is very important for the development of a healthy foetus, as it can significantly reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida.Taking folic acid supplements before pregnancy is important because closure of the neural tube is normally complete by 4 weeks post-conception when many women may not be aware they are pregnant.

All women who could become pregnant are therefore advised to take a daily supplement of folic acid (400 µg) prior to conception and until the 12th week of pregnancy ( https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5bab98a1e5274a55e18d2c12/Folic_Acid_and_the_Prevention_of_Neural_Tube_Defects__1992_.pdf ). Folic acid supplements of 5 mg per day are recommended to prevent the occurrence of neural tube defectsin the offspring of men or women with spina bifida themselves or women with a previous pregnancy affected by NTD ( https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5bab98a1e5274a55e18d2c12/Folic_Acid_and_the_Prevention_of_Neural_Tube_Defects__1992_.pdf ). https://www.diabetes.org.uk/guide-to-diabetes/life-with-diabetes/pregnancy recommends that all women with diabetes planning a pregnancy should also take a folic acid supplement of 5mg per day. This indicator is new for 2024 and is classed as an official statistic in development. It has been derived from the Maternity Services Data Set version 2.0, which is a new data set. There may be some data completeness issues for some providers of data, this is expected to improve over time and the publication of this indicator will help to drive that improvement .

Indicator: Early access to maternity care
Rationale: The first appointment with a midwife (booking appointment) should happen before the woman is 10 weeks pregnant.A booking appointment allows scheduling of an ultrasound scan, identification of women who might need more than usual care, either because of medical history or social circumstances, for discussion of antenatal screening, taking blood pressure and measuring the woman’s height and weight, identification of risk factors such as smoking and offering support, discussion of mood and mental health. Indicator: Drinking in early pregnancy
Rationale: Modifiable risk factors in pregnancy can have health impacts on both mother and child. At the first antenatal appointment, midwives or other health professionals will ask questions and perform tests to ascertain these risks and advise on recommended actions.Alcohol is a ‘teratogen’, which means that it can affect foetal development and cause birth defects or complications during pregnancy. Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is an umbrella term for conditions that can occur in a person whose mother consumed alcohol during pregnancy. The most severe form is known as foetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). Whilst FASD is less severe than FAS, it can result in physical, mental and behavioural problems including learning disabilities which can have lifelong effects. The risk of such problems is likely to be greater the more you drink. Ref:  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5b6c5703ed915d3119112af6/alcohol_public_health_burden_evidence_review_update_2018.pdf The Chief Medical Officers’ guideline is that: If you are pregnant or think you could become pregnant, the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all, to keep risks to your baby to a minimum. Drinking in pregnancy can lead to long-term harm to the baby, with the more you drink the greater the risk.The risk of harm to the baby is likely to be low if you have drunk only small amounts of alcohol before you knew you were pregnant or during pregnancy. If you find out you are pregnant after you have drunk alcohol during early pregnancy, you should avoid further drinking. You should be aware that it is unlikely in most cases that your baby has been affected. If you are worried about alcohol use during pregnancy do talk to your doctor or midwife. Ref:  https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a80b7ed40f0b623026951db/UK_CMOs__report.pdf This indicator is new for 2024 and is classed as an official statistic in development. Indicator: Drug misuse in early pregnancy
Rationale: Modifiable risk factors in pregnancy can have health impacts on both mother and child. At the first antenatal appointment, midwives or other health professionals will ask questions and perform tests to ascertain these risks and advise on recommended actions.The effects of different drugs of misuse during pregnancy are broadly similar and are largely non-drug specific. Intra-uterine growth retardation and pre-term deliveries contribute to increased rates of low birthweight and increased perinatal mortality (1). In the UK, around 3% of stillbirths and 2% of neonatal deaths are drug misuse-related and 12% of maternal deaths 6 weeks to 1 year post pregnancy are caused by alcohol/drugs (2,3). Higher rates of early pregnancy loss and third-trimester placental abruptions appear to be major complications of maternal cocaine use. Increased rates of stillbirth, neonatal death and sudden infant death syndrome are found in women who misuse cocaine. Women who misuse heroin have a higher rate of small for gestational age (SGA) babies and pre-term delivery, even when allowing for other confounding factors. People who misuse drugs are also more likely to misuse alcohol. 18% of opiate users and 54% of non-opiate drug users in treatment also have alcohol use disorders. Alcohol can also affect foetal development and cause complications during pregnancy or birth defects, including Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). Parental drug (and alcohol) use and co-sleeping are established risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).Women who misuse drugs may not use general health services—due to guilt and fear that children’s services will be involved—until late into pregnancy and this increases the health risks for both the mother and child (4). However pregnancy may act as a strong motivation for women who misuse drugs to reduce or stop their drug use and, where appropriate, to engage in specialist drug treatment. It is important that midwives recognise this opportunity and offer non-judgemental, person-centred support and reliable information about the effect of drug use on their child(ren) to their patients.The national clinical guidelines on drug misuse and dependence and other key clinical guidance make the case for early identification and intervention (5). Women who attend drug treatment services, even those who continue to use illicit drugs, usually have better antenatal care and better general health than women who are not in treatment. Therefore, services are advised to fast-track pregnant women into drug treatment to allow for the earliest engagement possible. Outcomes in opioid-dependent pregnant women are better, both in terms of the pregnancy and the child, for women who enter opioid substitute treatment programmes during pregnancy and cease illicit drug use, than for those who do not.Engagement of partners who misuse drugs in treatment is also important to reduce any impact of the partner’s drug use on the child(ren) and family’s well-being.(1)  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drug-misuse-and-dependence-uk-guidelines-on-clinical-management (2) https://www.npeu.ox.ac.uk/assets/downloads/mbrrace-uk/reports/MBRRACE-UK%20Perinatal%20Mortality%20Surveillance%20Report%20for%20Births%20in%202017%20-%20FINAL%20Revised.pdf (3) https://www.npeu.ox.ac.uk/assets/downloads/mbrrace-uk/reports/MBRRACE-UK%20Perinatal%20Mortality%20Surveillance%20Report%20for%20Births%20in%202017%20-%20FINAL%20Revised.pdf  https://www.npeu.ox.ac.uk/assets/downloads/mbrrace-uk/reports/MBRRACE-UK%20Maternal%20Report%202019%20-%20WEB%20VERSION.pdf (4)  https://www.bmj.com/content/336/7656/1303 (5)  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg110  ;  https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241548731 This indicator is new for 2024 and is classed as an official statistic in development. Indicator: Fast food outlets per 100,000 population
Rationale:
The environment in which we live and work has positive and negative effects on our health and wellbeing. One component of the built up environment is food outlets and the choices they provide. Meals eaten outside of the home tend to be associated with higher calories, and portion sizes tend to be bigger, which can make it more challenging to eat healthily [1,2] . The neighbourhood food environment is one important modifiable determinant of dietary behaviour and obesity.[3]

The availability of fast food in our environment is one issue, within a complex system[4], which is associated with a range of negative health outcomes and contributes to the obesogenic nature of some of our neighbourhoods. Fast food is more abundantly available in the most deprived areas of England where obesity in children and adults and the associated health conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease are most prevalent.[5,6]

This indicator is designed to help users understand the number of fast food outlets in an area taking the size of the population into account. It is intended to support national policy making and influence planning activities in local authorities[7] with the aim of reducing the availability of fast food, where this is deemed desirable, in order to improve health outcomes.[1] https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sugar-reduction-programme-industry-progress-2015-to-2020 [2] https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/calorie-reduction-programme-industry-progress-2017-to-2021

[3] Dietary inequalities: What is the evidence for the effect of the neighbourhood food environment?

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1353829213001317?ref=pdf_download&fr=RR-2&rr=884266335a67642b

[4] A foresight whole systems obesity classification for the English UK biobank cohort

https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-022-12650-x

[5] The Association between Fast Food Outlets and Overweight in Adolescents Is Confounded by Neighbourhood Deprivation: A Longitudinal Analysis of the Millennium Cohort Study

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8703340/

[6] The association between the presence of fast-food outlets and BMI: the role of neighbourhood socio-economic status, healthy food outlets, and dietary factors

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35897088/

[7] No new fast-food outlets allowed! Evaluating the effect of planning policy on the local food environment in the North East of England

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35724588/
Definition: Crude rate per 100,000 population: the number of fast food outlets is divided by the population of the area and multiplied by 100,000.
Data source: OHID, based on Food Standards Agency data
Definition of numerator: <span style="line-height: 107%; mso-fareast-font-family: Calibri; mso-fareast-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-ansi-language: EN-GB; mso-fareast-language: EN-US; mso-bidi-language: AR-SA;">The numerator is a count, at a specific point in time, of fast food outlets in each geographic area. The inclusion criteria for counting fast food outlets is described in the methodology section below.
Source of numerator: Food Standards Agency (FSA), Food Hygiene Rating Scheme
Definition of denominator: Count of the population in each geographic area from Office for National Statistics (ONS) mid-year population estimates 2023.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
Crude rate per 100,000 population: the number of fast food outlets is divided by the population of the area and multiplied by 100,000.

While not all fast food is unhealthy, it is typically high in saturated fat, salt and calories. For this analysis fast food has been defined as food that is https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9002576/ and available quickly usually via a counter service and for consumption on or off the premise. It covers a range of outlets that include, but are not limited to, burger, pizza, kebab, chicken, and fish and chip shops.

The data is sourced from the Food Standards Agency (FSA) Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) data 7 February 2024. The information provided on businesses is held on behalf of local authorities participating in the national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme in England, which is all the local authorities in England.

An inclusion criteria for selecting fast food outlets has been developed to select food premises from the FHRS data that fit the definition of fast food. The FHRS data categorises food premises into business types, all premises from the ‘Takeaway/ sandwich shop’ business type have been included. Additionally, fast food outlets have been selected from other business types within the FHRS data based on the business name using the main chains and a keyword search.

The main chain name search on business name selects the largest chain outlets with a cut-off criteria of 100 outlets nationally from the following business types;restaurant/cafe/canteen, retailers, and other catering premises.

The keyword search on business name selects relevant premises from the following business types; mobile caterer, other catering premises, restaurant/café/canteen. The keywords used in the search are grill, burger, chicken, chip, fish bar, pizza, kebab, India, China, Chinese.

Lower tier local authority is assigned within the FSA FHRS data and higher geographies are assigned by OHID based on the recorded local authority.
Frequency: Published every three years. Data for the latest three years will be added at each three yearly update.
Rounding: Rates rounded to one decimal place.
Caveats:
The impact of food delivery services

In recent years there has been a large growth of food delivery services and meal delivery apps (MDAs). The food delivery companies allow customers to order food on a mobile phone application or website to be delivered to a chosen address. The availability of fast food via MDAs and websites expands the geographic coverage of fast food outlets. This makes it more likely that some customers will order food for delivery from outlets in neighbouring local authority areas, particularly in urban areas. These apps increase the potential exposure or reach of their outlets beyond the immediate resident or visiting population.

Cross local authority movements

Some people may travel in person to neighbouring local authorities to visit fast food outlets. Data which shows the fast food outlets located in an area may underestimate the exposure to fast food for the resident population. When viewing the data, users should consider the values for neighbouring local authorities to get a wider picture of the exposure to fast food for people living within the local authority of interest.

The impact of non-resident populations

It is also important to consider the impact of movements of the population for purposes such as work, shopping, entertainment or tourism. Some local authorities with larger numbers of fast food outlets per 100,000 resident population may be areas with a large non-resident workplace or visitor populations. These groups are not included in the population denominator but are potentially exposed to the outlets.Data source and methods

It is likely that the data here does not show the complete picture for fast food outlets. Many of the outlets that could be considered 'fast food' are likely to be multi-functional; sit-down and eat in, takeaway and home delivery. As a result businesses may have been recorded under the category of restaurant or café which would mean they may not have been included here despite selling similar types of food to those included in this analysis. The further inclusion based on business names will mitigate against this but some may still not be picked up. Equally, there will be outlets included in the category of ‘Takeaway/ sandwich shop’ that might not be considered ‘fast food’.

Data recorded in the FSA FHRS data is presumed to be correct but there is the potential for error in the collection, collation and data entry. The FHRS FSA dataset was not developed for the analysis of fast food and categorisation of outlets may vary between the local authorities that collect and record the data. For example, in some instances an outlet that sells sandwiches and tea and coffee might be recorded in Restaurant/Cafe/Canteen and in other areas in Takeaway/sandwich shop.

There are different possible sources of data for fast food and take aways, numbers will differ between different datasets as the definitions vary and are subject to categorisation differences. Therefore, numbers presented here may not match numbers presented elsewhere. The data presented here is a count of businesses identified as fast food outlets rather than a direct measure of access for individuals which will be affected by factors such as opening hours, price and ease of car parking or delivery options. That is it looks at the use of a premise rather than being a direct measure of access to fast food.City of LondonCity of London is an extreme outlier and is suppressed in this profile for data presentation purposes. In City of London in 2024, there were 2,406.8 fastfood outlets per 100,000 population (confidence intervals: 2151.8 to 2683.6, total count of outlets: 324).

Indicator: Hypertension patients treated to appropriate threshold
Rationale:
Blood pressure is recorded with two numbers. The systolic pressure (higher number) is the force at which the heart pumps blood around the body. The diastolic pressure (lower number) is the resistance to the blood flow in the blood vessels. They are both measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).

Following a diagnosis of hypertension, regular monitoring and a reduction of blood pressure to specific treatment thresholds is recommended, to reduce the risk of developing problems such as heart attacks or strokes. Blood pressure can be managed through lifestyle changes and/or medications. There are different treatment thresholds for blood pressure depending on a person’s age and whether they have other comorbidities such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease. This indicator only uses the treatment thresholds depending on their age and not their level of comorbidity.

The NICE hypertension guidance recommends that adults with hypertension should be reviewed every year and patients aged under 80, should have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg (or a home or ambulatory blood pressure reading under 135/85mmHg) and adults aged 80 and over a clinic blood pressure below 150/90mmHg (or if home or ambulatory blood pressure reading under 145/85mmHg).

This indicator measures two aspects of hypertension care. Firstly that regular blood pressure monitoring is taking place, and secondly that blood pressure is managed to the age appropriate treatment threshold. It combines two age dependant hypertension management indicators from CVDPREVENT (Management for patients 18 to 79 and management for patients 80+) to give a summary for all patients aged 18 and over.

This indicator is intended to inform changes in clinical practice by highlighting areas where monitoring or treatment levels vary. It measures two processes, regular blood pressure measurement and treatment to the threshold levels. Higher percentage of patients managed to threshold can represent better quality of care, lower levels can represent low levels of testing or low numbers of patients achieving the hypertension treatment thresholds. This indicator can be used to identify areas of good practice and areas for improvement.

Patients aged 79 and under <=135/85mmHg

Indicator: Patients with QRISK ≥ 20% treated with lipid lowering therapy
Rationale:

High cholesterol is when there is too much cholesterol in the blood, which can increase the risk of having a heart attack or stroke. Lipid-lowering therapy with a high-intensity statin or other lipid-lowering medication can reduce cholesterol levels and is a clinically effective treatment option for the prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD), which includes heart attack and stroke events.

 https://qrisk.org/ is a predictive tool used by medical practitioners to assess the potential risk of CVD in patients. It is only used on patients with no previous history of CVD. It calculates the likelihood of a patient having a stroke or heart attack in the next 10 years. The higher the score, the greater the risk.

NICE guidance suggests that adults with a 10-year risk of CVD of 10% or more for whom lifestyle changes are ineffective or inappropriate, are encouraged to discuss the risks and benefits of starting statin therapy with their healthcare professional.

Indicator: CKD patients with a record of monitoring ACR test
Rationale:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition where there is a gradual loss of kidney function over time, it is classified as grades G1 to G5 (G5 being the most severe). Patients with CKD have an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease.

Indicator: CKD patients treated to appropriate blood pressure threshold
Rationale:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition where there is a gradual loss of kidney function over time, it is classified as grades G1 to G5 (G5 being the most severe). Patients with CKD have an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease.

A patient with CKD should have regular urine and blood tests to find out if there is any kidney damage, how serious the condition is, whether it is getting worse and what treatments are needed to manage symptoms. A simple urine test called the urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) is performed to look for signs that protein is leaking into the urine (a condition called albuminuria or proteinuria). This is an important sign of kidney damage.

Blood pressure control is an important factor in reducing the progression of CKD, this indicator uses a specific ACR level to guide blood pressure treatment levels. Most patients with CKD will have ACR levels below 70mg/mmol.

The NICE CKD guidelines recommend that patients with CKD and an ACR level below 70mg/mmol should have their blood pressure managed to a clinic threshold of less than 140/90 mmHg (or a home or ambulatory blood pressure reading under 135/85mmHg). For patients with CKD and higher levels of albuminuria (70mg/mmol or more), a lower clinic blood pressure threshold of 130/80 mmHg (or a home or ambulatory blood pressure reading under 135/85mmHg) is recommended.

This indicator is intended to inform changes in clinical practice by highlighting areas where monitoring or treatment levels vary. It measures two processes, regular blood pressure measurement and treatment to the threshold levels. Higher percentages of patients managed to target can represent better quality of care, lower levels can represent low levels of testing or low numbers of patients achieving the blood pressure treatment thresholds. This indicator can be used to identify areas of good practice and areas for improvement.

Clinic blood pressure reading

Indicator: People with type 1 diabetes who received all 9 care process checks (including retinal screening) - Retired

These are five risk factors for further complications causing deteriorating health including body mass index measure, blood pressure check, smoking status recorded, blood tests for glucose levels (HbA1c) and a measure of cholesterol. In addition, there are four tests to identify early signs of complications including urine albumin creatinine ratio (to assess kidney risk), serum creatinine measure (an indicator for renal function), foot nerve and circulation examination, and retinal screening.
Effective control and monitoring of diabetes can reduce mortality and morbidity in this population. There are differences in the population with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, leading to a discrepancy in receiving care processes. Understanding this discrepancy at a local level is important for assessing the needs of the local population with diabetes and where improvements can be made.
Definition: The percentage of people with type 1 diabetes who have received all 9 care processes as recorded by practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) during the audit period. These care processes include a measure of body mass index, a blood pressure check, having smoking status recorded, a blood test for glucose levels (HbA1c), a measure of cholesterol, urine test for albumin, serum creatinine measure, foot check, and retinal screening. For children under 12 years of age, 'all 9 care processes' is defined as receiving HbA1c blood test only.
Data source: NHS England, National Diabetes Audit
Definition of numerator:
Total number of people with type 1 diabetes who have received all 9 care processes and are registered with a practice participating in the NDA. A person with diabetes has to receive all 9 care processes in the 15-month audit period to be included in the numerator.

Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator: Total number of people with type 1 diabetes who are registered with a practice participating in the NDA.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)

Rounding: Numerators and denominators are rounded to the nearest 5. Numerators and denominators between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5. Values were calculated from these rounded values. <div style="line-height: 20px;">
Since November 2017, providers of publicly funded health services have been  https://digital.nhs.uk/about-nhs-digital/corporate-information-and-documents/directions-and-data-provision-notices/data-provision-notices-dpns/community-services-data-set-csds-data-provision-notice . This indicator is based on CSDS and has been developed as part of the process of discontinuing the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/childrens-public-health-0-to-5-years-national-reporting  established in 2015. Once the voluntary aggregate collection ceases, CSDS will be the only source of data for the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme .Breastfeeding prevalence at 6 to 8 weeks is a well-established population indicator of early infant feeding practices and an important marker of child and maternal health. Measurement at this time point captures both initiation and continuation of breastfeeding and reflects the effectiveness of early postnatal and health visiting support, which are central components of the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme .
There is strong evidence that breastfeeding is associated with improved health outcomes for infants, including lower risk of gastro-intestinal and respiratory infections, otitis media (middle-ear infections) and hospital admission in early life. Systematic reviews in high-income settings also show associations between breastfeeding and healthier growth trajectories, including lower risk of rapid weight gain and childhood obesity ( https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/156/1/e2025071516/201741/Breastfeeding-and-Health-Outcomes-for-Infants-and ). For mothers, breastfeeding is associated with reduced risk of breast and ovarian cancers, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK605414/ ).
Improving breastfeeding prevalence has wider public health and economic benefits. UK evidence indicates that higher breastfeeding rates have the potential to reduce costs to the NHS through reduced treatment of infant infections and longer-term maternal conditions, alongside broader health system benefits. ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK605414/ ,  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35062928/ ).
National and international guidance continues to recommend exclusive breastfeeding for approximately the first six months of life, with continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods thereafter. This recommendation is endorsed by the  https://www.who.int/health-topics/breastfeeding  and is reflected in  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng247 , which emphasises the importance of sustained breastfeeding support in the early postnatal period to enable continuation beyond the first few weeks.
Within England, breastfeeding prevalence at 6 to 8 weeks aligns with the universal mandated health visitor review and local authority public health responsibilities. This indicator supports monitoring of population trends, and encourages continued prioritisation of breastfeeding support at local level.

Indicator: Mean height (cm) of 5 year old girls
Rationale:
Genetic factors have a powerful influence on the height of children and their growth though childhood, with ethnic origin being an important genetic determinant of height and growth patterns.1

Evidence from research literature suggests that around 80% of the variance in height can be attributed to genetic factors, leaving 20% explained by environmental influence.2 There are many environmental factors that influence a child’s height and growth that start in utero and continue through postnatal growth through to puberty and up to adulthood. These include maternal smoking in pregnancy, parental and other passive smoking, diet and nutrition, living conditions, childhood diseases and psychological stress.3

At a population level the environment, both home and wider society, plays a key modifiable role in child growth. Child height and growth patterns can be reflective of conditions in society; improvement or worsening of the social and economic environment can impact growth patterns in children.4

Evidence from research literature shows that obesity is associated with accelerated height gain in childhood, but then a ‘catch-down’ of reduced height gain in adolescence, and earlier onset of puberty.5-8

This indicator will enable valuable monitoring of the patterns of child height over time and across demographic and socioeconomic groups.

Definition of numerator: Sum of height z score of girls in reception year measured in the NCMP. A z score (also known as a standard deviation score) is a statistical measurement describing the distance a value is from the mean in a normal distribution, with positive values being above the mean and negative values below. The height z scores calculated for children adjust for age and sex, based on the distribution of height measurements within the British 1990 (UK90) growth reference. This helps improve the comparability of data between geographic areas and over time as children’s height changes with age the use of the height z score rather than actual height values will adjust for any small differences in the age of children within and across measurement years.

Definition of denominator: Count of girls in reception year measured in the NCMP

Methodology:
The National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) collects height and weight measurements of children primarily in mainstream state-maintained schools in England. Since the proportion of records from independent and special schools is low and varies each year, analysis of NCMP data by NHS England and DHSC excludes such records to ensure consistency over time.

This indicator is calculated by summing the height z scores of all girls in reception (aged 4 to 5 years) and dividing by the count of girls measured.

The mean height z score is converted to the equivalent height in centimetres of a child aged exactly 5 years and 0 days as this is a more meaningful measure. The https://www.healthforallchildren.com/shop-base/shop/software/lmsgrowth/ is used to convert the z score to centimetres, LMSgrowth uses VBA functions to convert physical measurements to standard deviation scores (SDS) and vice versa based on a specified growth reference; for this analysis the UK90 growth reference was used. The UK90 growth reference centile curves show the distribution of a measurement (e.g. height, weight, BMI) as it changes according to age and sex. The LMS method summarises the changing distribution by three curves representing the median (M), coefficient of variation (S) and skewness (L), the latter expressed as a Box-Cox power. The L, M and S values are used to calculate z scores adjusted for the sex and age at measurement for a child, and can also be used to calculate the measurement from the z score. For population monitoring purposes, a child’s BMI is classed as overweight or obese where it is on or above the 85th centile or 95th centile, respectively, based on the UK90 growth reference data. Some of the variation seen between geographic areas is likely to be due to differences in the number of children across ethnic groups in the population.
Local authority and region geographies are derived from the postcode of child residence; only children with valid geographic coding (postcode of residence) have been included in the analysis. All records are included in the calculation of values for England. The proportion of records with such coding has increased over the years of the NCMP. In 2006/07 (the first year of the NCMP) around 57% of child records included valid postcode of residence. This increased to 95% in 2007/08, and to over 99% in 2008/09 and subsequent years. The participation rate in Torbay was very low (51.7% in Reception and 38.2% in Year 6) due to the use of an opt-in system of data collection, this resulted in poor validity in the prevalence data. Data from Torbay and Hinckley and Bosworth are included in the aggregated values for higher geographies i.e. County, Region and England.
Impact of COVID-19:
The 2019/20 NCMP data collection stopped in March 2020 when schools were closed due to the coronavirus COVID-19 pandemic. In a usual NCMP collection year, national participation rates are around 95% (over a million) of all eligible children, however in 2019/20 the number of children measured was around 75% of previous years. Despite the lower than usual number of measurements, analysis by NHS England indicates that figures at national and regional level are directly comparable to previous years, for all breakdowns. The data at local authority level and below are not as robust because of the fewer measurements than usual. Therefore, the local authority figures have been split into three levels: a. reliable – coverage of greater than 75% b. fit for publication but interpret with caution – coverage of between 25% and 75%, these areas have the following data quality flag ‘Interpret with caution - see Notes section in Definitions for details’ c. unreliable, suppressed (not published) – coverage of less than 25%, data for these areas is not shown in the Profile and has the following data quality flag ‘Value suppressed due to incompleteness of source data’ The reliability indicator calculations for the data presented in the Obesity Profile are available to download in a spreadsheet for each local authority by school year. More information on the data quality assessment of the 2019/20 data is available in the NHS England annual report, appendices, and data quality statement. The start of the 2020/21 NCMP data collection was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic response. In March 2021 local authorities were asked to collect a representative 10% sample of data because it was not feasible to expect a full NCMP collection so late into the academic year. This sample has enabled national and regional estimates of children’s weight status (including obesity prevalence) for 2020 to 2021 and contributes towards assessing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on children’s physical health. As the final sample was not fully representative of the child population, weighting was applied to the analysis to adjust for under or over representation of demographic and socioeconomic groups and make it comparable to previous years of NCMP data. More information about the weighting of data is available in the methodology and data quality chapter of the NHS England NCMP 2020 to 2021 annual report.

The 2021/22 NCMP was the first data collection since the COVID-19 pandemic that was unaffected by school closures and other public health measures. Over 1.17 million children were measured in which is 92% of all children that were eligible to take part. This participation rate, though high, is lower than pre-pandemic years where participation had been at 95% since the data collection in 2014 to 2015. This is likely to be due to resourcing issues within some local authorities during the pandemic recovery process. From the 2022 to 2023 NCMP onwards data collection was unaffected by issues linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Rationale:
Genetic factors have a powerful influence on the height of children and their growth though childhood, with ethnic origin being an important genetic determinant of height and growth patterns.1 Evidence from research literature suggests that around 80% of the variance in height can be attributed to genetic factors, leaving 20% explained by environmental influence.2 There are many environmental factors that influence a child’s height and growth that start in utero and continue through postnatal growth through to puberty and up to adulthood. These include maternal smoking in pregnancy, parental and other passive smoking, diet and nutrition, living conditions, childhood diseases and psychological stress.3 At a population level the environment, both home and wider society, plays a key modifiable role in child growth. Child height and growth patterns can be reflective of conditions in society; improvement or worsening of the social and economic environment can impact growth patterns in children.4 Evidence from research literature shows that obesity is associated with accelerated height gain in childhood, but then a ‘catch-down’ of reduced height gain in adolescence, and earlier onset of puberty.5-8 This indicator will enable valuable monitoring of the patterns of child height over time and across demographic and socioeconomic groups. Indicator: Year 6 prevalence of short stature (height <2nd centile)
Rationale:
Genetic factors have a powerful influence on the height of children and their growth though childhood, with ethnic origin being an important genetic determinant of height and growth patterns.1 Evidence from research literature suggests that around 80% of the variance in height can be attributed to genetic factors, leaving 20% explained by environmental influence.2 There are many environmental factors that influence a child’s height and growth that start in utero and continue through postnatal growth through to puberty and up to adulthood. These include maternal smoking in pregnancy, parental and other passive smoking, diet and nutrition, living conditions, childhood diseases and psychological stress.3 At a population level the environment, both home and wider society, plays a key modifiable role in child growth. Child height and growth patterns can be reflective of conditions in society; improvement or worsening of the social and economic environment can impact growth patterns in children.4 Linear growth is an important indicator of a child’s health. Poor growth in early childhood is associated with impaired physical, neurodevelopmental, and educational outcomes and can increase the risk of chronic disease and premature mortality later in life.5-7 This indicator will enable valuable monitoring of the patterns of short stature in children over time and across demographic and socioeconomic groups. Indicator: Percentage of population from an ethnic minority background.
Rationale: The population who consider themselves from an ethnic minority background has increased between the 2011 and 2021 Census, both in terms of number and proportion, in most areas in England. This makes it an important social and health care policy issue in terms of service delivery, developing to assess the needs of different population groups and meeting statutory obligations relating to ethnicity and equality.
Definition: The percentage of people stating they were from an ethnic minority background in the 2021 Census as a percentage of the total number of respondents to the census question.
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Census 2021.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census
Definition of denominator: Total population answering the ethnic category question as per the 2021 census returns.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census
Frequency: This indicator is census based so is not updated routinely.
Disclosure control:
ONS will sometimes make changes to data if it is possible to identify individuals. This is known as statistical disclosure control. In Census 2021, ONS:

  • Swapped records (targeted record swapping), for example, if a household was likely to be identified in datasets because it has unusual characteristics, ONS swapped the record with a similar one from a nearby small area. Very unusual households could be swapped with one in a nearby local authority.
  • Added small changes to some counts (cell key perturbation), for example, ONS might change a count of four to a three or a five. This might make small differences between geographies depending on how the data are broken down when perturbation applied.
Notes: The question about the ethnic group people feel they belong to is self-identified and is subjectively meaningful to the person answering the question. This means that how a person chooses to identify can change over time.The person response rate for Census 2021 was 97% of the usual resident population of England and Wales, and over 88% in all local authorities.

Indicator: Infants who have received a new birth review, CSDS-based (Official Statistics in Development)
Rationale:
Since November 2017, providers of publicly funded health services have been  https://digital.nhs.uk/about-nhs-digital/corporate-information-and-documents/directions-and-data-provision-notices/data-provision-notices-dpns/community-services-data-set-csds-data-provision-notice . This indicator is based on CSDS and has been developed as part of the process of discontinuing the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/childrens-public-health-0-to-5-years-national-reporting  established in 2015. Once the voluntary aggregate collection ceases, CSDS will be the only source of data for the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme .The new birth health and development review is one of the five mandated universal contacts delivered by health visiting teams as part of the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme in England. The HCP is the national framework for improving child health and wellbeing through prevention, early identification of need, and early intervention, with delivery aligned to the principle of proportionate universalism to help reduce inequalities in outcomes.
 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/delivery-of-the-healthy-child-programme/part-2-health-visiting-ages-0-to-5  identifies the antenatal, new birth, and 6 to 8 week health and development reviews as particularly important early contacts, and recommends the home as the most appropriate setting for these reviews. The new birth review, delivered when the baby is around 10 to 14 days old, supports continuity of care following transfer from midwifery services, enables health visitors to establish an early relationship with the family, and provides an opportunity for early identification of risks to infant health, parental wellbeing, and safeguarding that may not be apparent in other settings. The review typically includes assessment of the infant’s health and feeding, discussion of safe sleeping and infant care practices, consideration of parental mental health and wellbeing, and identification of any additional support needs, with appropriate follow-up or referral where concerns are identified.
The immediate postnatal period is a critical time for infant health, parental adjustment, and establishing patterns of care and support. Universal health visiting services aim to ensure that all families receive core preventative support at this early stage, while enabling additional and targeted input for families with greater need.Evidence indicates that mandated health visiting contacts have near-universal reach and form an important infrastructure for identifying vulnerability and providing early, proportionate support, including for families experiencing adversity. Policy and academic literature emphasise the role of health visiting in recognising adverse childhood experiences, supporting parental capacity, and mitigating risks through timely intervention, even where direct causal links to long-term outcomes cannot always be quantified. ( https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736%2824%2902065-8/fulltext , https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/90153/html/ , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12723622/ )
Monitoring coverage of the mandated new birth review provides an important measure of access to a core component of the HCP. Variation in coverage may indicate barriers to service delivery or access and may contribute to missed opportunities for early identification of need and support. This indicator supports local authorities and partners to assess delivery of the HCP, inform commissioning and service planning, and identify potential inequalities in access to early years support.

Indicator: Obesity prevalence in adults, (using measured height and weight)
Rationale:
Obesity is a global and complex public health concern. It is associated withreduced life expectancy and is a risk factorfor a range of chronic diseases, includingcardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes,at least 12 kinds of cancer,liver, andrespiratorydisease,and can also impact onmental health. The risk and severity of these diseases increases with a higher body mass index (BMI).The proportion of adults in England living with obesity has seen large increases in the last four decades. Analysis of data from the1980 National Heights and Weights Surveyestimates that the prevalence of obesity in England stood at 6% of men and 9% of women aged 16 and over with 0.1% of men and 0.4% of women living with severe obesity. In 1993 theHealth Survey for England reported that the prevalence of obesity among men and women in this age group was 13% and 16% respectively which has increased to 29% of men and 31% of women in 2024.

Understanding the data, the trends and patterns enables us to make the case for national and local action, which includes policy and approaches to create health promoting environments; healthier food and activity options; social marketing campaigns to support behaviour change; and to work with partners to design and tailor approaches to meet needs of particular groups of people.

This indicator uses data from the Health Survey for England (HSE) which collects measured height and weight of survey participants and provides the best available estimates of population level obesity prevalence for England and the regions. The HSE does not provide local level data, therefore data from the Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS) is used for local authority level indicators (with regional and national level comparators) as it provides routine, robust data for BMI calculations which will support local monitoring of obesity estimates.

The ALAS local authority level indicators for overweight (including obesity) and obesity prevalence are available in the https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/national-child-measurement-programme/data#page/0/gid/1938133368/pat/15/par/E92000001/ati/502/are/E09000002/iid/93881/age/168/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1 .

Definition of numerator: Number of adults aged 16+ years with valid height and weight measurements classified as living with obesity. Adults are defined as living with obesity if their body mass index (BMI) is greater than or equal to 30kg/m².
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Health Survey for England (HSE)
Definition of denominator: Number of adults aged 16+ with valid height and weight measurements.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Health Survey for England (HSE)
Methodology: The data for this indicator has been sourced directly from NHS England Health Survey for England (HSE) data tables, these tables and the report along with HSE methods and survey documentation are available on the NHS England website.
Frequency: The data is updated annually.
Confidence interval details:
England data uses published confidence intervals provided with the HSE data. The confidence intervals have been calculated for the observed regional data using Byar’s Method. These have then been adjusted using the design effect factors published by ONS for the England data and applied to the standardised regional estimates.

Further information on confidence intervals is available in the HSE methods report https://files.digital.nhs.uk/6C/753EC3/Health%20Survey%20for%20England%202022%2C%20Methods.pdf

Full details of fieldwork processes can be found in the https://files.digital.nhs.uk/6C/753EC3/Health%20Survey%20for%20England%202022%2C%20Methods.pdf .

The England and regional data for this indicator will be different to the data on obesity prevalence using Active Lives Adult Survey (ALAS) data. The ALAS data uses self-reported height and weight for adults aged 18 and over and as adults tend to underestimate their weight and overestimate their height when providing self-reported measurements the analysis adjusts the data to give estimates of the likely actual height and weight values.

However, this only gives estimated height and weight values so the best indicator of obesity prevalence for adults at a national and regional level comes from the Health Survey for England (HSE), which uses physical measurements of height and weight to calculate body mass index (BMI). However, the survey sample size is not sufficient to produce robust estimates at local level. The ALAS data is currently the best source for local authority data and is widely used to help inform local action to improve the health of the population now and into the future.

The England and regional level data from the HSE has been added to feed into the https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/health-trends-in-england/England/overview.html .

The data collection for the 2020 HSE was stopped in March 2020 and no data was published for that year and the 2021 HSE data largely contains self-reported heights and weights due to pandemic related restrictions in place at the time.

Therefore 2021 data is not comparable with previous years and therefore not included in this indicator. More details of the data collection in 2021 can be found in the HSE 2021 Methods report.

The 2022 Health Survey for England saw a return to face-to-face interviewer visits following disruption to the survey methodology during the pandemic, and there remained an option for remote interviews if required.

Indicator: Loneliness: Percentage of adults who feel lonely often or always
Rationale:
Feeling lonely frequently is linked to early deaths and its health impact is thought to be on a par with other public health priorities like obesity or smoking[1]. Lonely people are more likely to be readmitted to hospital or have a longer stay and there is also evidence that lonely people are more likely to visit a General Practitioner or Accident and Emergency and more likely to enter local authority funded residential care[2]. At work, higher loneliness among employees is associated with poorer performance on tasks and in a team, while social interaction at work has been linked to increased productivity[3].

The government’s work to tackle loneliness currently focuses on reducing the stigma associated with loneliness; supporting organisations across society to take action; and improving the evidence base on loneliness, including understanding rates of loneliness in England. This builds on work which began in 2018 in response to the 2017 Jo Cox Commission on Loneliness, which was co-chaired by Rachel Reeves. This work is led by the Minister for Tackling Loneliness, Stephanie Peacock, as part of her wider role as Minister for Civil Society, with input from other departments that have a key role to play in building a more connected society, including the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC).

Loneliness is defined as : “a subjective, unwelcome feeling of lack or loss of companionship. It happens when we have a mismatch between the quantity and quality of social relationships that we have, and those that we want.” This is a definition first suggested by Perlman and Peplau in 1981[4]

Loneliness can affect us all, at any time of our lives, with a negative impact on community and individual wellbeing. When people feel lonely most or all of the time, this is referred to as chronic loneliness. Chronic loneliness can have a serious impact on an individual’s well being, and their ability to function in society.

The loneliness evidence base has grown exponentially over the last 5 years and we now understand more about the prevalence and impact of chronic loneliness within different demographics. However, more research is needed to understand the root causes of chronic loneliness and what works to tackle it.

That is why it is important to continue including a loneliness measure in the PHOF. This will tell us what percentage of a population is chronically lonely and help us understand the characteristics of chronically lonely people, in order to inform and focus future work on loneliness at both a national and local level, providing a focus to support strategic leadership, policy decisions and service commissioning. When reporting the prevalence of loneliness, ONS advise using the responses from the direct question, “How often do you feel lonely?”. The measure is designed to show the percentage of a population that is chronically lonely (respondents who answer ‘Often or Always’). The measure is designed for all adults, however research is currently underway to determine if bespoke measures are required to accurately measure loneliness within demographics.

[1] Holt-Lunstad, J. et al. (2015) Loneliness and Social Isolation as Risk Factors for Mortality: A MetaAnalytic Review.

[2] Social Finance (2015) Investing to tackle loneliness - a discussion paper.

[3] Ozcelik, H., & Barsade, S. (2011) Work loneliness and employee performance. In Academy of management proceedings Vol. 2011, No. 1, pp. 1-6. Briarcliff Manor, NY 10510: Academy of Management.

[4] Perlman D and Peplau LA (1981) 'Toward a Social Psychology of Loneliness', which can be found in Gilmour R and Duck S (editors) (1981), Personal relationships. 3, Personal relationships in disorder, London: Academic Press, pages 31 to 56.

Indicator: Prevalence of type 1 diabetes among practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit
Rationale:
Diabetes is a lifelong condition that causes a person's blood sugar level to become too high. There are two main types of diabetes:

type 1 diabetes – where the body's immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin
type 2 diabetes – where the body does not produce enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to insulin

Type 1 and type 2 diabetes have different risk factors and management.
Diagnosing diabetes and recording it on GP registers may mean that a patient is more likely to be reviewed or investigated further and if appropriate, offered ongoing lifestyle advice, monitoring, and treatment, in accordance with National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance.
This indicator is intended to inform changes in clinical practice by highlighting areas where prevalence varies. Variation in recorded prevalence may indicate differences in case ascertainment.
Definition: Percentage of people with GP recorded type 1 diabetes mellitus, among practices that participate in the National Diabetes Audit (NDA).
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Definition of numerator: Total number of people of all ages registered with type 1 diabetes among practices that participate in the National Diabetes Audit.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator:
Total number of people of all ages registered with practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit.
Practices were mapped to geographies according to the mapping used for NDA registrations data for a given audit period.
Patient totals were taken from the month following the end of the audit period. For example, for 2022-23 data, list sizes for April 2023 were used as the denominators for all practices.
For 2023: Patients Registered at a GP Practice -  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice/april-2023  was used.
For patient registrations at other times in the year (or in previous years), please visit the  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice .
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), Patients registered at a GP practice
Methodology: Numerator divided by denominator multiplied by 100.
Rounding: Numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Numerators between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5. Values were calculated from these rounded counts. Because of this, values for areas with small denominators should be treated with caution, as rounding has a larger impact on the calculated percentage.
Caveats:
While there are similarities in the data reported by the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) indicator for diabetes prevalence, there are key differences between this and the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) data. NDA data report for all ages, whereas QOF data is reported for those aged 17 and over. While QOF data is reported for all types of diabetes combined, NDA data is split into ‘Type 1’ and ‘Type 2 and other’. Because of the differences however the total of ‘Type 1’ and ‘Type 2 and other’ will not match the registrations reported by QOF.
A number of people with diabetes are excluded if they are not registered with a GP practice at the time of collection. While information on children is captured by the NDA extraction of primary care data, information is not collected from paediatric specialist units. Where data for children with diabetes is only available through this route (and not through primary care or adult specialist services), they will not be included in this indicator. Therefore, there are some children with type 1 diabetes missing from the data used for this indicator. Instead, this data is currently only collected as part of the National Paediatric Diabetes Audit. Data from the audit shows that there were around 30,600 children and young people registered with type 1 diabetes in England in 2022-23. The majority of which were aged 14 or under. It is not possible to determine how many are missing from the Core NDA data used here.
In addition, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance changes through adolescent years and GPs are not incentivised to record diabetes data for those under the age of 17.
The participation of GP practices in the audit has varied over time. Over recent years, the participation rate has been around 98% of GP practices in England. Recent years of data are a very good representation of the care and treatment of people with diabetes. However, there is some variation in the participation rate between areas. These data should be treated with caution when comparing between years and should be considered in conjunction with participation rates.
There is a very small proportion of missingness in recording of age and sex for patients reported in the NDA data (0.1% or less for all areas). Because of this, these patients will be missing in the data available for inequalities.As of 2023-24, the NDA began reporting data from detained facilities. As the number of registered patients for these faciltities is not reported from NHS Digital as with other GP practices, no denominator was available. Therefore, this registrations are excluded from the numerator. Only England was impacted by this.
Where practices have a list size of less than 750, values are not reported.
Further details of the data quality for previous years are available here: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-diabetes-audit/report-1-care-processes-and-treatment-targets-2021-22-full-report/data-quality-statement-copy
Notes: The NDA includes data recorded about all people of all ages with diagnosed diabetes in England and Wales before the audit period end date. Included are people with all types of diabetes mellitus, with the exclusion of gestational diabetes, impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG). The audit integrates data from both primary and secondary care sources. The information collected from GP practices for the audit is individual level data and contains demographic information such as age, sex, ethnicity, diabetes duration and geographic variables - equivalent data is collected from secondary care settings.

Indicator: Percentage of adults who abstain from drinking alcohol
Rationale:
The health risks associated with drinking alcohol include accidents, injuries, cancer, heart disease and reduced life expectancy. These risks tend to increase with higher consumption.Since 2016, UK guidelines have focused on regular weekly consumption, with the recommendation that men and women should not normally consume more than 14 units of alcohol a week, and that this should include some days where no alcohol is drunk. This indicator shows the proportion of the adult population who are at no direct risk of alcohol-related harm from their current consumption behaviour.

Measures of usual weekly consumption are presented in line with the https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/545937/UK_CMOs__report.pdf

  • lower risk (up to 14 units for men and women)
  • increasing risk (above 14 and up to 50 units for men, above 14 and up to 35 units for women)
  • higher risk (above 50 units a week for men, above 35 units for women) There is often a lag between alcohol consumption and alcohol-related harms, particularly for chronic conditions where the lag can be many years. Some individuals who currently abstain from alcohol or drink at low risk might have drunk at risky levels in the past and hence remain at risk of developing alcohol-related conditions.
Definition: Percentage of adults who abstain from alcohol based on average weekly alcohol consumption.

Disclosure control: The HSE is a sample survey and hence it's not possible to identify specific individuals.

Simple Definition: Percentage of people aged 16 and over whose consumption puts them at higher risk of alcohol-related harm

Indicator: Possible alcohol dependence according to AUDIT
Rationale:
The health risks associated with drinking alcohol include accidents, injuries, cancer, heart disease and reduced life expectancy. These risks tend to increase with higher consumption.

The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) is a questionnaire used to assess problem drinking in the Health Survey for England (HSE). AUDIT is widely considered to be the best screening tool for detecting problematic alcohol use. It comprises ten indicators of problem drinking: three indicators of consumption, four of use of alcohol considered harmful to oneself or others, and three of physical dependency on alcohol. In addition to alcohol consumption, the AUDIT questionnaire includes questions measuring the social impact of alcohol consumption, harm caused by excessive drinking and whether friends or health professionals have suggested a need to cut down.In line with the World Health Organisation (WHO) guidelines on using the test, responses to each of the ten AUDIT questions in HSE were assigned values of between 0 and 4, and a total score between 0 and 40 was calculated. Categories for interpreting AUDIT scores were applied as follows: 0-7: 'Low risk drinking behaviour', 8-15: 'Increasing risk drinking behaviour', 16-19: 'Higher risk drinking behaviour', 20+: 'Possible alcohol dependence'.This indicator concerns the category '20+: possible alcohol dependence' only.The questionnaire, scoring and interpretation guidelines can be found https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6357a7af8fa8f557d85b7c44/Alcohol-use-disorders-identification-test-AUDIT_for-print.pdf .

Indicator: Regular e-cigarette users, 15 year olds
Rationale:
Vaping (consumption of e-cigarettes) is substantially less harmful than smoking because they do not contain tobacco, and therefore can be an effective tool in supporting smoking cessation. Vaping is already estimated to contribute to an extra 50,000 to 70,000 smoking quits per yearin England. Ensuring that vapes continue to be available to current adult smokers is vital to reducing smoking rates.However, the long-term health impacts of vaping are unknown, and the nicotine contained within them can be highly addictive, with withdrawal sometimes causing anxiety, trouble concentrating and headaches.Legislation came into force in England and Wales on 1 October 2015, introducing a minimum age of sale of 18 for e-cigarettes and prohibiting the purchase of these products on behalf of someone under the age of 18. However, the Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) reportUse of e-cigarettes among young people in Great Britainshows that the number of children using vapes has tripled in the past 3 years with 20.5% of children in Great Britain having tried vaping in 2023.

Due to nicotine content and the unknown long-term harms, vaping carries risks to health and lifelong addiction for children. The health advice is clear: young people and those who have never smoked should not vape. The UK Government has a duty to protect children from the potential harms associated with underage vaping while their lungs and brains are still developing. Encouraging children to use a product designed for adults to quit smoking and then addicting them is not acceptable ( https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/stopping-the-start-our-new-plan-to-create-a-smokefree-generation/stopping-the-start-our-new-plan-to-create-a-smokefree-generation ).
