Caveats: SDD participants are aged between 11 and 15. For each survey, around 1 in 7 secondary schools in England is randomly chosen to take part. Nearly every type of school with pupils in years 7 to 11 is eligible for selection, and only very small schools and special schools are excluded.In 2023 the survey was administered online for the first time, instead of paper-based surveys as in previous years. <span style="text-align: justify;">Designed to make the study easier for schools<span style="text-align: justify;"> to administer, the online survey approach is also easier for students to complete as they are automatically routed to sections that are relevant to them, rather than having to follow complex routing instructions, which in turn improves data quality. An additional benefit of automatic routing is that it reduces the survey length; in this case to less than 30 minutes, compared to 40-50 minutes for the paper version.<span style="text-align: justify;">Further information about the background to and development of the SDD, along with survey questionnaire is available on the NHS England website:  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/areas-of-interest/public-health/smoking-drinking-and-drug-use-among-young-people-in-england Since the survey began in 1982, school response rates have declined. 2023 was the first year since 1999 where the response rate increased. Indicator: Estimated prevalence of diagnosed and undiagnosed type 2 diabetes
Rationale:
Diabetes is a lifelong condition that causes a person's blood sugar level to become too high. There are two main types of diabetes:

type 1 diabetes – where the body's immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin
type 2 diabetes – where the body does not produce enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to insulin.

The NHS Long Term Plan published in 2019 included an ambition to prevent 150,000 strokes, heart attacks and dementia cases by 2029 by improving the detection and treatment of patients with high-risk conditions. This includes improving effectiveness of the NHS Health Check as well as supporting access to weight management services for people with type 2 diabetes and committing to expanding the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and Path to Remission Programme.
There are policy and epidemiological reasons to focus on type 2 diabetes prevalence only. The risk factors for developing type 2 diabetes are well understood. Additionally, as type 2 diabetes is preventable with many risk factors being modifiable, understanding the risk for type 2 diabetes in the local population specifically can support prevention activity. Early detection and diagnosis of type 2 diabetes can help delay or prevent disease progression. Understanding the numbers of people with type 2 diabetes supports local areas to understand the potential scale of the population who are at greater risk of complications including heart attacks, strokes and other microvascular and macrovascular events.
Healthcare professionals and commissioners can use these estimates to help plan service use for people with diabetes, alongside these other sources. These can be used to support work on whether testing, coding or both need to be improved in an area, based on the level of risk estimated to be in the population.
The  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/health-survey-for-england  includes data on diagnosed and undiagnosed (total) diabetes prevalence for England, based on a combination of survey respondent self-reported diagnosis and blood glucose (HbA1c) measurement, using a representative sample of the population. However, there are no estimates of total diabetes for local areas below England level due to the sample size available.
Therefore, the HSE data has been used to model estimates of the diagnosed and undiagnosed type 2 diabetes prevalence at a local level, based on the risk profile of local populations.
Definition:
Modelled estimated prevalence of diagnosed and undiagnosed type 2 diabetes for people aged 16 years and over.
Diagnosed diabetes is defined as self-reported doctor diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
Undiagnosed diabetes is defined as having a HbA1c reading of greater than or equal to 48mmol/mol and did not self-report having a diabetes diagnosis.
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics and NHS England data
Definition of numerator:
The numerator was defined as the estimated count of people in 2021 aged 16 years and over who self-reported being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by a doctor or nurse or they had a HbA1c reading of greater than or equal to 48mmol/mol and did not report having diagnosed diabetes.
The numerators were estimated using combined HSE 2015 to 2018 data.
This was undertaken using the following steps:

Identifying participants of HSE survey respondents with the HSE definition of diagnosed or undiagnosed type 2 diabetes aged 16 and over with a valid HbA1c reading. These were grouped by sex, 6 age groups (16 to 34, then 10-year bands through to 75 years and older), 3 ethnic groups (White-Mixed-Other, Black, and Asian) and area deprivation quintile (based on the Index of Multiple Deprivation quintile of their residence).
A multivariate complex samples logistic regression model that included sex, age group, ethnic group, and area deprivation demonstrated that each of these variables significantly contributed to the prediction of whether someone had type 2 diabetes or not. The adjusted probability of having type 2 diabetes for all distinct groupings of predictor variables was generated.
For each geographical area, the probability was then multiplied by the size of the sub-population.
Resulting numbers were summed across all groups to give the estimated number of people with type 2 diabetes for each area.

A  /documents/dmt2prev_technical2025.html  for more information about the method is available.
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on NHS England (NHSE) and Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Definition of denominator:
Denominators were generated from a combination of data sources for resident populations. Using record-level 2021 Census data, a bespoke dataset of usual resident counts for those aged 16 years and over and stratified by sex, age, ethnic group, and area deprivation quintile was extracted using the  https://integrateddataservice.gov.uk/ . These were grouped by sex, 6 age groups (16 to 34, then 10-year bands through to 75 years and older), 3 ethnic groups (White-Mixed-Other, Black, and Asian) and area deprivation quintile (based on the Index of Multiple Deprivation quintile of their residence). These were extracted for all local areas required and England.
ONS mid-year population estimates for 2021 were extracted at Lower Super Output Area 2021 (LSOA) level and aggregated by age, sex, and area deprivation quintile to higher geographies. The corresponding proportional split by ethnic groups from the Census data was applied to the mid-year population estimates stratified by each age, sex, and area deprivation quintile grouping. The final denominator is the sum of these estimates across the stated geography.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Methodology: The final values for each geography were calculated by estimating the numerator (see definition) then dividing the estimated numerator by estimated population denominator (see definition) for ages 16 and over and multiplying by 100.
Confidence interval details:
Uncertainty limits were calculated using statistical simulation. A large number of randomly generated proportions for each age, sex, ethnic group and IMD quintile grouping were generated for each grouping of the predictor variables.
For each grouping, the logit transformation is applied to the probability from the model (equation 1). The corresponding standard errors are estimated, based on the confidence intervals of the probabilities calculated using robust standard errors (equation 2).
Equation 1: lp = log⁡(p)/log⁡(1-p)
Equation 2: ls = ((log⁡(ucl/(1-ucl) )-log⁡(lcl/(1-lcl)))/z97.5)/2
For each simulation, a random number from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1 is generated (using the Mersenne Twister algorithm) for each grouping. These numbers were transformed to the binomial distribution with means (lp) and standard errors (ls) estimated from the HSE data as above. These transformed numbers were randomly generated logit-transformed probability of people in each grouping. They were then transformed back to counts and summed across all groupings (equation 3).
Equation 3: ∑(i to n) (exp⁡(lpi+zRilsi)/((1+exp⁡(lpi+zRilsi ) ) ) Ni )
Where:
n = Number of groupings
N = Grouping population
p = Grouping probability estimate from model
lcl = Lower 95% confidence limit for the probability
ucl = Upper 95% confidence limit for the probability
z97.5 = 97.5th percentile point of the standard normal distribution (≈1.96)
zR = Value of the standard normal distribution for randomly generated probability (between 0 and 1)
lp = Logit of the probability
A total of 10,000 simulations were undertaken for each geography. The total simulated counts for each geography were ordered and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the distribution of counts were extracted. These were then divided by the population aged 16 and older and expressed as the 95% uncertainty limits around the central estimated percentage prevalence for each geography.
Disclosure control: The statistical disclosure control applied to extracted 2021 Census data causing suppression of small cells (<10) means a small amount of population data was lost in this process. This was minimised where possible by testing of different group combinations for age and ethnicity to reduce the number of small cells whilst maintaining model performance. There was a total of around 15,000 residents across all counties and unitary authorities in England suppressed due to small counts. Larger geographies were impacted less by this.
Rounding: Numerators and denominators have been rounded to the nearest whole number.
Caveats:
The data to assess undiagnosed diabetes uses only a single measure of HbA1c from the Health Survey for England (HSE). This differs to the recommended criteria set out by NICE, of two confirmed tests above the recommended threshold. Therefore, this can only be seen as indicative of an individual having diabetes and would not meet the diagnostic criteria. Data for blood glucose available in HSE is only recorded for HbA1c, however diabetes can also be diagnosed with fasting plasma glucose readings instead.
Any participants with missing values for sex, age, ethnic group and area deprivation were excluded from the multivariate analyses (0.07% of available sample), giving an unweighted sample size of 14,915 aged over 16 with a valid HbA1c reading for this analysis.
Due to the need for population denominators which can break down by all groupings used in the analysis, the estimates do not take into consideration other population risk factors that are known to influence the risk of having type 2 diabetes (either diagnosed or undiagnosed). For more information, please see the technical document.
Where possible, people with type 1 or gestational diabetes were excluded from this outcome variable. There were a small number of participants that reported having diagnosed diabetes that also reported not knowing their type. To resolve these cases, those with diabetes diagnosed at 40 or younger were assumed to not have type 2 diabetes and those diagnosed aged over 40 were assumed to have type 2 diabetes. It was also assumed that people with HbA1c in the diabetic range but were not diagnosed had undiagnosed type 2 diabetes, and not another form of diabetes. This is consistent with previous methodology used by ONS. It is possible that people with rarer forms of diabetes not captured by the survey are still included in this outcome variable.(1)For more information and data on type 1 diabetes please see the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/diabetes-ft/supporting-information/resources  page.
Comparisons with other published sources should be done with caution due to discrepancies between these and the prevalence estimates. Existing sources, such as the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) and the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) both report GP-recorded diagnoses of diabetes. This only includes those who have had their HbA1c tested and registered with diabetes. The QOF reports all diabetes for those aged 17 and over. The NDA reports registration for all ages and includes counts for type 2 diabetes specifically but also other rarer forms of diabetes (excluding gestational diabetes). The Fingertips indicator ‘Prevalence of type 2 diabetes among practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit’ uses the latter. Because of this, it is based on GP practice registered populations, whereas the prevalence estimates are based on resident populations. The HSE data is based on a resident population and Census 2021 data was determined to be the most robust estimate of ethnic group population denominators, and this is based on place of residence. Therefore, it was chosen to base the estimates on resident population denominators.
The HSE data used for modelling type 2 diabetes prevalence was collected between 2015 and 2018. Multiple years of data were included to allow for an appropriate sample size for analysis. However, this data may not represent the current picture of diabetes prevalence in England in 2021. Due to more recent HSE data not being available and issues with comparability of relevant variables, the data used here was the most recent available to use for this analysis.
Prevalence estimates are not provided for Isles of Scilly or City of London local authorities. This is because the population of those area is too small to allow for robust estimates. Instead, these areas have been combined with Cornwall and Hackney respectively.

Indicator: Mortality rate from pancreatic cancer, all ages
Rationale: https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/pancreatic-cancer  states that, in the UK, pancreatic cancer is the 10th most common cancer, yet is the 5th most common cause of cancer death, and in 2017 to 2019, it accounted for 6% of cancer deaths. Pancreatic cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Doctors don't know what causes most pancreatic cancers, but there are factors that may increase your risk of developing it, including tobacco use, being overweight/obese, getting older, genetic factors and chronic pancreatitis, which is often caused by long term drinking of alcohol. This indicator monitors progress in reducing the number of deaths from this cause.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate from pancreatic cancer, per 100,000 population, for all ages
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths from pancreatic cancer (classified by underlying cause of death recorded as ICD-10 code C25) registered in the respective calendar years, in people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9,…, 90+).Numbers of deaths may have been adjusted using comparability ratios. More information on comparability ratios is available in the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Mortality/Comparability_ratios.html .
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area. This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
Frequency: The data will be updated annually
Caveats: Please note data may not match published Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures due to differences in the version of postcode lookup used and the application of comparability ratios in Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) data

Indicator: Emergency admissions for gastroenteritis (0 to 4 years)
Rationale: This indicator can be used to monitor success in treatment outside hospital of types of childhood gastroenteritis that have limited morbidity or need for hospital-based care, and low mortality. This could be through better management of infections and better support for young parents in the management of illnesses in the home. It also can be used to monitor the success of preventative measure such as encouraging breastfeeding, better diet and hygiene.Treatment and prevention interventions could take the form of providing support as well as facilitating access to health advice and therapy through the NHS.
Definition: Crude rate of emergency admissions for gastroenteritis in children aged 0 to 4 years per 10,000 population.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England and Office for National Statistics data
Definition of numerator: Number of emergency admissions for children aged 0 to 4 years for gastroenteritis, as defined within the codes A020, A04, A05, A072, A080, A081, A083, A084, A085, A09, K520, K521, K522, K528, K529 in the primary diagnosis position.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Admitted Patient Care (APC)
Definition of denominator: ONS, Mid-year population estimates: single year of age and sex for local authorities in England and Wales; estimated resident population (aged 0 to 4 years)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Crude rate: the numerator is divided by the denominator and multiplied by 10,000.
Disclosure control: New data added from March 2020 onwards is subject to new HES disclosure rules - all sub-national counts are rounded to the nearest 5, and counts of 1-7 are suppressed. Rates are calculated using rounded counts, and confidence intervals are calculated using unrounded counts. For previous data counts 1-5 were suppressed.
Caveats:
NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust in 2023 to 2024. The Trust reported a large proportion of missing values in the sex field between October 2023 and March 2024. NHS England identified a data quality issue affecting University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust in 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025. Indicator: Hospital admissions for drug-related mental and behavioural disorders
Rationale:
Drug misuse is a contributing factor to hospital admissions and deaths, and is estimated to cost the NHS nearly £1 billion per year [1] and society almost £20 billion annually [2]. Beyond the financial toll, the human cost is immeasurable, leading to countless lost and shattered lives. Drug dependence often co-exists with other health disparities, like poor mental health and homelessness, making it a complex public health challenge.The government's 10-year drug strategy [2] outlines an ambitious plan to address drug abuse not merely as a law enforcement issue but a complex societal challenge that requires coordinated efforts across health, social care, and justice systems. This indicator plays a key role in supporting this ambition by enabling the monitoring of drug-related hospital admissions at both local and national levels, providing essential insights to inform targeted interventions.

While drug-related hospital admissions serve as an indicator of need, they also reflect how well local treatment and support services are functioning. Strong local drug and alcohol services, including harm reduction initiatives and community-based treatment programmes, can help manage drug misuse more effectively and prevent unnecessary hospital admissions. Early intervention, accessible treatment pathways, and integrated support across healthcare and social services are vital in reducing the burden of drug-related harm. Tackling harmful drug use remains a key priority for the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, ensuring that individuals receive the necessary support before their condition escalates to the point of requiring hospital care.

[1] Understanding organised crime

https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5c780c25e5274a0ecbe9a231/understanding-organised-crime-mar16-horr103-2nd.pdf

[2] From harm to hope: A 10-year drugs plan to cut crime and save lives

https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/from-harm-to-hope-a-10-year-drugs-plan-to-cut-crime-and-save-lives/from-harm-to-hope-a-10-year-drugs-plan-to-cut-crime-and-save-lives
Definition: Hospital admissions with a primary diagnosis of drug-related mental and behavioural disorders. Directly age standardised rate per 100,000 population (standardised to the European standard population).
Data source: OHID, based on multiple sources
Definition of numerator: The numerator includes NHS Finished Admission Episodes with a primary diagnosis of drug-related mental and behavioral disorders (ICD-10 codes F11-F16, F18, F19). This covers hospital admissions for individuals residing in England as well as those with no fixed abode.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)
Definition of denominator: The denominator consists of population estimates from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) mid-year population estimates, providing the baseline population for rate calculation.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
A Directly Standardised Rate (DSR) adjusts for differences in population age structures, allowing for fair comparisons between different areas or time periods. It is calculated by applying age-specific rates from the study population to a standard population (in this case, the European standard population).
The numerator consists of NHS Finished Admission Episodes where the primary diagnosis is a drug-related mental and behavioral disorder (ICD-10 codes F11-F16, F18, F19), including admissions for residents of England and individuals with no fixed abode.
The denominator is derived from ONS mid-year population estimates.
Both numerator and denominator were aggregated by five-year age groups (0-4, 5-9, ..., 85-89, 90+ years) and sex for each area of residence. Directly standardized rates per 100,000 population were then calculated, using the European standard population as the reference.
The resulting rate is expressed per 100,000 population, standardised to account for age distribution differences.
Disclosure control: Data has been suppressed in line with the latest HES suppression methodology in order that individuals can’t be identified in the data. This means that in LA tables, the number of admissions have been rounded to the nearest 5, with small numbers between 1 and 7 suppressed. Age standardised rates have been rounded to the nearest whole number.
Rounding: All rates rounded to the nearest whole number.
Caveats:
Mental health providers have historically submitted to both HES and to the Mental Health Services Data Set (MHSDS). To reduce the burden on these providers it was decided that while they are mandated to submit to MHSDS they are not also required to submit the same activity to HES. Some providers who previously submitted to HES have now stopped doing so. As a result, the data published in this indicator is impacted; the exact impact has not yet been quantified.There is also likely to be some effect on the data in relation to data from 2020/2021 onwards, due to the coronavirus illness (COVID-19) disruption. It is known that many hospitals reported zero or significantly less activity from March 2020 onwards.
While NHS England has yet to quantify [1] the impact of reporting changes, our initial investigation shows a decline in admissions for this indicator, from 7,025 in 2019/20 to 4,299 in 2022/23 - a reduction of approximately 39%. However, it remains challenging to determine the exact contribution of each factor at this stage. We anticipate that the impact of mental health reporting changes is minimal, but further analysis is needed to fully understand the drivers behind this trend.
[1]  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-public-health/2023
Notes:
Please note that admissions do not represent the number of in-patients, as a person may have more than one admission within a year. This indicator does not also include outpatient activity as the quality of diagnosis codes are not sufficient to be sure the activity carried out was related to drug misuse.
Where the observed total number of admissions is less than 10, the rates have been suppressed as there are too few admissions to calculate directly standardised rates reliably. The cut-off has been reduced from 25, following research commissioned by PHE and in preparation for publication which shows DSRs and their confidence intervals are robust whenever the count is at least 10.

Indicator: Percentage of reception children remaining overweight (including obesity) in year 6
Rationale:
There is concern about the rise of childhood obesity and the implications of obesity persisting into adulthood. The risk of obesity in adulthood and risk of future obesity-related ill health are greater as children get older. Studies tracking child obesity into adulthood have found that the probability of children who are overweight or living with obesity becoming overweight or living with obesity as adults increases with age.[1,2,3]

Data published by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) shows that at a national level in England most children who start primary school (in reception, age 4 to 5 years) with a healthy weight retain this healthy weight status until the end of primary school (in year 6, age 10 to 11 years). However, the flow of children from a healthy to an unhealthy weight (underweight, overweight or living with obesity) was larger than the flow of children from an unhealthy to a healthy weight. This is reflected in the increase in obesity prevalence seen between reception and year 6. Additionally, clear demographic and geographic inequalities across England are evident in the change of BMI category of children during the primary school years; children living in more deprived areas and children from some ethnic groups are less likely to remain a healthy weight compared to the national average. [4,5]

These indicators provide local authority level estimates, with regional and national comparators, examining how child BMI category changes between reception (age 4 to 5 years) and year 6 (age 10 to 11 years) to support local public health action on prevention and reduction of child obesity.

The health consequences of childhood obesity include: increased blood lipids, glucose intolerance, Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, increases in liver enzymes associated with fatty liver, exacerbation of conditions such as asthma and psychological problems such as social isolation, low self-esteem, teasing and bullying.

The National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence have produced guidelines to tackle obesity in adults and children -Obesity: the prevention, identification, assessment and management of overweight and obesity in adults and children.The 2025 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-health-plan-for-england-fit-for-the-future set out plans to raise the healthiest generation of children through a range of initiatives including decisive action on the obesity crisis.

2 Serdula MK, Ivery D, Coates RJ, Freedman DS, Williamson DF, Byers T. Do obese children become obese adults? A review of the literature. Preventative Medicine 1993;22:167-77.

3 Starc G, Strel J. Tracking excess weight and obesity from childhood to young adulthood: a 12-year prospective cohort study in Slovenia. Public Health Nutrition 2011;14:49-55.

4 Office for Health Improvement and Disparities 2022. https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/changes-in-the-weight-status-of-children-between-the-first-and-final-years-of-primary-school .

5 Office for Health Improvement and Disparities 2025. Changes in the body mass index (BMI) category of children between the first and final years of primary school, 2023 to 2024.
Definition:
The National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) measures the height and weight of children in reception (age 4 to 5 years) and year 6 (age 10 to 11 years) in primary schools in England. The measurements taken at these two time points are linked for individual children to help understand how body mass index (BMI) tracks through childhood.

This indicator uses 3 years of NCMP data combined and shows the proportion of children classified as overweight or living with obesity when they were first measured in reception (aged 4 to 5 years) who were also overweight or living with obesity when they were subsequently measured in year 6 (age 10 to 11 years). The time period shown for the indicator covers the years that the children were measured in year 6.

Clinical body mass index (BMI) thresholds, recommended for use when assessing individual children, were used to assign children to a BMI category as the analysis tracks individual children. Therefore, proportions of children within each BMI category will be different to published population level prevalence estimates, shown elsewhere in this profile, that use the population monitoring BMI thresholds. The population monitoring cut offs for overweight and obesity (85th and 95th centiles respectively) are lower than the clinical cut offs (91st and 98th centiles for overweight and obesity) used to assess individual children; this is to capture children in the population in the clinical overweight or obesity BMI categories and those who are at high risk of moving into the clinical overweight or clinical obesity categories. This helps ensure that adequate services are planned and delivered for treatment and prevention of obesity.
Data source: Department of Health and Social Care, National Child Measurement Programme
Indicator source: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC)/ NHS England
Definition of numerator: Number of children measured in year 6 (age 10 to 11 years) who were classified as overweight or living with obesity (BMI greater than the 91st centile of the UK90 growth reference) and had a linked measurement in reception (age 4 to 5 years) which was also classified as overweight or living with obesity (BMI greater than the 91st centile of the UK90 growth reference).
Source of numerator: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP)
Definition of denominator: Number of children measured in year 6 (age 10 to 11 years) who had a linked measurement in reception (age 4 to 5 years) which was classified as overweight or living with obesity (BMI greater than the 91st centile of the UK90 growth reference).
Source of denominator: Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP)
Methodology:
The National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) collects height and weight measurements of children primarily in mainstream state-maintained schools in England. Since the proportion of records from independent and special schools is low and varies each year, analysis of NCMP data by NHS England and DHSC excludes such records to ensure consistency over time.

Record matching of NCMP measurements taken at reception and year 6 time points was completed by NHS England using NHS number and date of birth, or surname, forename, postcode, sex and date of birth where NHS number is not available. NHS England provides a linking file which allows OHID to link NCMP data without receiving any of the listed personal identifiable data items.

The indicator is calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and then multiplying by 100 to produce the percentage.
Frequency: This indicator uses three years of data combined; the next update is expected in 2029 to include children measured in year 6 in academic years ending 2025, 2026, and 2028. The 2020/21 NCMP data is not included in this analysis (see further information in the Impact of COVID-19 section). Following the 2029 publication, data will be updated with a new set of three year data every three years.
Disclosure control:
City of London totals have been included with Hackney and Isles of Scilly totals with Cornwall UA to prevent potential disclosure of individuals.

Any value based on a numerator that is 7 or less is suppressed. Any sub-national statistics require the numerators and dominators to be rounded to the nearest 5. The prevalence rates and data quality indicators for all sub-national geographies are calculated using these rounded values. Confidence intervals are calculated on the unrounded numerators and dominators.Further information on this method of disclosure control is available from NHS England.
Caveats:
A https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/announcements/changes-in-the-weight-status-of-children-between-the-first-and-final-years-of-primary-school-a-longitudinal-cohort-analysis-of-data-from-the-national--2 has been published alongside these indicators showing, for each local authority, the number of records included in the analysis from each measurement year and the proportion of records that have been linked. Overall, for England 85% of the child reception year records (from academic years ending 2016, 2017 and 2018) were matched to a year 6 measurement record (from academic years ending 2022, 2023 and 2024). This information relating to data matching should be considered when examining differences between local authorities and comparisons of local authority data to region and England data, as variation in these indicators may explain some of the different patterns in the data.It is important to note that areas with lower proportions of children remaining overweight (including obesity) still see a large increase in prevalence of overweight and obesity between reception and year 6.

Though these indicators group overweight children and those living with obesity, some children may have moved between these groups between their reception and year 6 measurements. A decrease in BMI centile from living with obesity to overweight is a positive change, but children in this category remain at higher risk of living with obesity in adulthood and associated future ill health.

Movements from and to underweight between reception and year 6 have not been included in the local authority data due to very small numbers in these groupings and consequently too many data points requiring suppression to avoid individual identification. Patterns of movement from and to underweight can be examined at England level in the national report.

NCMP data is of very high quality, however there is some potential for error in the collection, collation and interpretation of the data (bias may be introduced due to poor response rates and selective opt out of children with a high BMI for age/sex which it is not possible to control for).There is not a good measure of response bias and the degree of selective opt out, but participation rates (the proportion of eligible school children who were measured) may provide a reasonable proxy; the higher the participation rate, the less chance there is for selective opt out, though this is not a perfect method of assessment. Participation rates in each year of the NCMP for each local authority are available in theNCMP Data Quality topicof this profile.

Participation in the NCMP has been consistently high; since 2010/11 between 93% and 95% of eligible children have been measured each year (with the exception 2019/20 and 2020/21 due to the COVID-19 pandemic). Therefore, the potential errors described above will have had minimal impact on the data collection.
Notes:
Data linkage in the national NCMP data set of measurement records of individual children has been possible since 2013, this enabled the first linkage of measurements between reception and year 6 to take place in 2019/20 when children who were in reception in 2013/14 reached year 6. Subsequently reception and year 6 measurement data has been linked between the following measurement years:

  • reception in 2015/16 and year 6 in 2021/22
  • reception in 2016/17 and year 6 in 2022/23
  • reception in 2017/18 and year 6 in 2023/24

    These indicators combine the latest 3 years of linked data (shown in the bullet points directly above) to enable a large enough sample at local authority level to produce reliable estimates.

    Local authority and region geographies and deprivation quintile/decile are derived from the postcode of child residence in the reception measurement record. Where postcode of child resident in reception is missing the year 6 value is used, where both are missing the school postcode is used.

    Ethnicity recorded in year 6 is used as it was the most recently recorded. If the ethnicity in year 6 was not stated or missing, then the ethnicity from reception is used.

    As child BMI category is defined using sex specific growth charts, records were removed from the analysis where the sex at birth recorded for a child was different between reception and year 6.

    2017/18 data matched to 2023/24 data for Torbay, and Hinckley and Bosworth local authorities have not been included in this tool due to data quality issues. The participation rate in Torbay was very low (51.7% in Reception and 38.2% in Year 6) due to the use of an opt-in system of data collection, this resulted in poor validity in the prevalence data. Data errors in height measurement were identified in data for children measured in Hinckley and Bosworth local authority. Data from Torbay and Hinckley and Bosworth are only included in the aggregated values for higher geographies: county, region and England.
Impact of COVID-19:
The start of the 2020/21 NCMP data collection was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic response. In March 2021 local authorities were asked to collect a representative 10% sample of data because it was not feasible to expect a full NCMP collection so late into the academic year. This sample enabled national and regional estimates of children’s weight status (including obesity prevalence) for 2020 to 2021 and contributes towards assessing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on children’s physical health. However, as only a relatively small sample of children were measured in 2020/21 this data is not included in the analysis linking reception and year 6 measurements.

The 2021/22 NCMP was the first data collection since the COVID-19 pandemic that was unaffected by school closures and other public health measures. Over 1.17 million children were measured in which is 92% of all children that were eligible to take part. This participation rate, though high, is lower than pre-pandemic years where participation had been at 95% since the data collection in 2014 to 2015. This is likely to be due to resourcing issues within some local authorities during the pandemic recovery process.

From the 2022 to 2023 NCMP onwards data collection was unaffected by issues linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Co-morbid mental health and MSK conditions have serious implications, affecting people’s motivation and ability to self-manage and adapt healthy behaviours, such as exercising. For example, depression can make pain feel worse, the person is less likely to self-manage resulting in poorer health behaviours such as reduced physical activity, and some medications taken for mental health conditions can have impact on weight gain and the development of MSK conditions.
Delivery of care is often built around the individual conditions, rather than the way the person experiences them collectively. Definition:
The odds of those with a long-term musculoskeletal condition also having a mental health condition compared with those with no musculoskeletal condition.
The definition of "long-term" is a condition lasting or expected to last 12 months or more.

Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (based on the GP Patient Survey, NHS England)
Definition of numerator: See methodology.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: See methodology.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology:
The value is presented as an odds ratio. An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an event. The OR represents the odds that an event will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the event occurring in the absence of that exposure. This is calculated as:
Event Yes No Exposure Yes a b No c d Odds Ratio = odds of the event in the exposed group / odds of the event in the non-exposed group Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d)which can be simplified toOdds Ratio = ad/bc This odds ratio represents the likelihood of those with a long-term musculoskeletal condition also having a mental health condition compared with those with no musculoskeletal condition. The odds ratio for this indicator represents the odds that an event (having a mental health condition) will occur in the presence of a certain exposure (having a musculoskeletal health condition), compared to the odds of the same event (having a mental health condition) occurring in the absence of the exposure (not having a musculoskeletal health condition). The odds of the event in the exposed group is: The number of people who reported having a mental health condition and a musculoskeletal health condition (a) divided by the number of people who did not report having a mental health condition but did report having a musculoskeletal health condition (b). The odds in the event in non-exposed group is: The number of people who reported having a mental health condition but did not report having a musculoskeletal condition (c) divided by the number of people who did not report having a mental health condition or musculoskeletal healthcondition (d). This is illustrated by:
Mental health condition Yes No Musculoskeletal health condition Yes a b No c d

Patients were asked the following question regarding long-term conditions:

Which, if any, of the following long-term conditions do you have?

A long-term musculoskeletal condition was indicated by the response – “Joint problems, such as arthritis”.

A long-term mental health condition was indicated by the response – “A mental health condition”. The Odds Ratio was calculated by: Odds Ratio= (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc The sample is restricted to respondents age 16+ years, with a valid response to the question "Which of the following long-term health conditions do you have...". Participants were excluded if their local authority of residence was invalid or outside of England. The number of respondents has been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights consider survey design and non-responserates. Weights are calibrated to population counts by GP practice as well as population counts by age and gender by CCG. Full details on weighting within the GP Patient Survey can be found at https://www.gp-patient.co.uk/surveysandreports
Confidence interval details:
Confidence intervals are calculated as follows:lower 95% CI = e^( ln(OR) - 1.96 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d))upper 95% CI = e^( ln(OR) + 1.96 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d))

lower 99.8% CI = e^( ln(OR) – 3.09 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d))upper 99.8% CI = e^( ln(OR) + 3.09 √ (1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d)) where:OR = odds ratio a = reported a long-term mental health condition and long-term MSK conditionb = did not report a long-term mental health conditionbut did report a long-term MSK conditionc = reported a long-term mental health condition but did not report a long-term MSK conditiond = reported no long-term mental health condition and no long-term MSK conditiona to d are weighted counts
Disclosure control: Odds ratios calculated with values under 10 in categories a, b, c or d (as described in methodology) have been suppressed.
Rounding: Odds displayed to 1 decimal place but no further rounding is applied during the calculation.
Caveats:
These data have not been age-standardised and, therefore, variation between area values may be a result of differences in population structure.
Small sample sizes may cause fluctuations for smaller geographical areas, which should be interpreted with caution.
Notes: An odds ratio of 1 represents no difference between long-term mental health condition prevalence rates in the two groups. If the 95% confidence intervals overlap 1, we can say with 95% confidence that there is no significant difference in the prevalence of mental health conditions between the groups.The long-term condiitons question was changed in the 2024 GP Patient Survey, meaning this indicator is not comparable with the trend displayed for93742. Indicator: Proportion of records with an NHS number in the NCMP
Rationale:
The National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) is an annual programnme that measures the height and weight of children in reception (age 4 to 5 years) and year 6 (age 10 to 11 years) in state maintained primary schools in England. The data is used to monitor patterns and trends in the prevalence of overweight and obesity.Data on participation in the NCMP and data quality indicators are included to support interpretation of the prevalence and child body mass index (BMI) tracking indicators and help drive improvements in data quality. Data quality is monitored by the NCMP national and regional teams in the Department of Health and Social Care so work can be done with local authorities to make improvements.
Collection of child NHS number was included in the NCMP from 2013 to 2014 to enable linkage of records within the NCMP and with other data sources. The proportion of records with an NHS number has improved considerably across England since 2013 to 2014 where 61.5% of records had an NHS number to over 90% in 2023 to 2024.

Although collection of NHS number is now high nationally, there continues to be variation between local authorities with some having low completion. NHS number is the primary variable used to link individual child measurement records in the NCMP from a child's measurement in reception (aged 4 to 5 years) to their subsequent measurement in year 6 (aged 10 to 11 years). Where a low proportion of records are linked within a local authority it may not be possible to publish reliable data for the area. Further information on linkage of records in the NCMP is available in the report  https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/changes-in-the-body-mass-index-bmi-category-of-children-between-the-first-and-final-years-of-primary-school-2023-to-2024 .
Definition: Proportion of records with an NHS number in the National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP)
Data source: NHS England, National Child Measurement Programme
Definition of numerator: Number of records with an NHS number
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP)
Definition of denominator: Number of children measured by the NCMP
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP)
Methodology: The indicator is calculated by dividing the numerator by the denominator and then multiplying by 100 to produce the percentage.
Frequency: Annual measurements during academic year. Data published in the final quarter of the calendar year.
Disclosure control: City of London totals have been included with Hackney and Isles of Scilly totals with Cornwall UA to prevent potential disclosure of individuals.Any value based on a numerator that is 7 or less is suppressed. Any sub-national statistics require the numerators and denominators to be rounded to the nearest 5. The prevalence rates and data quality indicators for all sub-national geographies are calculated using these rounded values. Further information on this method of disclosure control is available from  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/find-data-and-publications/statement-of-administrative-sources/methodological-changes/changes-to-the-national-child-measurement-programme-2019-20-publication-content-and-disclosure-control-methodology
Rounding: The numerators and denominators for sub-national statistics have been rounded to the nearest 5 for disclosure control (see above in the Disclosure control section for more information).
Caveats: The data presented only includes children participating in the NCMP in state maintained schools, any measurements taken at independent and special schools are excluded from the analysis.
Notes: Local authority geographies are assigned based on the local authority submitting the data. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) publish the reasons provided by local authorities why they have low percentages of NHS numbers in the NCMP annual report. [we will add link once known]
Impact of COVID-19:
The 2019/20 NCMP data collection stopped in March 2020 when schools were closed due to the coronavirus COVID-19 pandemic. In a usual NCMP collection year, national participation rates are around 95% (over a million) of all eligible children, however in 2019/20 the number of children measured was around 75% of previous years. Participation rates are not calculated for the 2019/20, instead data is available on the coverage by each local authority showing the proportion of children measured in 2019/20 compared to the average of those measured in the three previous measurement years. More information on the data quality assessment of the 2019/20 data is available in the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-child-measurement-programme/2019-20-school-year

The start of the 2020/21 NCMP data collection was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic response. In March 2021 local authorities were asked to collect a representative 10% sample of data because it was not feasible to expect a full NCMP collection so late into the academic year. This sample has enabled national and regional estimates of childrens weight status (including obesity prevalence) for 2020 to 2021 and contributes towards assessing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on childrens physical health. As the final sample was not fully representative of the child population, weighting was applied to the analysis to adjust for under or over representation of demographic and socioeconomic groups and make it comparable to previous years of NCMP data. More information about the weighting of data is available in the methodology and https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-child-measurement-programme/england-provisional-2021-22-school-year-outputs/data-quality .

The 2021 to 2022 NCMP was the first data collection since the COVID-19 pandemic that was unaffected by school closures and other public health measures. Over 1.17 million children were measured in which is 92% of all children that were eligible to take part. This participation rate, though high, is lower than pre-pandemic years where participation had been at 95% since the data collection in 2014 to 2015. This is likely to be due to resourcing issues within some local authorities during the pandemic recovery process.

From the 2022 to 2023 NCMP onwards data collection was unaffected by issues linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Indicator: Economic inactivity due to long term illness or disability
Rationale:
“Reversing the increase in economic inactivity caused by ill health is a national priority” https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/get-britain-working-white-paper

In England in 2025 to 2026, an estimated 2.0 million people aged 16 to 64 were economically inactive due to long term sickness, which represented more than a quarter of all those economically inactive.

Economically inactive people are those not in employment who have not been seeking work within the last four weeks and/or are unable to start work within the next two weeks.

The main economically inactive groups are students, people looking after family and home, long term sick and disabled, temporarily sick and disabled, retired people and discouraged workers.

People who are economically inactive due to long term illness or disability are likely to face multiple barriers in returning to the labour market. Most have several long-term health conditions and no recent work history. They are also more likely (than the population as a whole) to have no qualifications, and some may also face other complex disadvantages, including homelessness, drug or alcohol addiction and contact with the criminal justice system.

This indicator provides further understanding of economic inactivity, to supplement data published by Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) as part of https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/the-employment-of-disabled-people . The DWP statistics provide an estimate of the number of people by reason for economic inactivity (Table EIA023).

Summary estimates of https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peoplenotinwork/economicinactivity/datasets/economicinactivitybyreasonseasonallyadjustedinac01sa are also published regularly by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The summary ONS estimates report the number of people economically inactive due to long-term sickness as a percentage of those economically inactive.

This indicator uses the same estimates of the number of economically inactive due to long term sickness as DWP and ONS, expressed as a percentage of the total working age population rather than only those that are economically inactive. Using the total population as the denominator means that the indicator values are not affected by changes in the number of people who are economically inactive for other reasons.

This indicator is calculated as a directly standardised proportion, presented as a percentage. The use of directly standardised proportions makes it easier to compare populations with different age structures. It allows for more consistent comparisons of labour market trends across different regions and time periods.
Definition: The number of people economically inactive due to long term illness or disability as a directly standardised proportion of the working age population (aged 16 to 64 years)
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Annual Population Survey (APS)
Definition of numerator:
Weighted number of persons aged 16-64 years who were economically inactive due to long term illness or disability from the Annual Population Survey.

The main reason for economic inactivity is derived from a series of questions relating to why the respondent is not in current employment.

Long term illness or disability is self reported and is defined as any physical or mental health conditions or illnesses lasting or expecting to last 12 months or more.

The number of respondents has been weighted with a derived population weight in order to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights take into account survey design and non-response.

For further information see the weighting the LFS sample using population estimates section of the Labour Force user guide.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS)
Definition of denominator:
Weighted number of respondents aged 16 to 64 years from the Annual Population Survey.

The number of respondents has been weighted with a derived population weight in order to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights take into account survey design and non-response.

For further information see the https://doc.ukdataservice.ac.uk/doc/9307/mrdoc/pdf/lfs_user_guide_vol1_background_2024.pdf#page70 section of the Labour Force user guide.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual Population Survey (APS)
Methodology:
The age specific proportions from the survey are used to calculate directly standardised proportions which are presented as percentages. This is the weighted number of respondents aged 16 to 64 who were economically inactive due to long term illness or disability divided by the weighted number of respondents aged 16 to 64, standardised to the European Standard Population, multiplied by 100.

The directly standardised proportion is calculated by summing the product of the age specific proportions in the survey population and the corresponding age specific proportions in the European Standard Population, then dividing by the sum of the standard population's age specific proportions.

Age specific proportions were calculated for 5 year age bands. The 16 to 19 age group is only 4 years and doesn’t match the standard 15 to 19 age group. The standard population total for the 15 to 19 age group was multiplied by 0.8 to provide an estimated standard age group.
Confidence interval details:
Wilson Method for Stratified Sample [1]

Unweighted data has been used to produce approximate confidence intervals for stratified proportions, which are then applied to the weighted directly standardised value.

The weighted data was not appropriate to use, as the values have been scaled up to the whole population and would provide a misleading level of certainty to the estimates.

The following process was used to calculate the confidence intervals from the Wilson Method for Stratified Sample:

  • Calculate the directly standardised proportions using weighted data and use these as the values
  • Calculate the directly standardised proportions with confidence intervals using unweighted data
  • Divide the unweighted upper and lower confidence limits by the unweighted values
  • Multiply the (divided) confidence limits by the weighted directly standardised values [1] Yan X, Su XG (2010). Stratified Wilson and Newcombe Confidence Intervals for Multiple Binomial Proportions. Statistics in Biopharmaceutical Research, 2, 329-335.
Caveats: This indicator reports the main reason for economic inactivity; this means that the number of people that are economically inactive due to long term illness or disability may be under represented if their long term illness or disabilitywas not the main reason for inactivity. Whilst long term illness or disability may be their main reason, there may be other reasons such as being a carer or student that contribute to their economic inactivity status.This indicator only reports on those that were long term ill or disabled and does not include those that were temporarily sick or disabled.Long term illness or disability is self reported and is defined as any physical or mental health conditions or illnesses lasting or expecting to last 12 months or more.
Notes:
The reported region of residence is used to assign respondents to a region rather than the region of work.

This indicator is related to the economic inactivity rate indicator but is not directly comparable, as the economic inactivity due to long term illness or disability indicator is presented as a directly standardised proportion rather than a crude proportion.
Simple Name: Economic inactivity due to long term illness or disability
Simple Definition: The percentage of people aged 16 to 64 who are economically inactive (neither in employment nor unemployed) due to long term illness or disability

Indicator: Mortality rate for deaths involving chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, all ages
Rationale: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the name given to a range of lung conditions which can cause breathing difficulties. In many people with COPD, the underlying cause of death is related to co-existing conditions such as cardiovascular disease and cancer. The condition cannot be cured or reversed, but there is well established evidence that healthcare and public health interventions reduce disease progression and mortality in people with COPD. This indicator shows mortality from COPD in all causes of deaths fields (all cause of death fields including the underlying cause of death). Looking at all deaths that involved COPD, in comparison with deaths that were due to COPD, allows us to understand better the role COPD plays in mortality from other conditions given its association with comorbidities.
Definition: Directly age-standardised mortality rate for deaths involving chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, per 100,000 population, for all ages
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics data
Indicator source: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths involving chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (classified by underlying cause of death or mention of death on death certificate recorded as ICD-10 codes J40 to J44) registered in the respective calendar years, in people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9,…, 90+)
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Annual mortality extract (produced for OHID)
Definition of denominator: For single years: Population for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+) For three-year rolling averages: Population-years (aggregated populations for the three years) for people of all ages, aggregated into quinary age bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9, …, 90+)
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Numerator data for each age band are divided by the denominator population data for each age band respectively to give age specific death rates for the area. These age specific rates are multiplied by the standard population for each age group respectively and aggregated across all the age groups to give the age adjusted count of deaths for the area. This age adjusted count of deaths is divided by the total standard population for the whole age range included in the indicator, and multiplied by 100,000 to give the age standardised mortality rate for the area.
Frequency: The data will be updated annually
Caveats: Please note data may not match published Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures due to differences in the version of postcode lookup used in Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) data
Notes: Population estimates produced by the Office for National Statistics for mid-2022 and mid-2023 have been revised, to account for updated estimates of international migration for England and Wales. Data for England, regions, local authorities, ICBs, NHS regions and local authority-based deprivation deciles covering the 2022 and 2023 period have been revised to use the revised population estimates. The resultant revisions to rates are very small and do not introduce any meaningful changes to results previously presented. Data for LSOA deprivation deciles will be revised in a future profile update.Data have been presented as single years and also three-year rolling averages. This is to allow users to monitor effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. Data for this indicator have local authority data presented with three-year rolling averages only. This is to enable consistency across all the mortality indicators and to avoid presenting indicators will high levels of suppression.Where the observed total number of deaths is less than 10, the rates have been suppressed as there are too few deaths to calculate directly standardised rates reliably.This indicator replaces indicator 93643 - mortality rate from COPD as a contributory cause, which has not been updated since deaths registered in 2020.

This indicator does not show a similar drop, suggesting that COVID-19 was considered the underlying cause of death on a proportion of deaths that would have been COPD.

Indicator: Model-based estimated prevalence of severe mental illness
Rationale:
Mental health is a priority for the 10 Year Health Plan for England [1]. The plan includes commitments to create dedicated Mental Health Emergency Departments, and to expand Mental Health Support teams in schools and colleges. As part of this work, severe mental illness (SMI) has been identified as an early priority for the development of a Modern Service Framework (MSF).

Neighbourhood health services [2] are a core element of the 10-Year Health Plan, aiming to improve support for people with complex needs. These services build on existing approaches to reducing health inequalities, including Core20PLUS5 framework [3], which identifies people living with SMI as one of 5 priority population groups for accelerated improvement.

People living with SMI experience some of the widest health inequalities in England. Their life expectancy is 15 to 20 years shorter than that of the general population [4]. They also have a much higher risk of developing preventable physical conditions [5].

To ensure that both the mental and physical health needs of people living with SMI are adequately supported, data on the local prevalence of SMI (including breakdown of individual condition groups) is essential. This data on local prevalence is required to plan, commission and deliver services that meet local needs of people with SMI across England.

People with SMI are included within a priority population group for national and hospital service planning. This wider group is increasingly recognised as ‘adults and older adults whose lives are severely impacted by mental health problems’. It includes, but is not limited to, people with: SMI, complex post traumatic stress disorder, personality disorder and those who experience complex emotional needs, eating disorders, severe manifestations of common mental health problems, and co-existing frailty, neurodevelopmental conditions and addiction.

This indicator estimates the level of local SMI overall, and for bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and other psychosis separately, and is part of action to enable effective planning for this wider group.



[1] Department of Health and Social Care (2025). 10 Year Health Plan for England: fit for the future. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-health-plan-for-england-fit-for-the-future
[2] NHS England (2025). Neighbourhood health guidelines 2025/26. https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/neighbourhood-health-guidelines-2025-26/ 
[3] NHS England. Core20PLUS5 (adults) – an approach to reducing healthcare inequalities https://www.england.nhs.uk/about/equality/equality-hub/national-healthcare-inequalities-improvement-programme/core20plus5/
[4] NHS England (2025). Improving the physical health of people living with severe mental illness (https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/improving-the-physical-health-of-people-living-with-severe-mental-illness/
[5] Public Health England (2018). Severe mental illness (SMI) and physical health inequalities: briefing.
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/severe-mental-illness-smi-physical-health-inequalities
Definition:
Model-based estimated prevalence of recorded diagnoses of severe mental illness (SMI) and component conditions (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and other<span data-teams="true">psychosis) in people aged 14 and over.

People under the age of 14 are unlikely to be diagnosed with SMI and therefore are not covered by this indicator.
Data source: OHID, based on Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency, Clinical Practice Research Datalink, Office for National Statistics and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government data
Definition of numerator:
The numerator is the estimate number of people aged 14 and over who are expected to have a severe mental illness (SMI), defined as bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or other psychosis. The estimated counts are based on resident population.

The following steps were used to estimate the numerator:

A sample of 12,467,991 patients 14 and over was identified from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) Aurum database. All patients had a permanent active, registration within a GP practice in England on 30 September 2023. This registration-based sample was used to develop a model for estimating SMI prevalence for England and sub-national resident populations.
Patients with SMI [1] were identified based on evidence of recorded diagnosis, treatment or symptoms, resulting in a SMI group of 147,374 patients. Each patient was assigned to the overall SMI and to one specific condition group (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or otherpsychosis) using an agreed algorithm [2].
A multivariable logistic regression model was fitted using sex (males and females), age (14 to 24, 25 to 34, 35 to 64, and 65 and over), ethnicity groups (Asian, Black, Mixed, Other and White) and deprivation (quintiles) as independent variables [3). Probabilities of having SMI were produced for all 200 distinct groups. This process was repeated for each condition group (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or otherpsychosis).
For each geography (England, regions (statistical), NHS regions, counties and UAs, and Integrated Care Boards (ICBs)), the CPRD-derived probabilities were applied to resident population sub-groups from the 2021 Census. Details on how the resident populations were derived are provided in the ‘Definition of denominator’ section.
The estimated counts were then summed to produce an estimated total number of people with SMI (and either bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or other psychoses) for each area.

[1] Case identification - people were identified as having SMI using SNOMED CT and READ codes for 'diagnoses', ‘lithium therapy’, ‘treatment’ or 'symptoms’.
[2] Assignment to condition groups - people were assigned to mutually exclusive condition groups in the following order:

Diagnosis codes: schizophrenia, then bipolar disorder, then other psychoses.
Administrative lithium therapy codes (past 6 months): bipolar disorder.
Other treatment codes: first assigned to bipolar disorder; if not applicable, assigned to otherpsychosis.
Symptom codes: otherpsychosis.

Each person contributes to the overall SMI prevalence and to one condition group only. No one is counted in more than one group.
[3] While some studies are inconclusive, evidence shows that sex, age, ethnicity and deprivation are statistically significant predictors for a diagnosis of SM. Within the logistic regression model, each of these variables was statistically significant.
Source of numerator: Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD), Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), English indices of deprivation
Definition of denominator:
Number of people aged 14 and over in 2021.

The following steps were used to produce the denominator populations:

The Lower Super Output Area (LSOA) population data from Census 2021 (by sex, age and ethnicity) was linked to the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019 (IMD 2019).
LSOAs were aggregated to deprivation quintiles by sex, age groups and ethnicity to obtain their distributions among IMD quintiles within the specific geography. These distributions were used for subsequent population adjustments.
For each geography (England, regions (statistical), NHS regions, Counties and UAs, and ICBs), LSOA populations were summed up to deprivation quintile by sex, age and ethnicity. These populations were also used to calculate the estimated counts as specified in the ‘Definition of numerator’ section.
The final denominator was derived by summing the population sub-groups across the stated geography.

Note: The Census 2021 LSOAs data used cell swapping to protect personal data and ensure statistical disclosure control. As a result, summed figures may differ slightly from direct Census 2021 extract. The differences were adjusted across the 2019 IMD quintile distribution to reduce the impact.
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), English indices of deprivation
Methodology: The numerator is divided by the denominator to give a prevalence proportion.
Frequency:
Every 2 to 4 years.

Note: Census 2021 was used to source local population counts, including ethnicity. Future updates depend on the availability of post census local ethnicity estimates.
Confidence interval details: Because of the way the estimates are derived, calculating confidence intervals would produce very narrow ranges that reflect the sample size of the CPRD and not the size of the local population. Therefore, confidence intervals are not published for this indicator. We will explore adding confidence intervals as we improve the method in future updates.
Disclosure control: The count estimates are based on CPRD derived probabilities and local demography, so there is no issue of disclosure.
Rounding: The indicator is rounded to 2 decimal points.
Caveats:
This indicator estimates how many people aged 14 and over are expected to have SMI in each area. Prevalence estimates are based on:

Schizophrenia: 'diagnoses'
Bipolar disorder: ‘diagnoses’, ‘lithium treatment’ (in the last 6 months) and ‘symptoms’ (in the last 12 months)
Other psychosis: ‘diagnoses’, and ‘symptoms’ (in the last 12 months)excluding people with a dementia diagnosis in the last 2 years

These estimates reflect SMI recorded by a healthcare professional in primary care records. They do not include undiagnosed conditions, or diagnoses recorded only in other care settings that have not yet been added to primary care records.

The CPRD Aurum database contains routinely collected data from GP practices that use EMIS electronic patient record system. Practices using Vision and SystmOne software are not included. CPRD Aurum covers around 25% of registered population and around 21% of GP practices in the UK.

This indicator included only patients with sex recorded as female or male. Patients recorded as other gender made up 0.01% of records in the CPRD Aurum and were excluded. This indicator excluded patients with missing ethnicity in CPRD Aurum (3.68%).

Area-level deprivation quintiles were assigned using the patient’s place of residence. If the residence-based quintile was unavailable, the GP practice postcode was used to assign deprivation quintiles.

These estimates include people with SMI who are managed in, or present to, primary care. The following caveats should be considered:

Primary care recording of SMI varies between practices and over time.
Only people registered with a GP practice are included. Some groups at higher risk of mental health problems, such as people experiencing homelessness and some migrant groups, may be under-represented.
CPRD is a large, non random sample. Not all regions are equally represented.


The indicator is calculated using sex, age, ethnicity and deprivation. Other local factors not captured in the model might be important predictors of SMI diagnosis. Therefore, the actual prevalence may differ from the indicator value.

The population aged 14 to 24 was derived from the 0 to 24 population. The age 14 population was estimated from the 9 to 14 age band. For these estimates, it was assumed that the IMD2019 quintile distribution for those aged 14 to 24 is the same as for those aged 0 to 24.
Notes:
Prevalence estimates of SMI from CPRD are consistent with published research using primary care data. The indicator shows geographical variation in SMI prevalence at UTLA level ranging from: 0.82 to 1.58% for SMI overall, 0.21 to 0.62% for schizophrenia, 0.29 to 0.53% for bipolar disorder and 0.25 to 0.52% for other psychosis. The indicator highlights the variation in the composition of the SMI population across the 3 component conditions.

A direct comparison with population surveys is difficult. However, the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (APMS) reports data on the prevalence of psychiatric disorder in the past year among adults 16 and over in England. It provides prevalence for bipolar disorder, based on a screening tool rather than a clinical assessment. The 2023/24 APMS reports prevalence at 1.9% for bipolar disorder and 0.4% for psychotic disorder. Prevalence based on screening tools is generally higher than figures based on clinical diagnoses.

This indicator uses the following definitions:

Severe mental illness and specific conditions groups are defined using guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. This includes: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management; Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management; and Coexisting severe mental illness (psychosis) and substance misuse: assessment and management in healthcare settings.
Prevalence is defined as cross-sectional prevalence based on primary care records. Individuals with recorded evidence of SMI are counted as a prevalent case. This indicator uses a combination of diagnosis, symptom and medication codes.

All code lists have been validated internally and externally by academic and clinical experts.

The Isles of Scilly and City of London data have been aggregated with Cornwall and Hackney, respectively.

Indicator: Deprivation score (IMD 2025)
Rationale:
Deprivation covers a broad range of issues and refers to unmet needs caused by a lack of resources of all kinds, not just financial. The English Indices of Deprivation attempt to measure a broader concept of multiple deprivation, made up of seven distinct dimensions, or domains, of deprivation.The English Indices of Deprivation 2025 are measures of multiple deprivation at the small area level. The model of multiple deprivation which underpins the indices of Deprivation 2025 is based on the idea of distinct domains of deprivation which can be recognised and measured separately. These domains are experienced by individuals living in an area. People may be counted in one or more of the domains, depending on the number and the types of deprivation that they experience. Each domain represents a specific form of deprivation experienced by people and each can be measured individually using a number of indicators. The Index of multiple deprivation (IMD) is the weighted aggregate of the seven domains.The seven distinct domains are (weighting in brackets):

Income Deprivation (22.5%)
Employment Deprivation (22.5%)
Education, Skills and Training Deprivation (13.5%)
Health Deprivation and Disability (13.5%)
Crime (9.3%)
Barriers to Housing and Services (9.3%)
Living Environment Deprivation (9.3%)
Definition: The Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025 (IMD 2025) is an overall measure of deprivation experienced by people living in an area. It is the combination of 7 deprivation domains and the official measure of deprivation in England.
