Indicator: Smoking prevalence in adults (aged 18 and over) - current smokers (GPPS)
Rationale:
Smoking is the single most important entirely preventable cause of ill health, disability and death in England (1). Smoking harms nearly every organ of the body. It causes lung cancer, respiratory disease and cardiovascular disease, as well as many cancers in other organs including lip, mouth, throat, bladder, kidney, stomach, liver and cervix. Smoking reduces fertility and significantly raises the risk of developing type 2 diabetes, eye disease and dementia. It leads to decreased bone mineral density and is associated with increased risk of osteoporosis, bone fractures, back pain and degenerative disc disease. Secondhand smoke is dangerous for anyone exposed to it, but children are especially vulnerable due to breathing more rapidly and having less developed airways, lungs and immune systems (2).

As a result, smoking puts significant pressure on the NHS. Almost every minute of every day someone is admitted to hospital because of smoking, and up to 75,000 GP appointments could be attributed to smoking each month - equivalent to over 100 appointments every hour. Those who are unemployed, on low incomes or living in areas of deprivation are far more likely to smoke than the general population. Smoking attributable mortality rates are 2.1 times higher in the most deprived local authorities than in the least deprived. It is estimated that the total costs of smoking in England are over £17 billion. This includes an annual £14 billion loss to productivity, through smoking related lost earnings, unemployment, and early death, as well as costs to the NHS and social care of £3 billion (2).The government aims to create the first smokefree generation with legislation to ensure that children will never be legally sold tobacco products. This will prevent future generations from ever taking up smoking, as there is no safe age to smoke (3). References:(1) Stopping the start: our new plan to create a smokefree generation https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/stopping-the-start-our-new-plan-to-create-a-smokefree-generation/stopping-the-start-our-new-plan-to-create-a-smokefree-generation (2) Smoking and tobacco: applying All Our Health https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/smoking-and-tobacco-applying-all-our-health/smoking-and-tobacco-applying-all-our-health

(3) Tobacco and vapes bill https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/the-tobacco-and-vapes-bill-2024
Definition: Proportion of the population who classify themselves as either occasional or regular smokers according to the GP Patient Survey
Data source: NHS England, GP Patient Survey
Indicator source: Calculated by Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) from GP Patient Survey (GPPS) data.
Definition of numerator: The number of people who responded either "regular smoker" or "occasional smoker" to the question "Which of the following best describes your smoking habits?"
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Definition of denominator: The number of people who responded to the question "Which of the following best describes your smoking habits?"
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), GP Patient Survey (GPPS)
Methodology: The prevalence is calculated by dividing the weighted number of self-reported smokers aged 18 and over by total number of respondents (with a valid smoking status) aged 18 and over, expressed as a percentage.<span style="line-height: 107%; mso-fareast-font-family: 'Times New Roman'; border: none windowtext 1.0pt; mso-border-alt: none windowtext 0cm; padding: 0cm; mso-fareast-language: EN-GB;">The number of respondents has been weighted to improve representativeness of the sample. The weights consider survey design and non-response. Non-response weights were constructed using a model-based approach to estimate the probability of taking part in the survey based on the age and gender of the patient and the socio-economic characteristics of the neighbourhood in which the patient lived. These weights aim to reduce the demographic and socio-economic differences between respondents and non-respondents.Full details on weighting within the GPPS can be found in the Technical Annex https://gp-patient.co.uk/technical-annex-introduction-2025
Confidence interval details:
An approximate 95% and 99.8% confidence interval was derived from 10,000 simulations of current smoking prevalence for each area. Each prevalence simulation was calculated by

1. drawing a number of ‘successes’ randomly from a binomial distribution ~Bin(n,p) when n is the unweighted total population estimate and p is the weighted prevalence of current smokers.

2. dividing the number of ‘successes’ by the unweighted total respondents

The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of these prevalence estimates were then found to give the 95% and 99.8% confidence intervals respectively.
Disclosure control: None applied.
Rounding: None applied
Notes:
Values suppressed where count <10 as sample size too small to produce reliable estimate.The publication of the 2024 survey results is the start of a new time series for GPPS. This means that trend data for previous years will not be presented alongside the 2024 results in Fingertips as it would normally be. The 2024 results are not comparable with previous years because of changes to both the questionnaire and the mailing strategy. The previous version of this indicator was 92304.The GPPS questionnaire was redeveloped ahead of the 2024 survey to reflect how primary care services are delivered and patients experience them.This provided the opportunity to improve other areas of the questionnaire, for example, ensuring that where possible, demographic questions are aligned with other major NHS patient experience surveys and the ONS harmonised standards. And all remaining existing questions were reviewed to ensure that they were understood and answered as expected by participants. This resulted in changes to question wording and response codes across the whole questionnaire, meaning that even for those individual questions where the wording has remained the same as in previous years, analysis has shown that trends cannot be reliably presented due to context effects.

The GPPS methodology has historically used a simultaneous push-to-web approach, offering the option to take part online and a paper questionnaire in every mailing. From 2024 onwards, the contact strategy for GPPS has changed to a sequential push-to-web methodology. This was a result of a series of experiments conducted in 2022 and 2023 which demonstrated that it was possible to save a significant amount of money by removing a paper questionnaire from the first two mailings and, where a mobile phone number was available, to replace the second physical mailing with an e-letter.

Analysis of these experiments showed that while there was no significant impact on the demographic profile of patients taking part in the survey, there were significant differences in answers to key survey questions. For example, patients in the experiment group reported poorer experiences, were more likely to have avoided making an appointment (because it was too difficult) and were more likely to have used online services. This indicated that moving to a sequential push-to-web approach would result in a break in trends across the survey results as a whole.For more information please see the GPPS methodology pages: https://gp-patient.co.uk/report-summary-of-changes

Methodology:
The value is presented as an odds ratio. An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an event. The OR represents the odds that an event will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the event occurring in the absence of that exposure.

Specifically, an odds ratio compares the odds that an event (smoking) will occur in the presence of a certain exposure (having a long-term mental health condition) to the odds of the same event (smoking) occurring in the absence of the exposure (having a long-term mental health condition).

The odds of the event in the exposed group is:

(a) The number of people who reported smoking and having a long-term mental health condition

(b) The number of people who reported not smoking and had a long-term mental health condition

The odds in the event in non-exposed group is:

(c) The number of people who reported smoking and not having a long-term mental health condition

(d) The number of people who reported not smoking and not having a long-term mental health condition

Indicator: Population vaccination coverage: Flu (secondary school aged children)
Rationale:
Influenza, also known as flu, is a highly infectious viral illness that can cause significant morbidity in children and young people. While most recover within a week, some develop complications requiring hospital care, even if they are otherwise healthy.[1]
Vaccinating secondary school aged children (Years 7–11) provides direct protection, reducing their risk of illness, hospitalisation, and disruption to education and daily life. [2]
Children are key drivers of influenza transmission. By immunising secondary school pupils, the programme reduces the spread of flu within schools, families, and the wider community, including to vulnerable groups such as infants, older adults, and those with underlying health conditions. This indirect effect is a major public health benefit, as it helps prevent outbreaks and reduces the overall burden of disease.
High vaccine uptake among school-aged children is associated with fewer GP consultations, hospital admissions, and emergency department attendances for flu and its complications. By preventing illness in school-aged children, the programme helps to ease winter pressures on primary care and hospital services.
The Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) recommends the annual flu vaccination programme includes all healthy children aged 2 to under 18, including secondary school pupils, to maximise both direct and indirect protection. [3]
Delivering the vaccine in schools ensures high coverage and equitable access, particularly for those who might otherwise miss out due to barriers in accessing healthcare.

Indicator: Estimated total prevalence of non-diabetic hyperglycaemia
Rationale: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NDH, also known as pre-diabetes or impaired glucose regulation) refers to individuals with raised blood glucose (42-47 mmol/mol) that are just below the diabetic range (48 mmol/mol and above). These individuals are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes, where the body does not produce enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to insulin. Subsequently, there is an increased chance of serious complications including heart attacks, strokes and other diabetes-related conditions. Identification of individuals with NDH is important. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that people with NDH should have their body mass index (BMI) and blood glucose measured and monitored every year to help prevent progression to type 2 diabetes. However, currently, NDH is differentially recorded across areas in England. Preventing people from developing to type 2 diabetes is a public health priority. As part of the 10 Year Health Plan, government has committed to shift towards prevention of disease. This includes improving effectiveness of the NHS Health Check to identify high-risk individuals as well as supporting access to weight management services and new weight loss medications for people with obesity. Additionally, the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme continues to be supported throughout England and Wales. https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/health-survey-for-england  includes data on blood glucose (HbA1c) levels based on blood samples taken, using a representative sample of the England population. There are available data on recorded instances of NDH from  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-tools-and-services/data-services/general-practice-data-hub/quality-outcomes-framework-qof . However, there are no direct estimates of total NDH prevalence for local areas below England level due to the sample size available. Therefore, the HSE data has been used to model estimates of total NDH prevalence at a local level, based on the risk profile of local populations.Healthcare professionals and commissioners can use these estimates to help plan prevention activity and service use for people at highest risk of developing type 2 diabetes. These can be used to support work on whether testing, coding or both need to be improved in an area, based on the level of risk estimated to be in the population.
Definition: Modelled estimated prevalence of non-diabetic hyperglycaemia for people aged 18 years and over. Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia is defined as having a HbA1c reading of between 42 and 47 mmol/mol (inclusive) and did not self-report having a diabetes diagnosis.
Data source: OHID, based on Office for National Statistics and NHS England data
Definition of numerator:
The numerator was defined as the estimated count of people in 2021 aged 18 years and over who had a HbA1c reading of between 42 and 47 mmol/mol (inclusive) and reported not having a diabetes diagnosis.The numerators were estimated using combined HSE 2014 to 2019 data. Blood weights were used and adjusted to maintain a mean of 1 across combined survey years.This was undertaken using the following steps: 

Identifying participants of HSE survey respondents with the definition of non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NDH) aged 18 and over with a valid HbA1c reading. These were grouped by 7 age groups (18 to 24, then 10-year bands through to 75 years and older) and 2 ethnic groups (White-Mixed-Other, Black-Asian).
A multivariate complex samples logistic regression model that included age group and ethnic group demonstrated that these variables significantly contributed to the prediction of whether someone had NDH or not. The adjusted probability of having NDH for all distinct groupings of predictor variables was generated.
For each geographical area, the probability was then multiplied by the size of the sub-population.
Resulting numbers were summed across all groups to give an estimated number of people with NDH for each area.
BMI category (underweight/healthy weight, overweight or obese) was found to be a significant predictor also, however it was not possible to include in the model due to the local level data available. Therefore, a post-hoc adjustment was calculated for each area. Using local estimates of overweight and obesity prevalence from the  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/diabetes-ft/data#page/6/gid/1938133138/pat/159/par/K02000001/ati/15/are/E92000001/iid/93088/age/168/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1  for the corresponding year, an adjustment factor was calculated. The distribution of the population within each BMI category were calculated for each area. These data were combined with the relative risks of having NDH in each category nationally to create an adjustment index.
This adjustment factor was applied to the previous estimates to generate a final estimate for all areas, adjusting for overweight and obesity prevalence.

Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on NHS England (NHSE) and Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Definition of denominator: Denominators were generated from a combination of data sources for resident populations. Using 2021 Census data extracted from  https://www.ons.gov.uk/datasets/create , a dataset of usual resident counts for those aged 18 years and over and stratified by age and ethnic group was extracted. These were then grouped into 7 age groups (18 to 24, then 10-year bands through to 75 years and older), 2 ethnic groups (White-Mixed-Other, Black-Asian). These were extracted for all local areas required. ONS mid-year population estimates for 2021 were extracted for all areas, stratified by age. The corresponding proportional split by ethnic groups from the Census data was applied to the mid-year population estimates stratified by each age grouping. The final denominator is the sum of these estimates across the stated geography.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on Office for National Statistics (ONS) data
Methodology: The final values for each geography were calculated by dividing the numerator by the population denominator and multiplying by 100.
Confidence interval details:
Uncertainty limits were calculated using statistical simulation for both stages of modelling.
For the logistic regression model (first stage), a large number of randomly generated proportions for each age, and ethnic group combination were generated, using simulation-based inference following the method of Krinsky and Robb (1986).
This was done by drawing sets of simulated coefficients from a multivariate normal distribution with means equal to the original model’s estimated coefficients and variances equal to the model’s variance-covariance matrix. These sets of coefficients were used to compute sets of proportions. Counts were then calculated from these and summed across all groupings, producing estimates of NDH prevalence.
For the post-hoc adjustment accounting for overweight and obesity prevalence (second stage), simulations were generated by drawing a number of ‘successes’ randomly using a binomial distribution. This produced an estimate of overweight and obesity prevalence which was then used to produce an adjustment for a given area, using the same method described in the section above.
A total of 100,000 simulations were undertaken for each geography and for both stages of the simulation. The simulated count of NDH prevalence estimates from the model had a simulated post-hoc BMI adjustment applied to it at random. This produced 100,000 estimates of NDH prevalence using both simulated stages. The final simulated counts for each geography were ordered and the 2.5th and 97.5th and 0.1th and 99.9th percentiles of the distribution of counts were extracted. These were then divided by the population aged 18 and older and expressed as the 95% and 99.8% uncertainty limits around the central estimated percentage prevalence for each geography.


Reference
Krinsky, I., and A. L. Robb. 1986. On Approximating the Statistical Properties of Elasticities. Review of Economics and Statistics 68 (4): 715–9.
Disclosure control: Statistical disclosure control is applied to extracted 2021 Census data. Techniques used for these tables include targeted record swapping and cell key perturbation.Office for National Statistics (ONS), released 9 March 2023, ONS website, methodology,  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/protectingpersonaldataincensus2021results .
Rounding: Numerators and denominators have been rounded to the nearest whole number.
Caveats: The data to assess non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NDH) uses only a single measure of HbA1c from the Health Survey for England (HSE). This differs to the recommended criteria set out by NICE, of using a risk assessment combined with blood test. Tests can alternatively be done using fasting plasma glucose or oral glucose tolerance tests. Therefore, this can only be seen as indicative of an individual having NDH. Data for blood glucose available in HSE is only recorded for HbA1c. Any participants with missing values for age, ethnic group or measured BMI were excluded from the multivariate analyses (10% of available sample), giving an unweighted sample size of 20,150 aged over 18 with a valid HbA1c reading for this analysis. Due to the need for population denominators which can break down by all groupings used in the analysis, the estimates do not take into consideration other population risk factors that are known to influence the risk of having NDH. Available data did not allow for robustly stratifying population denominators by BMI category (underweight/healthy weight, overweight or obese). However, analysis demonstrated the importance of accounting for variation on overweight and obesity prevalence at a local level to estimate NDH prevalence. A post-hoc adjustment was determined to be the most appropriate method to allow for this. While there is some association between age and BMI and ethnicity and BMI, collinearity with BMI was low when also adjusting for age and ethnicity. It is likely that a post-hoc adjustment for BMI also adjusts for some variance in risk associated with age and ethnicity, however sensitivity analysis indicated that this was likely to be minimal. Data from the Active Lives Adult Survey was used to calculate the post-hoc adjustment for each area. This uses self-reported height and weight, adjusted for self-report bias to estimate closer to measured BMI. The data from HSE used for this adjustment uses measured BMI, as recorded during the nurse visit. For this analysis, it was assumed that these two measures were consistent. The HSE data used for modelling NDH prevalence was collected between 2014 and 2019. Multiple years of data were included to allow for an appropriate sample size for analysis. However, this data may not represent the current picture of NDH prevalence in England in 2021. Due to more recent HSE data not being available, the data used here was the most recent available to use for this analysis. For more information on methodological decisions, please see the technical document.

Indicator: Diagnosed prevalence of type 2 diabetes among adults aged under 40
Rationale:
Diabetes is a lifelong condition that causes a person's blood sugar level to become too high. There are two main types of diabetes: 

type 1 diabetes – where the body's immune system attacks and destroys the cells that produce insulin
type 2 diabetes – where the body does not produce enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to insulin

Type 1 and type 2 diabetes have different risk factors and management. The number of people with early-onset type 2 diabetes (typically defined as the development of type 2 diabetes in people aged under 40 years) has been increasing over time. It can be asymptomatic but early identification and management can reduce the risk of diabetes complications and the risk of developing CVD. Compared with a diagnosis later in life, an earlier-onset diagnosis carries an unexplained excess risk of microvascular complications, adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death. Diagnosing early-onset type 2 diabetes means that a patient is more likely to be reviewed and if appropriate, offered ongoing lifestyle advice, monitoring, and treatment, in accordance with  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng18 . However, this diagnosed group are still significantly less likely to receive recommended care processes and achieve HbA1c treatment targets compared to those 40 and over. Diabetes UK have previously recommended sustainable, long-term investment for programmes of targeted support for those at highest risk of complications from diabetes - especially those with early-onset type 2. By identifying and managing people with early-onset type 2 diabetes, there is an opportunity to prevent further complications, delay disease progression and improve long-term health outcomes. This indicator is intended to inform changes in clinical practice by highlighting areas where prevalence varies. Variation in recorded prevalence may indicate differences in case ascertainment or alternative differences in population structure, as the risk of early-onset type 2 diabetes is greater for females, those with overweight and obesity, those living in more deprived areas and those from black and Asian ethnic groups.This indicator uses a different data source to other prevalence indicators in this profile and is therefore not directly comparable. This data is sourced from National Diabetes Audit (NDA) dataset linked to National Paediatric Diabetes Audit (NPDA) dataset and has undergone additional criteria to determine whether individuals have type 2 diabetes. The other type 2 prevalence indicator in this profile uses Core NDA data alone as this is the only source for diabetes registrations for all ages. The Core NDA data also includes other rarer forms of diabetes too – not just type 2 (see https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/diabetes-ft/data#page/6/gid/1938133438/ati/15/iid/94177/age/187/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1 for more information on this).For a more granular breakdown of data for young people with type 2 diabetes (including care processes and treatment targets), visit the NDA publication  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-diabetes-audit-yt2 .
Definition: Percentage of adults aged 19 to 39 determined to have type 2 diabetes mellitus among practices and services that participate in the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) and National Paediatric Diabetes Audit (NPDA).
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Definition of numerator: Total number of people of aged 19 to 39 identified as having type 2 diabetes that have been identified through practices and services that participate in the National Diabetes Audit and National Paediatric Diabetes Audit. Through linking paediatric services and GP practice records, people are identified as having type 2 diabetes through a series of criteria based on diabetes type registration, blood glucose readings, age and drug prescriptions (including metformin, oral hypoglycaemics and insulin). For more information please see the  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-diabetes-audit-yt2/young-people-with-type-2-diabetes-detailed-report-2021-22/methodology .
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator: Total number of people aged 19 to 39 registered with practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit. Practices were mapped to geographies according to the mapping used for NDA registrations data for a given audit period. Patient totals were taken from the month following the end of the audit period.For 2023: Patients Registered at a GP Practice -  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/patients-registered-at-a-gp-practice/april-2023  was used. Rounding: Numerators are rounded to the nearest 5. Values were calculated from these rounded counts.
Caveats: This indicator does not exactly describe early-onset type 2 diabetes prevalence as it is typically understood or defined - though no clinical definition currently exists. It does not account for people that have been diagnosed before they were 40 but have aged out of this cohort. By definition, these people have early-onset type 2 diabetes. These individuals will still have the same consequences of having early-onset as these often only manifest later in life. Additionally, children are not included here. Children are most often managed and treated through paediatric services, not necessarily primary care. This indicator is simply the prevalence of type 2 diabetes among people aged 19 to 39. In a separate collection from the Core NDA, the NPDA collects data on the care and outcomes of children and young people with diabetes from paediatric diabetes services in England and Wales. Additionally, it reports on patient and parent experiences of care and service delivery. The data source for this indicator combines data from these two audits to obtain a cohort of young people with type 2 diabetes. For more information on this data source see the NDA publications  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-diabetes-audit-yt2 .

Indicator: People with type 1 diabetes who achieved all three treatment targets (new definition)
Rationale:
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends treatment targets for HbA1c levels (glucose control), blood pressure and statins prescribed for combined prevention of CVD (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng17). Effective control of diabetes can reduce mortality and morbidity in this population. By reducing HbA1c in people with diabetes, this decreases the risk of all diabetic complications. By reducing blood pressure, this decreases the risk of vascular complications and the progression of eye disease and kidney failure. CVD prevention with statins aims to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent future cardiovascular events, among the appropriate population with diabetes.

There are differences in the population with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, leading to a discrepancy in achieving treatment targets. Understanding this discrepancy at a local level is important for assessing the needs of the local population with diabetes and where improvements can be made.
Definition: The percentage of people that met all three treatment targets for HbA1c, blood pressure and combined cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention for people registered with type 1 diabetes among practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) during the audit period. For children under 12 years of age, 'all three treatment targets' is defined as Hba1c only as other treatment targets are not recommended in the NICE guidelines for this age group. If a person falls into none of the primary or secondary prevention groups, 'all three treatment targets' is defined as HbA1c of less than or equal to 58mmol/mol and blood pressure of less than or equal to 140/90 only.
Data source: NHS England, National Diabetes Audit
Definition of numerator:
Total number of patients with type 1 diabetes who have met all three treatment targets and are registered with a practice participating in the NDA. Treatment targets are defined as:
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> The most recent HbA1c blood test is less than or equal to 58 mmol/mol recorded during the audit period.
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> The most recent blood pressure reading is less than or equal to 140/90 recorded during the audit period. Both systolic and diastolic pressures must be within their respective limits for this treatment target to be met.
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> Prescribed statins for combined (primary or secondary) prevention of CVD. Either a person aged between 40 and 80 years old with no history of CVD has been prescribed statins (primary prevention) or a person of any age has a history of CVD and has been prescribed statins (secondary prevention).

A person with diabetes has to achieve all three targets in the audit period to be included in the numerator. However, if a person does not fall into either primary or secondary prevention, then ‘three treatment targets’ is defined as meeting the HbA1c and blood pressure targets only. For children under 12 years of age, 'all three treatment targets' is defined as ‘HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol or less’ only as other treatment targets are not recommended in the NICE guidelines for this age group.

CVD history is determined by use of primary care records and hospital records. A history of CVD means the individual has had a hospital admission record mentioning angina, stroke, myocardial infarction, or heart failure in the ten years up to the period and/or are recorded in their NDA record as having ischemic heart disease.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator: Total number of patients with type 1 diabetes who are registered with a practice participating in the NDA. Patients 12 and older without a valid reading for HbA1c and/or blood pressure and patients aged under 12 without a valid reading for HbA1c in the audit period are excluded as it is not possible to determine if they have met either of these targets.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Methodology: Numerator divided by denominator multiplied by 100.
Rounding: Numerators and denominators are rounded to the nearest 5. Numerators and denominators between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5. Values were calculated from these rounded values. Because of this, values for areas with small denominators should be treated with caution, as rounding has a larger impact on the calculated proportion.
Caveats:
A number of people with diabetes are excluded if they are not registered with a GP practice at the time of collection. While information on children is captured by the NDA extraction of primary care data, information is not collected from paediatric specialist units. Where data for children with diabetes is only available through this route (and not through primary care or adult specialist services), they will not be included in this indicator. Therefore, there are some children with diabetes missing from the data used for this indicator. Instead, this data is currently only collected as part of the National Paediatric Diabetes Audit. In addition, NICE guidance changes through adolescent years and GPs are not incentivised to record diabetes data for those under the age of 17.

As of 2023-24, the NDA began reporting data from detained facilities. Therefore, data for England reported here includes these facilities in the numerator and denominator. This was around 0.1% of all reported registrations in 2023-24.

Those that do not have a valid HbA1c and/or blood pressure measurement are excluded here. Therefore, areas with lower recording of HbA1c or blood pressure as part of the care processes may impact achievement of this indicator as the denominator will be smaller/bigger. Caution should be taken when assessing HbA1c or blood pressure treatment target achievement for areas with a low proportion of HbA1c or blood pressure checks being completed.

The participation of GP practices in the audit has varied over time. Over recent years, the participation rate has been around 98% of GP practice in England. Recent years of data are a very good representation of the care and treatment of people with diabetes. However, there is some variation in the participation rate between areas. These data should be treated with caution when comparing between years and should be considered in conjunction with participation rates.

Further details of the data quality for previous audit periods is available here: https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/national-diabetes-audit/report-1-care-processes-and-treatment-targets-2021-22-full-report/data-quality-statement-copy. While these data quality issues predate the time series, many are still relevant to this data – particularly those related to data collection and processing.
Notes:
This indicator is very similar to indicator 94150 which it is superseding, found  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/diabetes-ft/data#page/4/gid/1938133135/ati/15/iid/94150/age/1/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1/page-options/car-do-0 .The audit period has changed from a 15-month period from 1st January to 31st March the following year, to a 12-month audit period covering the financial year – 1st April to 31st March. Due to these changes, the new definition is not comparable to the old definition and so a new time series must be created.

This is important as obtaining target blood pressure reduces the risk of target blood pressure reduced the risk of vascular complications and the possible progression of eye disease and kidney failure. Indicator: People with type 1 diabetes who received retinal screening
Rationale:
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends 9 care processes for diabetes, including retinal screening. Retinal examinations are used to check for possible signs of retinopathy - a condition where the retina is damaged causing at least partial loss of vision. People with diabetes are vulnerable to retinopathy due to blood vessel damage caused by the disease.
Effective control and monitoring of diabetes can reduce mortality and morbidity in this population. There are differences in the population with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, leading to a discrepancy in receiving care processes such as retinal screening. Understanding this discrepancy at a local level is important for assessing the needs of the local population with diabetes and where improvements can be made.
Definition: The percentage of people with type 1 diabetes aged 12 and over who have received retinal screening check among practices participating in the National Diabetes Audit (NDA) during the audit period.
Data source: NHS England, National Diabetes Audit
Definition of numerator:
Number of people with type 1 diabetes aged 12 and over who received a retinal screening check and are registered at practices that participate in the NDA. A check is counted if it occurred during the 12-month audit period.
For children under 12 years of age, only HbA1c blood test are recommended in the NICE guidelines for this age group. Therefore, they are excluded from this indicator.
Source of numerator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Definition of denominator: Number of people with type 1 diabetes aged 12 and over who are registered at practices that participate in the NDA.
Source of denominator: NHS England (NHSE), National Diabetes Audit (NDA)
Methodology: Numerator divided by denominator multiplied by 100.
Rounding: Numerators and denominators are rounded to the nearest 5. Numerators and denominators between 1 and 7 are rounded to 5. Values were calculated from these rounded values. Because of this, values for areas with small denominators should be treated with caution, as rounding has a larger impact on the calculated proportion.

Therefore, there are some children with diabetes missing from the data used for this indicator. Instead, this data is currently only collected as part of the National Paediatric Diabetes Audit. In addition, NICE guidance changes through adolescent years and GPs are not incentivised to record diabetes data for those under the age of 17.
Where denominators are 20 or below, values are not reported.As of 2023-24, the NDA began reporting data from detained facilities. Therefore, data for England reported here includes these facilities in the numerator and denominator. This was around 0.1% of all reported registrations in 2023-24.

Rationale:
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends certain treatment targets for people with diabetes. People with diabetes are at greater risk of CVD complications and comorbidities. Effective control and monitoring can reduce mortality and morbidity in this population. Statin therapy helps to lower levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) cholesterol and is associated with a reduction in myocardial infarction (MI), coronary heart disease (CHD), and stroke. Indicator: Percentage of less active children and young people
Rationale:
TheUK Chief Medical Officers' (CMOs') recommendthat children and young people (5 to 18 years) are physically active for an average of at least 60 minutes per day across the week. The evidence suggests, however, that a significant proportion of adolescents do not meet this minimum standard.Regular moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA) improves health and fitness, strengthens muscles and bones, develops coordination, maintains healthy weight, improves sleep, makes you feel good, builds confidence and social skills and improves concentration and learning.Good physical activity habits established in childhood and adolescence are also likely to be carried through into adulthood. If we can help children and young people to establish and maintain high volumes of physical activity into adulthood, we will reduce the risk of morbidity and mortality from chronic non communicable diseases later in their lives.

The 2025"Fit for the future: 10 Year Health Plan for England"set out plans to raise the healthiest generation of children through a range of initiatives focusing on prevention and healthy choices that aim to make physical activity and healthy eating easier for families.

The Active Lives Children and Young People Survey is the only national data source for physical activity levels that is available at local authority level and the data will shape and influence local decision making as well as inform and supporting monitoring of government policy on the Primary PE and Sports Premium, the 10-year health plan and other cross departmental programmes.The percentage of children and young people doing less than an average of 30 minutes of moderate to vigorous intensity activity a day across the week varies geographically across local authorities in England. Additionally, the percentage of less active children and young people is higher among people from Asian and Black ethnic groups, higher among girls than boys, and lower in children in school years 1 and 2.

Indicator: Infants whose mothers received an antenatal review, CSDS-based (Official Statistics in Development)
Rationale:
Since November 2017, providers of publicly funded health services have been  https://digital.nhs.uk/about-nhs-digital/corporate-information-and-documents/directions-and-data-provision-notices/data-provision-notices-dpns/community-services-data-set-csds-data-provision-notice . This indicator is based on CSDS and has been developed as part of the process of discontinuing the  https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/childrens-public-health-0-to-5-years-national-reporting  established in 2015. Once the voluntary aggregate collection ceases, CSDS will be the only source of data for the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme .The antenatal health and development review is one of the five mandated universal contacts delivered by health visiting teams as part of the  https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/healthy-child-programme in England. The HCP is the national framework for improving child health and wellbeing through prevention, early identification of need, and early intervention, with delivery aligned to the principle of proportionate universalism to help reduce inequalities in outcomes.
 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/delivery-of-the-healthy-child-programme/part-2-health-visiting-ages-0-to-5  identifies the antenatal, new birth, and 6 to 8 week health and development reviews as particularly important early contacts, and recommends the home as the most appropriate setting for these reviews. The antenatal review provides an opportunity for health visitors to establish early contact with families during pregnancy, begin a relationship prior to birth, and identify factors that may affect the health and wellbeing of the baby and family. This early engagement supports continuity of care across the transition from maternity services to health visiting and enables early identification of risks to parental wellbeing, infant health, and safeguarding that may not be apparent in other settings. The review typically includes discussion of maternal and family health, preparation for parenthood, infant feeding intentions, safe care practices, and emotional wellbeing, as well as assessment of any additional support needs. Where concerns are identified, the review provides an opportunity for early support, referral, or planning of proportionate follow-up following birth.
Pregnancy represents a critical period for influencing early life outcomes and addressing factors that contribute to health inequalities. Universal health visiting services aim to ensure that all families receive core preventative support at this early stage, while enabling additional and targeted input for families with greater need. Policy and academic literature emphasise the role of early health visiting contact in identifying vulnerability, supporting parental capacity, and mitigating risks through timely intervention, even where direct causal links to long-term outcomes cannot always be quantified. Indicator: Proportion of adults who scored 8 or higher on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI)
Rationale:
Gambling is associated with serious harms including suicide, domestic violence, financial hardship, and family breakdown [1]. Gambling-related harms are not limited to those who meet the criteria for a clinical diagnosis. Many individuals who do not meet diagnostic thresholds nevertheless report experiencing adverse personal, social, financial, or health-related consequences as a result of gambling [2]. Gambling related harms can affect not only the individual who gambles but also their families, friends, and relatives around them, resulting in wider costs to communities and society [3]. Importantly, while gambling harms can affect anyone, the greatest harm from gambling is experienced by socioeconomically disadvantaged groups [4].

Gambling-related harm is linked to an estimated annual cost to society of between £1.05bn and £1.77bn. The increased accessibility of gambling brings a growing public health threat, which could further drive inequalities and increase costs to/harms experienced by individuals, families, communities, and society [5].

The Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) within the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) is responsible for the prevention of gambling-related harms in England, and is the designated gambling harms prevention commissioner for England under the statutory gambling levy. OHID is leading an industry-independent, evidence-led public health approach to preventing gambling related harms [6].

The proportion of persons (aged 18 and over) who scored an 8 or higher on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), indicating ‘problem gambling’ whereby a person will have experienced adverse consequences from gambling and may have lost control of their behaviour. Indicator source: Two years of Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB)data combined were used for the modelled estimates, where it is displayed as 2023-24 it means that it covers data from survey years 2023 and 2024.
Definition of numerator:
The number of people who scored 8 or higher on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). The number has been modelled using a multinomial logistic regression based on data provided by the Gambling Survey for Great Britain and applied to a population matrix based on the following criteria:
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> age and sex
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> ethnicity
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) quintiles
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> region
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> resident qualifications
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> economic activity
•<span style="white-space: pre;"> proportion of area classed as ‘Coastal’
Source of numerator: Gambling Survey of Great Britain Gambling Commission
Definition of denominator: Adult (18 and over) Population of Local Authority
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology:
The figure was obtained using a modelled approach with 2 years of the Gambling Survey for Great Britain dataset  https://www.kcl.ac.uk/research/local-authority-small-area-estimates-of-gambling .

A Multinomial Logistic Regression was applied to the results of the GSGB datasets against a set of explanatory variables including demographic, local authority characteristics, deprivation domains, and gambling premises for each local authority in order to predict where specific demographics would fall in one of four PGSI categories (0, 1-2, 3-7, and 8+).

Each of the models regressed the full list of explanatory variables onto the outcome. Only those explanatory variables with a statistically significant association (p-value <0.05) with the outcome measure were retained to ensure a parsimonious model. This generated risk ratios for each category in each variable.

The completed model risk ratios were applied to the population matrix for each local authority (a breakdown of populations across each of the explanatory variables). The model coefficients were used to generate predicted probabilities for each of the cells in the population matrix (i.e. a percentage of the population in each cell likely to have scored a PGSI 8+). These figures were summed to produce the final numerator. This was then used as a proportion of the local authority 18 and over population to generate a percentage prevalence figure
Confidence interval details:
Upper and lower bounds were generated for each estimate. These indicate how precise the estimate is considered to be and providing a credible range in which we expect the true value to lie. These upper and lower bounds are generated using boot-strapping methods; 1000 simulations of the predicted probabilities were run. The 2.5th and 97.5th largest of these simulated probabilities were used as lower and upper limits, respectively.

The full published methodology document can be found here: https://www.kcl.ac.uk/research/local-authority-small-area-estimates-of-gambling

Rounding: No rounding applied to data
Caveats:
Survey variables could only be included in the modelling step if corresponding population-level information was available for the local authority. Because the definition of both the survey and population measures need to be as similar as possible to improve the accuracy of the estimation, this limited the choice of survey variables included in the modelling.

The Gambling Survey for Great Britain uses a push-to-web methodology and is presented as a gambling survey when recruiting participants. These aspects of the design have the potential to overestimate gambling prevalence and harms. This is discussed more fully in both the GSGB technical reports and an independent review of the data.The estimates are based on self-reported survey responses and not true population values. Therefore results could be affected by bias (such as recall bias and non-response bias) and measurement error (for example when reporting expenditure or frequency of participation in gambling). The impact of self-report bias is not necessarily in a single direction; some measures may be underreported while others may be overreported, depending on how respondents recall, interpret, and disclose their gambling behaviour.
Modelled estimates are subject to uncertainty arising from both the survey data and the modelling process. The precision of estimates may vary between areas and results should be interpreted as indicative rather than exact measures of prevalence.National and regional estimates are based on two years of survey data and will therefore differ from estimates published by the Gambling Commission which are based on one year of data.

Indicator: Healthy life expectancy at birth 2021 Census based
Rationale: This indicator is an important summary measure of mortality and morbidity, which adds a quality of life dimension to estimates of life expectancy. It provides an overall summary of the health status of populations in small areas in England.
Definition: A measure of the average number of years people can expect to live in ‘good’ general health. For the period 2019 to 2023, for each given area, it estimates how long a newborn would be expected to live in good health, if mortality rates and levels of good health for that period remained constant throughout their life. Figures are calculated from deaths from all causes, mid-year population estimates and self-reported health status from Census 2021. Estimates reflect the prevalence of good health and mortality among those living in an area in 2019 to 2023. The figures are not therefore the number of years a baby born in the area could actually expect to live in good health, both because levels of good health and mortality rates of the area are likely to change in the future and because many of those born in the area will live elsewhere for at least some part of their lives.
Data source: Office for National Statistics
Indicator source: Office for National Statistics (ONS),  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/datasets/healthstatelifeexpectancyestimatesformiddlelayersuperoutputareasenglandandwales
Definition of numerator: Number of deaths registered in the calendar years 2019 to 2023 and the prevalence of people self-reporting good or very good health in Census 2021.
Source of numerator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), 2021 Census
Definition of denominator: ONS mid-year population estimates (for construction of life tables) and Census 2021 resident populations (to derive health prevalence estimates).
Source of denominator: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Mid-year population estimates
Methodology: Healthy life expectancy was calculated by ONS using the  https://ined-legacy.reves-network.org/fichier/s_rubrique/20182/sullivan.guide.pre.final.oct2014.en.pdf .For these MSOA estimates, health prevalence is derived from Census 2021 self-reported general health data. Individuals reporting their health as "Very good" or "Good" are classified as being in good health, while those reporting "Fair", "Bad" or "Very bad" health are classified as not being in good health.Mortality rates are based on deaths registered during 2019 to 2023 and corresponding mid-year population estimates. Life expectancy estimates are period-based estimates derived from abridged life tables with a final age group of 90 years and over. Male and female estimates were produced separately. Further details of the methodology are available from the ONS publication  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectancyestimatesformiddlelayersuperoutputareasenglandandwales/2019to2023
Standard population/values: Not applicable, as a standard population is not used in estimation of healthy life expectancy.
Frequency: Published by ONS following each Census. Estimates are not available annually because health prevalence is derived from Census data.
Confidence interval details: Healthy life expectancy estimates are presented with 95% confidence intervals, which are calculated from the variance of both mortality and health state prevalence estimates. Further information on the confidence interval methodology is available in  https://ined-legacy.reves-network.org/fichier/s_rubrique/20182/sullivan.guide.pre.final.oct2014.en.pdf , as referenced by  https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/bulletins/healthstatelifeexpectancyestimatesformiddlelayersuperoutputareasenglandandwales/latest .
Disclosure control: Disclosure control not applied as the estimates do not reveal any information about individuals. Estimates are published at Middle Layer Super Output Area (MSOA) level, the smallest geography considered sufficiently robust for publication.
Rounding: Healthy life expectancy estimates and confidence intervals are presented to one decimal place.
Caveats: Estimates for small geographic areas are subject to greater uncertainty than national estimates and should be interpreted alongside their 95% confidence intervals.Healthy life expectancy estimates in this indicator should only be compared with other estimates published within the same indicator, including the higher-level geographies presented alongside the MSOA estimates. Comparisons with healthy life expectancy estimates published in other indicator series or publications are not appropriate, as differences in methodology, data sources and reference periods can result in systematically different values.Estimates should not be compared directly with the previous small-area health expectancy estimates published by ONS in 2015, because the current methodology uses a final age group of 90 years and over, whereas the earlier release used a final age group of 85 years and over.To improve the robustness of estimates for small populations, mortality data are aggregated over a five-year period and some mortality rates, population estimates, and health prevalence values have been imputed where insufficient data was available. MSOAs where imputation was required are identified in the ONS dataset. Areas where ONS identified implausible life expectancy estimates were classified as unreliable and no healthy life expectancy estimate was calculated for those areas.
Notes: Census 2021 health status information is used to represent health prevalence across the entire 2019 to 2023 period. This assumes that health prevalence measured in Census 2021 is representative of the wider five-year period. The estimates do not imply that the first period of life is in a "good" health state followed by a period in a "not good" health state. Rather, they represent the average expected years spent in good health based on mortality and health prevalence patterns.
Impact of COVID-19: The period (2019 to 2023) includes the COVID-19 pandemic. Mortality patterns observed during this period are reflected in the resulting healthy life expectancy estimates.

Indicator: Smoking status at time of delivery (MSDS based) (current method)
Rationale:
Smoking in pregnancy has well known detrimental effects for the growth and development of the baby and health of the mother. On average, smokers have more complications during pregnancy and labour, including bleeding during pregnancy, placental abruption and premature rupture of membranes.
Encouraging pregnant women to stop smoking during pregnancy may also help them stop for good and thus provide health benefits for the mother and reduce exposure to secondhand smoke by the infant.Smoking during pregnancy can cause serious pregnancy-related health problems. These include complications during labour and an increased risk of miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, low birthweight and sudden unexpected death in infancy.
The inclusion of this indicator will ensure that the local tobacco control activity is appropriately focused on pregnant women. Inclusion of this indicator will also encourage the continued prioritisation of action to reduce smoking at delivery. Decreases in smoking during pregnancy will result in health benefits for the infant and mother, as well as cost savings to the NHS.
Definition: The number of mothers known to be smokers at the time of delivery as a percentage of all maternities with known smoking status.
Data source: OHID, based on NHS England data
Indicator source: NHS England (NHSE), Statistics on Women's Smoking at a Time of Delivery (SATODv2) https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-women-s-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england
Definition of numerator: The number of pregnant women who were current smokers, this can be recorded 3 days before or after the labour onset date. This include any cigarettes or tobacco at all, but excludes non-combustible nicotine products, such as e-cigarettes or other nicotine containing products. Smoking status is identified via clinical coding in MSDS, for further information on the codes used please refer to  https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-women-s-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england .This indicator presents SATOD v2 local authority values based on local authority of residence. Values for ICBs and NHS England regions are based on sub-ICB of responsibility and may differ from aggregated local authority values.
Source of numerator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on NHS England (NHSE) data
Definition of denominator: The number of maternities with known smoking status. A maternity is defined as a pregnant woman who gives birth to one or more live or stillborn babies of at least 24 weeks gestation, where the baby is delivered by either a midwife or doctor at home or in a NHS hospital (including GP units).This indicator presents SATOD v2 local authority values based on local authority of residence. Values for ICBs and NHS England regions are based on sub-ICB of responsibility and may differ from aggregated local authority values.
Source of denominator: Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID), based on NHS England (NHSE) data
Methodology: <span style="white-space: pre-wrap;">Percentage: Numerator is divided by denominator and multiplied by 100
Disclosure control: In accordance with the suppression methodology guidance for the Maternity Services Dataset, rounding has been applied to all figures as follows: counts of zero are shown as zero, counts of 1 to 7 are rounded to 5, and all other counts are rounded to the nearest 5, with rates (where relevant) calculated from the rounded numerator and denominator numbers. Confidence intervals were not calculated where no women were known to be smokers recorded in the period or where due to low reliability resulting from small number of maternities in period (less than 100). Any Confidence Interval ranges where total maternities (all) are fewer than 100 are suppressed.
Caveats:
Smoking prevalence at time of delivery is calculated using only maternities with a known smoking status. Mothers with unknown smoking status are excluded from the denominator. As a result, values may be higher than if all maternities were included and comparisons should consider differences in data completeness between areas and over time.

If smoking status is more likely to be missing for certain groups (for example, smokers, younger mothers, or certain providers), then: areas with poorer data completeness may not be comparable with areas with more complete recording the indicator may understate or overstate true smoking prevalence trends could be affected if data completeness changes over time The number and percentage of women whose smoking status was not known at time of delivery are available from the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/statistics-on-women-s-smoking-status-at-time-of-delivery-england .Sub-totals may not add up to National totals, due to a known issue with duplication in MSDS. More information can be found in the Data Quality statement of the https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/maternity-services-monthly-statistics NHS England include people with Chinese ethnicity in the "any other ethnic group" rather than in the "Asian or Asian British" group.The sum of the ethnicity groups are not used to derive England level totals. This is because duplicate records may be inconsistently included across the ethnicity groups where maternity care has been provided at different locations at different points in time.
